Cost, Latency and Model Selection

What is the smallest model that clears the bar within budget?

A Tuesday morning in Bengaluru

On a Tuesday morning in March 2026, Ritika Desai, vice-president of product at Sarvatra Health, a Bengaluru maternal-and-infant-health platform, sat down with a one-page memo from finance and a decision she could no longer defer. Sarvatra's product let expecting and new mothers describe a symptom in their own words — swelling in the ankles, a missed kick count, a fever that would not break — and receive an AI-generated urgency assessment: see a doctor today, this week, or monitor at home. The memo capped the AI-serving budget for this one feature at ₹75,000 a month, a figure Ritika's team had derived two quarters earlier from the product's unit economics. The clinical safety board had separately set the bar: any model powering triage had to score at least 92% against a 400-transcript evaluation set, built from real anonymised conversations and labelled independently by two triage nurses. Engineering had its own ceiling — a 95th-percentile response time under 3.5 seconds, because a woman typing symptoms on a shared 4G phone in a district town would not wait much longer before closing the app, or trusting her own guess instead.

Exhibit 1 — the three numbers on Ritika's desk before she looked at a single model

ConstraintValue
AI-serving budget, this feature₹75,000 / month
Clinical eval bar≥ 92% on a 400-transcript set
Latency ceiling (95th percentile)< 3.5 seconds
Current volume40,000 conversations / month

Three candidate models sat on her screen, priced roughly ten times apart from smallest to largest. Her first instinct — an instinct shared by almost everyone who has not yet done this arithmetic — was to reach for the most capable one and call the decision safe. The rest of this page explains why that instinct is usually wrong, and what discipline replaces it.

The idea

Model selection, in the sense used here, is the exercise of choosing the smallest and cheapest model that still clears a task-specific accuracy bar within a fixed cost ceiling and a fixed latency ceiling. It is narrower and more useful than "pick the best model," because "best" means nothing until it is anchored to a bar, a budget and a clock. The problem it was invented to solve appeared only after 2023, once providers began selling several sizes of the same model family — small, fast and cheap at one end, large, slow and expensive at the other — at prices that could differ by a factor of twenty for an identical call shape. Before that menu existed, there was nothing to select between; after it existed, teams that defaulted to the largest model were quietly paying for capability, and latency, their product never used. Stanford researchers Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia and James Zou gave the problem its sharpest early name in a 2023 paper on what they called FrugalGPT, showing that cascading calls — trying a cheap model first and escalating only what it could not handle — could match a top-tier model's accuracy at a fraction of its cost.

The sentence Ritika could repeat in any meeting without sounding glib: "The smallest model that clears the bar within budget is the right model — anything larger is a tax the product doesn't need to pay."

This idea builds on two things the reader has likely already met: the recognition that when a feature is powered by a model rather than hand-written logic, its cost and latency move with every input and output token in a way ordinary software never did, and the pricing discipline that turns a company's unit economics into a hard ceiling. Ritika's ₹75,000 was not a guess — it came from exactly that discipline, applied a topic earlier.

How it actually works

Choosing correctly starts with writing down three numbers before looking at a single model, because the order in which a team does this determines whether the exercise is honest or merely decorative. The first is the eval bar: a task-specific score measured on a held-out set of real examples from the product's own distribution, not a public leaderboard result — a model that tops a general benchmark can still fail badly on the narrow, specific way a pregnant woman in Kanpur describes reduced fetal movement. The second is the latency ceiling, expressed as a percentile rather than an average, because an average of 1.8 seconds can hide a slow tail where one request in twenty takes eight seconds — and it is exactly that unlucky user who forms the product's reputation. The third is the cost ceiling, translated from the company's unit economics into a hard monthly rupee figure for this one feature.

With those three numbers fixed, the selection step itself is comparative: every candidate is run against the same eval set, timed under realistic concurrent load, and priced against the same expected traffic pattern, producing three scores per model that can sit side by side. The models that clear both the eval bar and the latency ceiling form a shortlist; among that shortlist, the cheapest wins, because nothing here rewards spending more once "good enough" has already been reached. The step teams most often skip is the concurrent-load timing — measuring latency one request at a time, then being surprised in production when twenty simultaneous users each experience a queue the single-request test never revealed.

A worked example

Three models were on Ritika's shortlist that Tuesday, sold by one vendor under names that map cleanly to size: Argus-mini, Argus-standard and Argus-pro, each priced per thousand tokens of input and output. A typical triage conversation ran to about 600 input tokens — the symptom description plus a short history — and 150 output tokens, the assessment and its explanation.

Exhibit 2 — base case, 40,000 conversations a month, 600 in / 150 out tokens each

Model₹/1K in₹/1K outCost / conv.Monthly costEval acc.p95 latency
Argus-mini0.080.24₹0.084₹3,36088.4%1.1s
Argus-standard0.401.20₹0.42₹16,80093.6%1.9s
Argus-pro2.006.00₹2.10₹84,00097.1%4.6s

The arithmetic for Argus-mini: (600⁄1000 × ₹0.08) + (150⁄1000 × ₹0.24) = ₹0.048 + ₹0.036 = ₹0.084 per conversation, or ₹3,360 a month — but it scored 88.4% against the 92% bar and was disqualified on accuracy alone. Argus-standard came to (0.6 × ₹0.40) + (0.15 × ₹1.20) = ₹0.24 + ₹0.18 = ₹0.42 per conversation, ₹16,800 a month, scoring 93.6% and landing at 1.9 seconds — clearing every constraint with ₹58,200 of budget headroom. Argus-pro came to (0.6 × ₹2.00) + (0.15 × ₹6.00) = ₹1.20 + ₹0.90 = ₹2.10 per conversation, ₹84,000 a month — over budget before accuracy was even discussed, and its 4.6-second tail breached the latency ceiling too. Argus-pro scored highest, at 97.1%, and was still the wrong answer.

Now change one input. In June, Sarvatra's hospital-referral partner asked the clinical board to raise the bar to 95% on a harder eval set built from near-miss incident reports. On this harder set, Argus-standard fell to 90.8% and no longer cleared it; Argus-pro scored 96.3% but, run wholesale, would have cost ₹84,000 against a ₹75,000 ceiling and still breached the latency ceiling. The fix was not to swap models but to split the traffic: a lightweight classifier flagged roughly one conversation in four as ambiguous — mentions of bleeding, severe pain, or reduced movement — and routed only those to Argus-pro, leaving the rest on Argus-standard.

Exhibit 3 — the cascade that met the 95% bar without leaving budget

PathShareModelAccuracy on subsetMonthly cost
Routine75% (30,000)Argus-standard95.9%₹12,600
Escalated25% (10,000)Argus-pro96.3%₹21,000
Blended100%—96.0%₹33,600

The one genuine complication was latency: Sarvatra could not pretend the escalated quarter ran at 1.9 seconds, so the team gave that path its own, honestly communicated budget — a visible "checking this with extra care" state, ceilinged at 6 seconds — rather than quietly missing the SLA it had promised for routine cases.

Nuances a learner must sit with

Your eval set, not the leaderboard

A model's ranking on a public benchmark says almost nothing about how it will do on your product's own distribution of inputs. The only score worth trusting is one measured on real examples from your own logs, ideally labelled by the people accountable when the model is wrong.

Percentiles, not averages

A latency ceiling stated as an average hides the slow tail users actually remember, and for anything that streams its answer, time to the first visible token shapes perceived speed even when total generation time is identical.

Cost per request is not cost to serve

The token price on a vendor's rate card ignores retries after a guardrail rejection, a separate embedding call for retrieval, and any orchestration step that calls the model more than once per user turn — all of which belong in the real monthly number, not just the sticker price.

The bar moves

A model that clears today's eval set can fail tomorrow's, not because the model changed but because the product's inputs did, or because a regulator, a partner or an incident report raised the standard — exactly what happened to Sarvatra in June. The eval set needs a version number and a re-run cadence, not a one-time pass.

Cascades carry real operating cost of their own

Routing traffic between two models is not free: it needs a classifier that itself must be evaluated, monitored and occasionally corrected when it routes a genuinely urgent case down the cheaper path. A cascade earns its place when the arithmetic demands it, not because it looks clever.

Accuracy cannot tell you what an error costs

A 96% score treats every mistake as equally bad, but in a maternal-health product a false reassurance on a genuine emergency and an unnecessary clinic visit are not symmetric harms. No single eval number captures that asymmetry; it has to be reasoned about separately, often by weighting the eval set toward the errors that matter most.

"Smaller" is a name, not a guarantee

A model marketed as the compact option can still turn out chattier in practice, generating longer explanations than a larger competitor and, at high output-token prices, costing more per conversation despite a lower price per token. The only number worth trusting is the measured rupees-per-conversation, never the rate card alone.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and company stage

Exhibit 4 — how the same three numbers get weighted differently

DimensionConsumerB2BMarketplace
Revenue per interactionNear zeroHigh, per seatThin, a take-rate
Cost sensitivityExtremeModerateExtreme
Latency sensitivityHigh, visibleLowerHigh
Typical defaultSmallest passing modelLarger model toleratedAggressive cascades

In a high-volume consumer product like Sarvatra's, cost per conversation must be tiny because revenue per conversation is close to zero and latency is highly visible — which pushes the default toward the smallest passing model and toward cascades once volume climbs into the hundreds of thousands. In a B2B product, an assistant sold into a hospital's billing office at a few thousand rupees per seat a month, a single wrong answer can cost a renewal, so buyers tolerate a slower, pricier model far more readily than a wrong one, and the conversation tilts toward accuracy first. In a marketplace product, where the model sits inside a thin take-rate rather than a subscription, cost discipline is often the most extreme of the three, because every rupee spent on inference comes straight out of a margin the marketplace does not fully control.

Company stage matters just as much. An early-stage team like Sarvatra has a small eval set, no volume discount from any vendor, and no infrastructure to fine-tune a model even if that were cheaper, so it leans on cascades built from off-the-shelf tiers. A large, scaled company can negotiate committed-use pricing that changes the arithmetic, can afford to fine-tune or distil a smaller model against years of accumulated eval data, and can justify a flagship model on its single highest-stakes journey while still cascading everything else — the same three numbers, applied with a far larger toolkit.

Common mistakes

Exhibit 5 — symptom, misunderstanding, and the cheapest way to catch it

SymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Always reaches for the flagship modelConflates capability with requirementMultiply real ₹/conversation by monthly volume; compare to budget
Ranks models by public benchmarkAssumes leaderboard mirrors your distributionScore 100 real logged examples per model
SLA holds in testing, breaks liveMeasured single-request, not concurrent, latencyLoad-test at expected peak concurrency
Bill balloons after launchMissed retries, chattiness, multi-call agent patternsAudit real production token counts per conversation

Each of these has the same shape: a team substituted a plausible-sounding proxy — reputation, a leaderboard, a single-request timer, a vendor's example prompt — for a measurement it could have taken from its own production data in an afternoon. The fix is rarely a better model; it is usually the fifteen minutes of arithmetic the team skipped.

What good looks like

By the following January, Sarvatra's triage feature looked, from the outside, unremarkable — which was the point. The team had turned the June episode into standing practice rather than a one-off fire drill.

The eval set carried a version number and was re-run every quarter against fresh, anonymised transcripts, with any drop below the current bar triggering a review before it triggered an incident. The classifier that routed conversations was itself evaluated and monitored like any other model in production, not treated as plumbing beneath notice. And a single dashboard showed three numbers side by side for every model in the stack — rupees per conversation, 95th-percentile latency, and current eval score against the live bar — so no one had to reconstruct Ritika's Tuesday-morning arithmetic from scratch each time a vendor released a new tier. Nothing about this required the newest or largest model available; it required treating the bar, the budget and the clock as three numbers to be satisfied together, continuously, rather than one capability question settled once.

What Ritika decided

Exhibit 6 — the decision, March 2026

ItemDecision
Model selectedArgus-standard
Monthly cost @ 40,000 conversations₹16,800 of ₹75,000 budget
Eval accuracy93.6% vs. 92% bar
p95 latency1.9s vs. 3.5s ceiling
Contingency builtClassifier + escalation path, quarterly eval re-run

Ritika chose Argus-standard that Tuesday, not because it was the safest-sounding name on the list but because it was the only model that cleared the clinical bar, fit inside the budget finance had set from the product's real unit economics, and met the latency ceiling engineering had committed to — with enough headroom left to fund the classifier and monitoring the team would need before the bar moved again, as she suspected it would. What her team took up next was the question this topic unlocks: whether, once a cascade like theirs stabilises, it is cheaper in the long run to buy a bigger model for the hard cases or to fine-tune a small one specifically on the errors their own eval set keeps surfacing — a build-fine-tune-or-buy decision that only makes sense once the cost-latency-quality arithmetic here has already been done honestly. Two questions are worth sitting with before moving on: what would your own eval bar have to measure to catch the one failure mode your product cannot survive, and how would you know this quarter, not next year, if the bar had quietly moved without anyone updating the eval set to match it.

Kalrav Voice Network: Seven Hundred Milliseconds

A case on cost, latency and model selection in a vernacular voice product

1. Sunday night, Hyderabad

At twenty past eleven on Sunday, 18 October 2026, Kavya Sreenivasan was at the dining table of her flat in Jubilee Hills with a page of hotel notepaper in front of her. On it were four letters — A, B, C and D — and beside each a number in rupees and a number in milliseconds. In nine hours she would chair the architecture review at Kalrav Voice Network's Madhapur office and say which would answer the phone for Jamuna Credit Network from February.

The binding dates were Friday, 30 October, when Jamuna's board committee expected a signed agreement, and 8 November, Diwali, after which the collections season begins. Jamuna's draft carried a service level Kalrav's own engineers had written into their September proposal: a 95th-percentile response latency of 1.50 seconds and a task-completion rate of 92 per cent. Two weeks earlier Kavya believed all four candidates could clear both. By Friday she believed none could, at a price the company could afford.

2. How Kalrav got here

Kalrav Voice Network was founded in March 2018 in Hyderabad by Lakshman Pai, previously a collections-technology head at a housing financier, and Jayesh Thorat, an engineer from Pune. Its first product replaced the touch-tone menus of two electricity utilities with a Telugu and Hindi speech interface, and by 2022 it had 180 employees and a reputation in a narrow trade: outbound calls Indians finish, in languages they speak at home.

The decision that shapes Kavya's Monday was taken in August 2023. Hosted speech recognition then handled code-mixing badly — a Coimbatore borrower saying "EMI next week pay pannitten" defeated it — and licence fees scaled with every call. Jayesh argued that recognition was the moat and had to be owned; Lakshman agreed. Kalrav signed a reserved-capacity contract with Lagan Compute Industries, a Mumbai data-centre operator, on 20 November 2023: twenty-four accelerators, ₹19.50 lakh a month, forty-two months from 1 December 2023 to 31 May 2027, non-cancellable, ₹819.00 lakh in all. By 30 September 2026, thirty-four months had been paid, ₹663.00 lakh; ₹156.00 lakh remains.

In June 2024, at about 7,00,000 connected minutes a month, Keerthana Vasudevan's team set transfer prices to charge the fleet back to products: ₹0.55 a minute for recognition, ₹0.40 for synthesis. Those recovered ₹6.65 lakh against the ₹19.50 lakh commitment, and the shortfall was called investment. Nobody revisited them. In February 2025 Kalrav replaced its hand-built dialogue flows with a language model, and in October 2025 standardised on ₹6.00 per connected minute, bundling telephony, recognition, the dialogue model and synthesis. That single number is the ceiling on everything Kavya can spend.

3. The industry

Indian conversational-AI vendors crowd this market: Yellow.ai, Gupshup, Jio Haptik, Exotel and Ozonetel sell voice automation to lenders, and open Indian-language work from Sarvam AI and AI4Bharat at IIT Madras has made small models credible rather than a curiosity. Kalrav's differentiation was never the model, but that the call sounds like someone from the borrower's own district.

The regulation is specific. The Reserve Bank of India's fair-practices expectations for recovery agents govern what may be said on a collections call and when; the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India's rules govern header registration and consent; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs recordings carrying names, loan account numbers and family circumstances. Jamuna's outsourcing policy, written to sit with the RBI's directions on outsourcing of IT services, requires personal data to stay in India absent a carve-out.

Since April 2026 Joshua Kiptoo has also run a Nairobi pilot for a Kenyan asset-finance lender in Swahili — proof the platform travels, and the reason Kalrav knows what happens when the model sits eight thousand kilometres away.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Jamuna Credit Network, a Chennai vehicle financier with a loan book of about ₹18,400 crore and roughly 11 lakh live contracts across Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, issued a request for proposal on Monday, 6 July 2026 for pre-due and early-delinquency calling. Jatin Oberoi won a shortlist place in August, and a six-week pilot ran from Monday, 24 August to Sunday, 4 October: 1,00,000 connected calls averaging 2.40 minutes, 2,40,000 minutes in all, split four ways so each candidate carried its own traffic.

Four September beliefs are no longer safe. First, engineering reached its end-to-end figure by adding the pieces: 350 milliseconds for recognition to finalise, 300 for the first byte of synthesis, 150 for telephony and jitter, 700 left for the dialogue model, 1,500 in all. Percentiles do not add, and the pilot's measured figures are worse than that sum. Second, the lab benchmark of 25 September (Exhibit 2) was single-stream; the pilot telemetry (Exhibit 3) shows every candidate slower under concurrency, the mid-size model nearly twice as slow. Third, the automated evaluation of 9 October (Exhibit 4) was judged by the largest model in the set, scoring its own transcripts among others; the human audit of 16 October (Exhibit 5) keeps the ranking but lowers every candidate, least of all the judge. Fourth, the volume under every rupee figure is not contracted: Exhibit 1 shows the committed floor and the forecast diverging by 47,00,000 minutes, or ₹2.82 crore.

Figure 1. From board minutes, the Lagan contract and the pilot run book. The reserved contract ends 31 May 2027, four months into the ramp.

5. The people

Kavya owns the decision and a bonus tied to gross margin. Seven colleagues own pieces of it.

Lakshman Pai, co-founder and chief executive, Hyderabad. He wants the Jamuna logo before January's Series C conversations, having told the board Kalrav's language advantage is owned, not rented. Unsaid: the reference matters more to him than the margin, and he treats Lagan as his own mistake to redeem.

Jayesh Thorat, co-founder and head of engineering, Pune. He wants Option C, fine-tuned on the fleet Kalrav pays for whether it is used or not. Unsaid: his team has never shipped a fine-tune at this scale, and his ten-week plan assumes Katarzyna's group drops its Swahili work.

Keerthana Vasudevan, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Her rule is cost-to-serve within 55 per cent of revenue, of which she allots the dialogue model ₹1.30 a minute, and she defends the 2024 transfer prices. Unsaid: at 36,00,000 minutes a month those prices recover ₹34.20 lakh against a ₹19.50 lakh commitment, flattering every margin.

Lalita Mazumdar, quality and evaluation lead, Kolkata. She will not certify any candidate on the automated evaluation and insists the contractual audit be human. Unsaid: her own language cells carry an interval of about ±9 points, wider than the differences she is adjudicating.

Jatin Oberoi, head of enterprise sales, Gurugram. He has offered Jamuna ₹5.25 a minute for three years with a take-or-pay floor and awaits Keerthana's approval; he thinks the latency clause negotiable, the audit clause not. Unsaid: he has already shown Jamuna the lab latency table.

Katarzyna Zielinska, applied science lead, Warsaw. She built the recogniser and thinks the dialogue model is the wrong place to look: abandoned calls cluster in the silence before the agent speaks, which a 250-millisecond acknowledgement would cover. Her team costs 2.6 times the Pune rate. Unsaid: she would rather spend ten weeks on Swahili.

Joshua Kiptoo, regional lead for East Africa, Nairobi. He wants something deployable near his callers, and reads Option C as the only candidate that qualifies. Unsaid: his lender's tender closes in March, so a decision to self-host is made for him too.

7. Voices

"Sixteen lakh a month to rent intelligence we own the hardware to run. The Lagan invoice arrives on the first of every month until May whether we use it or not. Ten weeks and three engineers."

Jayesh Thorat, engineering review, 12 October

"Ten weeks from Monday is 28 December; the ramp starts in February. If the fine-tune is late there is no load-tested fallback, and I will be explaining to Jamuna's committee why we rejected this model in October."

Jatin Oberoi, reply on the same thread

"I will not sign the automated number: the judge is one of the candidates. Of thirty-six failures on B, four were phrasing outside the approved script. Four in three hundred, on a collections call, is a compliance finding."

Lalita Mazumdar, email to Kavya, 16 October

"Look at where callers hang up. Not after a bad answer — during the silence before any answer. Play a 250-millisecond 'haan ji, dekh rahi hoon' and 1.6 seconds stops being 1.6 seconds of nothing."

Katarzyna Zielinska, chat thread, 14 October

"At ₹5.25 the 55 per cent rule leaves ₹2.89 for cost-to-serve, ₹0.89 for the model after telephony, recognition and synthesis. A is arithmetically impossible at that price."

Keerthana Vasudevan, finance note, 15 October

8. The options as Kavya sees them

Option A, the frontier hosted model for every turn. It alone clears 92 per cent on the human audit, at 94.0 per cent, with two script breaches in three hundred. It alone breaks Keerthana's budget, at ₹1.5088 a minute against ₹1.30, or ₹54.32 lakh a month against ₹46.80 lakh. Its production p95 of 1,620 milliseconds is over twice the 700-millisecond allowance, its end-to-end p95 of 2,240 breaches the 1.50-second clause, and it has no Indian region, so it needs a carve-out.

Option B, the mid-size hosted model for every turn. In September this was the obvious answer: 92.75 per cent automated, 540 milliseconds in the lab, ₹16.53 lakh a month. Exhibit 3 took the latency away and Exhibit 5 the pass rate. Its end-to-end p95 of 1,540 milliseconds misses the service level by 40 milliseconds — a rounding error or a breach, depending on who drafts the clause.

Option C, the small open-weight model, fine-tuned and self-hosted. It is the cheapest at ₹6.98 lakh a month, the fastest at 420 milliseconds, the only one wholly inside India, and the only one consuming capacity already bought. It is also the worst on quality: 83.0 per cent audited, fifteen language-drift failures, 19.4 promises to pay per hundred calls dialled against the frontier model's 21.2. The fine-tune would cost ₹30.00 lakh of Pune engineering time plus ₹2.80 lakh of labelling, ₹32.80 lakh in all, which the saving against Option B repays in about three and a half months — or just over six if a Warsaw engineer joins for the ten weeks, adding ₹26.00 lakh at 2.6 times the Pune rate. Nobody can say what it will score.

Option D, the router. A classifier sends 68 per cent of turns to the small model, 25 per cent to the mid-size and 7 per cent to the frontier, for ₹13.36 lakh a month and 89.0 per cent audited. Its p95 is a frontier p95, since escalated turns are by construction the slow ones — and the 7 per cent escalated are the hardest conversations, the most sensitive ones, which leave India.

All four are on the notepaper. What is not is that three of the numbers she compares them with may be the wrong numbers. The 700-millisecond allowance is the residue of a subtraction, not a measurement of what a borrower tolerates, and Exhibit 3 suggests callers abandon in the first second of silence whichever model speaks. The 92 per cent bar measures task completion, but Jamuna renews on promises to pay, where best and worst are 1.8 points apart. And the ₹1.30 allowance descends from a price Jatin is discounting.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The agreement must be signed by Friday, 30 October, and the ramp begins with Jamuna's 14,00,000 committed minutes a month from February 2027 — 38.9 per cent of the planning volume. The draft sets a 95th-percentile latency of 1.50 seconds and a task-completion rate of 92 per cent, both audited monthly by human reviewers, with service credits of 5 per cent of monthly fees for each month either is missed, capped at 15 per cent, and termination for convenience after a 90-day cure period. Jatin's ₹5.25 price is unapproved; the 55 per cent rule is a board commitment in the FY27 plan. The Lagan contract runs to 31 May 2027 at ₹19.50 lakh a month, and the renewal quotation is 22 per cent higher, ₹23.79 lakh. Jayesh has three engineers and ten weeks. Data residency is a clause, not a preference. And after Diwali on 8 November the collections season starts, when a financier finds out whether its agents work.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Reconstruct the bar. What must a candidate clear — which metric, measured how, over which traffic mix — and where did each threshold come from?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 disagree about latency; Exhibits 4 and 5 about quality. For each pair, which would you commit to contractually, and what first?
  3. Exhibit 6 puts every candidate except A inside the ₹1.30 allowance. Is that the right constraint? Rebuild it from Jatin's ₹5.25 price, and say what the Lagan transfer prices do to it.
  4. Option D is cheaper than B and better on both quality measures, yet its p95 is a frontier p95. What does that say about optimising a blended average, and what would bring its tail inside the budget?
  5. Katarzyna claims the abandon problem is a product problem, not a model problem. Using Exhibit 3, estimate what Kalrav gains if she is right, and what it risks in signing a latency clause on that assumption.
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Kavya decide, what does she commit to on 30 October, and what does she tell the board in January if the first audit returns 88 per cent?

Past midnight, Kavya drew a line under the four letters and wrote one more thing in the margin, where nobody would see it: which number is the product? She did not know whether she meant the rupees, the milliseconds or the promises to pay. The Lagan invoice would arrive in thirteen days, Jatin's price was unapproved, and Joshua, two and a half hours behind her, had not yet woken to read the thread. She turned off the lamp without turning the page over.

Cost, Latency and Model Selection

What is the smallest model that clears the bar within budget — and what does an expert see in that question that a competent practitioner does not?

1. Two desks, ten days apart

On 14 April 2026, Meghna Bhosale, vice-president of product at Nukkad Kitchens, a Pune company whose app takes food orders in free-form Hindi, Marathi and English — "wahi wala biryani jo pichli baar liya tha, bina raita" — sat with a finance memo and a growth chart that disagreed. The assistant handled 6.2 million assisted orders in March and was growing eleven per cent a month. Finance had capped model spend at ₹0.30 per assisted order, from a contribution margin of about ₹11: ₹18.6 lakh a month at March volume, ₹43 lakh at October's. Operations had set the bar at 97.5 per cent order-correctness on 2,000 real transcripts, a wrong order costing about ₹140 in refund and support. Engineering had set the clock at 900 milliseconds to first token at the 95th percentile, because a customer who saw nothing for a second began typing again.

Ten days later and 150 kilometres west, Farida Kazi, chief product officer of Godhuli Risk Systems in Mumbai, faced the same question with every parameter inverted. Godhuli sold eleven insurers a reviewer that read a forty-page proposal file and flagged material omissions — an undisclosed prior claim, a missing medical annexure — before a human underwriter signed. Volume was 240,000 files a month, each about 34,000 tokens, and nothing was interactive: files arrived nightly, the SLA promised 2,000 reviewed files in four hours. At ₹46 a file and a promised 72 per cent gross margin, model spend had ₹9 to live in. The bar was not an average but 99.0 per cent recall on omissions, since a miss was the insurer's regulatory exposure, and 82 per cent precision, since an underwriter interrupted by false flags stops reading them.

Exhibit 1 — the same three numbers, two products

ConstraintNukkad KitchensGodhuli Risk Systems
Unit of workOne assisted orderOne 40-page underwriting file
Volume / month6,200,000240,000
Cost ceiling / unit₹0.30₹9.00
Quality bar97.5% order-correctness99.0% recall, ≥82% precision
Latency constraintp95 first token < 900 ms2,000 files in 4 hours (throughput)
Cost of one error≈ ₹140Regulatory exposure, unbounded

Both women were about to be told by somebody senior that the answer was obvious — Meghna to take the cheapest model, Farida the strongest. Both counsels answered with a preference instead of an arithmetic. The rest of this page is that arithmetic, and where it stops being arithmetic and becomes judgement.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Model selection, stated precisely, is the choice of the cheapest serving configuration whose measured quality on a task-specific evaluation set meets a stated bar, subject to a latency or throughput constraint, at the traffic the product sees. Four words carry the weight. Configuration, not model: the choice is over a system — model, prompt, context, caching, routing. Measured: on your distribution, not a leaderboard. Cheapest: rupees per unit of resolved work. Bar: a threshold somebody accountable wrote down in advance.

The problem is young. Before 2023 there was no menu; you used the model you had. Once providers sold several capability tiers of one family at prices differing twenty- or thirty-fold for an identical call, a selection problem appeared. Chen, Zaharia and Zou's 2023 FrugalGPT work showed a cascade — try a cheap model, escalate what it cannot handle — matching a flagship's accuracy at a fraction of its cost; Hinton, Vinyals and Dean's older idea of distillation supplied the other half of the toolkit. What was new was not the techniques but the economics: inference became a variable cost of goods sold, which conventional software had spent thirty years not having. Four schools now argue about what follows, and it is worth being exact about what each would sign.

Exhibit 2 — four positions, and the proposition each refuses

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Frontier-default"Build on the strongest model; unit prices fall an order of magnitude a year, salaries do not.""Spend six engineering weeks to save ₹4 lakh a month."
Frugal routing"Most traffic is easy; pay flagship prices only where needed.""One model for the whole distribution is simpler and therefore better."
Small & specialised"On a narrow, stable task a fine-tuned small model beats a general large one on quality, cost and latency at once.""Task definitions are stable enough to bet fixed costs on."
System-first"Retrieval, prompt structure and caching move cost and quality more than model choice; fix the system, then take the cheapest model that survives.""Model choice is the primary lever."

The disagreement is not decoration: frontier-default and small-and-specialised give Farida opposite advice, both defensible. What separates them is a claim about the future — how fast prices fall, how stable her task is — that no evidence available in April 2026 could settle.

3. Mechanics, worked rather than named

Start with the cost identity, which most teams never write down: C = (Tin · pin + Tout · pout) / 1000. Output tokens are priced three to four times input and generated one at a time, so they drive latency as well as cost; input tokens are the larger count, so a long repeated context can be most of the bill even at the cheaper rate.

At Nukkad a typical order carried 850 input tokens — 620 of them menu and policy text, identical on every order at that restaurant — and 90 output tokens, against a vendor family priced per thousand at ₹0.05/₹0.15, ₹0.30/₹0.90 and ₹1.60/₹4.80:

Exhibit 3 — Nukkad Kitchens, cost per assisted order at 850 in / 90 out

ConfigurationInput ₹Output ₹₹ / order₹ lakh / month at 6.2MEval
Kestrel-Flash0.0430.0140.0573.595.1%
Kestrel-12B0.2550.0810.33620.897.9%
Kestrel-Max1.3600.4321.792111.198.6%
12B + cached menu prefix0.0880.0810.16910.597.9%

Cached prefix at 10% of input rate: (0.62 × ₹0.03) + (0.23 × ₹0.30) + (0.09 × ₹0.90) = ₹0.169.

Read the last row carefully. Neither the model nor the eval score changed; the bill halved, because 620 of the 850 input tokens were the same bytes on every call and the vendor charged a tenth of the rate to reuse them. Priced naively at ₹0.336, Kestrel-12B breached Meghna's ceiling and would have been rejected in favour of a model that failed the bar; restructured so the invariant menu sat in a cacheable prefix, it came in at ₹0.169 with 44 per cent headroom. The System-first school exists because of results like this.

Now the cascade. With q the fraction escalated from small model to large, blended cost is Cs + q·Cl + Cr — escalated traffic pays twice, the small model's tokens being spent either way — and blended quality is (1−q)·As|easy + q·Al|hard: not the average of headline scores but of each model's accuracy on the slice it actually sees. That is where the arithmetic is fudged, and it cuts both ways — the small model beats its headline on the easy slice, the large model falls short of its own on the hard slice, which was selected for being hard.

Farida's team worked exactly this curve. Kestrel-Max on a whole file cost 34 × ₹1.60 + 1.8 × ₹4.80 = ₹63, seven times her ceiling; Kestrel-12B cost ₹11.82, still over; Flash cost ₹1.97 but recalled 91.4 per cent. The natural move — retrieval, sending only the 6,200 most relevant tokens to the 12B model for ₹3.48 — dropped recall to 97.1 per cent, for a reason worth stating as a principle: you cannot retrieve what is absent. A retriever ranks chunks by similarity to the query, so the pages that say nothing about a prior claim are the ones it discards.

What worked was a screen-then-reason cascade over the whole document. Flash read all 34,000 tokens and emitted 400 tokens of page-level flags for ₹1.76; Kestrel-12B then reasoned over the flagged pages — 9,000 in, 1,800 out — for ₹4.32. Total ₹6.08, recall 98.6 per cent: still short. The last 0.4 points came from a deterministic checklist over six structurally detectable categories — annexure present or not, signature block present or not — costing ₹0.23 and taking recall to 99.2 per cent. The cheapest way to clear the last stretch of a bar is frequently not a model.

Latency has its own identity: response time = queue wait + time to first token + (output tokens × time per token). Three terms, three fixes. Queue wait is capacity, and behaves badly: as utilisation ρ approaches one, waiting scales roughly as 1/(1−ρ), so a system comfortable at 70 per cent utilisation is three times worse at 90. Time to first token is mostly model size and prompt length; the third term is verbosity, the one a product manager can fix without touching infrastructure, by asking for less.

Nukkad's first latency crisis was diagnosed as a model problem and was not one. Against a 900-millisecond target, p95 was 2.4 seconds: 610 milliseconds of queue wait from running the pool at 91 per cent utilisation at the 8 pm peak, and 1,270 milliseconds generating 190 tokens where 90 would do. Headroom and a shorter answer bought more than the proposed downgrade to Flash, and cost quality nothing.

4. When the rule applies, and when it misleads

"Smallest model that clears the bar" is a rule with preconditions, and they are testable. First: the bar is a real threshold, not a preference. Nukkad's 97.5 per cent passes, derived from a ₹140 error cost against a ₹11 margin. Godhuli's 99.0 per cent passes in form only: it came from a risk committee that could not say what 98.7 per cent would have cost, which makes it a negotiating position in a threshold's clothes. Second: quality above the bar has no value. True at Nukkad, where an order is right or wrong; false at Godhuli, where precision above 82 per cent kept underwriters reading the flags and adoption drove renewals. Third: the eval set represents production traffic. Both passed in April; one stopped passing by August. Fourth: cost is dominated by inference. True for Nukkad; not for Godhuli, where a ₹6 model bill sat beside reviewers sampling 4 per cent of files at ₹40 each — a smaller model that pushed sampling to 9 per cent would have cost more in total while showing a lower AI bill.

The rule actively misleads in three situations: when quality is the product's differentiation rather than its hygiene, so satisficing concedes the market to whoever optimises past the bar; when the whole model bill is a rounding error against salaries, and a team of six should optimise iteration speed, not tokens; and when the bar is what you are trying to discover, since only the strongest model tells you whether the task is solvable at all.

5. Hard edges: platforms, regulators, devices and seams

In multi-product companies the decision becomes an allocation. When one platform team serves twelve product teams from a shared pool, per-unit cost is a transfer-pricing artefact: charge average cost and heavy consumers are subsidised, charge marginal cost and the platform never funds its capacity. Godhuli hit the milder version — its reviewer and a newer claims-triage product shared a reserved-capacity contract, which changed the question from "cost per file" to "what does the marginal file cost on capacity already bought?" Near zero, until the pool saturates and then very expensive.

In two-sided products the party consuming inference is often not the party paying. Jhilmil Live, a live-commerce marketplace, captioned seller streams in real time: cost scaled with broadcast-hours, revenue with buyer purchases, and a seller streaming four hours to nine viewers destroyed margin. The fix was not a model but an entitlement — caption quality tiered by trailing conversion, a pricing decision dressed as a model-selection one.

Regulation changes what "smallest" can mean. Godhuli's insurers, supervised by IRDAI, required models processing policyholder data to run in Indian regions and every material change to be revalidated before production — turning selection from a monthly optimisation into a quarterly change-control event with a four-to-six week tail, so a cheaper model released in June could not ship until September. Under the DPDP Act, a vendor tier that trains on submitted data is not a procurement preference but a disqualification.

Hardware inverts the economics. Otla Devices, which builds a counter-top billing terminal for kirana stores with on-device Hindi speech recognition, chose its model against 4 GB of RAM and a bill of materials, not a rate card. Its inference cost is capex, paid once at manufacture, and the model cannot be swapped after shipping except over the air to devices that are often offline: a cloud team that picks wrong loses a month of margin, Otla loses a hardware generation. In AI-native companies the model bill is cost of goods sold, so six points of gross margin is a valuation difference — which is why their founders run this weekly and incumbents run it when finance asks.

The organisational seam matters more than the technical one. Finance can meet its ceiling by forcing a smaller model that raises review cost in operations; risk can raise the bar with no budget conversation; platform can meet p95 by over-provisioning into someone else's line. Mature companies do not fix this with a policy document: they put one number — fully loaded cost per resolved unit of work — on a dashboard all three owners see, and make one person accountable. What they say they do is collaborate; what they do is appoint an owner.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

Output tokens are the expensive ones, twice over

Output is priced three to four times input and generated serially, so it drives both the bill and the clock. The tell is a team that has spent two weeks compressing its system prompt while the model still answers in four polite sentences where a JSON field would do. "Our context is too long" is the wrong reading: input tokens are cheap, parallel and often cacheable. Verbosity is none of those.

Cost per call is not cost per resolved task

Any agentic or multi-step design multiplies calls per outcome, and retries after a guardrail rejection are invisible on a rate card. The tell is a bill growing faster than usage while the price per call is flat. Divide the invoice by user-visible outcomes, not API calls: the ratio between those counts is the most diagnostic figure in the exercise.

The eval bar is a decision threshold wearing a costume

A threshold like 97.5 per cent encodes an implicit exchange rate between false positives, false negatives and rupees, and the tell is that nobody in the room can say what a one-point drop costs. Experts push back to expected cost of error — error rate × cost per error × volume — and often find the bar was set two sizes too tight, buying an expensive model to prevent a cheap mistake.

Cheaper models move cost rather than removing it

Downgrade and you get more retries, longer compensating prompts, more human review. The tell is an inference bill down 60 per cent while total cost to serve is flat: Godhuli's sampling cost more per file than its models did, so a "cheaper" configuration that raised sampling would have been the expensive one.

Variance, not the mean, breaks the budget

Token counts are long-tailed: Nukkad's mean order was 850 input tokens, its 99th percentile — a family order with a long edit history — 6,400. The tell is a plan built entirely on averages. Budget from the mean, but cap inputs and alert from the tail, where latency violations and context-window failures also live.

A model swap is not a drop-in swap

Prompts are fitted to a model's quirks over months, so the incumbent's prompt run against a challenger measures transferability, not capability. The tell is a bake-off where every candidate got the same prompt and the incumbent won.

Perceived latency and measured latency are different products

A streamed answer beginning in 350 milliseconds feels faster than a silent one completing in 900. The tell is a team buying a faster model to fix a complaint that a skeleton state or an optimistic echo would have fixed. The corollary bites too: for a deliberative task, visible slowness reads as care.

The vendor's price is a policy, not a constant

Rate cards move, committed-use discounts of 30 to 50 per cent exist for predictable volume, and tiers get deprecated on ninety days' notice. The tell is a business case built on today's list price with no renegotiation date and no second source. Experts keep a tested fallback on another vendor or an open-weight model; that readiness is what makes the negotiation real.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

Exhibit 4 — where the binding constraint sits

TypeBinding constraintTypical resolution
Consumer, high volume₹ per unit; visible latencyCaching, output caps, cascades
B2B SaaSGross margin promised to investorsTwo-pass designs, rules for the last points of recall
Enterprise / regulatedChange control and residencyValidated configurations, not latest
Platform / marketplaceWho consumes vs who paysEntitlements and tiering, not model choice
HardwareRAM, battery, BOM, OTA reachDistilled on-device model; capex not opex
AI-nativeModel bill is COGSWeekly review; distillation at scale

Two commonly claimed differences are not real. The arithmetic does not change across types — identity, cascade formula and queueing behave the same everywhere — and enterprise buyers are not indifferent to latency; they are indifferent to milliseconds and acutely sensitive to whether the batch finishes before the 9 am shift.

Stage changes the toolkit, not the logic. A seed-stage team should use the strongest model it can afford and spend scarce engineering weeks on product-market fit, because ₹2 lakh a month of over-payment is cheaper than a month of delay. A growth-stage team — where both Meghna and Farida sat — has enough volume for the arithmetic to matter and enough eval data to trust it, and this is where caching, cascades and hard ceilings pay. A scaled company amortises fixed costs over volumes that make them trivially worthwhile, and its constraint becomes change management across dozens of teams.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

Nukkad Kitchens. What shipped was Kestrel-12B with a cached menu prefix and a 90-token output cap: ₹0.169 per order against a ₹0.30 ceiling, 97.9 per cent against a 97.5 bar. The headroom funded not a better model but a Flash first pass on the 41 per cent of orders that were verbatim repeats, costing ₹0.021 and scoring 99.4 per cent there, where the task is retrieval rather than comprehension. Blended: 0.41 × ₹0.021 + 0.59 × ₹0.169 = ₹0.108 per order at 98.5 per cent — ₹6.7 lakh a month, and eight months of growth inside the same budget.

Godhuli Risk Systems. With the two-pass design running at ₹6.31 a file, Farida's team modelled distilling a 9-billion-parameter open-weight model on 140,000 labelled historical files: ₹34 lakh fixed, then ₹11.4 lakh a month of reserved GPU capacity against ₹15.1 lakh of API spend — ₹3.7 lakh saved a month, break-even at 9.2 months. What decided it was not the break-even but the variance around it: reserved capacity does not fall if two insurers churn. Distillation converts a variable cost into a fixed one, which is a bet on volume stability, not a cost saving.

Bageecha Fresh — where it failed. The Nashik agri marketplace graded produce from photographs uploaded at packhouses. In February 2026 it replaced a flagship vision model with a distilled small one, cutting cost per consignment 82 per cent on an eval set showing 96.4 per cent against 96.9. By July, disputes had risen from 0.8 per cent to 4.3. The eval set had been collected in daylight at two modern packhouses on mid-range phones; monsoon consignments arrived photographed under tube lights on ₹6,000 handsets, and on fungal blemish in table grapes — 6 per cent of volume, 31 per cent of dispute value — the small model scored 71 per cent. The defect was in the eval set, not the model, and the small model was the more sensitive to it: smaller models degrade faster off-distribution.

The recovery is the instructive part, because it was not a reversion. Bageecha added an image-quality pre-check at upload, routed low-confidence gradings and all table-grape consignments to the flagship model, and rebuilt the eval set stratified by lighting, handset tier and season with a monsoon holdout. Cost settled at 31 per cent of the original rather than 18, and disputes returned to 0.9 per cent. The team had been right that a smaller model could do the job and wrong about what "the job" was — a distinction only a stratified eval set can make.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Exhibit 5 — symptom, diagnostic, and the price of a late catch

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost if caught late
Flagship by defaultNo one can state the bar"What score is good enough, and why that number?"Repricing the product
Leaderboard selectionShortlist built from vendor blogs"What did each score on 200 of our own cases?"Launch-week quality incident

Cascade decayEscalation rate creeping up"What is q this week versus at launch?"Silently paying flagship prices for everything

Cascade decay is the failure mode specific to the sophisticated: a router calibrated at 22 per cent escalation drifts as inputs change, and at Godhuli's 47 per cent the cascade would cost more than simply using the expensive model while carrying two code paths. Every entry in the table shares a shape — a cheap measurement sat in the team's own production data, and a plausible proxy was used instead.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Today's prices, or tomorrow's? The frontier-default camp points at a decline of roughly an order of magnitude a year in the price of a given capability level, and argues that anything built to save money — routers, distilled models, prompt gymnastics — is depreciating engineering debt: wait two quarters and the expensive model is affordable. Its evidence is the price history since 2023; it is wrong if compute stays supply-constrained, or if volume growth outruns the decline — Nukkad's case, where eleven per cent a month compounds to 3.5× in a year.

Are cascades worth their complexity? The one-model camp argues that two paths mean two prompt sets, two regression suites, two failure modes and a router that is itself a model needing evaluation, and that most reported savings do not survive a fully loaded accounting of engineering time; its evidence is the number of decayed, unmonitored cascades in production. The routing camp replies that on a long-tailed difficulty distribution a single model necessarily overpays on the easy majority, and that Godhuli's ninety per cent saving is unreachable otherwise. What would settle it — how savings hold up over eighteen months without maintenance — neither side has.

Is latency a constraint or a quality attribute? One camp treats it as a budget line: set a ceiling, satisfy it, move on. The other holds that speed is product quality, citing decades of evidence that response time moves conversion, and would spend real money to go from 900 milliseconds to 300. The second camp has the harder case in 2026: deliberative models trade time for accuracy explicitly, and users appear willing to wait for answers they read as considered — though whether that tolerance is durable or a novelty is unresolved.

Should there be a bar at all? A decision-theoretic minority argues that thresholds crudely stand in for the real objective — minimise expected total cost, of which model cost and expected error cost are two terms — and forbid sane trades, such as accepting 97.3 per cent to halve the bill. The threshold camp answers that expected-cost reasoning is indefensible where harms are not fungible with rupees, that it invites motivated re-estimation of error costs by whoever wants the cheaper model, and that a pre-registered bar is a governance device precisely because it is inflexible. The argument is about whether the organisation can be trusted with a dial.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a model comparison table. Someone who has internalised it arrives having asked what unit of work the bill should be divided by, and will not discuss models until that unit is agreed. They write the three numbers before opening a vendor page, and know which is binding, because effort spent on a non-binding constraint is wasted. They decompose by instinct: cost into input, cached input, output and retries; latency into queue, first token and generation. They are suspicious of their own eval set in a specific way — asking what population it under-samples, not whether it is "good" — and can state the escalation rate of every cascade they own from memory. They negotiate prices rather than accepting them, and keep a tested second source because that readiness is what makes the negotiation real. Most tellingly, they treat selection as a standing decision with a review cadence: the menu changes monthly, traffic weekly, the bar whenever a regulator or an incident says so.

12. What each of them did

Meghna shipped Kestrel-12B with a cached prefix, a 90-token output cap and a Flash fast path for repeat orders, at ₹0.108 blended against a ₹0.30 ceiling, and told her board the headroom was deliberate: at eleven per cent monthly growth, the ceiling to plan against was October's, not April's. The binding constraint was growth, not the current bill, and eight months of runway inside a fixed absolute budget was worth more than another ₹2 lakh of monthly saving.

Farida shipped the two-pass configuration with the deterministic checklist at ₹6.31 a file against a ₹9 ceiling, and declined the distillation despite its ₹3.7 lakh monthly saving: a nine-month break-even funded by converting a variable cost into a fixed one was a bet on eleven customers staying, two of them still on pilot contracts. She scheduled the review for the quarter after those pilots converted or did not.

Exhibit 6 — the two decisions side by side

  2. Godhuli's 99.0 per cent bar was set by an insurer's risk committee, and nobody could price a 0.3-point miss. Should Farida have contested the bar before selecting a model, and what would she have brought to that conversation?
  3. Bageecha's eval set was the defect, not the model. What would a monthly eval-integrity review check at Nukkad or Godhuli to catch that drift in four weeks rather than five months?

  • AI cost-to-serve and pricing — where the ceiling comes from, and when you can reopen it instead of obeying it.

  • Problem–model fit — the cheapest model is the one you did not need, as Godhuli's rules checklist showed.
  • The ML lifecycle — selection is a standing decision inside retraining, monitoring and re-release, not a procurement event.
  • Data strategy and data acquisition — a distilled model is only as cheap as the labelled data behind it.
  • Labelling and annotation — the eval set is a labelling programme; Bageecha's failure was a sampling failure in a model's clothes.
  • Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC — what a bar can and cannot mean, and why Godhuli needed two numbers.
  • Quality as a distribution — an average hides the slices where a small model has already failed.
case20v1-aipm.cost.latency:
Chakshu Works: Choosing the Invoice Reader

A decision case on cost, latency and model selection

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 5 October 2026, Aarti Bhandari, chief product officer of Chakshu Works, stood in front of a whiteboard in the company's Pune office. On it were three model names, three rupee figures and one date: Friday, 9 October. By that evening of the ninth she had to tell her leadership team which language model would read every supplier invoice that Chakshu's customers uploaded, because the add-on was due to open to paying customers on 19 October, three weeks ahead of Diwali, when distributors' billing volumes climb sharply.

The nine-week beta had gone well. Customers liked the feature.

2. Company background

Chakshu Works, founded in 2017 in Pune, sells accounting and GST-compliance software to small wholesale distributors: dealers in tiles, auto spares, stationery and packaged food who buy from a dozen suppliers and sell to several hundred shops. It has 31,000 paying business accounts. It competes with Tally, Zoho Books and Vyapar. Its pitch has always been that a distributor should never retype a supplier's invoice.

That pitch matters because of the GST regime. A distributor's input tax credit depends on matching each purchase invoice with what the supplier reported on the GST Network, and a mismatch can delay the credit until the supplier corrects it. The monthly return deadline around the 20th makes the busiest days at a distributor's counter the days its accountant is most impatient. Invoices contain names, phone numbers and GSTINs, so the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 shapes where and how they may be processed.

In June 2026 the board approved an "Invoice Reader" add-on. A distributor photographs or uploads a supplier invoice, a language model extracts twelve fields (supplier, GSTIN, invoice number, date, taxable value, tax rates and so on), and the product posts the entry for the accountant to confirm. The add-on is priced at ₹400 per account per month.

3. The situation

Since 3 August, 400 beta accounts had used a prototype built on a large frontier model. The prototype was accurate but slow and expensive, and Chitra Ahuja, the finance head, had written the constraint into the launch plan: the model bill for the add-on could not exceed 25 per cent of add-on revenue. Finance expected 8,000 accounts to adopt by December, at 150 invoices per account per month, or 12,00,000 invoices a month. Revenue is therefore 8,000 × ₹400 = ₹32,00,000, or ₹32.00 lakh, a month, and the model budget is ₹8.00 lakh.

Engineering agreed an eval bar with product. On a test set of 400 real invoices, 12 fields each (4,800 fields), a model had to read at least 94 per cent of fields correctly, which is 4,512 fields, and its 95th-percentile response time had to stay under 4.0 seconds. The second number came from customer-success: at the counter, an accountant who waits longer than four seconds usually types the entry by hand.

On 25 September, ten days before the whiteboard session, the team ran three candidates against the test set. They were a large hosted model, a mid-size hosted model, and a small open-weight model that Chakshu would fine-tune and host on rented GPUs. Exhibit 1 sets out the results, and Exhibit 2 puts them against the budget.

The beta had also surfaced a pattern the headline numbers hid. About a quarter of the invoices distributors upload are not printed GST invoices at all, but handwritten bills and phone photographs of carbon-copy slips from small suppliers. The test set reflected that mix: 300 printed invoices (3,600 fields) and 100 handwritten ones (1,200 fields). Exhibit 3 splits the accuracy.
