Exhibit 3 shows that the gap between the models is mostly a handwriting gap. On printed invoices all three models sit within 3.0 percentage points of one another, and the small model alone fails the bar overall because of the handwritten bills.

The distributed team reads the numbers differently. Bhaskar Chatterjee in Bengaluru sees an engineering opportunity in Option C. Beatriz Carvalho, who leads evaluation and design from Lisbon, has spent the beta reading wrong extractions line by line. Bindu Chandran, in Coimbatore, hears the complaints first.

4. The people

Bhaskar Chatterjee, head of engineering, Bengaluru. He wants the small model. It is cheapest at scale, keeps invoices on infrastructure Chakshu controls inside India, and would give his team a fine-tuning capability the company lacks. He estimates two engineers and eight weeks of work to reach production quality, which would miss the 19 October launch.

Chitra Ahuja, finance head, Mumbai. She wants the 25 per cent cap respected, with room to absorb price changes from the model vendor. She dislikes the fixed GPU commitment in Option C because it is paid whether or not customers adopt.

Beatriz Carvalho, evaluation and design lead, Lisbon. She wants quality protected. She points out that a wrong tax rate posted without notice costs a distributor real credit, and she is uneasy that the mid-size model clears the bar by only 24 fields, or half a percentage point, on one test set.

Bindu Chandran, customer-success lead, Coimbatore. She wants speed. Her beta accounts abandoned the large model's slow responses during the afternoon rush, and she believes accuracy beyond the bar is worth little if the accountant has already started typing.

5. The options

Option A: the large hosted model for every invoice. It has the best accuracy, 96.0 per cent, and the best handwriting performance. It breaks two limits: its p95 latency is 6.5 seconds against a ceiling of 4.0, and its cost of ₹13.20 lakh a month exceeds the ₹8.00 lakh budget by ₹5.20 lakh.

Option B: the mid-size hosted model for every invoice. It clears both parts of the bar, with 94.5 per cent accuracy and a 2.8-second p95, and costs ₹5.40 lakh a month, leaving ₹2.60 lakh of headroom. Its weaknesses are the thin accuracy margin and a 90.0 per cent handwritten score.

Option C: the small model, fine-tuned and self-hosted. It is the fastest, at 1.2 seconds, and the cheapest, at ₹4.04 lakh a month including ₹2.60 lakh of fixed hosting. But at 91.0 per cent it sits 3.0 points, or 144 fields, below the bar. No one can promise a fine-tune closes that gap by 19 October.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, which options clear the eval bar and the budget, and which fail on accuracy, latency or cost?
  2. What does Exhibit 3 tell you about where the models differ, and how would you test whether the mid-size model's half-point margin is real?
  3. How should Aarti weigh Bhaskar's case for owning the model against the fixed GPU cost and the launch date?
  4. Which option should she announce on Friday, and what evidence after launch would make her change it?

7. A note for the learner

This topic frames model choice as a constrained search. Set the bar first, covering accuracy on a representative test set and a latency ceiling set by what the user will tolerate, and set the budget from what the price of the product can bear. Then pick the smallest, cheapest model that clears all of them. Quality beyond the bar is not free: the large model is better, but its extra accuracy breaks the latency ceiling.

One defensible path: choose Option B and announce it on 9 October. It is the only option that clears accuracy (4,536 fields against the 4,512 required), latency (2.8 against 4.0 seconds) and budget (₹5.40 lakh against ₹8.00 lakh). Option A fails two limits and Option C fails the accuracy bar, so neither survives the first screen.

The path should carry conditions, because Beatriz's worry is fair. Before 19 October, re-run the eval on a fresh set of invoices and keep the model only if it still clears 94.0 per cent. After launch, track handwritten invoices separately, since Exhibit 3 shows they are where the model is weakest. If handwriting dominates complaints, the next experiment is to route only those invoices to a stronger model, provided the slower response is acceptable for them.

Bhaskar's proposal is deferred, not rejected. Once Chakshu has weeks of confirmed corrections, it will own the training data that Option C lacks, and the question of building, fine-tuning or buying a model can be asked again with evidence instead of hope.
case20v1-aipm.skillset:
Bhavishya Works: Who Should Own the AI Feature?

A decision case on the AI-era product manager

1. Opening

On Monday 5 October 2026, Kamini Joshi, chief product officer of Bhavishya Works, sat in a glass meeting room at the company's Pune headquarters with a printout she had marked in three colours. The board would meet on Friday 16 October, and chief executive Siddharth Bapat had told her that morning what he expected to hear there: who would own the company's first major AI feature, and whether it would reach merchants before Diwali, which fell on 8 November.

The feature was called Munim Sahayak. It read a small trader's purchase invoices, sorted them into GST categories, and drafted replies to the mismatch notices that the tax department sends when a return and a supplier's filing disagree. A pilot had just ended, well enough to excite everyone and badly enough to worry Kamini. She had eleven days to choose how her product team would be organised and skilled to take it to market.

2. Company Background

Bhavishya Works was founded in Pune in 2016 by Siddharth Bapat and a chartered accountant, who left within two years. Its flagship product, Munim, is a mobile and web application that helps small retailers and wholesalers raise GST invoices, track purchases and reconcile their books. By October 2026 the company employed 210 people and had 4,20,000 monthly active merchants, of whom 1,10,000 paid an average of ₹7,200 a year. Annual recurring revenue was ₹79.2 crore (1,10,000 multiplied by ₹7,200).

The market was crowded. Zoho Books and ClearTax served the more formal end of small business; Vyapar and Tally dominated the neighbourhood shop counter; and the Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN) kept changing portal rules in ways that every vendor had to follow. Munim's advantage was distribution through wholesalers and chartered accountants in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka, plus a reputation for getting the numbers right. Merchants forgave a clumsy screen but not a wrong tax figure, since the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) held them responsible.

Siddharth wanted an AI feature as a defence against better-funded rivals and as an upsell. The plan was an add-on at ₹2,400 a year. If 30 per cent of paying merchants bought it, that meant 33,000 buyers and ₹7.92 crore of new annual revenue, a gain of exactly 10 per cent on the existing base.

3. The Situation

The product team had six product managers, all hired between 2019 and 2023 for what the company then needed: turning merchant requests into clear specifications, coordinating with engineers, and keeping releases on schedule. They were good at it. The pilot, however, exposed a different job. From 3 August to 28 September, eight weeks in all, Munim Sahayak drafted 4,000 notice replies for 600 pilot merchants, each reviewed by a partner chartered accountant before sending. Exhibit 1 shows the result: 3,640 drafts needed no correction, but 360, or 9.0 per cent, had to be edited.

The most worrying line was the 150 drafts with a wrong input-tax-credit amount. A merchant who sent such a reply unread could admit to liability that did not exist. In the July demonstration that won board enthusiasm, the team had shown twenty hand-picked notices, and every one came out right. Nobody had written a test set of realistic, difficult notices, because nobody thought that was the product manager's job.

Kamini then asked a colleague in the data team to score her six product managers against four skills that the pilot had made important. In Exhibit 2 the team wrote clearly, with a mean of 3.83 out of 5, but scored only 1.83 on designing evaluations and 2.17 on understanding what each AI call cost.

Colleagues abroad saw the problem differently. Sanne de Wit, the lead designer in Amsterdam, said the drafts "read like a confident junior who has never been wrong". Amani Odhiambo, the data scientist in Nairobi, who sat two and a half hours behind Pune, could show which notice types failed most often. Gurpreet Anand, who led customer success from Melbourne and worked five and a half hours ahead of Pune, relayed what merchants told him on late calls: they liked the speed, but asked who was responsible if the draft was wrong.

4. The People

Siddharth Bapat, chief executive, Mumbai, wants the feature in merchants' hands by 2 November. He believes festival season is when buying intent peaks, and he has promised the board the ₹7.92 crore revenue line.

Rudra Hebbar, vice president of engineering, Bengaluru, leads thirty-eight engineers and favours speed. He argues that modern tools let any product manager write a good instruction to the model within a week, and that the team needs no new species of hire.

Amani Odhiambo, data scientist, Nairobi, wants a formal evaluation set built from real notices before anything ships, and wants someone on the product side to own it. She will not be the permanent author of tests for what are product decisions.

Gurpreet Anand, customer success lead, Melbourne, wants a launch that does not turn his team into a complaint desk. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 already makes merchants nervous about where their invoices go.

5. The Options

Kamini identified three distinct courses. Exhibit 3 sets out the first-year cost of each in ₹ lakh.

Option A: hire two senior AI product managers from outside. Total cost is ₹132 lakh, or ₹1.32 crore. The upside is immediate credibility; the cost is that the existing team might treat AI work as someone else's territory, and notice periods push the first result to about five months, past Diwali.

Option B: build the skills in the existing six. Total cost is ₹64 lakh. Product managers would learn to write evaluation sets, read failure patterns, and price each model call, with Amani as mentor. The upside is that ownership stays with the product decisions; the cost is slower delivery on other work and learning that may be shallower than hiring would give. In this option the launch is staged: invoice categorisation goes live on 2 November, while notice drafting waits until drafts pass a threshold the product managers themselves set.

Option C: outsource AI features to an external studio. Total cost is ₹82 lakh, with the quickest start at two months. The studio would own prompts, tests and tuning. The cost is that Bhavishya Works would be buying judgement it should hold.

6. Questions for Discussion

  1. What did the pilot in Exhibit 1 reveal about the work of the product manager that the July demonstration hid?
  2. Using Exhibit 2, which skills did a 2019 product manager need, and which new ones is the team missing? Why might clear writing matter more, not less?
  3. How should Kamini weigh the cost and timing in Exhibit 3 against Siddharth's Diwali deadline and Gurpreet's concern about merchant trust?
  4. If you were Kamini, which option would you take to the board on 16 October, and what evidence would make you change your mind?

7. A Note for the Learner

This case turns on a quiet change in the job. In 2019 a product manager mainly specified behaviour that engineers then made deterministic. With AI, behaviour is probabilistic, so the product manager has to define what good looks like, build the test that measures it, judge the output with taste, and understand what it costs to run. Prompt writing is the smallest part.

One defensible path is Option B with explicit gates. Exhibit 1 shows that every failure was detectable by someone who knew the domain and had a test set; hiring two outsiders (₹132 lakh against ₹64 lakh, roughly double) does not by itself create that habit in six people who will own the roadmap for years. Outsourcing removes the learning altogether. The reasoned plan is to launch categorisation on 2 November, keep notice drafting in reviewed mode with the chartered accountants, and have the product managers own the evaluation set, publishing a pass mark before notice drafting goes broadly live, ahead of the 31 December annual return rush.

The risk of Option B is a slow skill ramp. Kamini should reduce it by reassessing the Exhibit 2 scores at the end of the first quarter, and by hiring selectively if evaluation design is still weak.
exp40v2-aipm.skillset:
AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management

The AI-Era PM Skillset

What a 2019 product manager could safely not know — and what it now costs to not know it.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 9 February 2026, in a rented floor above a tyre showroom on Pune's Nagar Road, Aparna Kulkarni, VP Product at Tarkeeb Systems, watched a slide that said her company could take ₹1.66 crore a month of cost out of its customers' warehouses. Tarkeeb sold warehouse execution software to third-party logistics operators — the layer that tells a picker which bin, a supervisor which pallet, a control tower which shipment has gone wrong. Across Tarkeeb's fourteen enterprise accounts, roughly 92,000 exceptions surfaced every month: a scan that did not match the manifest, a carton photographed with a crushed corner, an address string that resolved to two pincodes. Every one of them went to a human resolver at a fully loaded cost of about ₹180. The slide proposed that a vision-plus-language model resolve them instead.

Aparna's engineering director had brought a single number: 94.3% accuracy on a held-out set of 18,000 historical exceptions. Her CEO had brought a customer, one of India's larger contract logistics firms, who had said in a QBR that he would sign a three-year renewal for this. Aparna had brought a question nobody in the room could yet answer: if the model takes the easy half of the queue, what happens to the cost of the half it leaves behind?

Eight days later and 590 kilometres north-east, in Indore, Kabir Deshmukh faced a problem with the same shape and none of the same furniture. Kabir was co-founder and chief product officer of Mausam Agri Intelligence, a four-year-old company whose Marathi- and Hindi-language voice assistant answered agronomy questions for 410,000 monthly active farmers across Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and southern Rajasthan. A farmer called, spoke a question into a ₹6,000 handset, and received an answer about spray timing, mandi prices or an irrigation window, stitched together from India Meteorological Department forecasts, state agriculture department advisories and the company's own plot-level history. Mausam charged ₹49 per farmer per season and had, on 17 February, discovered that its inference bill was consuming four-fifths of its gross revenue.

Neither problem is an AI problem. Both are product-management problems in which the thing managed happens to be probabilistic, and in which the classical toolkit issues no instruction at the decisive moment. This page is about the layer of judgement that does.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

The AI-era PM skillset is the set of capabilities a product manager needs in addition to the 2019 toolkit once a product's core behaviour is produced by a learned model rather than by rules the team wrote and can fully inspect. Five capabilities compose it: evaluation literacy (designing and reading tests that establish whether a probabilistic system is good enough for one specific decision); data-quality judgement (knowing what the system learned from, and therefore where it will fail); responsible-AI judgement (anticipating harm, bias and misuse as a pre-launch obligation); workflow-redesign fluency (treating the task, not the feature, as the unit of design); and probabilistic product economics (costing and pricing a system whose behaviour and marginal cost vary per call). It is not a new profession. It is the set of things the old profession was allowed to delegate when software was deterministic and is no longer allowed to delegate now.

The intellectual history is older than the vocabulary. Statistical decision theory gave us, in Abraham Wald's work of the 1940s, the idea that a decision rule should be chosen against a loss function rather than a hit rate. Signal detection theory, born from wartime radar, established that sensitivity and threshold are separable: the same detector yields many operating points, and choosing one is an act of policy, not of engineering. Lisanne Bainbridge's 1983 paper "Ironies of Automation" showed that automating the easy part of a task makes the residual harder and the human worse at it — the most under-taught result in this field. The 2021 "data-centric AI" turn argued that fixing the dataset beat fixing the architecture. What happened between 2023 and 2025 was not discovery but relocation: these results moved into the weekly decisions of ordinary product teams, because generative models put a probabilistic component into products whose teams had no tradition of reasoning about error. The strongest teaching programmes — Berkeley's SCET, Stanford's BUS311, IIM Calcutta, Cambridge — converged independently on the same four-plus-one curriculum, and on downgrading prompt writing to a craft skill of small and falling importance.

The field is not unanimous. Four schools recur, and it is worth being precise about the exact proposition each would sign.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Measurement-first
(evals, data-centric AI)		 "No model-driven decision ships without an eval set the PM can defend by sampling method." "A passing eval predicts that users will trust or adopt the system."
Sociotechnical
(human factors, Bainbridge, lean)		 "The unit of design is the whole task; automation reallocates work rather than removing it." "A better model resolves the problem without touching the workflow."
Velocity
(AI-native startups)		 "Where capability doubles every two quarters, heavyweight evaluation destroys more value than it protects; build many, kill fast." "Rigour scales down cleanly — a light process is just a heavy one with fewer steps."
Governance
(NIST AI RMF, DPDP-era compliance)		 "Harm assessment is a gate that binds independently of accuracy." "Post-launch monitoring can substitute for a pre-launch assessment."

Exhibit 1 — The four positions, stated as propositions rather than as attitudes. Most practitioners hold two of these and quietly violate a third.

The sentence that survives all four schools is narrow: an AI-era PM's job is to decide, with evidence, when a probabilistic system may be allowed to make someone else's decision — and to redesign the work around the cases where it may not. Everything below is an argument about the second clause, which is where the money is and where the teaching is thinnest.

3. Mechanics: the threshold, and the term nobody models

Expert practice begins by refusing the accuracy number. Aparna's 94.3% describes a classifier; it does not describe a decision. The decision is: for this exception, do we act automatically or route to a human? That decision has two costs. Routing to a human costs ₹180, certainly. Acting automatically costs nothing when right and ₹4,200 when wrong — the reshipment, the SLA credit and the control-tower time that follow a mis-resolved exception, as Tarkeeb's finance team had already measured from twenty-two historical incidents.

From those two numbers the threshold follows mechanically. Automate when the expected cost of automating is below the cost of escalating: (1 − p) × 4,200 < 180, where p is the model's probability of being correct on this item. Solving, p > 1 − 180/4,200 = 0.957. Tarkeeb should automate only where the model is at least 95.7% likely to be right — a bar the 94.3% average does not clear, which is the first reason the headline number was misleading rather than merely incomplete.

But p is not one number; it varies per item, and the model reports it. The step usually left implicit is checking whether that reported confidence is calibrated — whether items the model calls 90% likely are in fact right about 90% of the time. Aparna's team bucketed the 18,000 held-out exceptions by reported confidence and compared to ground truth.

The arithmetic that follows is elementary and is where most teams stop. Automating the top band covers 41% of 92,000 = 37,720 exceptions per month at an expected cost of 0.019 × ₹4,200 = ₹79.80 each, against ₹180 to have a human do it: a saving of ₹100.20 per decision, or ₹37.8 lakh a month. Aparna's engineering director had, in effect, computed this and stopped.

The second-order term is not a refinement of the business case. At Tarkeeb it was 93% of it.

The term he had not computed is Bainbridge's. The 54,280 exceptions left for humans are not a random 59% of the old queue; they are the hard 59%, selected by the model precisely for being hard. Tarkeeb's own time-and-motion data from two pilot sites showed average handling cost on the residual rising from ₹180 to ₹245 — partly because ambiguous address strings and disputed damage claims genuinely take longer, and partly because resolvers who no longer see easy cases lose the rhythm and the pattern library that made them fast. That is ₹65 × 54,280 = ₹35.3 lakh a month of cost created by the automation. Net saving: ₹2.5 lakh a month, or 1.5% of a ₹1.66 crore base, for a project with an eleven-month engineering commitment and a new class of ₹4,200 failures.

Expert practice does not stop at discovering this; it redesigns against it. The move Aparna eventually took was to stop treating the residual as a leftover and start treating it as the product. Bands two and three — 41% of all exceptions, the ones the model has an opinion about but not a trustworthy one — were routed to an assisted queue where the model drafted a resolution, cited the two manifest lines it had compared, and the human confirmed or corrected in a single click. Handling cost on that segment fell to ₹128. Only the bottom 18% went to unassisted human work at ₹245.

4. When the framework binds, and when it misleads

Three conditions make the threshold-and-residual apparatus load-bearing, and each can be stated as a testable claim. First: the decision has an asymmetric, monetisable cost of error. True at Tarkeeb, where ₹4,200 and ₹180 differ by a factor of 23. Partially true at Mausam, where a wrong mandi price costs a wasted trip and a wrong spray window can cost a season — different by two orders of magnitude within the same product, which means Kabir needs several thresholds, not one. Second: a human alternative exists and its cost is measurable. True at Tarkeeb. False at Mausam, where the counterfactual is not a human agronomist but silence, or a neighbour's guess, which no finance team can price. Third: the population the model sees is stable enough that last quarter's calibration predicts this quarter's. True at Tarkeeb, where exception types shift slowly. Sharply false at Mausam, where the question mix rotates completely between kharif and rabi and a calibration measured in July is worthless in December.

Where the idea is actively misleading is the case of small n with large variance. A pre-product-market-fit team with 300 users and forty labelled examples that builds a stratified eval set, computes a threshold to three decimal places and gates a launch on it has produced precision theatre: the confidence interval on a 40-item slice spans roughly ±15 points, wide enough to contain every decision. The velocity school is right about this case and usually arguing from it; the error is generalising to a company like Tarkeeb, where n is 18,000 and sampling error is under a point.

5. Edge cases and organisational seams

The framework frays predictably at five seams. Multi-product: Tarkeeb's model was licensed from Machaan Labs and served three products — exceptions, dock scheduling and returns triage — whose cost asymmetries were 23:1, 4:1 and 1.5:1. A single platform-set threshold cannot be right for all three; the correct design exposes it as a product-level parameter, and the political fight is about who owns it when the model team reports to engineering and the loss reports to each business line. Two-sided: an eval measuring only the demand side is structurally blind to half the harm, as Saudagar Markets discovered below. Regulated: Mausam's advisories touch pesticide dosage, and its data touches the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent requirements for farmer phone numbers and plot coordinates. A governance gate binds here whatever the eval says — a constraint on the design space, not a stage in the pipeline. Hardware plus software: Bhatti Foundry Systems, a Coimbatore firm running vision inspection on castings, cannot ship a model update on a software cadence — 1,900 cameras drift with lens film and lighting, and the re-calibration window is a plant shutdown, not a Tuesday deploy. AI-native: Mausam has no pre-AI workflow to fall back to, so "turn it off" is not a rollback but an outage.

What mature companies actually do, as opposed to what their process documents say, is maintain a few quietly hand-tuned thresholds that no dashboard reports, and a shadow list of accounts excluded from automation because someone senior once got a call. This is not hypocrisy; it encodes information the eval set does not contain. Expert practice is to make that list explicit and review it, not to pretend it away.

6. Nine distinctions that separate the expert

The denominator moves. Automating the easy cases changes the composition of what remains, so the per-unit cost of the residual is not a constant. The tell-tale sign is a business case whose "after" column uses the "before" unit cost. The obvious reading — that cost scales linearly with volume removed — is wrong because the model selects, and selection is never random.

Calibration is not accuracy. A model can be 94% accurate overall and useless for threshold-setting because its confidence scores do not track correctness; conversely a 78%-accurate but well-calibrated model supports a perfectly sound automation policy on its confident tail. The tell-tale sign is a team that quotes accuracy and confidence in the same breath without ever having plotted one against the other.

Cost of error is a distribution, not a scalar. Tarkeeb's ₹4,200 is a mean over twenty-two incidents that ranged from ₹600 to ₹47,000. If the tail is fat, the mean understates the risk of a policy that produces many small errors and occasionally a catastrophic one. The expert asks for the maximum, not just the average, and the tell-tale sign of a novice is a single-cell cost assumption presented without a range.

Golden sets become training targets. Any eval set a team looks at repeatedly gets optimised against, formally through fine-tuning or informally through engineers who have memorised its failures. The tell-tale sign is an eval curve that improves smoothly while support-ticket volume does not move; the remedy is a held-out set refreshed on a schedule and seen by nobody.

Taste is a prior over failure modes. The word is used loosely to mean aesthetic preference. In this context it means something more specific and more learnable: a well-shaped expectation, acquired by reading several hundred real model outputs, about which kinds of wrongness a given system produces. The tell-tale sign of someone who has it is that their first question about a new model is what it gets wrong, not how often it is right.

The PM's artefact changed. The 2019 deliverable was a specification of behaviour. The AI-era deliverable is a specification of a decision boundary: the confidence threshold, the escalation path, the segments excluded, the rollback trigger. The tell-tale sign of the shift is a PRD whose acceptance criteria are stated in probabilities and rupees rather than in screens.

Latency is priced in accuracy. Every pipeline sits on a frontier where more reasoning, more retrieval or a larger model buys correctness at the cost of response time and inference spend. Kabir's voice product cannot exceed about 2.5 seconds before farmers hang up, which removes the top of the accuracy curve from consideration entirely. The tell-tale sign is a team optimising accuracy with no latency budget written down.

Human backstops decay. The reviewer who approves 98% of what the model proposes stops reading by month four; this is automation complacency, measured in human-factors literature since the 1990s and reliably reproduced in every review queue. The tell-tale sign is a rising approval rate paired with falling review time. The design answer is injected known-bad cases and rotation, not exhortation.

Rollback capability is the real risk budget. How much model risk an organisation can responsibly take is set by how fast it can turn the model off — which is an engineering and contractual property, not an appetite. A firm that needs three weeks and a customer's written consent to revert should hold a far higher launch bar than one that can flip a flag. The tell-tale sign is a launch review that discusses confidence in the model and never asks how long reversal takes.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

The differences are real in three places and imagined in most others. In consumer products, errors are cheap and anonymous and feedback volume is enormous, so iteration substitutes for evaluation to a degree that would be reckless elsewhere; Mausam is consumer by interface but not by consequence, which is what makes it hard. In B2B and enterprise, every error has a name, a ticket and a renewal attached, and the binding constraint is usually the customer's own workflow, which you do not control — Aparna could redesign Tarkeeb's screens but not her client's shift roster. In platforms and marketplaces, the distinctive requirement is a supply-side slice in every evaluation, because the party bearing the harm is not the party generating the metric. In hardware, update cadence and sensor drift dominate everything else. In AI-native products there is no non-AI fallback, so the risk work moves from "should we ship" to graceful degradation.

Across stages the difference is narrower than commonly claimed. Seed-stage teams lack the data for stratified evaluation and should not fake it; what they can always do, at any size, is write down the cost of being wrong and the rollback path, which costs an afternoon. Late-stage companies have the data and the harnesses and lose instead on reversal speed. The claim that rigour is a luxury of scale is half true: the measurement is, the decision arithmetic is not.

8. Three worked cases

Mausam: the unit economics of a probabilistic feature

Kabir's 410,000 monthly actives placed 3.4 voice sessions each — 1,394,000 sessions a month. Each session ran speech recognition, a frontier language model with retrieval over IMD and state advisories, and text-to-speech, at a blended ₹2.10. That is ₹29.3 lakh a month against revenue of ₹49 per farmer per season, two seasons a year, or ₹8.17 per farmer-month: ₹33.5 lakh. Gross margin before any other cost: 12.5%.

DesignSessions on small modelInference costGross margin
Frontier model for everything0₹29.3 L12.5%

Exhibit 2 — Mausam's routing options, monthly. The distilled 3-billion-parameter model costs ₹0.28 per session against ₹2.10. The middle row is the one a cost spreadsheet recommends; the bottom row is the one a PM recommends.

The difference between rows two and three is an entire skillset. Routing all forty recurring intents to the cheap model saves ₹18 lakh a month, but the router itself misroutes about 4.1% of sessions, and among the forty intents are spray-timing and dosage questions where a degraded answer is not recoverable inside the call — the farmer acts on it, and the feedback arrives three weeks later as a damaged crop. Kabir routed only the twenty-two intents whose errors are visible and correctable within the same conversation: mandi prices, weather windows, scheme eligibility. He paid ₹4.3 lakh a month for that restraint and could say exactly what he had bought with it.

Saudagar Markets: the case that failed

Saudagar, a Jaipur wholesale marketplace connecting 11,400 craft producers to 46,000 buyers, launched a model-generated listing quality score in August 2025 that reordered search results. The pre-launch evaluation was serious by the standards of the measurement school: 9,000 labelled listings, stratified by category, buyer-side A/B test over six weeks. Click-through rose 14% and order conversion 6.2%. Nobody ran a supply-side slice.

Exhibit 3 — The supply-side consequences that the demand-side evaluation could not have detected. By day 90 the buyer-side click-through gain had decayed from +14% to +3% as selection thinned.

The score had learned that listings with studio-grade photography and long descriptions converted better, which was true, and demoted producers who photographed on a handset in courtyard light, which correlated with being small and rural rather than with being bad. The failure was not the model; it was an evaluation whose unit of analysis was the buyer session. Recovery took 140 days: a cap limiting any listing's demotion to 30% of baseline impressions, an appeals workflow with a five-day SLA that reinstated roughly 900 sellers, a photography assist that cleaned phone images, and a standing seller-decile slice in every ranking evaluation thereafter. Category GMV returned to within 4% of trend; about 600 producers never came back.

Bhatti Foundry: the discipline of the update

Bhatti Foundry Systems inspects castings for porosity with vision models on 1,900 cameras. A retrained model improved held-out defect recall from 91% to 96% but, deployed to 14 plants at once, raised the false-reject rate on one customer's aluminium line from 2.1% to 7.8%, because that line's lighting had drifted since the training images were collected: ₹31 lakh of scrap in nine days. The fix was procedural — staged rollout by plant, a 72-hour shadow period in which the new model scores but does not reject, and an acceptance test defined per line rather than per model.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Demo-driven commitment. Early sign: a senior stakeholder has seen three impressive live examples and stopped asking questions. Diagnostic: "were these cases sampled from the eval set, or chosen?" Caught late, the cost is a public commitment that makes the segmented numbers politically unsayable.

Evaluating against the workflow you are about to change. Early sign: the eval set is historical human decisions, and the plan is to remove the humans. Diagnostic: "what will the input distribution look like six months after launch?" Caught late, this is the Tarkeeb trap — a business case that evaporates in production.

Thresholds set by the model team. Early sign: the PM cannot state the cost of a false positive in rupees without checking. Diagnostic: exactly that question, asked without notice. Caught late, the organisation discovers it has been running an unexamined risk policy for a year.

Monitoring without an owner or a trigger. Early sign: a dashboard exists and nobody is rostered to look at it. Diagnostic: "what number, at what value, turns this off, and whose phone rings?" Caught late, degradation is discovered by a customer.

Backstop atrophy. Early sign: reviewer approval rate climbs above 97% while average review time falls. Diagnostic: seed the queue with ten known-bad cases and count catches. Caught late, the human-in-the-loop control that the entire risk case rested on has been fictional for months.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Evaluation rigour versus velocity. The measurement school holds that untested probabilistic systems impose costs that surface as churn and liability, and points to cases like Saudagar's. The velocity school holds that in a domain where the underlying models improve every quarter, elaborate evaluation amortises over a shorter and shorter lifetime, and that the firms winning AI-native categories have shipped and killed a dozen features in the time a rigorous competitor evaluated two. The measurement school would be wrong if error costs in a category were genuinely small and reversible; the velocity school would be wrong if the harms were irreversible or fell on parties without recourse. Both are right within their domains, and most arguments between them are really arguments about which domain the product is in.

How technical the PM must be. One camp holds that a PM who cannot read a confusion matrix, question a sampling frame and inspect a hundred model outputs is not doing the job — that the judgement is inseparable from contact with the data. The other holds that this recruits for the wrong thing: the scarce skill is deciding what is worth building and for whom, and technical depth is available from specialists at lower cost than customer judgement. The second camp would be wrong if the specialist's incentives systematically diverge from the product's, which in most organisations they do: the model team is measured on accuracy, not on residual cost. The first would be wrong if technical PMs demonstrably built worse products, and the evidence there is thin in both directions.

Is responsible AI a gate or a metric? The governance school treats harm assessment as a separate pre-launch obligation. Integrationists argue that a separate gate gets gamed and that fairness constraints belong inside the eval set as slices with their own thresholds — that Saudagar's failure was a missing slice, not a missing committee. The gate camp would be wrong if slice-based evaluation reliably caught harms nobody thought to slice for; it does not. The integrationists would be wrong if gates actually blocked things; in many firms they do not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in identifiable ways. They ask what the system gets wrong before asking how often it is right. They can state the cost of a false positive in currency, from memory, in a meeting. They treat the residual queue as a design surface rather than a leftover, and can name the second-order term in their own business case. They know the reversal time for every model-driven decision they own. They read model outputs personally, in volume, and can describe the characteristic shape of the system's wrongness in a sentence. They prefer a narrower thing with a defensible boundary to a broader thing with an average. And they can say which of the four schools above they are borrowing from and why it fits this decision — the difference between having judgement and having a methodology.

12. Decisions, and three questions

Aparna took the proposal to her CEO on 3 March with the naive case, the residual term and the assisted-queue redesign on one page. Tarkeeb shipped automation on the confident band in May and the assisted queue in July, sold as a ₹46.6 lakh saving rather than a ₹37.8 lakh one, with a contractual right to revert within 24 hours written into two renewals. Kabir shipped the twenty-two-intent router in March, took 53% gross margin instead of 66%, and gated the eighteen withheld intents on a Marathi agronomy eval set that Mausam is still building with two Krishi Vigyan Kendras.

  1. Tarkeeb's residual cost rose because resolvers lost their easy cases. Is that a cost of the model, a cost of the workflow design, or a cost the customer's operations team should bear? Who you assign it to determines whether the project is approved.
  2. Kabir paid ₹4.3 lakh a month to avoid errors he could not observe. What evidence would justify that premium to an investor, and is "we cannot measure this harm" an argument for caution or an argument that the harm is small?
  3. Saudagar's evaluation was rigorous and still catastrophic. If the missing slice was unknowable in advance, does the measurement school have an answer — or does this case belong to the governance school?

13. Going deeper

  1. How AI is reshaping the PM role — the demand side of this skillset; explains why these five capabilities became load-bearing rather than optional.
  2. AI-native teams — who owns the threshold when the model sits in a platform team; unlocks the organisational design that makes the residual queue anyone's job.
  3. Problem–model fit — the upstream question of whether a model is the right instrument at all; catches the failure before any threshold matters.
  4. The ML lifecycle — the cadence within which retraining, drift and staged rollout live; makes Bhatti's shadow period a standard step rather than an invention.
  5. Data strategy and data acquisition — why Mausam's Marathi eval set is a roadmap item with a twelve-month lead time, not a prerequisite.
  6. Labelling and annotation — where ground truth comes from and what its disagreement rate does to every number on this page.
  7. Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC — the formal vocabulary behind Figure 1; unlocks the ability to argue with a data scientist's chart rather than accept it.
  8. What's different when the feature is a model — the compact statement of the whole shift; the right page to reread after this one.

Gunjan Systems: What the Advisory Was Worth

A case on the product manager's craft when the product is a judgement

1. The night before

On the night of Sunday 22 November 2026, Aparna Kotwal sat at the dining table of her flat off Avinashi Road in Coimbatore with three printouts in front of her. Two were face up. The third she had turned over twice.

The first was a billing summary from her finance team: in the year ended 31 March 2026, Gunjan Systems had invoiced its nine outcome-contract mill groups ₹23.40 crore as its share of downtime those mills had not suffered. The second, assembled by Marisol Agbayani's customer-success team in Manila from the mills' own maintenance systems, showed rather less downtime avoided, for the five groups where the exercise was possible at all. The third, face down, was a September capability survey of Aparna's own product organisation, which she had shown nobody.

The board met on Friday 27 November. On Thursday 19 November, Vedant Sabnis, who had founded the company and still ran it, had sent two lines: Bring one slide. Who owns Faisla, and what does it cost to make them able to own it. Jaagran Faisla — a verdict — was the advisory layer built on top of Gunjan's machine-monitoring product, and it had just finished a twelve-week pilot that everyone described, accurately and unhelpfully, as promising.

What Aparna could not decide was whether she faced a staffing problem, a measurement problem, or a problem with the promise the company made in 2021 and has billed against ever since.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2021

Gunjan Systems was founded in Coimbatore in March 2016 by Vedant Sabnis, a vibration-analysis engineer who had spent nine years commissioning ring frames, and Thangaraj Velusamy, who wrote the firmware. Their insight was unglamorous: in a spinning mill an unplanned stop costs money by the hour, the warning signs are present days in advance, and almost nobody was listening.

Jaagran reached its first recognisable form in 2019: sensors, an edge box in the shed, threshold alarms, a weekly report. By the year ended 31 March 2026 the company employed 430 people, monitored 40,000 machines across 152 plants, and reported revenue of ₹167.40 crore — ₹61 crore of hardware, ₹68 crore of subscription at ₹17,000 per machine per year, ₹23.40 crore of outcome share and ₹15 crore of commissioning and training services.

Two early decisions shape what is possible in November 2026. The first, in June 2021: to win large groups sceptical of software, Gunjan offered a contract taking 12.5 per cent of the value of downtime avoided — the agreed baseline of unplanned machine-line hours, frozen from a 2019–20 study, minus the hours actually recorded, multiplied by ₹18,000 per hour. Nine groups signed. The arithmetic was attractive and the measurement was never built: avoided hours were settled in quarterly reconciliation meetings between a Gunjan account manager and a mill's maintenance head, from whatever records each brought. A clause allows either party to demand re-measurement of the baseline and the rate from 1 April 2027.

The second, in February 2022: mills objected to shop-floor signals leaving the premises, and Gunjan turned the objection into a promise that all inference would run on the edge box inside the plant. "No signal leaves the shed" went onto the sales deck and into eleven master agreements. It also meant models small enough for a box with no accelerator, and field updates requiring a technician's visit or a shutdown window; in the south, Ayudha Pooja in October and Pongal in January.

3. The industry

Gunjan sells into the Indian spinning, knitwear and home-textile clusters: Coimbatore, Tiruppur and Erode, and Surat, Ichalkaranji, Solapur, Panipat and Guntur beyond. Its customers buy machinery from Lakshmi Machine Works and European suppliers and sell to domestic buyers including Reliance Retail and Myntra as well as export houses. Large integrated players such as Arvind, Welspun, Trident and KPR Mill run engineering teams of their own and are the hardest sales to make, because they can build a version of Jaagran themselves.

At the top of the market, Siemens, ABB, Honeywell and Schneider Electric sell condition monitoring inside a wider automation estate, priced per plant and sold to mills with reliability departments of their own. Gunjan sits below them: cheaper hardware, Tamil and Hindi interfaces, engineers who answer at eleven at night, and very little asked of the mill up front.

Three forces now press on that position. The first is energy: under the Bureau of Energy Efficiency's schemes, and more sharply under European buyers' demands flowing from the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, export-facing mills must produce verified energy figures per kilogram of yarn, and several customers have asked whether Faisla could report them. The second is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: maintenance logs carry operator names, shift timings and disciplinary notes, so the moment Gunjan moves them off the plant to give a model context it is processing personal data under a promise made in 2022.

The third is talent. Coimbatore and Chennai are also where Zoho and Freshworks hire, and a product manager who can credibly claim to have shipped an AI feature can ask either for a Bengaluru salary. Gunjan's exposure is not only Indian: its largest customer by outcome share is the Nusantara Spinning Group in Jakarta, and its fastest-growing line is a North American book of home-textile mills sold out of Austin.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Faisla began in January 2026 as an answer to a complaint: Jaagran raised alarms and mills ignored them. The proposal was to issue advisories instead — a recommendation in the operator's language naming the machine, the suspected fault, a window for acting and the cost of a failure. A supervisor could accept it, creating a work order, or reject it with a reason.

In March 2026 a demonstration ran Faisla over forty curated vibration signatures from past failures. All forty produced the correct recommendation. The project note recorded the belief that the hard part was the model and that it was done. Nobody had built a test set of hard, unlabelled cases; it had not occurred to anyone that writing one was product work rather than data-science work.

In June 2026, with renewals approaching, Vedant bundled Faisla into the subscription at no extra charge: monetisation could wait, adoption could not. Dale Whitcomb, who runs the Americas, argued then for pricing it separately.

The pilot ran from Monday 13 July to Monday 5 October 2026 — twelve weeks exactly — at 24 plants covering 3,600 machines. Exhibit 1 is its outcome. Of 6,480 advisories, supervisors acted on 3,402 and confirmed a fault in 2,106, a precision of 61.90 per cent. They declined 3,078, and in 324 of those the machine failed within thirty days.

On 28 August, Vanmalai Spinning Mills in Tiruppur received 61 advisories in nine days, all pointing at humidification plant. The site engineer assumed a faulty sensor. Niamh Gallagher, the principal data scientist in Dublin, found worse: the model had tied a seasonal ambient-humidity pattern to a failure mode seen three times in training, in the same cluster and month. It was doing what it had been taught.

On 18 September, Niamh ran a stratified check nobody had asked for. Splitting the 3,402 acted-upon advisories by whether the plant kept digital records, she found 1,890 at digitised plants, of which 1,350 were confirmed — 71.43 per cent — and 1,512 at paper-records plants, of which 756 were confirmed, exactly 50.00 per cent. The aggregate 61.90 per cent in Exhibit 1 is the average of two very different products, and at a paper-records plant a confirmation is a supervisor's recollection.

On 20 October, during the Ayudha Pooja shutdown, Marisol's team extracted unplanned-downtime hours from client systems; her compilation became Exhibit 3. On Friday 6 November, Sulekha Rathi, the chief financial officer, circulated it with a note putting ₹6.49 crore of annual outcome share at question for five groups. On Thursday 12 November, Bayu Prasetyo, engineering director at Nusantara in Jakarta, asked for joint re-measurement of baselines before the group's renewal, due on 31 December 2026. On 19 November, Vedant asked for the slide.

5. The people

Vedant Sabnis, founder and chief executive, Coimbatore. Position: Faisla must reach all 152 plants in the Pongal window, because the 2027 renewal conversation begins in February. Incentive: a Series D circling since August, in which the outcome-share line proves Gunjan is paid for results. What he is not saying: he has been told one investor's diligence will test that measurement, and would rather it happened after the round.

Thangaraj Velusamy, co-founder and chief technology officer, Coimbatore. Position: precision is a tuning problem and tuning is engineering work; two quarters and three machine-learning engineers will lift it above 80 per cent, and product managers can return to requirements. Incentive: his team's credibility is at stake in the Vanmalai episode. What he is not saying: he would exclude paper-records plants, removing about half the installed base from the January rollout.

Ipsita Mohapatra, head of the reliability desk and the model platform, Hyderabad. Position: human review is not scaffolding, it is the product; her six reviewers read every advisory before a supervisor sees it. Incentive: her desk is the reason the pilot did not embarrass the company. What she is not saying: at rollout volumes she would need about nineteen reviewers, and she has not told Sulekha, because the number will be read as the cost of failure rather than of care.

Niamh Gallagher, principal data scientist, Dublin, five and a half hours behind Coimbatore. Position: until Gunjan has an evaluation set, every claim about Faisla is an anecdote. She has specified one: 900 historical cases stratified by cluster, machine type, season and record-keeping quality, labelled by a retired mill engineer. Incentive: she will not certify quality against a definition of good she did not write. What she is not saying: she has turned down an offer to lead Faisla, because the role as described is not a data science role.

Marcin Sokolowski, design lead, Warsaw, four and a half hours behind Coimbatore. Position: the advisory is too confident — it names a fault and a deadline with no indication of how sure it is, and supervisors have learned to accept or ignore everything. Incentive: he has asked for a redesign since July. What he is not saying: his design, showing a confidence band and the signals behind the call, would make the 50.00 per cent confirmation rate at paper-records plants visible to the customer.

Marisol Agbayani, director of customer success, Manila, two and a half hours ahead of Coimbatore. Position: she compiled Exhibit 3 and distrusts it — partial logs, windows that do not match the contract quarters, mills that changed machinery mid-year — and wants the rollout delayed until measurement is settled. Incentive: her team absorbs every argument at reconciliation. What she is not saying: two of her five regional managers have been quietly agreeing generous avoided-hour figures to protect relationships.

Dale Whitcomb, head of sales for the Americas, Austin, eleven and a half hours behind Coimbatore. Position: Faisla should be a paid module from January at ₹2,400 per machine per year, and Exhibit 6 shows the appetite. Incentive: his 2027 quota assumes a new module. What he is not saying: his survey went to the mills most likely to say yes.

Sulekha Rathi, chief financial officer, Coimbatore. Position: the outcome-share line must be defensible before anything else, and the cost of Faisla must be known before it is given away. Incentive: she will sign the representations in a Series D data room. What she is not saying: she has modelled outcome share renegotiated downwards across all nine groups from April 2027, and has not circulated it.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"Precision of 61.90 per cent is not a number I would publish, nor one I would panic about. Two quarters and three engineers and it starts with an eight. What I cannot give you is a definition of good, because that is not mine to write."

Thangaraj Velusamy, engineering review, Coimbatore, 9 November 2026

"We keep saying the pilot went well. It produced 324 machines that broke after we told somebody they would. If I were the mill I would not ask about precision. I would ask who is responsible."

Marisol Agbayani, chat thread, 10 November 2026, 06:14 Manila time

"The 900-case set takes a retired mill engineer seven weeks and costs under ₹12 lakh. The reason it does not exist is not money. Nobody owns the question of what a good advisory is, and the answer I get is that we will know it when we see it. We saw forty in March and learned nothing."

Niamh Gallagher, email to Aparna Kotwal, 11 November 2026

"Exhibit 3 is the first honest thing anyone has put in front of me and I do not trust it either. Five groups of nine, the wrong twelve months, two with new machines. What I trust is that we invoice ₹2,250 an hour against a number two people agree to in a room with no instrument in it."

Sulekha Rathi, note circulating Exhibit 3, 6 November 2026

"If Faisla ships in January without a confidence indicator, we are teaching five hundred supervisors to stop reading. A redesign in April will not undo that."

Marcin Sokolowski, design review, Warsaw, 13 November 2026

"Before we renew, we would like to measure the baseline again, together, with meters. We are not disputing that the system helps. We are saying that neither of us knows by how much."

Bayu Prasetyo, Nusantara Spinning Group, Jakarta, 12 November 2026

"Six people read 6,480 advisories in twelve weeks and rewrote or killed a good number. Nobody has asked what we changed or why. That log is the evaluation set you are all looking for."

Ipsita Mohapatra, Hyderabad, 18 November 2026

8. The options as Aparna sees them

She has written three on the back of the face-down printout.

Option A: buy the capability. Two senior product managers from Bengaluru with evaluation and AI-product experience at a fully loaded ₹68 lakh each, one evaluation engineer at ₹32 lakh, and ₹14 lakh of search fees: ₹182 lakh in the first year. Notice periods mean the first lands in February, after the Pongal window. The deeper cost is cultural: the sixteen who will own the roadmap for five years learn that this work belongs to somebody flown in.

Option B: build it in the sixteen. One day a week for twenty-six weeks across sixteen product people is 416 person-days at a loaded ₹11,000, or ₹45.76 lakh; forty days of Niamh's time at ₹26,000 is ₹10.40 lakh; labelling and tooling for the 900-case set is ₹18 lakh. Total ₹74.16 lakh, and a fifth of the organisation's capacity withdrawn from a roadmap already carrying the energy-reporting module. Whether twenty-six Fridays produce judgement or a certificate is not knowable in advance.

Option C: give it to engineering. Thangaraj takes Faisla as a machine-learning deliverable with a precision target, and the reliability desk becomes permanent. Three engineers redirected for two quarters is ₹52 lakh; thirteen additional reviewers at ₹6.4 lakh each is ₹83.2 lakh a year, a total of ₹135.20 lakh — though the review cost already sits inside the ₹264.96 lakh run-rate in Exhibit 4, so the two must not be added. The attraction is that someone would finally own a number; the risk is that the number would be precision, and precision is not what the mill is buying.

Reading them again, Aparna is uneasy about the frame rather than the choices. All three ask who should acquire a skill. None asks whether a share of hours nobody measures survives a system producing 24,000 advisories a month. Ipsita's remark has stayed with her: six reviewers have been making exactly the judgement the product needs, 6,480 times, and nobody has read their log. A fourth possibility is that the skill already exists in the building and the chart points at the wrong room; a fifth, that the 2022 promise, not the skillset, makes Faisla expensive and impossible to evaluate centrally.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Friday 27 November 2026. Nusantara's master agreement, which carries ₹486.00 lakh of outcome share and the largest single subscription book, lapses on 31 December 2026, and Bayu has asked for joint re-measurement before it is renewed. The re-measurement clause in all nine contracts can be invoked from 1 April 2027, leaving one quarter to build a measurement Gunjan can defend or to accept whatever the mills bring. The Pongal shutdown of 14 to 17 January 2027 is the only window before April in which edge models can be updated across the installed base without buying production time.

The board has capped incremental FY2027 operating spend at ₹4 crore pending the Series D, against which the ₹264.96 lakh run-rate for Faisla at full scale is already two-thirds, before any of the three options. The product organisation is sixteen: three joined after 1 July, two are contractors on hardware. Moving maintenance logs to a Mumbai-region service brings operator names and shift records into scope under the DPDP Act, beside eleven master agreements promising the data stays in the shed. And the ₹18,000 per hour is Gunjan's own number: if re-measurement moves it, every line in Exhibit 2 moves with it.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the March 2026 demonstration of forty curated signatures establish, and what did it conceal? Who was responsible for noticing the difference, and what would they have needed to know?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 describe the same customers and disagree. Identify every reason in the footnotes why both might be accurate. Which could Gunjan close by the end of the quarter, and which could it not?
  3. Niamh's split — 71.43 per cent confirmed at plants with digital records, 50.00 per cent at plants without — averages to the 61.90 per cent in Exhibit 1. What would a manager who saw only the average decide differently, and who should be designing the measurement?
  4. Exhibit 4 shows a cost of ₹92.00 per advisory against a budget of ₹34.00, on a volume 50 per cent above assumption. How much of that gap is forecasting failure, how much design choice, and how much the price of the 2022 edge-only promise?
  5. Exhibits 5 and 6 are both incomplete in ways their footnotes admit. If you may commission one further piece of evidence before 27 November, what is it, and what would you refuse to decide without it?
  6. What should Aparna Kotwal do on Monday morning, 23 November, and what will she say to the board on Friday? If the board asks for the one number that proves Faisla is working, what number does she offer, how is it produced, and who is accountable for it?

At half past eleven she turned the third printout over and read the last row again: a mean of 2.89 across eleven of sixteen people, who had rated themselves. Underneath it she wrote two lines. The first was Niamh's: nobody owns the question of what a good advisory is. The second was Bayu's: neither of us knows by how much. The same sentence, she thought, written from two ends of the company — and she could not tell whether the slide Vedant wanted was about hiring, about measurement, or about a promise made in 2021 by people who had not imagined a product making 24,000 claims a month about a machine's future. She switched off the lamp without a third line.

AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management

The AI-Era PM Skillset

What does an AI-era product manager need that a 2019 product manager didn't?

A Tuesday in Bengaluru

On the second Tuesday of March 2026, Meera Iyer sat in a glass-walled meeting room at Drishti Commerce Cloud with a slide deck she did not fully believe in. Drishti sold inventory and pricing software to mid-market retail chains across India — grocery, pharmacy, electronics — and its flagship product told store managers what to reorder each night. Meera, a group product manager with six years at the company, was two weeks from the deadline she had set herself: ship an AI-powered "Smart Reorder" feature before the April renewal cycle, when forty customers worth roughly ₹14 crore in annual recurring revenue would decide whether to keep Drishti or switch to a cheaper rival.

A contracted data science team had built the model over three months. Their final readout reported 81% precision — of every hundred reorder recommendations, eighty-one matched what a skilled store manager would have ordered by hand. In a live demo the week before, the model had impressed two customer advisory-board members by correctly predicting a Diwali sweets surge for a Nashik store. Her VP of Sales wanted it in the release notes for the renewal pitches. Her own instinct said the number sounded fine. But Meera had learned enough in the past year to know that 81% was not a fact about the product — it was a fact about one way of measuring it, and she had not yet asked whether it was the right way.

What Meera lacked was not classic product sense. She knew how to run discovery interviews, sequence a roadmap, and manage a renewal conversation. What she lacked was a newer layer of judgment — the layer this reading page is about — for deciding when a system that is right most of the time, but wrong in ways no one has yet characterised, is safe to hand a decision to.

The Idea: A Second Layer of Judgment

The AI-era PM skillset is the set of capabilities a product manager needs on top of the classical PM toolkit — discovery, prioritisation, roadmapping, stakeholder management — once a product's core behaviour is produced by a model rather than by rules the team wrote and can fully inspect. It is not a replacement for the 2019 skillset; it is layered on it, and it becomes load-bearing precisely where the old skillset runs out of things to say. Five capabilities make up this layer: evaluation literacy, the ability to design and read tests that measure whether a probabilistic system is good enough for a specific decision, not just accurate on average; data-quality judgment, knowing what a model was trained and tested on and therefore where it is likely to fail; responsible-AI judgment, anticipating harm, bias and misuse before launch rather than after a complaint; workflow-redesign fluency, because an AI feature usually changes how work gets done, not merely what button exists; and probabilistic product economics, the discipline of costing and pricing a system whose behaviour and compute cost vary from one call to the next.

No single person invented this layer the way Robert Cooper is credited with stage-gate development. It crystallised between roughly 2023 and 2025, as generative and predictive AI moved from research labs into mainstream product teams faster than product education could keep pace, and it is visible today in how the strongest programmes teach AI product management — Berkeley's SCET, Stanford's BUS311, IIM Calcutta, and Cambridge all converge on evaluation, data quality, responsible AI and workflow redesign as the actual curriculum, deliberately downplaying prompt-writing as a craft skill that matters far less than the judgment around it. The sentence Meera could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: an AI-era PM's job is not to write better prompts; it is to decide, with evidence, when a probabilistic system is trustworthy enough to make someone else's decision for them — and to redesign the work around the cases where it isn't.

How It Actually Works

Applying this judgment is a sequence, and most of its failure modes come from skipping a step silently rather than getting a step wrong. Walked through with Smart Reorder, the sequence looks like this.

Step 1 — Name the decision and its cost of error

Before touching a metric, Meera needed to state precisely what decision the model was making and what each kind of mistake cost. An over-recommendation ties up working capital and shelf space; an under-recommendation causes a stockout and a lost sale, plus, for a repeat offender, a lost customer. These costs are rarely symmetric, and the whole eval effort is calibrated against them.

Step 2 — Build a stratified eval set, not a convenient one

The contractor's 81% came from a random sample of past orders. A random sample over-represents whatever is common — in Drishti's data, fast-selling staples — and under-represents the rare, high-variance SKUs that generate most of the complaints. A defensible eval set is stratified deliberately across the segments where behaviour is expected to differ.

Step 3 — Choose metrics that match the decision, not metrics that are easy to report

Aggregate accuracy answers "how often is it right," which is a data-science question. The product question is "when it is wrong, how much does that cost, and who bears it" — which usually means precision and recall broken out by segment, weighted by that segment's cost of error.

Step 4 — Set a confidence threshold and an escalation path

Every model can, in principle, report how confident it is in each recommendation. The PM's job is to decide the threshold below which a human reviews the recommendation before it reaches a customer, and to make sure that review queue actually exists as a workflow, not just as a checkbox in a design document.

Step 5 — Redesign the workflow around the failure cases

Shipping a model into an unchanged workflow — replacing a trusted number with an untrusted one and calling it done — is usually worse than not shipping. The store manager's screen, the escalation queue, and the override mechanism all need to change together.

Step 6 — Price it and monitor it

Inference has a marginal cost per call, and a model's accuracy drifts as the world it describes changes — a monsoon, a festival calendar shift, a competitor's price war. The PM sets a re-evaluation cadence before launch, not after the first complaint.

A Worked Example

The contractor's 81% figure was real, but it was a blended average across three SKU tiers Meera had not seen separated until she asked for the breakdown. Fast-moving SKUs — items ordered more than three times a week, 2,000 of them in the sample — scored 94% precision, or 1,880 correct recommendations out of 2,000. Slow-moving SKUs — 600 items ordered less than once a week — scored only 58%, or 348 correct out of 600. A third tier of 200 erratic or newly listed SKUs, with too little order history for the model to have learned a reliable pattern, scored 20%, or 40 correct out of 200.

SKU tierSample sizeCorrectPrecision
Fast-moving2,0001,88094%
Slow-moving60034858%
Erratic / new2004020%
Blended2,8002,26881%

The arithmetic behind the headline number is (1,880 + 348 + 40) ÷ 2,800 = 2,268 ÷ 2,800 = 81%. The figure the contractor had led with was correct and also nearly useless on its own, because 71% of the sample — the fast-moving tier — was carrying the entire average while the tail dragged the blended number down without anyone being able to see which customers would feel that tail.

Now change one input: restrict the initial launch to fast-moving SKUs only. Precision on the covered set rises to 94%, but coverage of the catalogue falls to 2,000 of 2,800 SKUs, or 71%. To see whether that trade is worth making, Meera priced the errors. Drishti's finance team estimated an over-recommendation costs roughly ₹800 in tied-up working capital per unit, and an under-recommendation costs roughly ₹2,400 in lost margin and goodwill per unit — a threefold asymmetry, since a stockout on a shelf a customer was actively shopping is far more expensive than excess stock in a backroom. Assuming errors split evenly between the two types, the blended cost per error is (800 + 2,400) ÷ 2 = ₹1,600. Expected cost per SKU-decision is then the error rate multiplied by ₹1,600: for fast-movers, 6% × ₹1,600 = ₹96; for slow-movers, 42% × ₹1,600 = ₹672; for erratic SKUs, 80% × ₹1,600 = ₹1,280. Weighted across the full catalogue, expected cost per SKU is (2,000×96 + 600×672 + 200×1,280) ÷ 2,800 = 851,200 ÷ 2,800 ≈ ₹304. Restricting the launch to fast-movers alone cuts that exposure to ₹96 per SKU — a threefold reduction in expected cost for a 29-point reduction in catalogue coverage. That asymmetry, not the headline 81%, is what actually told Meera how to scope the launch.

Eight Nuances Worth Sitting With

An eval score is not a fact about the product

It is a fact about one sample, one metric, and one moment. The same model can report 81%, 68%, or 94% depending on how the eval set was drawn, and a PM who cannot describe the sampling method is not yet entitled to an opinion about the number.

Aggregate accuracy hides the tail that generates complaints

Customers do not experience an average; they experience the specific recommendation made about the SKU in front of them. Stratification by the segments where cost or behaviour differs is the only way to see where harm concentrates.

This is routinely confused with prompt engineering

Writing a good prompt is a craft skill, useful and quick to learn. The AI-era PM skillset is a judgment skill about when to trust a prompt's output, however well written, and what to do when it is wrong. Teams that invest only in prompt craft ship confidently and fail quietly.

It does not apply with equal weight to every decision

A low-stakes, reversible recommendation — reordering the featured products on a browsing screen — tolerates a light evaluation and fast iteration. A high-stakes, hard-to-reverse decision — auto-placing a purchase order against a customer's working capital — earns the full six-step sequence. Matching the rigor to the stakes is itself a judgment call.

An eval cannot tell you whether a specific customer will trust the system

Precision and recall describe historical correctness; they say nothing about whether a store manager in Nashik will actually act on the recommendation, override it out of habit, or lose trust in the whole platform after one bad Diwali. That requires field research, not a bigger eval set.

It is also confused with the data science skillset itself

A PM does not need to build the eval harness. A PM does need to be able to read it, question its sampling, and own the threshold decision. Delegating the threshold entirely to the data science team is not efficient division of labour — it is abdication of the one judgment call that is the PM's alone.

Four questions worth asking before relying on any of this

What is the cost, in real currency, of a false positive versus a false negative? Who is the human backstop when the model is wrong, and does that role exist in the org chart today? How was the eval set sampled, and does it represent the segments customers actually complain about? And what signal will tell the team the world has shifted since the last evaluation?

Shipping into an unchanged workflow can do more harm than not shipping

If Smart Reorder simply replaced the number a store manager used to trust with a number nobody has taught them to question, Drishti would have converted a known, correctable human error rate into an unknown, silent one.

Consumer, B2B, Marketplace — and Scale

In a consumer product, an individual bad recommendation is cheap and anonymous; users tolerate quirks, and feedback from millions of interactions lets teams iterate their way to a better model faster than any eval harness could. In B2B — Meera's world — every error has a name attached to it, surfaces in a renewal conversation with a real buyer, and is remembered for a year. That is precisely why the cost-of-error arithmetic above was not academic: it was the number Meera would have to defend in the April renewal meetings. In a marketplace, the calculus doubles, because a bad recommendation to a buyer is simultaneously a bad outcome for a seller, and an eval measuring only one side misses half the harm. Scale changes the picture again: an early-stage company usually has too little historical data for a rigorous eval set and must accept more risk because the blast radius of a mistake is small; a large, established company has the data and compliance apparatus for real rigor, but slower reflexes, so the harder problem becomes turning a flawed feature off quickly once it is live.

Common Mistakes

Shipping on the strength of a demo. The symptom is a leadership team that saw three impressive live examples and stopped asking questions. The underlying error is demo bias — a handful of cases were, consciously or not, selected because they worked. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask for the eval set the demo cases were drawn from and check whether it was sampled or curated.

Chasing one aggregate number. The symptom shows up weeks after launch, as complaints cluster suspiciously in one customer segment. The underlying error is measuring accuracy without stratification. The diagnostic is to cut the metric by every segment where behaviour plausibly differs before launch, not after.

Treating an AI feature like an ordinary feature launch. The symptom is a model that quietly degrades for weeks before anyone notices. The underlying error is no monitoring plan and no rollback trigger. The diagnostic question is simple: what specific signal tells us to turn this off, and who is watching for it?

Outsourcing the threshold decision entirely to the vendor or data science team. The symptom is a PM who cannot explain, in plain rupee terms, what an 81% precision figure means for the business. The diagnostic is that exact test: can the PM state the cost of being wrong, out loud, without notes?

What Good Looks Like

Meera restructured the launch rather than delaying or forcing it. Smart Reorder went live for fast-moving SKUs only, covering 71% of catalogue volume at 94% precision and roughly ₹96 of expected cost exposure per SKU-decision. Slow-moving and erratic SKUs kept the existing manual reorder workflow, with the model's output shown as a low-confidence suggestion a store manager could accept or ignore, feeding a review queue that the data science team used to keep improving that tier. The renewal pitch led not with "81% accurate" but with the segmented numbers and the cost logic behind the phased rollout — a harder story to tell in one slide, and a far more defensible one in a follow-up call from a customer's finance team. A quarterly re-evaluation was scheduled before launch, tied to the festival calendar where demand patterns shift fastest.

The Decision, and Two Questions

Meera shipped Smart Reorder on the fast-mover tier alone, deferred the rest, and told her VP of Sales the truth: the headline number was real, but it was the wrong number to lead with. What she needs to learn next is how to design and read evaluation harnesses without depending entirely on the data science team to interpret them for her, and how India's Digital Personal Data Protection framework will shape what customer order history a vendor like Drishti can use to build these eval sets at all. Two questions worth sitting with: when the aggregate metric and the segmented metric disagree, which one should determine the launch decision, and why is that not always the same answer? And if a model can only be evaluated honestly on the segment it already performs well on, is a phased launch genuine risk management, or a way of postponing a harder decision the organisation would rather not make?
