case20v1-aipm.trust.ux:
Disha Goes Live

A decision case on trust and AI user experience at Unnati Claims Exchange

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday 1 October 2026, Ujwala Bapat, chief product officer of Unnati Claims Exchange, sat in a glass-walled meeting room at the company's Pune headquarters with an audit sheet and a calendar. The sheet summarised a six-week pilot of Disha, the company's AI assistant for health-insurance policyholders. The calendar had one date circled twice: Monday 2 November, when enrolment opened for the corporate groups that made up most of Unnati's business.

Sumedh Kalgutkar, the co-founder and chief executive, wanted Disha live for everyone on that date. He had told two insurer clients so. Ujwala had until Monday 5 October to tell him which version of Disha could be ready, because engineering had to start that week. The assistant worked most of the time; the audit sheet showed when it did not.

2. Company background

Unnati Claims Exchange was founded in Pune in 2016 by Sumedh Kalgutkar and two insurance-operations colleagues. It sells a claims and policy-service platform to health insurers and to large employers that run group health cover. Policyholders reach it through white-labelled apps carrying the client's name, not Unnati's. By 2026 the platform served nine insurers and forty corporate groups, covering about 61 lakh lives, with revenue of roughly ₹212 crore.

The market around it is crowded. Consumer platforms such as Policybazaar and Acko had taught customers to expect instant answers, and Plum pitched the same promise to employers. The regulator, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI), expected insurers to treat grievances seriously, with complaints escalating to its Bima Bharosa portal and the insurance ombudsman, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 placed consent obligations on every use of health data.

For Unnati the economics were plain. Each time a policyholder phoned to ask what a policy covered or where a claim stood, a human contact cost the company about ₹95. Disha, built on a large language model and grounded in each client's policy documents, handled the same question for about ₹6. It could also act: intimate a claim or update a nominee, with the change written to the insurer's system.

3. The situation

The pilot ran from Tuesday 18 August to Monday 28 September 2026, with two insurers and three employer groups. Disha answered 1,90,000 questions. The data science team drew a random sample of 12,000 answers and had trained claims reviewers mark each as right or wrong against the policy wording. Disha scored its own confidence on each answer, and the team sorted the sample into three bands (Exhibit 1).

Exhibit 1: Audit of 12,000 pilot answers by confidence band
Confidence bandAnswers auditedShare of sampleWrong answersWrong rate
High (0.85 and above)7,20060%2163.0%
Medium (0.60 to 0.85)3,60030%50414.0%
Low (below 0.60)1,20010%50442.0%
Total / overall rate12,000100%1,22410.2%

Source: Unnati data science team audit, 18 August to 28 September 2026. Wrong rate is wrong answers divided by answers audited in the band. The band mix is assumed to hold at full volume.

Roughly one answer in ten was wrong, but unevenly: high-band answers failed three times in a hundred, while low-band answers failed 42 times in a hundred. The wrong answers were rarely absurd; a typical one quoted a room-rent limit from the base policy when the employer's top-up had changed it.

Disha showed every answer as the same confident paragraph, with no source and no hint of doubt. Femke Brouwer, the data scientist in Amsterdam who built the audit, wrote to Ujwala that the model knew when it was unsure but the interface did not tell the customer. Mariana Seixas, the designer in Lisbon, had built a prototype with three additions: a plain-language confidence label, a citation that opened the exact clause in the policy document, and a clear route to a human agent. A two-week test of the prototype with a small group suggested that a wrong answer shown with a label and a citation cost the company ₹150 in repeat contacts and complaint handling, against ₹400 for a wrong answer shown flat.

4. The people

Sumedh Kalgutkar, chief executive, Pune. He saw a good result: nine answers in ten were right, at under a tenth of the cost per contact. He feared a delay would strain two insurer relationships.

Ishita Warrier, head of machine learning, Bengaluru. She believed the score could support a clean policy, but worried it was calibrated on only five clients and might drift as new policy documents arrived.

Mariana Seixas, product designer, Lisbon. A hedged answer, she argued, is useful only if checkable in one tap, and an action such as filing a claim must be reversible. Working about five hours behind Pune, she held her design reviews at the edge of each day.

Pushkar Anand, head of claims operations, Chennai. His agents would receive every escalation. He supported escalation in principle but asked how many extra contacts his team could absorb in the Diwali-season spike.

5. Exhibits

At the full-rollout volume of 3,00,000 answers a month, the band mix of 60, 30 and 10 per cent gives 1,80,000 high-band, 90,000 medium-band and 30,000 low-band answers, and about 30,600 wrong answers a month if Disha speaks flatly to everyone. Exhibit 2 prices the three courses open to Ujwala; Exhibit 3 shows the time available.

Exhibit 2: Monthly cost at 3,00,000 answers a month (₹ lakh)
CourseHandled by DishaHandled by humansDisha costHuman costWrong-answer costTotal / month
A: Ship as is3,00,000018.00.0122.4140.4
B: Full trust layer2,70,00030,00016.228.540.585.2
C: Confident answers only1,80,0001,20,00010.8114.021.6146.4

Assumptions: Disha costs ₹6 per answer and a human contact ₹95. An answer that is wrong and shown flat costs ₹400; a wrong answer shown with a label and citation costs ₹150. Answers handled by humans are assumed to carry no wrong-answer cost. In B the wrong-answer cost is 5,400 high-band wrong answers at ₹400 (₹21.6 lakh) plus 12,600 medium-band wrong answers at ₹150 (₹18.9 lakh). Handling all 3,00,000 contacts by humans would cost ₹285.0 lakh a month.

Exhibit 3: Pilot and launch timeline, 18 August to 8 November 2026. The pilot ended on 28 September; the trust layer date assumes engineering starts on 5 October and takes three weeks.

Exhibit 3 shows that a three-week build starting 5 October finishes seven days before enrolment opens.

6. The options

Course A: ship as is. Disha goes live to all policyholders on 2 November exactly as piloted. The upside is speed and a large saving against a fully human service: ₹140.4 lakh a month against ₹285.0 lakh. The cost is that roughly 30,600 policyholders a month receive a wrong answer in the same confident voice as the right ones, and 12,600 of those arrive from the low-confidence band, where the system was wrong 42 per cent of the time.

Course B: build a full trust layer first. Engineering spends three weeks, at a one-time cost of ₹62 lakh, adding the confidence label on every answer, a citation to the policy clause, an undo for any action Disha takes, and automatic hand-off to a human with the conversation attached whenever the score falls below 0.60. Monthly cost falls to ₹85.2 lakh, ₹55.2 lakh below course A, so the build repays itself in a little over a month. The cost is 30,000 extra contacts a month for Pushkar Anand's agents.

Course C: confident answers only. Disha answers only the 60 per cent of questions in the high band and sends everything else to a human. It launches on 2 November with little design work, and only 5,400 wrong answers a month reach customers. But the monthly cost of ₹146.4 lakh is slightly above course A's, and the human queue grows by 1,20,000 contacts a month, four times the load of course B. It also discards 90,000 medium-band answers a month, 86 per cent of them correct.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, should a product team think of Disha's quality as a single accuracy figure or as a distribution? What does that make possible?
  2. For each confidence band, what should the customer see and be able to do? Which of label, citation, undo and hand-off matter most for answers, and which for actions?
  3. Using Exhibit 2, what does each course assume about how customers react to a wrong answer? Which assumption is least secure, and how could it be tested before 2 November?
  4. If you were Ujwala, which course would you recommend to Sumedh by 5 October, and what conditions would you attach to it?

8. A note for the learner

Trust UX begins from an admission: the system is sometimes wrong, and the interface should make that manageable, not hide it. Because accuracy varies with confidence, the product can behave differently in each band. A well-reasoned answer compares the courses on the whole cost of wrongness, not model cost or headline accuracy, and separates answers from actions that change a record.

One defensible path is course B, staged. Start the build on 5 October and ship the label, the citation and the low-band hand-off by 26 October, which leaves a week of testing before enrolment opens. Ship the undo for claim intimation and nominee changes in the same release, since they alter the customer's record. Phase the rollout by insurer if Pushkar Anand's team cannot absorb 30,000 extra contacts at once. The reasoning: B has the lowest monthly cost, ₹85.2 lakh against ₹140.4 lakh and ₹146.4 lakh, and keeps most of Disha's value while protecting policyholders where it is least reliable. Attach one condition: re-audit a fresh sample every month and widen the high band only if its wrong rate holds near 3 per cent. The case against A is that customers cannot see the errors; the case against C is that it refuses to use a system that is right most of the time.
case40v1-aipm.trust.ux:
What Ustaad Does Not Say

Wachan Field Works and the question of what a technician should be told about a machine that is sometimes wrong

1. Thursday night, 15 October 2026

The lights in the Wachan Field Works office on Avinashi Road in Coimbatore had been switched to the night circuit, leaving Nandita Ravishankar's corner of the fourth floor lit by two tubes and a monitor. It was a quarter past ten. On the monitor were four tabs she had been moving between for three hours: an engineering review of 2,400 job cards, a telemetry dashboard for September, a finance sheet her chief financial officer had sent that evening with the subject line Ustaad contribution, please read before Monday, and a memo from her largest customer's service director that used the phrase advisory accuracy four times.

On Monday 19 October, four days away, the product council would meet and Nandita, as chief product officer, would say what happened next to Ustaad, the artificial-intelligence assistant Wachan had put inside its technician app in March. On Friday 6 November she would say the same thing to the board, in fewer words and with a number attached.

What made the night long was not that Ustaad was failing. On most jobs it worked. A technician in front of a rooftop condensing unit in Hosur could type four words of symptom and a model number and get back a probable cause, a sequence of checks, a part number and a drafted service report. Supervisors said their junior technicians now closed jobs they would once have escalated. The trouble was that Ustaad said everything in the same tone of voice, whether it was reading a manual it had indexed last week or guessing at a unit it had never seen. Nandita had three proposals for changing that: the cheapest was the only one her engineering head thought could be built in time, and the most complete cost more than the budget left for the year.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2019

Wachan Field Works was founded in Coimbatore in 2014 by Giridhar Alagappan and a classmate from the pump industry, on the observation that India's after-sales service networks ran on paper job cards and WhatsApp. Its software — the Wachan Service Suite — issued job cards, tracked van stock, held annual maintenance contracts and measured service-level agreements for companies repairing air conditioning, refrigeration, elevators and generating sets. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it earned ₹268 crore from 340 customers, with about 1,42,000 technicians carrying the app and roughly 1.6 crore job cards closed on the platform.

One decision from 2019 shaped everything Nandita could now do. To win the service arm of a large cooling manufacturer, Wachan had committed to an offline-first app: a technician in a basement plant room or a lift shaft had to be able to open a job card, record readings, photograph a nameplate and close the job with no network, syncing later. The architecture that delivered this cached a compressed slice of asset history on the handset; it had never been designed to carry a document index, and Ustaad's retrieval, scoring and citation all ran server-side. In September 2026, of 14,50,000 job cards closed by Ustaad-enabled customers, 9,00,000 — 62 per cent — had an Ustaad session attached. The other 5,50,000, 38 per cent, did not, and the mobile team believed four in five of those — about 4,40,000 jobs, or 30 per cent of all cards — were done with no signal at all. Whatever trust mechanism Nandita chose would be invisible on those.

A second decision, taken in November 2025 before anyone knew what inference would cost, priced Ustaad as a flat add-on of ₹240 per technician per month, unlimited use, billed annually. Caleb Ostrander's team had sold it hard on that simplicity.

3. The industry

Indian after-sales service is a crowded, low-margin trade pressed between manufacturers and building owners. Room air-conditioner volumes had grown through a run of hot summers, and the service networks behind Voltas, Blue Star, Daikin and Carrier competed for the same shortage of trained technicians, as did the elevator majors Otis, Schindler and Kone and the process-cooling businesses of Cummins India and Thermax. Service-management software from Zoho, Freshworks, Ramco Systems and Facilio circled the same buyers, and Urban Company had taught households to expect a rating and an arrival window.

Regulation touched the work at three points. Refrigerant handling fell under India's commitments on ozone-depleting substances, administered through the Ozone Cell and the Central Pollution Control Board, and the move from R-410A to R-32 units meant a top-up instruction read off the wrong variant of a manual was a safety matter, not a clerical one. State lift and escalator legislation required a licensed mechanic for adjustments to brakes and door operators. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 bore on every site photograph Ustaad sent to a model, and on how long a cited manual snippet could be kept against a job card.

Wachan's exposure ran beyond India. Four customers held service contracts in West Asia and East Africa, eleven per cent of revenue came from customers headquartered outside India, and the product, design and data teams sat in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Warsaw, Tokyo, Austin and Manila — so a decision taken in Coimbatore on a Monday morning was argued over for the previous eighteen hours in three other working days.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Ustaad went to six pilot customers on Monday 16 March 2026. On Friday 24 April, Sharath Kodial's team in Hyderabad delivered a review of 600 pilot job cards in which senior engineers had marked each recommendation right or wrong: 37 were wrong, 6.2 per cent. The number travelled — into the general-availability note of Monday 4 May, seven weeks after the pilot opened, and into Caleb's deck as 94% accurate.

What nobody wrote down was that the pilot had run on split and ducted air-conditioning work at four customers, and that elevator jobs and parts identification were excluded because those manuals were not yet indexed. By July both were switched on.

On Wednesday 1 July the platform team moved Ustaad to a larger model with a longer context window. It handled multi-page manuals better and raised the cost of a session from ₹7.00 to ₹9.00, and then to ₹11.00 in August when retrieval was made to re-read the service bulletins on every query. Nobody updated the planning sheet the option costings were built on.

On Monday 24 August, at a cold-storage site in Jalandhar run by Himaank Coldchain Services, Ustaad answered a question about a refrigerant top-up by quoting the manual for a superseded variant of the condensing unit. The technician, eleven years in the trade, did not follow it; he photographed the screen and sent it to his supervisor. Himaank's safety officer filed a note asking why the assistant had not shown which document it was reading from.

Sixteen days later, on Wednesday 9 September, Shikhar Climate Systems — an original-equipment manufacturer whose warranty work flows through three Wachan customers — placed under review the 58,000 claims auto-filed through Ustaad in the quarter, worth about ₹36.54 crore, on the grounds that a claim generated from an assistant's inference without a photograph of the failed part did not meet its documentation standard. In September Ustaad had auto-filed 23,000 claims and Shikhar had rejected 1,260 of them, 5.5 per cent.

On Wednesday 30 September, Sharath's team delivered the quarterly review in Nandita's first tab. It covered 2,400 job cards from the 92 days of 1 July to 30 September, and it did not say 6.2 per cent.

5. The people

Nandita Ravishankar, chief product officer, Coimbatore. Three years at Wachan after a decade in industrial software. Her position is that this is not a quality problem but an interface problem: the system knows more about its own uncertainty than it tells anyone. Her incentive is a commitment she made in May that Ustaad would reach 60,000 seats by March 2027. What she is not saying is that she approved the 94% accurate line in Caleb's deck without asking what the sample covered.

Giridhar Alagappan, co-founder and chief executive, Coimbatore. He believes Wachan sells to businesses that live on first-time-fix rates, and that a visibly cautious assistant will be read as a weak one. His incentive is a Series C conversation in which Ustaad is the growth story. What he is not saying is that two of three investors who saw the deck asked how error costs were tracked, and that he answered in general terms.

Rituparna Das, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru. She has 14 engineers for the trust work and no more. Her position is that labels and citations are a fortnight each, and that undo for a filed warranty claim is the real work, because it must reverse a record in a customer's enterprise system. What she is not saying is that she thinks the offline-first commitment of 2019 is the actual constraint, and that nobody has priced its removal.

Sharath Kodial, head of applied machine learning, Hyderabad. He produced both reviews and is the only person who has read every wrong recommendation in them. He argues the confidence score is good enough to route on; his incentive is that routing is a change he controls and a redesign is not. What he is not saying is that the score was fitted on the same four customers the April pilot covered.

Haruna Ishizaki, senior data scientist, Tokyo. She joined in June from a reliability team and has been cutting the telemetry by job family. Her position is that one confidence threshold across all asset types is indefensible. Her incentive is methodological credibility in a company that has never had a measurement fight. What she is not saying is that her elevator finding rests on 90-day reopen windows she has not reconciled with the dashboard everyone else reads.

Zofia Kaminska, principal product designer, Warsaw. She has prototyped the trust layer — internally, Pehra — as four elements: a plain-language confidence line, a citation that opens the exact manual page, an undo on anything Ustaad writes to another system, and a one-tap route to a senior engineer. An answer a technician cannot check in one tap, on a ladder, is not hedged but unusable. What she is not saying is that the prototype has been tested with eleven technicians, all of whom read English manuals.

Imee Salonga, director of customer success, Manila. She holds the renewals and hears the complaints. Her position is that customers are not asking for better accuracy; they are asking to be told when to distrust the thing. Her incentive is retention against a window that opens on 1 December. What she is not saying is that one customer has already begun quietly withholding the Ustaad line item while it finishes its own review.

Padmini Iyengar, chief financial officer, Coimbatore. Her sheet is the third tab. Her position is that Ustaad is sold as a flat seat fee against a cost that scales with use, and that the margin is held up only by the customers not using it. What she is not saying is that she has not decided whether to show the board the contribution line at all.

8. The options as Nandita sees them

Course A: build Pehra in full. Fourteen engineers for eleven weeks from 19 October, landing on 4 January 2027, at a one-time ₹286 lakh: the confidence line, the citation, undo on every action Ustaad writes into another system, and hand-off below 0.55. On the planning sheet the monthly total falls from ₹859.24 lakh to ₹585.17 lakh; at the real unit cost, from ₹895.24 lakh to ₹621.17 lakh. It lands 34 days after the renewal window opens and 27 days before it closes, and it does nothing on the 30 per cent of job cards done with no network.

Course B: withdraw the two worst families. Switch Ustaad off for elevator and escalator work and for parts identification, ship by 23 November for ₹46 lakh, and keep the assistant where it is strongest. It is the cheapest line on Exhibit 5 at ₹543.15 lakh, or ₹570.15 lakh corrected. It also removes the assistant from the family where Bharat Kotecha has a contractual claim and a licensing exposure — and from 11,000 seats Wachan bills him for.

Course C: keep Ustaad as it is and staff around it. Four regional escalation desks, 48 senior engineers at ₹46.08 lakh a month, and a repricing at renewal from ₹240 to ₹390 per technician per month, lifting billed revenue on 48,000 seats from ₹115.20 lakh to ₹187.20 lakh, ₹72.00 lakh more a month. No engineering at all. It is the most expensive course on the sheet at ₹785.88 lakh, or ₹821.88 lakh corrected, and asks customers to pay 63 per cent more for a product their own reviews are questioning.

Rituparna had written in the margin twice. Against Course A: the undo is 6 of the 11 weeks; ship the citation alone in 3 and we are live before December. At the bottom: nobody has costed turning the actions off. Ustaad reserved parts and filed warranty claims because that was what made supervisors notice it in May. Nothing in Exhibit 5 priced an advisory-only assistant that recommended and wrote nothing — which would make the undo unnecessary, the claims dispute moot, and the three courses on the page a different three.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The discretionary product budget for the second half of the year is ₹340 lakh, of which ₹190 lakh is committed to the consent-ledger work the board promised to complete by 31 March 2027 under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and cannot slip. That leaves ₹150 lakh. Course A at ₹286 lakh needs a further ₹136 lakh, which only the board on 6 November can release.

There are 14 engineers and no more. Rituparna has told Nandita plainly that the offline-sync rewrite that would put citations on the 30 per cent of jobs done without a network needs nine people who do not exist, and a quarter nobody has.

Contracts covering 29,000 of the 48,000 contracted seats, just over 60 per cent, come up for renewal between 1 December 2026 and 31 January 2027. Two of them — Stambh Elevator Services at 11,000 seats and Himaank Coldchain Services at 4,200 — carry a clause permitting the customer to withhold the Ustaad fee if advisory accuracy, measured by the customer's own review, falls below 90 per cent. Together those 15,200 seats bill ₹36.48 lakh a month. Caleb's FY2027 pipeline holds a further 26,000 seats, an annualised ₹7.49 crore, in deals whose security reviews now ask how the assistant's errors are disclosed.

The Shikhar letter carries no reply deadline, which Imee reads as the worst kind.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 reports 14.3 per cent and Exhibit 2 reports 7.9 per cent. What is each measuring, which population does each exclude, and which should Nandita put in front of the board on 6 November?
  2. Exhibit 3 is positive and Exhibit 4 is large. Whose money is in each, and what does that difference imply about which number will move first?
  3. Exhibit 5 understates every course. Having corrected the unit cost, what else in it would you refuse to rely on, and what would you want measured instead?
  4. Sharath wants to route on the confidence score; Haruna says it is not calibrated by job family. What would settle that in four days, and what would you do meanwhile?
  5. Ustaad both answers and acts. Should both be governed by one mechanism, and what changes about Courses A, B and C if the acting powers are withdrawn rather than wrapped in an undo?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What does Nandita do, in what order, with ₹150 lakh and 14 engineers — and what does she tell the board on 6 November about the 38 per cent of job cards that record no Ustaad session at all?

11. A quarter past eleven

Nandita closed the finance tab and left the other three open. Zofia's prototype still ran in a fifth window: a confidence line, and under it a grey link reading from the installation manual, page 41. She tapped it. The page opened in a tenth of a second, and she thought, as she had the first time, that it was obviously right and obviously not enough — that the eleven technicians who tapped it were the eleven who could read page 41, that the reopen numbers would not tell her within a quarter whether any of this worked, and that in Punjab a man with eleven years in the trade had photographed a screen instead of believing it, which was the behaviour she was trying to design for and also the behaviour she was proposing to spend ₹286 lakh to make unnecessary.

On her notepad were three words and a question mark: label, citation, undo? — and below them, in different ink, the thing she had said to nobody, which was that she did not know whether she was deciding what Ustaad should show a technician, or whether Ustaad should be allowed to do anything at all.
exp40v2-aipm.trust.ux:
AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management · Exp40

Trust and AI UX Patterns

Confidence, citations, undo and escalation are not decorations on a model. They are the mechanism by which a product decides, case by case, how much of its own fallibility to pass on to the person in front of it — and at what price.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On 11 March 2026, Dr. Ritwika Sen, Chief Product Officer of Nabz Diagnostics Systems in Bengaluru, sat with a one-page incident note from a district hospital in Nanded. Nabz's chest-radiograph triage engine reads roughly 31,000 films a day across 140 sites, forty-six of them district hospitals in a state lung-health screening programme. Since November the product has run an "auto-normal" mode: films scored above a threshold are reported normal and never reach a radiologist, because the districts in question have one radiologist for every four lakh people and the alternative is not a careful human read but a fourteen-day queue. Auto-normal covers 46% of films. In the Nanded case it had reported normal a film with a small apical pneumothorax; the patient returned eight days later. Nothing had malfunctioned; the model did precisely what its threshold permitted. Nabz's licence under the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's device rules came up for renewal on 30 April, and the state's technical committee had asked a question harder than it looked: what threshold is defensible, and who decided it?

Six weeks earlier and 1,000 kilometres away, Kabir Anand, Head of Product at Amanat Money in Mumbai, had opened a different file. Amanat is a consumer personal-finance app with 4.2 million monthly users; its assistant answers about 2.6 lakh tax, portfolio and insurance questions a week. An audit of 900 sampled answers had found 7.4% materially wrong — a wrong capital-gains holding period, a confused old-versus-new regime deduction, a fund category mixed up. The same cohort rated the assistant 4.5 out of 5. That gap, not the 7.4%, was the finding: users failed to notice errors not from carelessness but because nothing in the interface varied between a right answer and a wrong one. Kabir's team now wanted the assistant to act — change a systematic investment plan, rebalance, push capital-gains data into a tax filing. The go/no-go was 20 April.

Ritwika's problem is a threshold on a regulated diagnostic; Kabir's is a permission on a consumer agent. They are the same problem: how much of a known, measured error rate the interface absorbs, how much it surfaces, and how much it simply hands to the user.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Trust UX patterns are the interface and control-flow choices that determine how a user's reliance on a fallible system tracks that system's actual, case-by-case reliability. The operative word is tracks. The canonical formulation is John Lee and Katrina See's 2004 Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance: the target is neither maximal nor minimal trust but calibrated trust, and the two failure states are misuse (relying on automation that is failing) and disuse (ignoring automation that works). The lineage runs back to Thomas Sheridan and William Verplank's 1978 ten-level taxonomy of automation, and to Lisanne Bainbridge's 1983 Ironies of Automation: automating the easy cases leaves the human a residual harder than the original job while removing the practice that made them good at it. Raja Parasuraman and colleagues added automation bias — errors of commission (following a wrong flag) and omission (missing what was not flagged) track how reliable a system is believed to be, not how reliable it is.

The problem, in the form product managers now meet it, is that fluency and correctness became statistically independent: a conventional system fails loudly, a generative one fails in the same typeface it succeeds in. Trust UX reintroduces the signal fluency erased. But "reintroduce a signal" is where consensus ends, and a PM who cannot state the disagreements will referee an argument they do not understand.

Five positions are held by serious people. The calibration school is decision-theoretic: produce a well-calibrated probability, display it honestly, and users will integrate it. It signs "a calibrated probability, well displayed, improves joint human–machine decisions," and will not sign "any uncertainty display beats none," because badly calibrated numbers demonstrably worsen reliance. The cognitive-forcing school, after Zana Buçinca and Krzysztof Gajos's 2021 work, holds that passive displays fail because people process them with fast, automatic cognition; only interrupting friction — withholding the model's answer until the human commits to their own — produces calibrated reliance. It signs "interruption is the active ingredient," will not sign "explanations improve reliance," and accepts that its remedy costs throughput. The reliability-first school treats trust affordances as compensating controls for an under-engineered model: below a certain accuracy do not ship, above it do not clutter. It signs "most trust UX is a tax that hides an evaluation failure," and will not sign that a badge substitutes for precision. The contestability school — Deirdre Mulligan and the accountable-algorithms literature — reframes the goal as recourse rather than psychology: can an affected person find out why, object, and get it changed. It signs "a consequential system that cannot be contested should not be deployed however accurate it is," and refuses that calibration discharges the obligation. The allocation school, descended from Sheridan and Bainbridge, argues the level of automation is the real lever and the widget is downstream. It signs "changing the level of automation dominates any display change," and will not sign that an interface pattern bolted onto an unchanged allocation accomplishes much.

Ritwika's technical committee is, without using the words, contestability school; Kabir's growth team is reliability-first. Neither is wrong.

3. Mechanics: what the numbers actually look like

Expert practice begins before any pixel, with whether the model's confidence means anything. A score is calibrated if, across cases scored 0.90, about 90% resolve as predicted. Modern networks are systematically overconfident out of the box — Chuan Guo and colleagues showed this in 2017 and gave the field temperature scaling as the cheapest post-hoc fix. The measurement is a reliability diagram: bucket predictions by stated confidence, plot empirical accuracy against it, read the gap. Nabz's data-science lead ran this over 30,000 auto-normal-eligible films.

Expected calibration error is the film-weighted average of absolute gaps: (1,180×0.056 + 1,940×0.017 + 3,420×0.018 + 6,860×0.049 + 7,410×0.038 + 9,190×0.023) ÷ 30,000 = 0.033. An ECE of 3.3 points would pass most internal reviews. It is also the number that concealed Nanded. Split by acquisition source, the 9,190 films at a mean stated 0.971 resolved at 0.961 on fixed-plate installations in metro hospitals and at 0.906 on the portable units the district programme actually uses — 6.5 points of overconfidence on exactly the subpopulation carrying the clinical risk. Calibration is a marginal statistic; a patient is a conditional one. Experts calibrate per slice — per device, site, language, segment — and report the worst slice, not the average.

Figure 1. The same model, two populations. The aggregate curve sits close enough to the diagonal to pass review; the portable-unit curve, where the screening programme actually runs, is overconfident in exactly the band used for auto-reporting.

With a trustworthy score, the second mechanic is the threshold, and here most teams commit a unit error: a threshold is expressed in probability, but the decision it encodes is expressed in money. The correct form is an expected-cost comparison. Let creview be the marginal cost of a human read (Nabz pays a panel radiologist about ₹38 a film), cmiss the expected cost of a missed actionable finding (Nabz's actuary and clinical lead settled on ₹1.4 lakh, blending remediation, programme liability and a quality-adjusted harm estimate), and k the probability a human reviewer actually catches what the model missed (0.85 on measured double-reads). Automating is cheaper when the residual probability of an actionable finding satisfies p × cmiss × k < creview, i.e. p < 38 ÷ (1,40,000 × 0.85) = 0.00032 — three in ten thousand. Stated that way, "we auto-report at 95% confidence" is roughly 150 times more permissive than the economics support.

Three things repay study. First, the shipped policy is suboptimal but not scandalous: about ₹74,000 a day worse than the best row, roughly ₹2.7 crore a year. Second, full manual review is worse than moderate automation, because radiologists working a fourteen-day backlog miss things too; the honest comparison is never against a perfect human. Third, the curve between 0.97 and 0.99 is flat — ₹10.66 lakh against ₹10.73 lakh, less than the error bars on ₹1.4 lakh. Inside a flat basin the threshold should be chosen on grounds the cost model cannot see: drift headroom and defensibility. Optimising to the second decimal there is arithmetic, not judgement.

Figure 2. Cost against coverage is U-shaped with a wide floor. The competent practitioner finds the minimum; the expert notices it is not a point, and asks what should decide the rest.

The second-order effect the table cannot contain is Bainbridge's. As coverage rises, the cases reaching the human are the residual — systematically harder, arriving in a stream that is now mostly confirmations. Nabz measured it: reviewer catch rate k fell from 0.86 at 22% coverage to 0.79 at 46% and 0.71 at 58%. That is the arithmetic of vigilance, documented since Norman Mackworth's radar studies in 1948. Feeding measured k back through the model adds about 2.3 missed findings a day at 58% coverage, steepening the curve's right arm and pushing the optimum toward caution. Any model treating human review as a fixed-efficiency backstop overstates its own safety, and the overstatement grows precisely as the product succeeds.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, each testable. (a) The error must be consequential and attributable. If a wrong output causes no traceable loss, calibration display is overhead. Nabz passes emphatically; Amanat passes for execution actions and only weakly for general informational answers. (b) The user must have a cheaper verification path than the system's own. If checking costs more than the error, the pattern is theatre. A radiologist verifying a Nabz flag against the film is cheap; an Amanat user verifying a capital-gains computation against Section 112A is not, which is why Amanat's escalation target must be a document or an adviser, not the user's own judgement. (c) Reliance must be adjustable. Where the user cannot decline — a screening programme with no second reader — a confidence display informs nobody who can act, and the work belongs in allocation, not display. (d) Confidence must be measurable at the level at which it is shown. Per-answer confidence in a multi-claim paragraph is often not measurable at all: the paragraph is right in four clauses and wrong in the fifth, and one badge on it is a category error.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When error is structural rather than stochastic — a stale field, a retrieval index missing a document class — patterns manage consequences while the root cause continues, and teams mistake an escape hatch for a fix. When displayed uncertainty becomes a liability shield: the tell is legal asking for a stronger disclaimer rather than a lower threshold. And when the population is adversarial: an insurance-claims assistant that escalates above ₹50,000 will see a great many claims for ₹49,500.

5. Hard edges: seams, regulators and things that cannot be undone

Three edges repay working through. Hardware and physical action. Aaftab Grid Analytics sells fault prediction into 220 kV distribution feeders; an automated trip cannot be undone, and a false trip means a town without power. Aaftab's answer is the most transferable pattern in this literature: place reversible actions in front of irreversible ones and raise the evidentiary bar at each step. Alarm at p ≥ 0.35, automatic derate at p ≥ 0.62, auto-trip only at p ≥ 0.93 and corroboration from an independent sensor channel. False trips fell from 11 a month to 2 while detection of genuine faults held at 88%. Undo, where it cannot exist downstream, is manufactured upstream as a staircase.

Two-sided markets. Manzil Freight Exchange suggests lane prices to shippers and truckers, and showed the confidence band to shippers only; disputed loads ran at 4.9%. When Manzil exposed the same band and its basis to truckers, disputes fell to 2.8% and acceptance of the suggested price fell from 71% to 58%, because truckers who could see the band was wide negotiated upward. Transparency did not create value; it moved surplus, and the take rate moved with it. In two-sided products a trust pattern is a pricing decision wearing an interface costume, and the PM who does not model the surplus transfer is surprised the quarter after launch.

Regulated products and the organisational seam. Nabz's threshold is at once a clinical-safety parameter under CDSCO device rules, a contractual service level with the state health department, a cost line and a config value in a YAML file — which in practice means nobody owns it. The seam shows up in incident reviews: Nanded was filed as a "model performance issue" and routed to data science, so the UX debt — that a report reaching a clinician carried no indication of which device produced it, and thus no way to discount it — was never logged where it would be fixed. Mature companies say they run a trust-review gate before threshold changes. What the better ones actually run is a threshold changelog with a named owner, a per-slice calibration refresh on every model update, and an escalation queue whose approval rate is monitored: above roughly 95% approval the queue is a rubber stamp and the safety story is fictional. That last metric is the cheapest honest instrument in the field and is almost never on the dashboard.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert

Calibration is conditional, not marginal. The tell is a single ECE figure on a model card. An expert asks for the worst slice and its sample size, because the aggregate is dominated by the easy population. "3.3 points, we're calibrated" is wrong because the user is never sampled from the aggregate; they are sampled from one slice, and the highest-stakes slice usually has the least data.

Displayed confidence changes verification non-monotonically. The tell is a verification-rate curve that is a cliff, not a slope: users check at 0.7, check a little less at 0.85, and essentially stop above 0.9. The naive reading is that the display works. It works too well at the top: a 0.93 that is really 0.88 now has no human check at all, so the display converted a moderate error rate into an undetected one.

The reviewed population is not the deployed population. The tell is reviewer accuracy declining while model accuracy improves — which looks like a training problem and is Bainbridge's residual plus vigilance decrement. "Our reviewers are sloppy" leads to monitoring reviewers; the correct reading leads to injecting known-answer cases into the queue and rotating people off high-automation streams.

A citation is a credibility cue before it is evidence. The tell is citation click-through under 2% coexisting with rising trust scores. A source changes perceived reliability whether or not anyone opens it, so provenance can reduce checking while appearing to enable it. The fix is not more citations but cheaper verification — source text inline, differences highlighted — so checking costs a glance, not a click.

Undo is a race between two distributions, not a button. The tell is undo usage concentrated in the first five seconds after an action. That is the distribution of typos, not of errors; real errors surface minutes or days later, when the counterparty responds. An undo window protects only where it exceeds time-to-detect for the errors that matter; the honest metric is the share of confirmed errors still reversible when discovered.

Reversibility is a property of the downstream system, not of your design. The tell is an interface offering "cancel" uniformly. A mutual-fund order Amanat places at 11 a.m. can be cancelled before the 3 p.m. NAV cut-off; the same order at 4 p.m. cannot be cancelled at all. The button was identical; the reversibility was not. A product that acts in the world inherits somebody else's clock, and the interface must show that clock rather than its own aspirations.

Escalation rate moves for reasons unrelated to difficulty. The tell is escalation rate correlating more strongly with hour of day, queue depth or shift handover than with any measure of case complexity. The obvious reading is that case mix varies. The mechanism is incentive: reviewers measured on throughput escalate less when the queue is long — exactly when the system is under stress and escalation matters most.

Hedging language is generated, not measured. The tell is that hedge frequency in model output is uncorrelated with accuracy. "I think" and "you may want to verify" are tokens produced because they were probable, not because an internal uncertainty estimate crossed a threshold. Teams treat verbal hedging as a trust pattern; unless it is wired to a measured score it misleads more reliably than a bare assertion, because it manufactures the appearance of calibration.

Trust loss and trust recovery are asymmetric and differently shaped. The tell, after a visible incident, is that usage counts recover within weeks while delegation depth does not — people keep asking the assistant and stop accepting its answers without checking. An engagement dashboard calls the incident closed; the metric that has not recovered is the one that carried the value. Experts instrument acceptance-without-edit, not sessions.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the individual stake is small and the aggregate stake is regulatory and reputational; the user will not read a calibration explanation, so the load falls on defaults and abstention. In B2B and enterprise the person best placed to catch an error rarely bears it, so escalation design and audit trail carry the weight, and the buyer's security review is the forcing function. In platforms and marketplaces the pattern is a surplus-allocation decision, as Manzil found. In hardware the constraint is irreversibility, answered with staged actions and independent corroboration. In AI-native products there is no non-AI fallback to escalate into: the escalation target must be built and staffed, and its capacity, not the model, binds how conservative the product can afford to be.

Where the difference is not real: the obligation to measure per-slice calibration, to know the rupee cost of an error, and to instrument acceptance-without-edit is identical everywhere, and claims that a domain is too fast-moving or too qualitative for this are almost always claims about budget. By stage, an early company should build one instrumented reversal path and one honest calibration measurement and skip the rest; a scaling company should establish threshold ownership before it has forty thresholds; a large company's characteristic failure is not absence but drift — patterns on paper, thresholds nobody has re-derived in two years, and a queue quietly approving 97% of what reaches it.

8. Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Nabz, and the cost-derived threshold. Ritwika's team raised auto-normal but not globally: they split the threshold by acquisition device, holding portable units at 0.985 and fixed plates at 0.97, on the per-slice curves rather than the aggregate. Coverage fell from 46% to 33%, daily read cost rose ₹1.6 lakh, expected missed findings fell from 3.6 to 1.9, and modelled cost fell about ₹40,000 a day. The committee was persuaded less by the arithmetic than by one artefact: a signed changelog showing who set the threshold, on what evidence, and when it would next be re-derived.

Daleel Legal Cloud, and the citation that hurt. Daleel, a Gurugram contract-review product, shipped inline clause citations in February 2026 expecting verification to rise. Across 1,180 reviewers, clause-level verification fell from 34% to 11%, self-reported trust rose from 4.1 to 4.6, and escaped material errors rose from 3.1 to 7.4 per thousand clauses — a 2.4× deterioration from a feature built to improve safety. The mechanism was the credibility-cue effect: the pin meant "grounded," and the reviewer stopped reading. Recovery took four months and three changes — clause text rendered inline rather than behind a link; a mismatch detector flagging where a summary's dates and amounts did not appear in the cited clause, catching 63% of escapes mechanically; and 5% of contracts served in cognitive-forcing mode, the summary withheld until the reviewer recorded their own reading. By June verification was 29%, escaped errors 2.2 per thousand — better than before citations existed — and time per contract 8% higher. The recovery was paid for in speed, which is the honest price of the friction school's remedy.

Amanat, and the window that was not theirs. Kabir's team estimated 6% of questions would convert to actions — about 15,600 a week — at a 2.1% error rate after retrieval improvements, giving 328 wrong actions weekly. Of those, 41% fall outside a cancellable window because of fund cut-off timing, leaving 134 irreversible errors a week at roughly ₹2,100 remediation plus goodwill: about ₹1.5 crore a year. Restricting execution to cancellable hours removes that liability and 41% of the feature's usage with it.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Five recur across every product type. Each has a cheap early indicator, and each becomes expensive in a characteristic way if the indicator is ignored.

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Calibration drift after a model or prompt changeConfidence distribution shifts while accuracy reports go stale"When was calibration last re-measured, on which slices?"Thresholds silently turn 5–10 points more permissive; surfaces as an incident, not a metric
Escalation queue as rubber stampApproval rate above ~95%; review time per case falling"What share of escalated cases were overturned last month?"The audited safety control is fictional; found in a regulatory review
Provenance as credibility cueCitation click-through under 2% with rising trust scores"Does verification rise or fall when we add sources?"A safety feature raised escape rate; costs a redesign and a speed regression
Undo shorter than time-to-detectUndo usage clustered in the first seconds"What share of confirmed errors were still reversible when found?"Every tail error becomes a remediation case with a refund or legal cost
Threshold with no ownerNobody can say who last changed it, or why"Show me the changelog and the rupee cost of one error."Post-incident, no reasoned basis for the company's own policy can be shown

The pattern across all five is that the early warning is a second-order metric — a rate of change, or a ratio between two quantities — while the dashboards teams build track first-order volumes. That is why these failures are caught late so reliably: the instruments point at the wrong order of derivative.

10. Where competent people genuinely disagree

Whether numeric confidence should be shown at all. The affirmative case rests on work such as Yunfeng Zhang, Q. Vera Liao and Rachel Bellamy's 2020 experiments, where displayed confidence improved reliance while feature-based explanations did not. The negative case rests on the cliff effect: a number good enough to display is good enough to be over-trusted, and the display that helps at 0.7 harms at 0.95. It would be falsified if verification declined smoothly rather than discontinuously with displayed confidence; the evidence is mixed across domains and nobody should claim it settled.

Whether human–AI complementarity is achievable. Gagan Bansal and colleagues showed in 2021 that human–AI teams frequently fail to beat the better of the two alone, because explanations increase acceptance of correct and incorrect outputs alike. The optimistic reply is that those studies used generic explanations and untrained participants, and that domain experts with a real stake behave differently. What would settle it is field evidence from trained reviewers with skin in the game; there is little, and both camps extrapolate.

Whether abstention is honest or corrosive. One school treats "I don't know" as the strongest trust pattern available. The other observes that abstention teaches users to go elsewhere, and the substitute is usually less safe — a user who gets "I can't advise on this" from Amanat asks a message group instead. Both are right about what they measured; they disagree about which counterfactual counts.

Whether contestability is separable. The contestability school holds that recourse is owed independent of accuracy — a position with regulatory backing in the EU AI Act's human-oversight provisions and, in India, in the grievance-redressal machinery of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the Reserve Bank's digital-lending guidance. The counter-position is that recourse without capacity is worse than none: a contest channel answering in six weeks converts a design failure into a false promise. The disagreement is empirically tractable, and almost nobody publishes the data.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks the rupee cost of an error before asking what the threshold is, and treats a threshold nobody can price as an unowned liability. They ask for the worst slice, not the average. They instrument acceptance-without-edit rather than engagement, and overturn rate rather than escalation volume. They know a safety feature can reduce safety, and they test trust patterns against escape rate rather than satisfaction. Faced with a flat basin they stop optimising and start arguing about defensibility, which is the correct argument. And they design the staircase before the button: which reversible action can precede the irreversible one, and whose clock governs whether reversal is possible at all.

12. Two decisions

Ritwika kept auto-normal, moved to device-specific thresholds of 0.985 and 0.97, made per-slice recalibration a release gate, and put the queue's overturn rate on the programme's monthly report to the state committee. She did not promise fewer errors; she offered a documented basis for the errors the programme had chosen to accept. Kabir shipped execution only inside the cancellable window, with the assistant telling users when an action could no longer be undone and offering to schedule it for the next morning. The 41% outside the window became a roadmap item aimed at the settlement clock, not the interface. Neither decision made the model better; both changed what the product would let the model do alone.

  1. Nabz's cost curve is flat between two thresholds. On what grounds should the choice inside the basin be made, and who should make it?
  2. Daleel's citations raised trust and raised escapes. Under what conditions should a product deliberately make its own outputs look less credible than they are?
  3. Amanat's reversibility is governed by a fund cut-off it does not control. Which trust patterns remain available when the reversibility of your product's actions belongs to someone else?
Design so the user's reliance rises and falls with measured reliability on their slice — not with the fluency of the output or the average on your dashboard.

13. Going deeper

Quality as a distribution
The source of the problem: until quality is a spread rather than a number, no threshold is derivable.
UX fundamentals for PMs
Trust patterns are ordinary interaction design under an unusual constraint; without them you reinvent affordance and feedback badly.
Conversational and generative UX
Where fluency and correctness decouple most sharply, and per-claim confidence becomes unavoidable.
Explainability and contestability
The step beyond calibration: recourse, and the legal duty that does not care how accurate you are.
Problem–model fit
Decides whether trust UX is the right tool at all, or whether the problem should never have been modelled.
The ML lifecycle
Calibration drift is a lifecycle event; thresholds belong to a release process, not a person's memory.
Data strategy and data acquisition
Worst-slice performance is a data-coverage fact, as Nabz's portable units were.
Labelling and annotation
Escalation queues are annotation pipelines in disguise; label quality caps what the loop can teach.
Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC
The vocabulary in which thresholds are argued; AUC hides the operating point that trust UX is entirely about.
What's different when the feature is a model
Generalises the argument: the specification is statistical, so the interface must carry uncertainty the spec cannot remove.
exp20v2-aipm.trust.ux:
AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management

Trust and AI UX Patterns

Confidence, citations, undo, escalation — how a product is designed once its makers accept that it will sometimes be wrong.

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Meera Iyer, VP of Product at Aashwasan Systems, read a legal notice forwarded by her largest client's general counsel. Aashwasan builds an AI copilot that drafts customer-service replies for lending and insurance contact centres; the client, a large vehicle-financing NBFC, ran it across 38,000 conversations a day. Two weeks earlier Meera's team had switched on "auto-send": replies the model scored above 92% confidence went to the customer without a human reading them first, freeing agents to handle harder cases. It covered 61% of ticket volume and, on an audited sample, was wrong 1.9% of the time — mostly harmless phrasing slips. One was not harmless. A customer had asked whether his loan foreclosure no-objection certificate had been issued. The model, reading a backend field that had updated optimistically before a downstream job actually completed, answered yes. The customer sold his car. The NOC had not, in fact, been issued. He was now suing, and two other clients worth ₹14 crore in annual contract value were watching Aashwasan's board decide whether "auto-send" was a feature or a liability.

Meera's instinct was to rip auto-send out. Her head of engineering's instinct was to raise the confidence threshold to 98% and call it fixed. Both instincts missed the actual problem, which had nothing to do with the number 92 and everything to do with what the interface let the model claim, and what it let the customer do about a claim that turned out to be false. That is the problem this topic exists to solve.

1. The idea

Trust UX patterns are the interface design choices that let a person calibrate how much to rely on a system that is right most of the time but not all of the time: showing how confident the system is, showing what its answer is grounded in, making its actions cheap to reverse, and routing it to a human when the stakes or the uncertainty are too high. The discipline did not begin with generative AI. Aviation and process-control researchers John Lee and Katrina See gave it its modern name in a 2004 paper, Trust in Automation, built on decades of watching pilots either ignore autopilots that were working (disuse) or defer to autopilots that had failed (misuse). Their conclusion was that the goal is neither high trust nor low trust but calibrated trust — trust that tracks the system's actual, moment-to-moment reliability. Microsoft's Human-AI Experience (HAX) guidelines (2019) and Google's People + AI Guidebook (2019) translated that idea into concrete interface patterns once large-scale ML products made "sometimes wrong" a daily condition rather than an edge case. The sentence Meera could repeat in a board meeting without sounding glib: the interface's job is to make the customer's confidence rise and fall with the system's actual reliability, not with how fluent its answer sounds.

The problem this was invented to solve is specific: fluency and correctness are uncorrelated in a large language model. A wrong answer reads exactly as confident as a right one, because both were generated by the same process predicting plausible next tokens. Traditional software fails loudly — a null pointer, a timeout, a red error banner. A generative system fails in exactly the same font as it succeeds. Trust UX is the set of patterns that reintroduce, deliberately, the signal that fluency erased.

Fig. 1 — The four pattern families Meera's team had to choose among; auto-send had quietly turned off three of the four.

2. How it actually works

The mechanics start earlier than the interface: they start with what the model is even capable of telling you. A confidence score is only useful if it is calibrated — if, across a thousand answers scored "90% confident," roughly 900 are actually right. Most raw model probabilities are not calibrated out of the box; they are typically overconfident, because the training objective rewards sounding sure. Product teams usually have to build a calibration layer: log thousands of predictions against outcomes, bucket them by the model's stated confidence, and check whether the buckets hold. Aashwasan's data science lead had done this once, at launch, and never rechecked it — the exact implicit step practitioners skip, because calibration drifts as the model, the prompt, and the underlying data all keep changing quietly underneath it.

Once a confidence number can be trusted, the second mechanic is deciding what to show, which is not the same as what to compute. A raw number ("87%") invites false precision and means nothing to a customer without a reference class. Calibrated language ("likely, but double-check the date") is more honest but harder to standardise across a product. Abstention — the system declining to answer rather than guessing — is the strongest pattern and the one teams reach for last, because it looks like a failure in a demo even when it is the correct behaviour in production.

Provenance works by tying the generated claim back to a retrievable source at generation time, not after the fact — Aashwasan's copilot, for instance, drafts a reply and separately fetches the loan-account fields and policy clauses it references, so the interface can underline "your NOC was issued on 3 September" and let the agent click through to the actual system-of-record field. The NOC error happened precisely because that citation pointed at a field that had updated before the process behind it had actually finished — the citation was real, current, and still wrong, which is the nuance most teams building this mechanic miss.

Reversibility and escalation are the two mechanics that matter most once the first two have already failed, which they will. A cheap undo — the reply held in a queue for ninety seconds before sending, or a "recall" the agent can hit — turns a wrong answer into an inconvenience. Escalation is the rule that decides, automatically, when a case is too uncertain or too consequential to let the system act alone, and routing it to a human with the system's own reasoning attached rather than a blank ticket.

3. A worked example

Meera's engineering lead proposed simply raising the auto-send threshold from 92% to 98%. She asked him to show the arithmetic first, using the prior month's 38,000 conversations a day and the calibration curve her data scientist had actually re-measured that week.

Confidence thresholdShare auto-sentMeasured error rate in that bandWrong replies sent per dayReplies routed to agents
92% (current)61% (23,180)1.9%44014,820
98% (proposed)29% (11,020)0.3%3326,980
92%, but foreclosure/NOC topics excluded58% (22,040)1.1%24215,960

The 98% option cut daily errors from 440 to 33 — a real improvement — but it also pushed 12,160 more conversations a day back onto human agents, erasing most of the labour saving the client had bought the tool for. Worse, it treated all errors as equally costly, when the actual damage from the NOC mistake had nothing to do with the model's confidence and everything to do with the topic: a wrong answer about a late-fee waiver is an annoyance; a wrong answer about a document that lets a customer sell an asset is a legal event. The third row — keeping the 92% threshold but forcing every reply that touches foreclosure, NOC, or settlement topics into human review regardless of confidence — cut daily errors on those specific topics from roughly forty to near zero, at a much smaller cost in agent hours, because those topics were a thin slice of total volume. The second pass changes one input, topic sensitivity rather than the threshold, and gets a materially better trade than moving the whole dial.

4. The nuances a learner must catch

Confidence is not correctness

A model can be perfectly calibrated in aggregate — 90% buckets really do resolve correctly 90% of the time — and still be badly wrong on a subclass, as Aashwasan's NOC field was. Calibration is a population statistic; a customer experiences one draw, not the population. Product teams must keep asking which subpopulations the average is hiding.

Showing a citation is not the same as being grounded

A citation proves the system consulted a source; it does not prove the source was current, complete, or the right one. The NOC citation was accurate and stale at once. Teams routinely equate "has a citation" with "is safe," which is the mistake that let auto-send ship in the first place.

Undo has a clock, and the clock is often invisible to the user

A ninety-second hold before sending only works as reversibility if the customer, not just the agent, can act inside that window. Many "undo" patterns are undo for the company and irreversible for the person who already read the message.

Escalation needs a reason attached, not just a routing rule

A handoff that dumps a raw transcript on a human without the system's own confidence, sources, and the specific point of doubt simply moves the cognitive load rather than reducing it — the agent re-does the diagnosis from scratch, usually under time pressure, which reintroduces the error the escalation was meant to prevent.

Trust UX cannot fix a model that is wrong for structural reasons

No amount of interface design repairs a system trained on stale account data, or one asked to answer questions outside its retrieval scope. These patterns manage the consequences of fallibility; they are not a substitute for the evaluation and data-quality work that reduces the fallibility itself.

High-frequency, low-stakes and rare, high-stakes cases need opposite designs

A pattern tuned for the bulk of ordinary tickets — light-touch confidence badges, no friction — will under-protect the rare cases that carry real cost, and a pattern tuned for the rare cases will annoy the customer on every ordinary one. The two need different thresholds, not one global setting.

Trust, once broken on one topic, migrates to every topic

Customers and regulators generalise from a single visible failure to the whole system. The NOC incident cost Aashwasan credibility on loan disbursal, EMI dates, and every other topic the copilot touches, even though those were unaffected — a fact worth remembering when arguing that "only one narrow case" failed.

5. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

A consumer app can rely on the user's own stake in the outcome as a natural brake: a shopper who gets an odd AI-written product description will simply not buy, so the cost of overconfidence is diffuse and self-correcting. A B2B tool like Aashwasan's sits between two parties — the agent using it and the customer receiving its output — so the person best placed to catch an error (the agent) is not the person who bears the cost of a missed one (the customer), which is exactly why escalation design, not confidence display alone, carries the weight in B2B products. Marketplace products add a third party: a mis-set AI recommendation or mis-priced auto-suggestion affects a buyer, a seller, and the platform's own take rate simultaneously, so provenance has to be visible to whichever side is likely to dispute the outcome, not just the side using the tool.

Early-stage companyLarge, established company
Dominant patternConfidence + undo, built fast, tuned by eyeCalibration pipelines, audited escalation SLAs, compliance sign-off
Failure modeNo one is measuring calibration at allPatterns exist on paper but drift silently as models change
What changes itFirst serious incident, or first enterprise buyer's security reviewA regulator, auditor, or repeat incident forcing re-verification

6. Common mistakes

Treating the confidence score as the whole design. Symptom: a number badge with nothing else. Underlying error: mistaking the easiest mechanic to build for the whole job. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what the user is supposed to do differently at 60% than at 95% — if the answer is "nothing," the score is decoration.

Calibrating once, at launch, and never again. Symptom: confidence bands that "feel" right in a demo but drift out of alignment with reality within weeks. Underlying error: treating calibration as a one-time model property rather than an operating metric. Cheapest diagnostic: pull last month's "high confidence" bucket and check its real accuracy — if no one can produce that number in an hour, it is not being tracked.

Building escalation as a dead end instead of a loop. Symptom: agents ignore escalated cases or resolve them without ever telling the system what the right answer was. Underlying error: treating the human handoff as a safety valve rather than a source of training signal. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether a single escalated case has ever changed a prompt, a retrieval source, or a threshold — if not, the loop is open, not closed.

Making undo available but not discoverable. Symptom: a recall button exists in the product but usage logs show it is essentially never used, even where errors are known to occur. Underlying error: assuming a feature that exists is a feature that is used. Cheapest diagnostic: watch five real users hit an error and time how long it takes them to find the correction path.

"Design the interface so the customer's confidence rises and falls with the system's actual reliability — not with how fluent its answer sounds."

7. What good looks like

Six months after the NOC incident, a similar near-miss surfaced at Aashwasan's second-largest client, a general insurer using the same copilot for claims-status replies. A customer asked whether his claim had been approved; the model's draft said yes, at 89% confidence, sourced to a claims-status field. But because "claim approved" now sat on the topic-sensitive list Meera's team had built after the first incident, the reply never auto-sent — it queued for an agent with the citation, the confidence score, and a flag reading "high-stakes topic: verify against claims system before sending." The agent found the field had, in fact, updated early, the same underlying bug as before, corrected the draft, and logged the discrepancy. Product got the log within the hour, not months later through a legal notice, and used it to fix the timing of the status update itself. The customer never saw the wrong answer at all. Nothing here required a smarter model — it required the interface to know, before generation, which topics could not afford to be wrong, and to route those regardless of how confident the model sounded.

8. Meera's decision

Meera kept auto-send on. She did not raise the global threshold to 98%, because the arithmetic showed that traded a large, diffuse labour cost for a small, already-manageable error rate. Instead she shipped topic-sensitive escalation — foreclosure, NOC, settlement, and claim-status topics routed to a human at any confidence level — rewired the provenance citations to show the source field's last verified timestamp rather than just its current value, and gave customers, not only agents, a visible correction channel on any AI-drafted message. The board approved the two pending client contracts on the strength of that redesign, not on a promise that the model would stop making mistakes. What Meera's team took up next was evaluation: the systematic measurement of where and how often the model is actually wrong, since trust UX can only route around failures that measurement has already found. Two questions worth sitting with: when your product shows a confidence number, can you say — with a real measurement behind the answer — what fraction of "high confidence" outputs are actually correct? And for the one output your system could get wrong tomorrow that would cost the most, does your interface currently treat it the same as every ordinary one?
exp40v2-aipm.problem.fit:
Problem–model fit

Is this actually a prediction, generation, ranking or classification problem — or none of them?

1. Two rooms, ten days apart

On Tuesday 4 August 2026 in Bengaluru, Omprakash Fulzele was shown a slide he had not written. Fulzele ran product at Ojhal Grid Systems, which sold meter-data software and edge hardware to state discoms. Prepared by the chief executive Falguni Ogale, it promised "an AI loss assistant" to the largest of Ojhal's six discom customers by March 2027. The discom pushed 400 million units monthly and lost 14.5 per cent; of the 58 million units lost, 34 million went to the network and 24 million to theft and metering fraud. At ₹6.20 a unit that commercial share — 41 per cent of the loss — was worth ₹14.88 crore a month. Its 120 vigilance teams made 18,000 inspections a month, confirming theft in 9 per cent — 1,620 cases, assessed at ₹25,000 each, ₹4.05 crore. Only 38 per cent was ever collected: ₹1.539 crore of the ₹14.88 crore lost, or 10.3 per cent. Fulzele disputed not the problem but the noun: nobody in that discom was short of sentences.

Ten days later, on 14 August, Fatima Oza sat through the same meeting in Hyderabad. Oza was chief product officer of Fanoos Home Services, a four-city appliance-repair marketplace handling 1,40,000 jobs a month, 5,600 a day, worked by about 1,120 of its 4,800 partners on any day, five jobs each. It promised a two-hour arrival window and missed it on 31 per cent of jobs, 43,400 of them; 22 per cent of all jobs, 30,800, were rescheduled at least once at an all-in ₹410, ₹1.26 crore a month. Farooq Ojha, the chief executive, had promised investors an "AI concierge" by Diwali; Onkar Fadia, Oza's head of machine learning, had run the numbers.

The two share one question: what kind of answer does the decision need, and can a learned model supply it at a price the decision can bear?

2. The idea, and the five camps that read it differently

Problem–model fit is the discipline of establishing what object a decision requires as input, and whether a model whose output is that object can be built and operated profitably. A model is a function fitted to examples; its output is always one of a few objects: a label from a fixed set (classification), a number over a horizon (prediction), an ordering (ranking), or a new artefact such as text or an image (generation). A fifth answer is no cop-out: the decision may need an object none of these produce — a plan, a rule, or a finding with legal standing.

The vocabulary predates the enthusiasm. Fisher separated discrimination from estimation in 1936; Dantzig's simplex method (1947) and Kuhn's Hungarian algorithm (1955) gave allocation under constraints a mature discipline half a century before anyone called it AI, which is why "optimisation, not learning" is so often correct and so rarely popular; Cranfield in the 1960s and Robertson's probability ranking principle (1977) formalised ranking. Beneath all of it sits Howard's decision analysis (1966): information is worth the improvement in the decision it changes, and nothing if the decision would not change.

Five positions are genuinely held. The prediction-machine camp, after Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb's Prediction Machines (2018), signs "AI is a collapse in the cost of prediction: hunt for decisions bottlenecked by a missing forecast", but not that the choice among families is a first-order product question. The decision-analytic camp signs "a model that moves no action is worth zero however accurate", but not that a lift in AUC is progress. The operations-research camp signs "most commercial problems are allocation under constraints; the learned part is a coefficient inside a program", but not that prediction and decision share one objective — though decision-focused learning signs exactly that, which is the live quarrel. The generality camp signs "prompt a general model into any family and measure", but not that you must know the output object before building. The workflow-redesign camp signs "fit is a property of the model-and-workflow pair", but not that a problem's shape is independent of how work is organised.

3. Mechanics: what actually fixes the operating point

Experts begin from the action, not the output object, asking two questions most briefs omit. Are the items independent, or do they compete for a shared resource? Is the number of actions per period free, or fixed from outside? Those answers fix the family and the operating point, and the operating point decides whether the project earns money.

Apply that to Ojhal. The action is an inspection, and the discom can make 18,000 a month — a number set by headcount and a negotiated service condition. That converts what the room called classification ("flag the thieves") into ranking ("order 9,60,000 meters, take the top 18,000"). Oindrila Fotedar, Ojhal's principal data scientist, had run a random audit of 6,000 meters that found 186 confirmed cases, a base rate of 3.1 per cent, implying about 29,760 offenders in the 9,60,000. She backtested a gradient-boosted scorer on twelve months of interval data, tamper flags and transformer energy balance, reporting the yield of each tranche of 18,000.
