4. The conditions, stated so they can fail

Four claims make this testable. One: the action exists, and someone can name who takes it. At Ojhal it is a vigilance team with a work order; at Fanoos a dispatcher, later a solver. Ogale's assistant failed here, its actor being "management". Two: the object is producible at the frequency the decision runs. Fanoos's assignment must solve in nine minutes at 21:00, which rules out better formulations. Three: the operating point comes from outside the model and is written down. Ojhal's is 18,000; Fanoos's is a two-hour window, a marketing promise product could have renegotiated. Four: the counterfactual is the cheapest thing that would work, not the absence of a system.

The idea misleads twice over: when the question becomes a stall, and when the workflow is not fixed — if work can be reorganised then shape is a variable, and treating Fanoos's window as physics is how good teams optimise inside a bad design.

5. Hard edges

Ojhal sells one model to six discoms, and the multi-product seam bites at once: capacity differs, so the operating point differs, so one scorer needs six cut-offs, six contracts, and a deck that cannot quote "23 per cent hit rate". The regulated seam is sharper: a theft assessment under the Electricity Act, 2003 is a quasi-judicial finding and a score is not evidence, so the permitted output object is a position in a queue, never a determination — the law selecting the family.

Two-sidedness bends Fanoos the other way. Showing customers a ranked list of technicians looked harmless: in a fortnight's test in Jaipur, 430 of the 4,800 partners — 9 per cent — took 61 per cent of bookings. A ranking correct for each customer is corrosive to supply, because the label the ranker learns from is generated by the ranker. In hardware the constraint arrives earlier: Falak Sensing Works, a Pune vibration-sensor maker, has an installed base reporting at 15-minute intervals, and no modelling recovers transients from 15-minute averages — a sampling decision three years old had already deleted two families from the menu. In AI-native products the seam moves to runtime, as at Farmaan Dispatch Cloud, whose agent picks its own shape per request.

What mature organisations do, as against what they publish, is put the operating point in a contract — Ojhal's came to specify cases confirmed per 1,000 inspections, audited jointly — because data science is rewarded on AUC, operations on visits and finance on rupees collected, and a contract number is the cheapest referee going.

6. Eight things the expert sees that the competent practitioner does not

The operating point belongs to the world, not the model. The tell is a deck quoting AUC with no k in it. AUC averages over thresholds the discom can never work, while the value sits in the top 1.875 per cent, where two models with identical AUC differ twofold.

A model earns only what it changes. The honest figure at Ojhal was never ₹10.35 crore but the incremental ₹6.30 crore over a process already finding 1,620 cases. Teams quoting the gross number have simply never been asked for the counterfactual.

Fit has a level, and the first level is usually wrong. Both Fadia and Fotedar first named a family for a problem stated a layer too high. The tell is a proposal whose output nobody consumes directly; a prediction feeding a bad dispatcher is worth a fraction of the same prediction feeding a good one.

Ranking launders accountability; classification accepts it. A ranker never decides, so a human still visits every meter it puts forward, which halves the political cost of error and makes ranking the right first shipment. It can also be a dodge: if the human cannot exercise judgement — 18,000 orders arriving as a bare list — you have shipped a classifier and pretended otherwise.

The top of the list is where data artefacts live. When Ojhal read what the first band contained, 4,851 of the 13,860 inspections that found no theft — 35 per cent — were meters whose gaps came from a failed communication module. The scorer had partly learned "this meter stopped reporting" — what theft looks like, and also a dead modem. The tell is a homogeneous top band, whose obvious reading is backwards.

Labels record the previous policy, including where it never looked. A capacity-constrained history holds outcomes only for meters somebody chose to inspect. This is why Fotedar's random audit of 6,000 mattered more than her model: without it every lift figure is guesswork.

Generation is an interface, not a problem shape. Ask what the artefact is worth once a competent person must read it. Fanoos's concierge would have answered 29,512 of 47,600 support contacts — 62 per cent — that were arrival-status queries. Those exist because the promise was wrong, so answering them pays to preserve the defect.

Better predictions do not monotonically improve decisions. Cutting mean absolute error from 31 minutes to 19 helps only if the residual error lands where it is cheap: ten minutes early costs idle time, ten late costs ₹410, so an expert tunes the estimator to over-predict. The tell is a review where the error metric improved and misses did not.

7. What actually differs by product type and stage

In consumer products errors are small, numerous and borne by strangers, so ranking dominates and the operating point is attention, not capacity. In B2B and enterprise every error has a named customer and a contractual consequence, which pushes the operating point into a document, as at Ojhal. In platforms and marketplaces the label is endogenous — Fanoos's ranker changes the supply it ranks — so "what does a wrong output cost?" has two answers that do not net out. In hardware and AI-native products the menu is set elsewhere — years earlier by sampling rate and bandwidth, or at runtime by the model itself — so the work is specification and constraint, not selection.

Stage matters less than is claimed, and the claim that early-stage companies should skip the question for want of data is false. With no labels the cheap baseline is nearly always a rule or a hosted general model, and knowing which leaf you are filling is what stops a seed-stage team assembling a training set for a decision that occurs eleven times a month. What changes with scale is the cost of error at the top of the list, and hence how much a company can afford to automate rather than merely order.

8. Three worked cases

One: the finding that needed no model

The communication-fault discovery was worth more per rupee than the scorer. A rule — six consecutive days of meter silence routes to maintenance, not vigilance — took those 4,851 visits out of the first band. Refilling the freed slots from the second band, at its 14.0 per cent hit rate, yields 679 more cases a month: confirmed cases rise from 4,140 to 4,819 on the same 18,000 visits, a hit rate of 26.8 per cent. Those 679 are worth ₹1.70 crore assessed and ₹64.51 lakh realised a month, ₹7.74 crore a year, from about ₹6 lakh of one engineer's time — found by reading what the model ranked, not by improving it.

Two: the prediction worth more than the optimiser

A three-week pilot in Nagpur over 11,200 jobs cut reschedules from 22 per cent to 14.5 per cent — 2,464 down to 1,624 — which across 1,40,000 jobs a month is 10,500 fewer reschedules at ₹410, ₹5.17 crore a year. The optimiser added an 18 per cent cut in riding distance, ₹0.75 crore a year on 8,28,800 km at ₹4.20, and released travel time for 4,620 extra jobs a month at ₹95 contribution, ₹0.53 crore a year.

10. Where competent people still disagree

The generality position at its strongest is not laziness. Between 2023 and 2026 general models absorbed classification, extraction and ranking tasks that had justified dedicated pipelines, often at better quality with no training data: the taxonomy described tooling, not problems. It would be wrong if capacity-constrained decisions resist it — a general model can rank 9,60,000 meters, but not at a price the discom will pay.

Decision-focused learning holds that separating prediction from optimisation leaves value on the table: train the estimator against the decision's loss and its errors land where they are cheap. Its evidence is a decade of results in which predict-then-optimise loses to joint training. It would be wrong if the joint objective proves unauditable where regulators look.

Workflow redesign holds that arguing about families before fixing the workflow is optimising inside somebody else's error; its evidence is Firozi's tape measure and Ojhal's silent modems. It would be wrong if workflow change proved slower and more political than model change — and in a state utility it often is.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the action before the data, and will not accept "management" as an actor. They ask for the operating point as a number from outside the model and write it into the document that governs the work. And they treat "none of these" as a finding to be hunted rather than an embarrassment, which means somebody reads fifty cases by hand before anyone opens a notebook. The studied practitioner recites four families; the fluent one spends the first meeting on Exhibit 2's fourth column and the last on who audits it.

12. What each of them did

On 11 September Fulzele took three items to Ogale rather than one. First, the silence rule: three weeks, ₹6 lakh, no model, ₹7.74 crore a year of realised recovery. Second, the ranking module, with the operating point written into the contract as cases confirmed per 1,000 inspections, audited jointly — ₹4.80 crore of annual revenue against ₹28.73 crore of realised benefit. Third, the loss assistant, demoted to a drafting aid for the inspector's site note, the one place where the required object really was free text. Ogale had wanted it first and settled for third: a regulator can audit a ranked queue, not a generated paragraph.

Oza's decision was narrower and harder to sell. She shipped the estimator into the existing dispatcher — row three of Exhibit 6 — declining the optimiser she agreed was structurally correct, and named the trigger for revisiting it: any city crossing 2,400 jobs a day, where density makes its advantage grow faster than its cost. She cancelled the concierge, keeping only the post-visit summary, which a technician reads and corrects. Ojha's Diwali promise went unmet.

Discussion questions. First: Oza rejected the structurally correct framing on cost grounds at 5,600 jobs a day. At what scale does that reverse, and what would you measure to know it? Second: the silence rule earned more per rupee than the model, and nobody's bonus depended on finding it. How would you make "none of these" a career-positive finding? Third: if the generality camp is right, Exhibit 2's second column becomes a runtime decision taken by the model. What does the product manager then own?

13. Going deeper

Validating a problem hypothesis is the gate before this. AI product design choices turns a family into an interface — a queue, a score, a draft. The ML lifecycle is what the choice commits you to operate; model metrics: precision, recall, AUC is the vocabulary for arguing about the first band. Discovery for AI products finds Exhibit 2's fourth column. Recommendation systems for PMs and vector search and similarity are ranking's machinery; forecasting and optimisation products is Fanoos's leaf. Data strategy and data acquisition, labelling and annotation, what's different when the feature is a model and quality as a distribution settle whether the family is buildable. What evals are and why PMs own them, evals and what they actually measure and building a golden set from real usage are how you learn whether it holds.

Rupantar Metals Exchange: Whose Grade Is It?

An ambiguous case for discussion. No teaching note.

1. The night before

On the evening of Thursday, 15 October 2026 — the fifth night of Navratri, garba drums carrying from the society ground two lanes away — Aditi Mhatre sat in the empty product room of Rupantar Metals Exchange's office off Sindhu Bhavan Road in Ahmedabad with eleven printed pages and a laptop she had stopped reading. The board met at ten the next morning.

It would allocate ₹145 lakh of new product and engineering money for the half-year. The chief executive, Harsh Lalwani, had circulated a pre-read whose single slide read “Rupantar Inspector: an assayer on every loading yard's phone”: ₹210 lakh over twelve months, ₹118 lakh of it before 31 March 2027. Aditi, vice-president of product, was listed to present it.

She did not think the slide dishonest. She thought it answered a question nobody had stated. In the quarter to 30 June 2026 the company lost ₹1.92 crore to quality and settlement claims — fifty-three per cent of the gross margin it earned on trades where it took title. Four colleagues had told her in four separate weeks what that number meant, and no two of them agreed.

What troubled her most was the eleventh page, printed twice. It showed where the company's training labels came from: each was a grade assigned at a mill's gate by the buyer who paid less when the grade was lower.

2. How Rupantar came to be exposed

Rupantar was founded in 2017 by Harsh Lalwani, then twenty-nine, out of a family brass business in Jamnagar, and Rohan Bhide, eleven years a scrap buyer in Mandi Gobindgarh. The idea was unglamorous: the ferrous scrap trade ran on telephone calls, cash advances and personal trust, and a platform showing verified lots, verified weights and same-week payment could take a thin slice of it. In the year to March 2026 it traded 2,40,000 tonnes at an average ₹32,000 a tonne — ₹768 crore of gross merchandise value — on ₹214 crore raised in three rounds: ₹28 crore, ₹76 crore and, in October 2023, ₹110 crore.

That round came with the decision that defines the present. Mills would not pay a premium for a grade they could not trust, and brokerage left Rupantar arguing between two parties who both blamed it. So in October 2023 the founders chose to take title on selected trades — buy the lot, guarantee its grade, sell it on — and on 1 November signed a master agreement with Rishabh Alloys, an induction-furnace group with three mills in Punjab and Haryana and today 31 per cent of volume. Clause 9.3 made the grade and weight recorded at the buyer's gate final for settlement.

The clause bought three years of growth. It also handed the definition of the truth to the party that gained from a downgrade, and created Rupantar's only systematic record of what its lots contained. The agreement renewed automatically unless either side gave ninety days' notice; notice for the term ending 31 October 2026 fell due on 2 August, and nobody served it. On 28 August the general counsel, Rhea Kamdar, confirmed 9.3 stood until 31 October 2027.

3. The industry around the decision

India consumes roughly 3 crore tonnes of steel scrap a year and imports perhaps 60 lakh tonnes, and the trade is being formalised from several directions: GST e-invoicing and the e-way bill have put a trail on once-invisible movements, imported scrap needs a DGFT pre-shipment certificate, mills run radiation portal monitors in line with Atomic Energy Regulatory Board expectations, and state legal metrology departments stamp the weighbridges every settlement rests on.

The field is not empty. Metalbook, OfBusiness and Zetwerk have built metals businesses with far more capital; Tata Steel and JSW run branded recycling channels that pull scrap upstream; and the aggregator who closes a deal on WhatsApp in twenty minutes is still the speed benchmark. Rupantar's 64,000 tonnes was under one per cent of national consumption.

Scrap prices are set globally — the London Metal Exchange, the Turkish heavy-melting index, container freight, domestic sponge iron — and move Rupantar's buy price more than anything it does. Imported lots, 11,520 tonnes of the 64,000, arrive with an inspection certificate, a chemistry report and a far more homogeneous profile than a truckload of mixed Punjabi offcuts; and induction furnaces on thin spreads scrutinise every load.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Until late 2025 the claims line was treated as friction, a “quality adjustment” and a cost of doing business. Two things changed that. In July 2024 a lot from a Ludhiana yard set off a mill's radiation portal; Rupantar paid ₹41 lakh and lost that mill for seven weeks. Then came arithmetic: by the April–June 2026 quarter claims had reached 2.17 per cent of principal gross merchandise value against 2.08 for the previous year, and against gross contribution before claims of ₹5.74 crore and operating costs of ₹4.55 crore, the ₹1.92 crore was the difference between a profit and a loss of ₹73 lakh.

In July 2026 Rohan's team tagged every claim by cause (Exhibit 2). Ahmedabad read it as vindication of the grading thesis: downgrades at the mill gate were ₹78 lakh, 40.6 per cent of claim value and the largest line by far. Harsh commissioned the inspector concept that month. In August, Althea Villamor's team in Manila produced its own cut from the mill-facing ticket system (Exhibit 3), covering six months and all trades; there, documentation was largest by a distance and grade disagreement third. Nobody noticed for three weeks that the two exhibits counted different things over different windows, or that one detained truck could generate nine tickets, one per follow-up email.

Also in August, Anjali Keskar's team in Bengaluru assembled a training set and hit the constraint nobody had anticipated. Of the 3,200 lots traded in the quarter, a final settled grade existed for only 1,088 — 34.0 per cent — because on brokered trades the mill settles directly with the supplier. Those 1,088 are 85.0 per cent of the 1,280 lots where Rupantar took title: not a sample of the business but a census of the trades it carried the risk on, graded by the counterparty who paid the bill.

From 3 August to 11 September the team piloted a downgrade-risk classifier on the corridor from Mandi Gobindgarh to Rishabh Alloys' Khanna mill. The pilot (Exhibit 5a) was the best news of the year; the holdout evaluation two weeks later (Exhibit 5b) was not, and nobody has reconciled them. On 29 September Astrid Hellström wrote from Stockholm that the annotation underneath both was unsound: of 600 photo sets double-annotated by trained graders, the two agreed on the exact grade in 372.

5. The people

Aditi Mhatre, 34, vice-president of product, Ahmedabad. Hired from a logistics software firm in Pune, she has no metals background and knows it counts against her in Mandi Gobindgarh. She believes the company skipped a step, and that saying so will sound like delay. Unsaid: she is unconvinced by the inspector concept.

Harsh Lalwani, 38, co-founder and chief executive, Ahmedabad. He wants Rupantar Inspector in the field before Diwali restocking: the judgement of a good assayer is what a model of photographs and text can learn, and a visible capability changes how Rupantar is valued. Unsaid: the Series D conversations opening in January have, in his reading, been priced on an AI story, and 9.3 was his own negotiation.

Rohan Bhide, 43, co-founder and chief operating officer, Mandi Gobindgarh. There is no mystery, he maintains: yard weighbridges are uncalibrated, moisture is never measured, the picklist is ignored for free text, and nobody checks a lot for sealed cylinders. Unsaid: three of the six worst yards are his own, and his ₹11,000 cost per flag is an afternoon's estimate his budget would bear.

Anjali Keskar, 36, head of data science, Bengaluru. The classifier is cheap, uses data that exists, and routes scarce inspector time to the riskiest lots. She is scrupulous about her labels in writing and less so in meetings. Unsaid: she thinks ₹11,000 a flag three times too high, her own ₹3,500 equally unmeasured, and the classifier the only proposal that justifies her three hires.

Hariharan Venkataraman, 31, lead machine-learning engineer, Pune. The discussion is small, he says: claims are ₹1.92 crore a quarter, while one per cent off the principal buying price is ₹88.32 lakh a quarter. His backtest calls the seven-day direction correctly on 56.8 per cent of days against 54.1 for carry-forward, which he calls an edge. Unsaid: he is interviewing with a Mumbai quantitative fund.

Rashmi Nagarkar, 45, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Her concern is the ₹6.80 crore of invoice value unpaid at 30 June against 196 lots with an open claim — just over half the ₹13.52 crore invoiced on them, and 5.96 times the ₹1.14 crore assessed. Carrying it costs ₹91.80 lakh a year at 13.5 per cent. Unsaid: she has modelled withdrawing cover on the two worst corridors.

Astrid Hellström, 39, principal designer, Stockholm. She has spent two weeks on what suppliers upload: three images a lot, at night under sodium lamps, from the top of a trailer. Rupantar is not automating a judgement, she argues, but creating a record both parties accept, which needs no model. Unsaid: she sent the annotator figure to a wide list rather than to Anjali.

Althea Villamor, 41, head of customer success for mill accounts, Manila. Despatch managers never raise grading, she reports; they say a dispute takes 11.4 days to close on average, against a median of six, while holding the whole invoice. Two accounts, including Ambar Ispat, have moved buying to rivals over it. Unsaid: she promised those two a four-day turnaround Rupantar cannot deliver.

8. The options as Aditi currently sees them

She has written them in the order the company argues about them, which is not necessarily the order that matters.

A. Build Rupantar Inspector. Photographs and the supplier's text go in; a grading report comes out. It is the only proposal that would appear in a Series D deck, and at ₹118 lakh before March it consumes most of the envelope to return ₹8.97 lakh a quarter: a payback of 70.2 months. Harsh's answer is that this is the wrong arithmetic: a grading capability changes what suppliers list and what mills pay, which nobody has measured either.

B. Ship the classifier. Cheap, fast, uses what exists. Whether it earns ₹112 lakh a year or loses ₹36 lakh turns entirely on the cost of acting on a flag, which two senior people have asserted and neither measured. It trains on a label the counterparty produces, so a well-fitted model may be a model of the buyer.

C. Build the price engine. The biggest number on the page, ₹88.32 lakh a quarter for a one per cent improvement, against a backtest edge of 2.7 points. It addresses margin, not claims, and does nothing for the ₹6.80 crore Rashmi is chasing.

D. Instrument the yards and change the contract. The cheapest package and the largest claimed effect, but much of its value sits behind supplier behaviour Rupantar has failed to change once already: in February 2025 a three-photograph mandate on the Jamnagar corridor cost it 29 of 104 enrolled yards (27.9 per cent) and a fifth of corridor volume in six weeks, and was withdrawn. A further ₹15.60 lakh needs the locked clause.

E. Stop guaranteeing grade where it hurts most. Rashmi's unpublished model: on the two worst corridors, 7,040 of the 25,600 principal tonnes, give up ₹99.58 lakh of gross margin, recover ₹38.86 lakh as brokerage, avoid ₹88.34 lakh of claims and come out ₹27.62 lakh a quarter ahead, building nothing. It also unwinds the decision on which the chief executive built the company.

What Aditi keeps circling is that all five answer a question that has been assumed. Exhibit 2 says grading; Exhibit 3, read naively, says paperwork; Exhibit 4 says Rupantar sees the outcome on a third of its trades, and only where it pays for the answer. Exhibits 5a and 5b measure one model two weeks apart and point opposite ways. Imported lots, which carry an inspection and a chemistry report, show a claim rate of 14.6 per cent against 34.5 for domestic lots — which might mean inspection works, or only that shredded scrap is more uniform. And the smallest category by count, eighteen lots of prohibited material, is second largest by value.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board sits at ten on Friday, 16 October 2026. Dussehra falls on 20 October and Diwali on 8 November; the restocking cycle that follows is the year's heaviest buying window, and anything meant to help must reach the yards this month. Harsh intends to leave with an approval, not a study.

The money is ₹145 lakh before 31 March 2027. On the Exhibit 6 figures A alone takes ₹118 lakh of it; B, C and D together take ₹126 lakh; A with B, C or D needs ₹164 lakh, ₹148 lakh or ₹168 lakh and fits with none. Only A with E fits: E costs nothing and leaves ₹27 lakh. Hiring is capped at four roles, and Anjali's plan claims three.

Clause 9.3 binds Rupantar to gate-assessed grade and weight on Rishabh Alloys volume — 31 per cent of trade — until 31 October 2027. Supplier photographs carry consent for platform use only; wider use of yard imagery needs fresh notice under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. A weighbridge in a supplier's yard is the supplier's asset and legal metrology's jurisdiction. And at ₹73 lakh a quarter of losses the company has four quarters before the Series D conversation becomes a different one.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Take the six causes in Exhibit 2 one at a time. Is each a prediction, a classification, a ranking or a generation problem, or none of these — and what share of the ₹192.04 lakh does your answer cover?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 disagree about Rupantar's worst problem. Reconcile them. Which figure would you ask for that neither contains?
  3. Exhibits 5a and 5b came from one team two weeks apart and point opposite ways. Which would you believe, and what single experiment would settle it before January?
  4. Clause 9.3 makes the buyer's assessment the label. What does that do to any supervised model built on it, and what would an independent ground truth cost Rupantar to create?
  5. Astrid Hellström argues for a shared evidence record rather than a model. Is that a product decision, a contract decision or an admission of defeat — and how would you know within a quarter whether it worked?
  6. You are Aditi Mhatre at seven on Monday morning, 19 October, whatever happened on Friday. What do you do first, and what do you say to the board about the question Rupantar has not answered?

11. Ten past eleven

The drums stopped a little after eleven. Aditi put the eleven pages in order, changed the order, then put the page about labels on top. She had drafted one slide saying, in the plainest words she could find, that Rupantar did not know what kind of problem it had, and a second recommending Option B for six months because it was cheap and would generate evidence. She did not believe the second, and suspected the board would approve only the first thing Harsh said aloud. Outside, a loaded trailer went past the end of the lane, heading north for Punjab, and she wondered what was in it and who would decide.
case20v1-aipm.problem.fit:
Gulmohar Services: The Second Visit

A decision case on problem–model fit

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Gauri Phadnis sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the third floor of Gulmohar Services' headquarters in Baner, Pune, with a printed one-page slide in front of her. The slide had been drawn by the chief executive, Uday Mehendale, and carried a single headline: “Gulmohar AI Assistant: a technician in every customer’s pocket.” Beneath it was a request that the board approve ₹1.8 crore to build a generative assistant that would look at a customer’s photograph and chat, and tell the household what was wrong with a washing machine before anyone was dispatched.

Gauri, the head of product, had until the board meeting on Friday, 23 October, a gap of seventeen days, to tell Uday and his directors what the company should build with its next tranche of engineering money. She had a quarter of operating data, three colleagues who each saw the problem differently, and a growing suspicion that nobody had yet asked the first question: what kind of problem was this?

2. Company background

Gulmohar Services was founded in 2018 by Uday and a former appliance-service manager to do one thing: send a vetted technician to an Indian household to repair a refrigerator, washing machine, air conditioner or water purifier, at a price shown before booking. It operates in Pune, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Jaipur through about 2,300 technicians who work as independent partners, and it has raised ₹95 crore across three rounds. In the quarter from July to September 2026 it completed 40,000 jobs at an average ticket of ₹1,450, which is bookings of ₹5.8 crore for the quarter.

The market is crowded. Urban Company sets the consumer expectation for app-booked home services, the manufacturers’ own networks, such as those of LG, Samsung, Whirlpool and Voltas, handle warranty work, and local mechanics found through a WhatsApp number on a refrigerator door remain the largest competitor of all. Gulmohar’s argument is reliability: fix it once, and charge what was quoted. Payments run through UPI and Razorpay, and the October to November season, when Diwali falls on 8 November and households want everything working before guests arrive, brings the year’s heaviest demand.

3. The situation

The trouble sat in a figure the operations team called the repeat-visit rate. Of the 40,000 jobs in the quarter, 6,800 needed a second visit, a rate of 17.0 per cent. Gulmohar’s finance team put the direct cost of a repeat visit, meaning technician payout and fuel, at an average of ₹1,000, so the quarter’s repeat visits cost ₹68 lakh, or about 11.7 per cent of bookings.

Otieno Kamau, who leads support analytics from Nairobi, had tagged the cause of each repeat visit by reading the ticket history. His breakdown is Exhibit 1. The largest single cause, two visits in every five, was that the technician arrived without the part the job needed. A further fifth were misdiagnoses, where the fault found on the first visit was not the real fault. The remainder was a mixture of absent customers, workmanship gaps and jobs that overran their time slot.

Exhibit 2, assembled by Joost van der Meer, the senior data scientist working from Amsterdam, shows what data Gulmohar actually holds on those 40,000 jobs. The fault description is always present, because the booking form demands it, but it is free text: “fridge not cooling”, “fridge making noise and warm”, or simply “problem”. 4. The people

Uday Mehendale, chief executive and co-founder, in Pune, has watched investors and rivals talk about generative AI for two years. He wants a visible, ambitious product for the board and the next funding round.

Joost van der Meer, senior data scientist in Amsterdam, joined from a European logistics firm. He believes the repeat-visit problem is largely one of prediction: given a booking, which part will the job need? He is candid that a model is only as good as its labels.

Otieno Kamau, head of support analytics in Nairobi, spends his days in customer complaints. What customers write, he reports, is not “your technician was wrong” but “nobody came with the part and I took another half-day off.”

Jagdish Saini, head of field operations in Jaipur, manages the technicians. He argues that vans carry no standard kit, bookings do not capture the fault in a usable form, and customers are not reminded to be home. He would rather fix these in a month.

5. How the team reads the numbers

Each person looked at Exhibit 1 and saw a different problem. Uday saw the 20 per cent misdiagnosis line and an opening for a generative assistant that could talk to customers. Joost saw the 40 per cent parts line and a classic classification task, since the history of what each job used was available for 24,400 jobs, which Exhibit 2 confirms. Otieno saw that absent customers and overruns, together a quarter of the repeat visits, had nothing to do with intelligence at all. Jagdish saw a process that had never been designed.

Two further considerations mattered. Photographs of kitchens and bedrooms are personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and Gulmohar holds consent only for the 8,800 jobs with a photograph. And the Diwali season left little room: any change to technician workflow had to reach the field early to help with peak demand.

6. The options

Option A: the generative photo-and-chat assistant. The assistant would talk to customers, request photographs and produce a diagnosis in plain language. It is the most visible option, but it addresses only the misdiagnosis cause, 1,360 repeat visits, which the product team assumes it could halve. Year-one build and running cost: ₹180 lakh.

Option B: a part-prediction classifier. At booking, a model would predict which part or parts the job is likely to need, so that the technician is dispatched with them. It targets the largest cause, assumed to cut those repeat visits by 40 per cent. Cost is ₹45 lakh, including cleaning historical labels and a six-week review of technician data entry.

Option C: fix the process first, with no model. Replace the free-text fault with a fixed picklist of faults, issue standard van kits for the twelve most common faults, send a WhatsApp confirmation the evening before every visit, and build a time buffer into estimates. These changes are assumed to remove a quarter of the parts-related repeat visits, half the access problems, and half the overruns. Cost is ₹12 lakh.

B and C both act on the parts cause, so their savings do not add.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, classify each of the five repeat-visit causes as a prediction, generation, ranking or classification problem, or as none of these. What share of the ₹68 lakh falls in each group?
  2. What does Exhibit 2 tell you about whether Option B is ready to be built today? Which field would you fix first, and what would it cost the business to wait?
  3. Option A is the most impressive and Option C the least. Why might the board rank them in that order, and what would persuade you that Option A solves a problem Gulmohar actually has?
  4. If you were Gauri, which option or sequence would you put to the board on 23 October, and what evidence would you promise to bring back by January?

8. A note for the learner

The lens here is problem–model fit: before asking which model, ask whether the problem is prediction, generation, ranking or classification at all, or whether it is a design and operations problem that no model will solve. Exhibit 1 does most of the work. Cause by cause, only the parts line is a clean prediction task, and misdiagnosis could be a classification task, with photographs only as one input. Absent customers, overruns and a free-text booking form are rule or process failures. In money terms, 40 per cent plus 20 per cent of the ₹68 lakh is ₹40.8 lakh that could possibly benefit from a model, while ₹27.2 lakh cannot.

A well-reasoned answer therefore starts with Option C, because its cost is smallest, its payback is 2.3 months and it can be in the field before Diwali. It also improves the data: a fixed fault picklist creates the labels Option B needs. After Option C, the parts cause falls from 2,720 to 2,040 repeat visits. A classifier on the residual then saves 40 per cent of 2,040, which is 816 visits, or ₹8.16 lakh a quarter, a payback of about 16.5 months on ₹45 lakh. That is still sound, but it should wait until the picklist has produced a quarter of clean data and the parts-used field is compulsory at closure.

Option A should be deferred, not rejected. At ₹180 lakh against ₹27.2 lakh a year it fails the economics today and rests on the weakest data in Exhibit 2. Gauri can still give Uday a story: fix the process now, predict the part next, and revisit a customer-facing assistant when clean data shows a diagnostic gap a photograph can close. The sequence is defensible because each step buys the evidence and the data that the next step needs, and because the first costs less than a fifth of the board’s original request.
exp20v2-aipm.problem.fit:
Problem–model fit

Is this a prediction, generation, ranking or classification problem, or none of them?

1. The pre-authorisation queue

On Monday 13 April 2026, Charulata Bhattacharjee, head of product at Ujjwal Claims Cloud, opened the quarterly review with one slide and one number. Ujjwal, a Pune-based administrator of cashless health claims, sat between forty hospitals and three insurers. Each month it received about 12,000 pre-authorisation requests: a hospital asks whether the insurer will pay for a planned admission, and a reviewer at Ujjwal answers. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) expects cashless decisions within an hour. In March, 31 per cent of Ujjwal's requests took longer than four hours. That is 3,720 patients waiting.

The chief executive, Chinmay Deshpande, had already decided what he wanted. Having watched a competitor demonstrate a language model that wrote decision letters, he asked for an "AI claims agent" by the September quarter, with ₹1.8 crore of engineering budget for the year. If the money went to the wrong kind of system, Ujjwal would have an impressive demo, no faster reviewers and possibly disputed approvals.

Charulata did not doubt that the problem was real. What she doubted was the sentence "use AI". Her data scientist, Uttam Kulshreshtha, put it precisely: "A model is a machine for one kind of output. We have not yet said which kind we need." The argument that follows runs one way: a problem has a shape, a model has an output shape, and value depends on whether they match and what a mismatch costs.

Fact (March 2026)Figure
Pre-authorisation requests per month12,000
Requests decided after four hours (31 per cent)3,720
Average reviewer time per request18 minutes
Loaded cost of a reviewer hour₹300
Engineering budget for the year₹1.8 crore

Exhibit 1. The starting position at Ujjwal Claims Cloud. Source: internal queue logs, as reported to the review.

2. The idea

Problem–model fit is the discipline of establishing, before any building begins, what kind of answer the problem needs and whether a machine-learning model of that kind can supply it economically. A model here means a function learned from examples rather than written by hand: it takes an input, such as a claim, and returns an output, such as a number. The output comes in a small number of shapes, and each shape defines a family of problems.

A prediction problem asks for a number or a future value: how many days will this patient stay, how many requests arrive next Tuesday. A classification problem asks for one label from a fixed list: routine or complex, genuine or suspect. A ranking problem asks for an order: which of the 400 waiting requests should a reviewer open first. A generation problem asks for new content: a letter, a summary, a draft reply. A fifth answer, unglamorous and often correct, is that the problem is none of these: it is a rule, a process change, a missing form field, or a decision that needs human judgement and not a statistical estimate.

The vocabulary predates the current enthusiasm: statisticians separated regression from classification in the early twentieth century, and information-retrieval researchers formalised ranking from the 1960s. The habit of asking the question first is younger, and comes from practice: product teams found that projects failed less from weak algorithms than from a mismatch between what was asked and what the model returned.

The sentence Charulata could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "Tell me what the output is, who acts on it, and what happens when it is wrong." The output fixes the model family, and the cost of error fixes whether the idea is worth building.

Read the figure from the top. Most conversations start at the bottom, with a model already chosen, and work backwards to a problem that seems to justify it. The tree runs the other way, and a single business problem, slow decisions, turns out to contain several branches.

3. How it works in practice

Charulata's team walked the queue through six steps, most of which practitioners perform in their heads, which is why they are skipped.

First, name the decision, not the topic. "Claims are slow" is a topic; "which requests can be approved without a doctor reading them?" is a decision. Second, write the output as a data type: here, one of two labels, so classification. Third, identify the actor and the action. This label lets a request skip the reviewer entirely, a strong action.

Fourth, price the two kinds of error. A wrong approval leaks money; a needless referral wastes reviewer minutes. They rarely cost the same, and only a person can tell the model so. Fifth, check that labels exist. Ujjwal had 26 months of decisions, but they recorded what reviewers chose, not what was correct. Sixth, compare against the baseline, which is not "no system" but the cheapest thing that would work, such as a rule or a form change.

StepQuestionUjjwal's answer
1What is the decision?Can this request skip clinical review?
2What is the output?One label: routine or needs review
3Who acts, and how?The system approves; no reviewer sees it
4What does each error cost?Wrong approval: leakage. Needless review: 18 minutes
5Do trustworthy labels exist?Partly: reviewer decisions, not verified outcomes
6What is the cheap baseline?A rule on package code and amount

Exhibit 3. The six implicit steps, applied to the pre-authorisation queue.

4. A worked example, line by line

Uttam trained a classifier on the 26 months of history and tested it on a month of 12,000 requests. Of these, 7,200 were routine (60 per cent) and 4,800 needed genuine clinical review (40 per cent). The model was set to approve automatically only when confident. It approved 5,760 of the 7,200 routine requests, an 80 per cent capture. It also approved 240 of the 4,800 requests that needed review, a 5 per cent miss. In total it auto-approved 5,760 + 240 = 6,000 requests, and sent the other 6,000 to reviewers.

Two headline metrics follow. Precision of the approve label is 5,760 ÷ 6,000 = 96 per cent. Overall accuracy is 5,760 approved routine plus 4,560 review cases sent onward (4,800 − 240), so 10,320 of 12,000, or 86 per cent.

Each automatic approval saves an 18-minute review. Across 6,000 requests that is 108,000 minutes, or 1,800 hours, worth 1,800 × ₹300 = ₹5,40,000 a month, or ₹5.40 lakh. Each wrongly approved request that needed review leaks money. Finance estimated the average leakage at ₹12,000 per case, so 240 × ₹12,000 = ₹28,80,000, or ₹28.80 lakh. The month's net effect is ₹5.40 lakh minus ₹28.80 lakh, a loss of ₹23.40 lakh, from a model that is 96 per cent precise.

Now change one input. Suppose approvals can be reversed cheaply because Ujjwal audits a sample after payment and recovers most of the leakage, cutting the net cost of a wrong approval from ₹12,000 to ₹1,200. The savings are unchanged at ₹5.40 lakh, but the leakage falls to 240 × ₹1,200 = ₹2,88,000, or ₹2.88 lakh, and the net becomes ₹5.40 lakh minus ₹2.88 lakh, a gain of ₹2.52 lakh. The break-even cost of one wrong approval is ₹5,40,000 ÷ 240 = ₹2,250. Above that figure, this model loses money at this threshold, however good its accuracy sounds.

Exhibit 4. Same model, same threshold, one input changed. Net = savings minus cost of wrong approvals.

5. The nuances a learner must become aware of

Accuracy is not fit

Ujjwal's model was 86 per cent accurate, yet approving everything would score 60 per cent and referring everything 40. Accuracy compares a model with nothing in particular; fit compares it with the decision's economics.

The same problem has several shapes

Slow decisions can be attacked as classification (approve or refer), ranking (most urgent first), prediction (forecast volume to roster reviewers) or generation (draft the hospital query). Each has different data needs and error costs, and choosing among them is the real product decision.

Ranking forgives what classification punishes

A ranker never makes a final decision; a human still reads every request, in a better order. A wrong rank costs minutes, not ₹12,000. Converting a classification problem into a ranking one often keeps most of the value.

Labels record decisions, not truth

Ujjwal's history held what reviewers chose, fatigue and inconsistency included. A model trained on it learns to imitate reviewers, not to be right.

Sometimes the answer is a rule

Uttam found that 31 per cent of the most delayed requests lacked a mandatory document field. The hospital portal needed a required field, not a model. If the logic fits in a sentence, write it.

What fit cannot tell you

Fit says a model of some shape can address the problem. It does not say users will trust it, the data is legally usable, or the organisation will change its process.

6. How it differs by product type and stage

In a consumer product errors are small and spread thinly, so ranking dominates. In a B2B product like Ujjwal's, each error is attributed to a named customer, often with a penalty, so the human stays in the loop. In a marketplace ranking must be fair between two sides: whose interest does the order serve?

Stage matters as much. An early-stage company has few labelled examples, so the honest answer is often a rule or a hosted generation service. A large company can afford a purpose-built classifier, but carries exposure that makes each automated approval dearer.

7. Common mistakes

Starting from the model. Symptom: a demo with no named user and no error cost. Misunderstanding: capability is a reason to build. Diagnostic: ask for the output as a data type and the person who acts on it.

Quoting accuracy. Symptom: a launch note with one percentage and no baseline. Misunderstanding: a high number implies value. Diagnostic: a two-line table of trivial-strategy score and error costs, as in Exhibit 4.

Treating generation as the default. Symptom: a language model choosing between three options, with variable results and a large bill. Misunderstanding: the most general tool is safest. Diagnostic: try a rule and a small classifier on fifty cases.

Forcing a model onto a process defect. Symptom: the model improves but the delay never falls. Misunderstanding: every delay is a prediction gap. Diagnostic: read twenty delayed cases end to end and count the human or form causes.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version starts with a one-page brief before any engineering request. It names the decision, gives the output as a data type, names the actor, prices both errors from finance's numbers, and states the cheap baseline. It shows at least three candidate shapes and commits to the least risky first, with a threshold set from the cost of error.

Above all, it is specific enough that an insurer's medical director could argue with it.

9. What Charulata decided

On 27 April she took three proposals to Chinmay. The first, a rule, made two document fields mandatory on the hospital portal; it cost almost nothing and addressed the 31 per cent of delayed requests with missing fields. The second was a ranking model to order the queue by urgency, with every request still read by a doctor. The third, the automatic approval classifier, she held back, showing him Exhibit 4: at ₹12,000 a wrong approval it lost ₹23.40 lakh a month, and it would pay only once the cost of an error fell towards ₹2,250. The letter-writing agent she reframed as a later drafting aid for reviewers.

His first reaction was disappointment; the agent had been the point. She held her ground with the sentence from section 2 and arithmetic he could check. He released ₹42 lakh for the first two and kept the rest of the ₹1.8 crore in reserve, because the ranking model matched the real bottleneck, kept a human accountable and could fail cheaply.

To judge whether a model like Uttam's works, study model metrics: precision, recall and area under the curve. To see how ranking is built, read recommendation systems. To turn a fit decision into a product, study AI product design choices and the machine-learning lifecycle; to ask whether a model deserves trust, evals.

Two questions to sit with. First: pick a product you know well and write its main problem as an output data type, an actor and an error cost. Does your first instinct for the solution still stand? Second: in the Ujjwal case, the break-even error cost was ₹2,250 per wrong approval. Who in your organisation actually knows what a wrong output costs, and have they ever been asked?

Ekatra Sourcing Exchange: Who Decides What "Good" Means?

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday 5 October 2026, Devika Narayanan, chief product officer of Ekatra Sourcing Exchange, opened a spreadsheet she had requested on Thursday and received late on Saturday. It had 600 rows, one for each real seller-support conversation, and a column recording whether the company's AI assistant had answered correctly. A week earlier the vendor behind the assistant's language model had offered a newer and cheaper model, advertised at 94 per cent accuracy, and asked for a signed twelve-month commitment by Friday 9 October. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, and the heaviest weeks of supplier payouts would begin well before it. Devika had five days to decide whether the new model went live, and on what evidence.

2. Company background

Ekatra Sourcing Exchange was founded in Pune in 2016. It connects 38,000 manufacturers and wholesalers with 6,50,000 small retailers and handled gross merchandise value of about ₹2,400 crore in the last financial year. It competes for the same retailers as Udaan, IndiaMART and Jumbotail, and it has begun listing selected catalogues on the ONDC network. Its edge is speed: suppliers are paid within two working days of delivery.

Because suppliers live on those payouts, they ask a great many questions about them. In February 2026 Ekatra launched an AI assistant to answer supplier queries in Hindi, English and Hinglish on payouts, GST invoices and tax deducted at source, returns and disputes, catalogue listings, and KYC. It now handles 4,00,000 conversations a month. Anything it cannot resolve passes to a human team of 60 agents in Indore.

3. The situation

The assistant had been judged since launch by containment, the share of chats that never reached a human. Containment rewards a confident answer whether or not it is right, and it would look much the same for either model. Nobody had written down what a good answer was.

The vendor's offer changed that. The new model would cost ₹1.90 per conversation against ₹3.20 today, and Dhruv Malhotra, the chief financial officer, had already put the saving in the board pack: 4,00,000 conversations at ₹1.90 is ₹7.60 lakh a month, against ₹12.80 lakh now, a gap of ₹5.20 lakh a month or ₹62.4 lakh a year. The vendor's 94 per cent came from a public benchmark of general questions, mostly in English.

Devika therefore asked Eshaan Kulkarni's team in Pune to draw 600 real conversations from the past quarter, in the proportions in which suppliers actually ask, and to run both models on them. Farah Siddiqui's senior agents in Indore labelled every answer correct or not. "Correct" was defined narrowly: right, complete, and safe for a supplier to act on without a second contact. Exhibit 1 shows the result.

Read as a single number, the sample favoured the new model: 88.0 per cent against 86.5. Read by type, it told a different story. The first two rows, payouts and GST, are the conversations where a wrong answer costs a supplier money. They make up 300 of the 600 cases. There the current model was right on 264 (88.0 per cent) and the new one on 249 (83.0 per cent). The other 300 cases went the opposite way, 255 correct (85.0 per cent) against 279 (93.0 per cent).

Faith Wanjiru, who leads customer success from Nairobi, two and a half hours behind Pune, looks after Ekatra's export suppliers and had been receiving their payout complaints overnight, when the Indore team was offline. She feared that any wrong settlement answer would reach her accounts hours before anyone could correct it.

4. The people

Devika Narayanan, Bengaluru, chief product officer, owns the assistant and must recommend. She wants a decision she can defend to the board and to suppliers.

Eshaan Kulkarni, Pune, head of machine learning, prefers the new model on engineering grounds and would like to ship it within the month. He notes that 600 cases is a small sample.

Farah Siddiqui, Indore, head of seller support, leads the human team that absorbs every wrong answer. She wants no change to payout and GST answers before Diwali.

Dhruv Malhotra, Mumbai, chief financial officer, wants the ₹62.4 lakh saving. He has asked, fairly, how much a wrong answer actually costs.

5. The cost of being wrong

Farah answered Dhruv's question with her team's records. A wrong payout or GST answer costs about ₹140 once the second contact, goodwill credit and finance-operations time are counted. A wrong answer elsewhere costs about ₹38, the price of one agent contact. Half the 4,00,000 monthly conversations, 2,00,000, are payout or GST queries, and the other half are not. Exhibit 3 applies the sample's error rates to that volume. The third column anticipates Option C below, in which each model handles only the queries where it did better.

The figures overturn the headline. Switching everything saves ₹5.20 lakh in fees and ₹6.08 lakh in cheaper errors elsewhere, but adds ₹14.00 lakh of costlier errors on payouts and GST, so the company would spend ₹2.72 lakh more each month, ₹32.64 lakh over a year. The routed arrangement saves ₹8.68 lakh a month, about ₹1.04 crore a year. Eshaan's caution still applies: with 300 cases per half, each percentage carries a margin of roughly four points either way, so the payout gap is suggestive rather than proven.

6. The options

Option A: sign the twelve-month deal for all traffic. The upside is the visible ₹62.4 lakh annual fee saving, better answers on returns and listings,. The cost, per Exhibit 3, is a net monthly loss of ₹2.72 lakh and a worse experience for suppliers at their most anxious moment, just before Diwali.

Option B: decline and stay on the current model. The upside is no risk to payout answers and a calm festive season. The cost is forgoing the ₹8.68 lakh monthly saving that routing offers, and leaving suppliers' returns questions at 80.0 per cent correct when 90.0 is available.

Option C: sign a three-month term and route by query type, under a written quality gate. The new model takes returns, catalogue, KYC and other queries immediately. Payout and GST queries stay on the current model until the new one meets a threshold Devika sets. The upside is most of the saving at little risk; the costs are about ₹4.5 lakh to build the router, roughly ₹1.2 lakh of agent time to double the golden set, and a vendor who must accept a shorter term.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Why did containment fail to show the difference between the models, and what would "good" have meant at Ekatra before the sample existed?
  2. Why does the 88.0 per cent overall figure mislead, and which cases deserve the heaviest weight?
  3. In Exhibit 3, which assumption would you test first, and how would a change in it move the ranking of the three columns?
  4. Whose job is it to set the payout threshold, Devika's or Eshaan's, and what should the other contribute?

8. A note for the learner

This case frames an eval as the product requirements document of an AI feature. A requirements document says what the product must do; an eval says, case by case, what a correct answer looks like. Someone must decide that definition, and it cannot be the model vendor, whose benchmark measures its own questions, nor the data scientist, who optimises whatever number is supplied. The definition rests on knowledge of suppliers and of what a wrong answer costs them. That knowledge sits with the product manager, which is why she owns it.

A well-reasoned answer separates the average from the distribution. Quality is not one number: the assistant is excellent in one place and poor in another, and an overall score hides which. It also weighs errors by consequence, as Farah's ₹140 and ₹38 do.

The defensible path is Option C. Devika should sign the three-month term, route returns, catalogue, KYC and other queries to the new model, and keep payout and GST on the current one. She should write the gate into the plan: the new model takes payout and GST traffic only if it scores at least 90 per cent on a doubled golden set of 1,200 real conversations that includes Hinglish and festive-season cases, re-run before each model change. Option A bets the festive season on a vendor's benchmark. Option B protects safety but ignores evidence that most of the saving is available at no added risk. Option C acts on what the sample proves and defers what it only suggests.

Evals: The PRD of an AI Product

Before a model ships, someone has to write down what "good" means. That someone is the product manager.

On the morning of 11 February 2026, Ananya Kulkarni pulled up a spreadsheet she had been avoiding for two weeks. Ananya was the product lead for Auto-Resolve, a feature inside Vachan Support Cloud, a Bengaluru-based helpdesk platform used by roughly 340 direct-to-consumer brands to run their WhatsApp and email support queues. Auto-Resolve used a large language model to read an incoming ticket, decide whether it could answer without a human, and, if so, send a reply and close the ticket on its own. For six weeks it had run in a supervised pilot with eleven customers, auto-drafting replies a human agent still had to approve before anything went out. The pilot had gone well enough that the growth team wanted to flip a switch: let Auto-Resolve send replies for a defined slice of tickets with no human in the loop, starting with four customers and a plan to widen it within the quarter.

The spreadsheet was supposed to answer one question before Ananya agreed to flip that switch: how good, exactly, was the model at this task, and how would anyone know if it got worse next month. Her engineering lead, Rohit Bhandari, had sent a dashboard showing the model's replies were approved by human agents 91% of the time during the pilot. Ananya's worry was that 91% approved was not 91% good. Agents were tired, the queue was long, and "approve" mostly meant "did not obviously embarrass us," not "resolved the problem, matched our refund policy, and used a tone we'd stand behind." If Vachan auto-sent to real customers on the strength of that number and it was measuring the wrong thing, the company would find out from a spike in complaints, not from a chart. Ananya's task was to define, precisely enough that an engineer could check a new model version against it in twenty minutes, what "a good reply" meant at Vachan. That definition is called an eval, and writing it was her job, not Rohit's.

The idea, defined plainly

An eval, short for evaluation, is a fixed, repeatable test that scores a model's outputs against a standard of quality a human has deliberately chosen, so "is this good enough" stops being opinion and becomes a number anyone can reproduce. An eval has three parts: a set of representative inputs the model will actually see (a "golden set"), a rule or a second judge that decides whether each output is acceptable (a "grader" or "rubric"), and a threshold for how good is good enough to ship. Run the same eval against two model versions and you get two comparable scores. Without it, a team compares anecdotes: "the new version felt smarter in the two examples I tried," which is not evidence, it is a mood. The term entered mainstream product vocabulary between roughly 2020 and 2023, as language models moved from research benchmarks — fixed academic test sets like SQuAD for reading comprehension or GLUE for general language understanding, built by university labs in 2016–2018 — into products where the question was no longer academic but "will this specific business logic hold up." OpenAI's teams, building GPT-3 and then InstructGPT, popularized "eval" for exactly this shift: a small, versioned test suite a team trusted more than its own impression of an output. The idea it borrowed from was older and mundane: engineers have run automated regression tests before every release since the 1990s, so a change to one part of a codebase does not silently break another. An eval is that discipline applied to a system whose logic lives in billions of learned parameters rather than in lines a person can inspect. The one sentence Ananya could say without sounding glib: an eval is the executable definition of "good" for this model, written before we ship it, not argued about after a customer complains.

This is why an eval is often called the PRD of an AI feature. A traditional requirements document tells engineers what to build and how to know it is done. A model takes no such document as input; it takes examples, human judgments, and a threshold. If the PM does not specify what counts as a correct, on-brand, policy-compliant reply, nobody else is positioned to make that call — not the engineer, who can only say the system runs, and not the data scientist, who can only say the loss went down. Only the PM sits close enough to the customer to say what "resolved" means here.

How an eval actually gets built

Building an eval for Auto-Resolve took Ananya and Rohit five steps, several of which teams skip in practice — usually the ones that feel like extra work with no visible payoff until something breaks. First, they pulled a representative sample of real tickets — not the easy ones, and not a hand-picked set that flattered the model, but a stratified sample of 400 tickets from the prior month, drawn proportionally across shipping delays, refund requests, product defects, and general questions. A golden set that is 80% easy "where is my order" questions produces a score meaningless for the 20% of tickets that carry real risk. Second, they wrote a rubric: what made a reply acceptable — correct facts (no invented tracking numbers or policy), correct policy (refund windows and escalation triggers matched the specific customer's actual stated policy, not a generic one), and correct tone (nothing dismissive toward a frustrated customer). This is the step most often left implicit: engineers frequently grade against whatever labels already exist, without a PM first writing down what the categories mean and where their edges sit. Third, two trained human raters independently scored a sample of 80 replies against the rubric, pass or fail, and Ananya checked how often the two agreed. Fourth, once agreement was high enough to trust, they built an automated grader — a second, larger language model prompted with the rubric to score replies the way a trained human would, a technique called "LLM-as-judge," spot-checked regularly against fresh human ratings so it did not quietly drift. Fifth, they set a threshold and a slicing plan: not one number for "the model," but a pass rate per category, since a model excellent at shipping questions and mediocre at refunds should not auto-send refunds just because its blended average looks fine.

The arithmetic, worked through

Ananya's 400-ticket golden set broke down as 160 shipping-delay tickets, 120 refund-request tickets, 80 product-defect tickets, and 40 general questions. Running the current model version through the grader produced the pass rates in Table 1.

CategoryTicketsPassed rubricPass rate
Shipping delay16015295.0%
Refund request1209075.0%
Product defect806885.0%
General question403997.5%
Blended40034987.25%

The blended figure, 87.25%, sits close enough to Rohit's original 91% that it might look like confirmation. But the category breakdown tells a different story: refund requests — the category with the most financial and legal exposure, where getting the window wrong means an unauthorized charge-back or a wrongly refused refund — pass only 75% of the time, nowhere near Ananya's working threshold of 90%. Trusting the blended number would have approved auto-send across the board; the sliced number told her to auto-send shipping and general questions immediately, hold defects for two more weeks, and keep refunds fully human-reviewed. Now the second pass: what happens when one input changes. Rohit's team retrained the refund logic to pull the customer's actual stated policy from a structured field rather than letting the model infer it from ticket text, and reran the same 120 tickets through the identical grader. Passes rose from 90 to 111, moving the pass rate from 75.0% to 92.5% — a genuine gain, verifiable because everything else held constant. That is the discipline in miniature: change one thing, hold the test fixed, and the number tells you honestly whether the change helped, rather than trusting Rohit's impression that "it feels better now."

What a learner needs to sit with

An eval is not the same thing as a benchmark

A benchmark, like the academic test sets above, measures a model's general capability on a standardized task, the same for every company using it. An eval is specific to one product's definition of success, built from that product's own data and rubric. A model can score brilliantly on a public summarization benchmark and still fail Vachan's eval, which checks whether the reply matches a specific customer's refund policy — a thing no public benchmark has heard of.

A high pass rate is not the same as a safe threshold

87% sounds high in isolation. Whether it is safe depends on the cost of the 13% that fails and the volume flowing through: at Vachan's roughly 9,000 tickets a month, that failure rate was over a thousand mishandled replies monthly if applied everywhere — why the category-level threshold, not the blended one, should gate a launch.

Human agreement must be checked before trusting the automated grader

An LLM-as-judge grader is only as good as its correlation with what trained humans would say. Teams often skip measuring that correlation, quietly reintroducing the unreliability the eval was built to remove.

An eval measures the distribution it was built from, not the world

Vachan's golden set came from the prior month's tickets. If a new product line launches next quarter with a different return policy, the eval keeps reporting a healthy score on old ticket types while saying nothing about the new one.

A pass/fail threshold hides how badly something failed

A rubric that only records pass or fail treats a reply that was 90% right and one that fabricated a nonexistent policy identically. Ananya's team later added a severity tag — cosmetic, policy-adjacent, fabricated — after one badly fabricated reply hid inside an otherwise reassuring pass rate.

Evals go stale the moment the product, policy, or model changes

A model provider ships a new version every few months; Vachan's own return policy shifts with the festive season. An eval run once at launch and never rerun is a snapshot of a world that no longer exists.

An eval cannot tell you whether the task should be automated at all

Even a model that passes every rubric item can be the wrong choice if customers in a segment simply prefer, or are legally entitled to, a human response — a judgment the score cannot make, since it only measures "assuming we automate this, is the output good."

A vendor's eval score is not the same as your eval score

Model providers publish their own results, run on their own golden sets, graded by their own rubrics. A vendor's claimed 95% accuracy on support tasks says nothing about Vachan's specific refund edge cases until Vachan runs its own eval on its own data.

"An eval is the executable definition of 'good,' written before we ship — not argued about after a customer complains."

Consumer, B2B, and marketplace, early-stage and large

Vachan's product is B2B: a wrong reply is visible to one paying customer's queue, which makes category-level thresholds and manual failure review economically sensible, since volume per customer is modest. In a high-volume consumer product — a shopping assistant answering millions of queries a day — the golden set must be far larger and grading must lean much more heavily on automation, since no review team can keep pace; scrutiny shifts from individual outputs to statistical monitoring of the aggregate over time. In a marketplace product, the eval must account for two audiences at once — a model that writes a compelling listing for a seller can still fail a buyer-facing accuracy standard, so a marketplace eval typically needs two rubrics scored on the same output. Early-stage companies, lacking labeled data or rater headcount for the full five-step process, often start lighter: a founder hand-scoring twenty to fifty examples before every release, a real eval, just a small one, and considerably better than shipping on vibes. Larger companies invest in standing infrastructure — versioned golden sets, a trained rater panel, automated regression runs on every model or prompt change — because at scale, an unnoticed three-point drop in pass rate is thousands of bad interactions before anyone notices.

Common mistakes

Grading on convenience, not the rubric that matters. The symptom is a dashboard that looks reassuring until a complaint reveals a category no one was measuring. The error is letting whatever labels already exist define the eval, instead of a PM deciding first what to measure. The cheapest diagnostic: ask whoever built the eval to name the three ticket types most likely to embarrass the company, and check the golden set has enough of each. Treating a blended average as a launch gate. The symptom is a team approving a rollout on one headline number, as Vachan nearly did at 87.25%. The error is averaging away exactly the categories where failure is most costly. The cheapest diagnostic: always ask for the worst-performing slice, not the average, before approving anything. Never rerunning the eval after the first launch. The symptom is a team that can no longer explain why quality quietly degraded over a quarter. The error is treating the eval as a one-time artifact rather than a living regression suite. The cheapest diagnostic: check when the golden set was last refreshed; if it predates the last product or policy change, the score is already stale. Letting engineering own the definition of "good" by default. The symptom is a rubric built entirely around what was easy to grade programmatically, with no traceable link to what the customer cares about. The error is a PM assuming evals are a technical artifact rather than a product decision in technical clothing. The cheapest diagnostic: ask the PM, without notes, to state the pass criteria for the highest-risk category; if they cannot, the eval was never really theirs.

What good looks like

Six weeks after the retrained refund logic pushed that category's pass rate to 92.5%, Ananya brought a different proposal to the same room. Instead of "we're ready to turn it on," she brought a table: current pass rate per category, the threshold required before auto-send, and a rerun schedule tied to every model or policy update. Shipping and general questions were live already, refunds crossed the threshold that week and joined them, and product defects stayed on human review with a dated plan to revisit once the labeling issue behind most failures was fixed. Nobody argued about whether the feature "felt" ready — the eval had already answered the question the meeting used to spend an hour debating, and what was left to debate was the threshold itself, a genuine risk decision, exactly the kind a PM is meant to own.

Closing

Ananya approved auto-send for shipping, general questions, and, as of that week, refunds — each backed by a category-level pass rate above 90%, each rerun after the model or policy changed, and each with severity-tagged failures reviewed weekly rather than folded into one reassuring average. Product defects stayed human-reviewed, not because the model was unusably bad at them, but because 85% was not yet good enough for a category where a wrong answer left a customer stuck with a broken product and no recourse. What she had built was not a one-time test but a standing instrument the team would keep consulting every time the model, policy, or product changed under it. The natural next step is to learn how a team turns raw production traffic into that golden set in the first place, and how a PM works day to day with the data scientists and ML engineers who build the graders — since authorship of the eval stays with the PM even when its automation does not. Two questions worth sitting with: if your team shipped an AI feature tomorrow with no eval at all, what number would you actually be trusting instead, and where did it come from? And for a feature you already know well, what failure is a blended average currently hiding from you?
