Nirmiti Vision Works: The Definition of a Defect

1. Sunday night, Baner

At twenty minutes to eleven on the night of Sunday 4 October 2026, Meghana Thipsay was still at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, with two spreadsheets open: the field reconciliation her team had finished nine days earlier, and the offline score sheet her machine-learning lead had sent on 7 September, the day he declared the new model ready. Each told a coherent story. They did not match.

Meghana was vice-president of product at Nirmiti Vision Works and owned Nigah, the camera-and-model station that sat on twenty-two production lines at five customer plants and decided, some forty times a minute across them, whether a forged or machined part was fit to pass. In nine hours she would tell her board whether Nigah's next model should be deployed. On Thursday she would face the quality head of her largest customer, who had spent the week computing numbers Nirmiti had never reported, and had not said what she meant to do with them.

What she could not put on a slide was what bothered her most: nobody at either company had ever agreed in writing what counted as a defect.

2. How Nirmiti got here

Narayan Ketkar founded Nirmiti Vision Works in Pune in 2019, after eleven years in process engineering at a Tier-1 supplier. The pitch was simple: plants inspected visually at the end of the line, the inspectors good but tired, and a camera that never blinked could sit upstream. In FY26 Nirmiti reported revenue of ₹58 crore. Nigah carried ₹16.4 crore of recurring revenue across 63 plants and 41 customers, priced per part inspected — ₹0.28 to ₹1.10 by part class — plus ₹1.8 lakh per line a year.

One decision from that period still shaped everything. In November 2024, bidding against machine-vision incumbents Indian Tier-1s had bought from for two decades, Nirmiti needed to win Mandara Auto Industries. Mandara's purchasing could not score a bid on anything it could not reduce to one comparable figure, and asked for accuracy. Narayan agreed: 98 per cent inspection accuracy, measured monthly per plant as correct decisions divided by parts inspected, with the reject rate capped at 3 per cent of parts inspected, and 12 per cent of the quarterly invoice held back on breach. The clause became the template for every Nigah contract since. Meghana, then a senior product manager, argued for a guarantee on escapes instead. She lost: escapes were harder to measure, and the rival had offered a number.

3. The industry around it

India's auto component industry, which ACMA puts at well over ₹6 lakh crore of annual turnover, had spent three years absorbing the production-linked incentive scheme, electrification and the demands of exporting. Tata Motors, Mahindra, Bajaj Auto, Hero MotoCorp, TVS and Ather all bought from plants within three hours of Pune, and all ran annual price-downs. IATF 16949 governed how a Tier-1 answered for a part that should not have shipped.

Two forces bore on Nirmiti directly. Its customers' customers were increasingly foreign: Mandara shipped a brake-component family to a Japanese two-wheeler maker whose quality office in Osaka, three and a half hours ahead of Pune, capped incoming defects at 150 parts per million. And talent was dear: its engineers could earn more at Zoho, Freshworks or Postman, and its one senior data scientist worked from Warsaw, three and a half hours behind Pune, on a contract expiring 31 December.

4. What happened, and what was believed

In January 2026 Meghana's team built the evaluation set everything since has rested on. Named Maapdand, it held 4,000 part images, all from Mandara's Chakan plant, enriched so that 1,200 of them — 30 per cent — were defective, a set at the true 1.2 per cent rate having little to learn from. Labelling fell to Manjula Hegde's eleven-person team in Hubballi, working to a one-page defect definition Meghana approved in four days to hold the February launch. The page listed six defect families but not what to do with a part that was arguably acceptable, and a line in the training document, author unidentified, told annotators to mark ambiguous parts acceptable.

Nigah v3 went live on nine Chakan lines in February 2026, scoring 93.3 per cent on Maapdand, and through the spring reached Ojhar Forge Works in Nashik, Nilgiri Fastener Works in Coimbatore, Nandur Pressings Industries in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar and Mahuli Castings Industries in Rajkot. The monthly report to each customer showed group accuracy above 98 per cent, and nobody asked for it plant by plant.

In July, under its own price-down pressure, Mandara changed the supplier of its forged blanks. The change went through sourcing; quality was told, Nirmiti was not. The new blanks brought a defect family the Chakan rig was never set up to see — sub-surface porosity, a faint shadow at an angle the January lighting did not use. Maapdand held 60 examples, 5 per cent of its defective parts.

Escape reports from Chakan rose through August. The theory, held three weeks, was calibration drift; recalibrating every station changed nothing. On 7 September Nachiket Dharwadkar's team shipped a v4 candidate with a new backbone and heavier augmentation, scoring 94.2 per cent on Maapdand against v3's 93.3. From 14 to 25 September Omkar Bhave's team reconciled all five plants (Exhibit 1), and 600 parts were labelled twice, by Hubballi and by Mandara's panel (Exhibit 3). On 28 September Mandara's quality head requested Chakan's raw decision logs under the contract's data clause, computed accuracy line by line, and found three of the nine lines below 98 per cent, the worst at 96.8. Prompted by that, Meghana's team computed accuracy plant by plant for the first time, and found three of five below the floor. On 30 September the quality council agenda arrived with item four: Nigah performance and renewal.

Figure 1. Twenty-three months from contract to board meeting.

5. The people

Meghana Thipsay, 41, vice-president of product, Pune. Must recommend on Monday; wants the renewal and the better model. She has told nobody that she approved the one-page defect definition herself, in four days, to hold a launch.

Narayan Ketkar, founder and chief executive, Pune. Wants v4 shipped and the renewal signed this quarter; he signed the 98 per cent clause and treats it as commercial detail. He has not told the product team that a Series B term sheet is in circulation, and a disclosed breach would reopen its pricing.

Nachiket Dharwadkar, head of machine learning, Bengaluru. Argues v4 is strictly better and should go live in the shutdown week; his quarterly objective is Maapdand accuracy and his bonus follows it. He has not volunteered that most of v4's gain sits in cheap families.

Oindrila Basu, senior data scientist, Warsaw. Holds that neither spreadsheet can support a decision, the set no longer resembling the plants. Her contract ends on 31 December. She believes the labels, not the model, are the binding constraint, and has written that only in a chat Nachiket has not opened.

Omkar Bhave, head of field engineering, at Chakan. Opposes any model change before the shutdown; his four operators absorb every false reject and he has no headcount. He has not escalated that two plants have run Nigah in advisory mode since 12 August, their flags being recommendations an operator may overrule.

Nandini Sridharan, head of customer success, Chennai. Wants everything put before Mandara on Thursday, with a jointly written defect taxonomy; renewals are her number. She has been told informally that Mandara's quality function has invited a rival bid, and has not passed it on.

Murtaza Rangwala, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Holds that finance's standard non-conformance rate is the right price for an escape, and on it v4 does not pay. He has already shown the board an FY27 plan carrying Mandara's two-plant expansion as committed revenue.

Niloufer Dastur, head of quality, Mandara Auto Industries, Chakan. Will not renew on a single accuracy number again; she wants escape guarantees by defect family. Her IATF audit falls in January and an escape reaching Osaka is her exposure. She has not told her management that her panel disagrees with Nirmiti's labels a fifth of the time, or with itself.

7. Voices

Murtaza Rangwala, board pre-read:

On the rate we have used since FY24, v4 raises Chakan's monthly cost by ₹2.18 lakh. I cannot recommend a change justified only by a rate two and a half times ours, produced by customer success last week.

Oindrila Basu to Nachiket, 29 September, 7.14 pm Warsaw:

We project v4's field performance by multiplying a field number by an offline ratio. That holds only if the offline mix matches the field. It does not: 47 per cent of September's escapes are a family with sixty examples in the set. We are not measuring the model, we are measuring January.

Niloufer Dastur to Nandini, 30 September:

Three of the nine lines at Chakan are under the committed accuracy, and the plant looks compliant only because the other six carry them. I am not invoking the holdback; ₹1.39 lakh is not my concern. I want to know how a station decides a part is good, because my auditors will ask me in January.

Omkar Bhave, 1 October:

Four people on the Chakan bench. v4 puts twenty-seven thousand parts a month on it. Either I get two more or the bench waves parts through, and your slide is fiction.

Manjula Hegde to Meghana, 25 September:

Ma'am, my team has been asking about shadow marks since April. The sheet says mark acceptable if unsure. They are following the sheet.

Narayan Ketkar, 3 October:

Ship the better model. Every week we debate this, the competitor is in Niloufer's office.

8. The options as Meghana sees them

A. Deploy v4 at all five plants in the shutdown week, 7 to 15 November, and renegotiate the accuracy clause afterwards. It cuts escapes fastest and is what the chief executive and machine-learning lead want, but breaches the accuracy floor and the reject cap everywhere on the day it goes live, and rests on a projection Oindrila calls unsupported.

B. Hold v3, rebuild Maapdand at ₹22.36 lakh over ten weeks, and decide in January. It is the only option that attacks the measurement problem, but leaves sub-surface porosity escaping through the festive season, overspends the ₹4.80 lakh left in the quarter, and, begun after the 8 October council, lands on 17 December, two weeks before Oindrila's contract expires.

C. Deploy v4 at Chakan only, in advisory mode, add two operators, and offer Mandara escape guarantees by defect family instead of the accuracy number. It gives Niloufer what she asked for, but spreads advisory mode, concedes the measured number was never right, and prices a guarantee on a quantity nobody can count to within 60 per cent.

Meghana had written all three on a page, and under them a line she had shown nobody: all three assume the question is which model. None changed who writes the defect definition, or how a change on Mandara's floor reaches Hubballi. A v5 trained on the same labels would be scored by the same set, which would again be right about January.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at nine on Monday 5 October and expects a recommendation this quarter. Mandara's quality council meets on Thursday 8 October, with the Chakan renewal worth ₹139.32 lakh over three years and the two-plant expansion worth ₹49.68 lakh a year at stake; Holdback exposure, if invoked, is ₹1.68 lakh for the quarter. The only production stoppage before January is the Diwali shutdown, 7 to 15 November; any change outside it stops a line. ₹4.80 lakh remains of the quarter's ₹14.00 lakh retraining budget, and Oindrila's contract expires on 31 December. The Osaka ceiling of 150 parts per million sits in Mandara's contract, not Nirmiti's.

Near midnight Meghana opened a blank slide, typed a title — Nigah: what we know — and stopped. She knew the number she had reported for eight months rested on a definition drafted in four days, labelled by a team told to resolve doubt in one direction, scored against a set from one plant in one month, and audited against a panel that disagreed with itself one time in five. What she did not know was whether to carry into Thursday a model, a number, or an admission.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 reports 97.94 per cent accuracy; Exhibit 2 reports 94.2 for the better model. Why do they differ, and which, if either, belongs in a customer report?
  2. Nigah's precision across the five plants is 42.4 per cent. Who bears that cost, and why has it not surfaced?
  3. Two expert panels agree on 81.3 per cent of parts. What does a contractual 98 per cent guarantee mean in that light, and what should Narayan have agreed to in 2024 instead?
  4. Exhibit 4 offers three escape counts and Exhibit 5 three prices for one. Which would you fix first, and how?
  5. Advisory mode at Nilgiri and Mahuli means part of Exhibit 1 measures recommendations, not outcomes. What else here measures something other than what its label claims?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Meghana recommend to the board, what does she say to Niloufer on Thursday, and which determines the other?

What Evals Are, and Why the PM Owns Them

An eval is not a test suite bolted on at the end. It is the specification, the roadmap and the launch gate of an AI product — and whoever writes it decides what the product becomes.

1. Two rooms, one week apart

On 3 March 2026, Meera Raghunathan had ten days to decide whether to swap the model underneath the most-used feature at Jhilmil Play. Jhilmil was a Bengaluru learning app — 4.1 million monthly actives, mostly Class 8 to 10 students, ₹149 a month — whose flagship feature, Samjhao, let a student photograph a maths problem and receive a worked explanation in English or Hindi. The proposal was to move Samjhao to a smaller model costing 38% less per call and answering twice as fast. On every public benchmark the vendor cited, it matched or beat the incumbent on grade-school mathematics.

Meera's problem was that Samjhao did not do grade-school mathematics. It read a blurry photograph of a handwritten sum in state-board notation, inferred which step the student had got stuck on, and explained it in language a fourteen-year-old would follow without feeling condescended to. No public benchmark measured any of that. Thumbs-up rates were 82%, but thumbs-up on a homework app measures relief as much as correctness; students rated an answer highly when it produced a number they could copy. The one instrument that could settle the question — a fixed set of real problems, a written standard for a good explanation, and a repeatable score — did not exist at Jhilmil in any form Meera trusted.

Two days later and eight hundred kilometres away, Arvind Menon was in a different version of the same room. Arvind ran product at Baaz Vision Systems, a Pune company selling a camera, an edge computer and a defect-detection model as one unit to auto-component plants. Sixty-one lines across fourteen plants ran on Baaz hardware, inspecting stamped and machined parts at roughly 90 parts a minute. Its contract with its largest customer, a tier-one supplier near Chakan, carried a clause: escapes — defective parts passed as good — were to stay below 0.5% of defective parts produced. On 12 March, Baaz planned to ship a hardware revision with a new sensor and lens, and with it a retrained model.

Arvind's team had a golden set: 8,400 labelled images collected over two years, on which the new model scored 95.4% against the incumbent's 93.1%. The number was real and, Arvind suspected, close to meaningless, because every image had been captured through the old lens on the old sensor. The eval measured a world the product was about to leave. Meera and Arvind faced one question in different clothing: what does "good" mean for this model, who is entitled to write it down, and what is a number worth when nobody can say what it is a number of.

2. The idea: a definition, a lineage, and four schools that disagree

An eval, stated precisely, is a four-part object: a dataset of inputs drawn from a defined population; a grader mapping each output to a score on a defined scale; an aggregation rule turning per-item scores into reported figures; and a decision rule converting those figures into an action — ship, hold, roll back, route to a human. Drop any one and you no longer have an eval. A dataset without a grader is a demo; a grader without a defined population is an anecdote generator; aggregation without a decision rule is a dashboard, a place where numbers go to be admired. The decision rule is what PMs most often omit and what makes the instrument load-bearing.

The lineage is older than large language models, and every argument practitioners have today was had before. Psychometrics came first: Cronbach and Meehl's 1955 paper on construct validity established that a test is valid not in the abstract but for an inference — a score means something only if you can state what unobservable quality it stands in for and show the correspondence holds. Information retrieval came second: Cleverdon's Cranfield experiments of the early 1960s produced the test-collection paradigm — fixed corpus, fixed queries, human relevance judgements, reproducible score — which became TREC in 1992 and remains the template for every golden set since. Machine translation came third, where BLEU (2002) introduced the now-dominant pattern of a cheap automatic proxy whose entire claim to legitimacy is a demonstrated correlation with human judgement. Software regression testing came fourth, contributing the discipline of running the same test on every change.

Public benchmarks — GLUE in 2018, HELM in 2022 — pushed the practice into the open and exposed its limits. By 2021, critics including Raji and colleagues argued that general benchmarks claimed construct validity they had never demonstrated. "Eval" entered product vocabulary around 2022 as the escape hatch from that critique — a team's own small, versioned test of its own definition of good, explicitly not a claim about the model in general.

Four schools disagree about what follows, and the disagreement is real rather than terminological. The measurement school, heir to Cranfield, holds that an eval must be frozen, versioned and statistically powered: it signs "no launch without a pre-registered threshold and a confidence interval," and refuses "a founder scoring twenty examples by hand is an eval." The experimentation school holds that offline scores are proxies for a proxy: it signs "let a randomised trial arbitrate," and refuses "a golden-set pass rate is sufficient evidence to launch." The error-analysis school, fastest-growing since about 2024, holds that rubrics must be induced bottom-up from failures: it signs "the PM reads a hundred failing traces before writing a rubric line," and refuses "buy a general eval suite and start scoring." The safety school holds that averages are the wrong object: it signs "one catastrophic failure fails the release regardless of the mean," and refuses "91% is better than 88%."

3. Mechanics: what the work actually consists of

Start where Meera started, with sampling. The naive move is to take the last thousand queries; the expert move is to define the population first and sample so the estimate can be reconstructed. Jhilmil's traffic split roughly 54% algebra, 21% geometry, 15% arithmetic word problems and 10% trigonometry, but failures clustered in geometry and trigonometry. Meera sampled disproportionately — 200 items per topic, 800 in total — buying enough items to say something about trigonometry, then re-weighted when reporting overall. With per-stratum pass rates of 0.91, 0.78, 0.94 and 0.69, the estimate is not the unweighted mean of 0.83 but 0.54(0.91) + 0.21(0.78) + 0.15(0.94) + 0.10(0.69) = 0.862. Nearly three points separate them. Skipping the re-weighting means a team cannot say whether a score moved because of the model or the sampling.

Next, the rubric — a written standard whose quality is measurable, since two trained humans applying it independently should agree. Meera had two tutors score 120 explanations; they agreed on 101, giving 84.2% raw agreement. Raw agreement flatters: two raters who both pass 85% of items agree by chance about 0.85² + 0.15² = 74.8% of the time. Cohen's kappa corrects for this: κ = (0.842 − 0.748) / (1 − 0.748) = 0.373 — poor. The rubric was not a standard; it was four adjectives. Rewriting it with explicit decision rules ("an explanation fails if it states a step the student has already completed correctly, or reaches the right answer by a method the board syllabus has not yet taught") pushed κ to 0.71 — the quarter's largest quality intervention, and not a model change, because everything downstream inherits the rubric's precision.

Only then is automation defensible. An LLM-as-judge is a second model prompted with the rubric to score at scale, and the honest way to use it is as a diagnostic test with known error rates. Meera measured hers against 240 human-labelled items: it passed 97% of genuinely good explanations and also 48% of genuinely bad ones, being lenient about answers that were fluent and wrong. The observed rate is then o = p(0.97) + (1 − p)(0.48). The judge reported 88.0%, so p = (0.880 − 0.480) / (0.970 − 0.480) = 0.816. True quality was 81.6%, six and a half points below the dashboard. Most teams never perform this inversion; they treat the judge as ground truth and then wonder why complaints do not track the chart.

The last step is statistical power. Comparing two models at around 90% pass, detecting a four-point difference at 5% significance and 80% power needs roughly 880 items per model when samples are independent — about 1,760 gradings. Run both on the same items and only the disagreements carry information: at 20% discordance running 65:35 in favour of the new model, roughly 87 discordant pairs suffice, meaning about 440 items scored twice — 880 gradings, half the cost. Paired designs are the largest efficiency available to an eval programme and are routinely left on the table because nobody ran the arithmetic.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions make an eval the right instrument. First: quality can be judged from the output plus its input, without waiting for the world to respond. Meera's case passes — a tutor can read an explanation and say whether it is good. Arvind's passes more cleanly: a part is defective or it is not. A churn model fails, because whether a prediction was "good" is knowable only months later and is confounded by everything the company did meanwhile. Second: the input distribution you sample from resembles the one you will face. Meera's passes for now and fails in June, when the syllabus changes. Arvind's fails outright on 12 March, because the lens changes. Third: the cost of a failure is roughly stable across items, or you are willing to weight it. Meera's fails silently: a fluent wrong explanation that teaches an incorrect method costs vastly more than a clumsy right one, and a pass rate treats them alike.

The idea becomes actively misleading in three situations. When the product's value is an aggregate behaviour rather than a per-output property — a feed, a pricing engine, a recommendation carousel — per-item grading measures a thing nobody buys. When the output is one step in a long agentic chain, per-step rates multiply into a figure unrelated to reality: ten steps at 95% is 60% end-to-end, and a team congratulating itself on 95% is describing a product that fails two times in five. And when the eval has been optimised against often enough to stop being a measurement and become a target — the phenomenon Goodhart named in 1975, which every eval programme eventually meets.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Two-sided products force two rubrics onto one output. Sohni Marketplace, a Jaipur handloom platform, generated product descriptions for sellers; a description that lifted conversion by being evocative could simultaneously fail a buyer-facing accuracy standard on fabric composition. Scoring the same 500 descriptions on both rubrics gave a 92% seller-appeal rate and a 71% accuracy rate; the useful artefact was neither number but the 24% that passed one and failed the other — the zone where the business had an unresolved position and the eval exposed it.

Regulated products change who the eval is for. At Adaab Money, a Chennai lender drafting adverse-action explanations for rejected loan applications, the eval had a second audience: a supervisor asking, during an inspection, how the firm satisfied itself the model was fit for purpose. That changes the artefact — versioned datasets with provenance, documented rater qualifications, a record of every threshold change and its approver. Model risk frameworks, imported into Indian finance from the Basel-influenced supervisory tradition, demand independent validation. The PM still owns the definition of good; they no longer own the sign-off.

Hardware plus software breaks the assumption of a stable input distribution — Arvind's problem exactly. A golden set of images is measurements from one optical path; change the sensor and scores on it are precise, reproducible and about the past. Mature hardware companies run two tiers: a frozen legacy set to catch gross regressions in model logic, and a rolling field set re-collected each revision, on which launch decisions are made. Baaz had the first and not the second.

Platforms push the boundary outward. When a company sells a model or an API, downstream quality depends on prompts and retrieval it does not control, so its eval measures the component, not the outcome — and that gap is where every escalation lives. The mature answer is to publish the eval itself, not just the score.

At the organisational seams, what mature companies do differs from what they say. They say a central quality team owns evals. What happens is that the central team owns infrastructure — sampling, storage, judge calibration, regression running — while rubric authorship stays with the PM closest to the customer, because centralised rubric writing produces rubrics that are general, defensible and useless.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The threshold is written before the score is known, or it is not a threshold. The tell is chronology: when a team reports 88% and then discusses whether 88% is acceptable, the number has already done its work on the discussion. An expert writes the decision rule into the eval definition — "automate at ≥ 92% on the highest-risk slice" — and dates it. The obvious reading is bureaucratic ceremony. It is instead the only defence against a ratchet in which every launch lowers the bar by exactly the amount needed to clear it, and no meeting ever feels like the one where standards slipped.

Pass rates are the wrong currency; expected cost is the right one. An expert asks what a failure costs before asking how often it happens. Take two models for clinical documentation at Tehzeeb Care Cloud: Model A passes 91%, with 2.0 of its 9 failure points being fabricated clinical facts at roughly ₹40,000 each and 7.0 cosmetic at ₹200. Model B passes 88%, but 0.3 points are fabrications and 11.7 cosmetic. Per thousand items, A costs 20(40,000) + 70(200) = ₹8.14 lakh and B costs 3(40,000) + 117(200) = ₹1.43 lakh. The worse model is five and a half times cheaper. Higher pass rate, better model is wrong whenever the failure distribution is skewed, which is nearly always.

A dataset scored many times is a dataset that has been optimised against. The tell is a score climbing smoothly over many iterations while every field proxy stays flat. Each time a team chooses between variants using the same items, it leaks information from those items into the product — adaptive overfitting, identified in the machine-learning literature around 2015. An expert rotates datasets and keeps a sealed holdout touched at most monthly. The obvious reading is that a held-out set is a formality because nobody trained on it; but selection is training, and forty rounds of selection on 300 items is meaningful training.

Inter-rater agreement is a property of the rubric, not of the raters. When agreement is poor, the competent response is more rater training; the expert response is to read the twenty items the raters disagreed about, because each marks a place where the rubric failed to state a rule, and fixing those twenty moves κ more than a day of training. The obvious reading treats disagreement as noise to average out; it is a precise map of where the product's definition of good has holes.

The automatic judge is a measuring instrument and drifts like one. The tell is a score that steps on a date with no code change — the vendor silently updated the judge model. An expert keeps a hundred frozen human-labelled items and re-runs the judge monthly, treating movement as an instrument fault rather than a product signal. The obvious reading is that a newer judge is a better judge, so a score change after an upgrade is good news. It is neither; it is uninterpretable until recalibrated.

Slices are not a reporting nicety; they are where the decision lives. Meera's blended 86.2% concealed 69% on trigonometry. The tell is the direction of attention: a competent PM presents the mean and answers slice questions; an expert opens with the worst decision-relevant slice and has to be asked for the mean. Nobody ships to an average user, and every complaint arrives from a slice.

The eval defines the roadmap, whether or not anyone intends it to. Once a rubric exists, engineering effort flows to what it measures, because that is what visibly improves. The tell is a backlog whose top five items map one-to-one to rubric categories. An expert treats rubric authorship as roadmap authorship, asking before adding a category whether they want a quarter of engineering spent there. The obvious reading puts the eval downstream of strategy; it is upstream, being the only artefact that makes progress legible.

Evals answer whether the output is good, never whether the task should be automated. A model can clear every rubric line and still be the wrong choice, because a segment is legally entitled to a human or because automating the task removes the only moment in which the company learns anything about its customers. The tell is a team that has stopped asking the second question because the first has a number attached. A high score removes one objection among several, and an expert names the others aloud so their absence from the dashboard is not mistaken for their absence from reality.

7. How this varies by product type and stage

In consumer products, per-user stakes are low and volume enormous, so evals lean on automated grading and statistical monitoring, and the binding constraint is judge calibration rather than dataset size. In B2B and enterprise, volume is modest and a bad output is visible to a named buyer, so category thresholds and manual failure review stay economic; enterprise adds a second audience — procurement and risk — who want the eval as a document, not a score. Platforms and marketplaces differ: a platform cannot observe the outcome it is judged on, while a marketplace can and must trade two rubrics against each other. In hardware, the golden set has physical provenance and expires with a revision. In AI-native products the eval is not a gate on the roadmap — it is the roadmap.

By stage, the difference is real but smaller than claimed. An early team with no raters and no labelled data should still have an eval: fifty items, a written rubric, hand-scored by the founder before every release. What changes with scale is not whether the eval exists but its infrastructure — versioned datasets, a standing rater panel, regression runs on every prompt or model change, scheduled judge recalibration. "Too early for evals" is almost always a claim that nobody has written down what good means, dressed as a resourcing argument.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Jhilmil Play. Meera rebuilt in eleven days: 800 stratified items, a rewritten rubric at κ = 0.71, a calibrated and inverted judge. The cheaper candidate scored a true 79.4% against the incumbent's 81.6% — but the slices diverged sharply.

A 1.8-point overall drop for a 38% cost saving is arguably worth making. A 15-point collapse in trigonometry is not, because trigonometry was where Jhilmil's Class 10 cohort — the segment that converted to paid — spent March. Meera routed by topic: the cheap model for algebra and arithmetic, the incumbent for geometry and trigonometry, capturing 69% of the saving with no slice regression beyond noise.

Baaz Vision Systems. Arvind held the launch ten days and spent them collecting 1,900 images through the new optical path on three live lines, stratified by shift and lighting. On that set the new model scored 88.6%, not 95.4%, with failures concentrated in low-light night-shift frames. The old golden set had not been wrong; it had been about a different camera. Baaz shipped the hardware with the incumbent model and retrained over five weeks.

Parwana Mail Cloud, the failure. Parwana, a Gurugram company whose model drafted marketing email copy for mid-market retailers, built a 300-item golden set in April 2025 and used it unchanged for eleven months. Across roughly forty prompt and model iterations the pass rate climbed from 74% to 93%, reported to the board as compounding quality. In March 2026, prompted by flat customer satisfaction, a new PM drew a fresh 300-item sample from the same window — same population, same rubric, same judge — and scored 79%. Fourteen of the nineteen points had been selection pressure on 300 specific items, not quality. Catching it late cost two quarters of roadmap pointed at improvements that were not improvements. Recovery was three rotating datasets, a sealed holdout scored at most monthly, and a rule that any gain under three points on a working set counts as zero until the holdout confirms it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Offline evals versus online experiments. The experimentation position at its strongest: quality is defined by what users do, not what raters say, and every rubric is a hypothesis a randomised trial tests directly; mature teams repeatedly find rubric wins that move no behavioural metric. The measurement position at its strongest: experiments are slow, underpowered for rare costly failures, and ethically unavailable when the failure harms someone — you cannot A/B test whether fabricated medical advice is bad. The first is wrong if rubric scores reliably predict behaviour; the second is wrong if costly failures are common enough to measure online. Both hold in some products and neither in all, which is why this does not resolve.

Is LLM-as-judge a primary instrument or a screening tool? The permissive view: judge–human agreement now routinely exceeds human–human agreement on well-specified rubrics, and a consistently biased instrument is adequate for detecting changes, which is what launch decisions need. The restrictive view: judges share failure modes with the systems they grade, prefer fluent output, and correlate exactly where correlation is most dangerous. The first is wrong if judge bias moves with model version; the second is wrong if periodic recalibration keeps drift inside the decision's tolerance.

Small curated datasets versus large synthetic ones. The curated camp holds that 200 items a PM has personally read beat 20,000 nobody has, because meaning lives in the reading. The scale camp holds that small sets cannot detect rare failures and that synthetic generation is the only affordable route to tail coverage. Underneath is which failure a business fears: common mediocrity or rare catastrophe.

Who owns the rubric. A minority but serious view holds that PM ownership is a conflict of interest — the person accountable for shipping should not define the bar — and that an independent quality function should, as model risk functions do in banks. The counter is that separated rubrics drift into generality and stop describing the product. Regulated contexts split authorship from certification; unregulated ones have not settled it at all.

The competent practitioner asks what the model scored. The expert asks what population the score is about, what the judge's error rate is, when the threshold was written, and which slice is worst — then asks the score.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied evals builds one, reports it, and defends it. Someone who has internalised them differs in four visible ways. They write the decision rule before the measurement, so the meeting where the number arrives is short. They read failures personally and in volume, treating a hundred bad outputs as primary research rather than a task to delegate. They treat every instrument in the chain — sample, rubric, judge, weighting — as something that can itself be wrong, auditing it on a schedule rather than when a result surprises them. And they retire an eval when the rubric no longer describes the product, accepting the loss of trend continuity rather than preserving a comparable series about the wrong thing. The last is hardest: a long clean trend line is the most seductive artefact a team can own.

12. Closing: two decisions

Meera neither swapped the model nor kept it. She routed by topic, took most of the saving, and added trigonometry to the June syllabus review — carrying operational complexity in exchange for not degrading the one slice her paying cohort cared about. Her reasoning: a 1.8-point blended movement was inside her uncertainty and a 15-point slice movement was not.

Arvind shipped the hardware and held the model. He had a defensible 95.4% and chose to disbelieve it, because the number described an optical path his product was about to stop having. Baaz absorbed five weeks of retraining and one uncomfortable customer conversation, and avoided learning about night-shift escapes from a penalty clause.

Three questions for discussion. First: Meera's inversion moved reported quality from 88.0% to 81.6%; if you were her CEO and had been quoting 88% to investors, what would you want done differently, and when? Second: under what circumstances is it legitimate to make a launch decision on a dataset you know is stale, and what would you require in exchange? Third: Parwana's fourteen points of illusory gain came from ordinary diligent work with no bad actor in the story — what specific mechanism, not exhortation, would have caught it in month three?

13. Going deeper

  1. Quality as a distribution — a score summarises a distribution, and the tail is where decisions live.
  2. What makes a good metric — an eval inherits everything separating a good metric from a vanity one.
  3. Building a golden set from real usage — the sampling craft assumed here: stratification, provenance, refresh cadence.

Building a Golden Set from Real Usage

1. Two desks, January and February 2026

On 14 January 2026, Aparna Menon, head of product for quality at Tathya Labs in Bengaluru, was asked to approve a change that would save her company ₹1.14 crore a quarter. Tathya's product is a free vernacular assistant answering questions about government schemes, forms and entitlements — pension eligibility, crop-insurance windows, scholarship deadlines — in eight Indian languages, and it served 2.6 crore queries in December. Engineering had distilled a smaller in-house model that cut inference cost from ₹0.42 to ₹0.07 a query. The only evidence it matched the frontier model it replaced was a 300-item test file written in English by two people in 2024 and machine-translated into the other seven languages. Eleven of its items named schemes since merged or closed.

Aparna's difficulty was not scarcity. Tathya logged every query, so any sample she drew would be real. Her difficulty was having no defensible way to choose which 400 of 2.6 crore queries would stand in for all of them — and no answer key, because for a question like "my father is 61, can he get the widow pension for my mother," correctness turns on a state rule that changed in September.

Three weeks later, on 3 February, Kabir Sheth faced the mirror image. Sheth leads product at Sanhita Systems, a Pune company whose assistant drafts credit-underwriting notes for eleven non-banking financial companies and two small finance banks — about 74,000 notes a year, roughly what Tathya serves in ninety seconds. Every note feeds a lending decision, and after an internal audit at one client flagged two notes citing a policy clause that did not exist, that client's chief risk officer asked for documented evidence the model did not fabricate. Sanhita had a 900-item "golden set," but the solutions team had built it from onboarding demonstrations: clean files chosen because they showed the product well. Sheth had labels without real usage; Menon had real usage without labels. Both faced the same question from people with the power to stop them — how do you know? — and in both cases the artefact they would point at did not yet exist.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A golden set is a fixed, versioned sample of real inputs to a system, each paired with a human-decided statement of what an acceptable output would be, composed as a known function of production traffic, and held out from everything the system learns from. Each clause is load-bearing. Fixed and versioned: the yardstick cannot move between measurements. Real inputs: from logs, not imagination, because practitioners are bad at guessing their own users' phrasing. Human-decided acceptability: a judgement recorded in advance, not reverse-engineered from whichever output arrived. Known function of traffic: not necessarily proportional — over-sampling rare, severe cases is normal — but the weights must be written down, because a score from a skewed sample means nothing until re-weighted back.

The lineage runs through information retrieval. Cyril Cleverdon's Cranfield experiments in the early 1960s established the pattern still in use: a fixed collection, a fixed query set, and human relevance judgements made once and reused, so two systems could be compared without re-running the humans. TREC formalised it from 1992. Machine learning inherited the held-out test set from the same instinct, and ImageNet showed both the power and the pathology — a frozen benchmark drives a decade of progress, then saturates, and people optimise the benchmark rather than the task. Product teams adopted "golden set" after 2022, when generative systems made the old question — did this release break anything? — unanswerable by deterministic tests. The problem it solves is comparability: without a fixed instrument, every release argument collapses into whoever demoed most persuasively.

Practitioners who accept that definition still disagree about what the set should contain; a PM will meet all four positions in one room. The measurement school, heirs of Cranfield, treats a golden set as a survey instrument: probability sampling from a defined frame, documented strata, intervals on every number. It signs "a set you edit between runs is not an evaluation set." It will not sign "weight the set toward known failures," which severs score from production quality. The regression school, from software testing, treats the set as institutional memory: every incident becomes a permanent case and the set grows monotonically. It signs "no bug we have already paid for should recur undetected." It will not sign "composition should mirror production traffic," which it sees as re-confirming cases you already pass.

The adversarial school holds that static sets saturate and stop carrying information, so items should be continuously regenerated by humans or models trying to break the system. It signs "an item everyone passes has information value zero," and will not sign "freeze the set for a year." The online school, from controlled experimentation, holds that offline evaluation is proxy measurement and only a live experiment on a business metric is evidence. It signs "an offline improvement that never moves a production metric was not an improvement." It will not sign "gate releases on an offline pass rate," which it regards as Goodhart's law with extra ceremony.

The competent practitioner picks one school. The expert runs three artefacts with different statistical contracts — a representative core, a regression annex, an adversarial probe — and never averages their scores.

3. Mechanics, worked rather than named

Aparna's team spent six weeks on what looked from outside like "pulling some logs." The work usually left implicit sits in three places: the frame, the allocation, and the reproducibility of labels.

Defining the frame

A sampling frame is the enumerated population you draw from, and the first expert move is noticing it is not "the logs." Tathya's logging wrote a row when a response was returned, excluding sessions abandoned mid-typing, sessions where retrieval timed out behind a fallback card, and the 6.2% where the language detector misfired and the user switched to English in frustration — a frame conditioned on the system having already succeeded at three prior steps. Aparna re-drew it at session start: every session with at least one query between 1 October and 31 December 2025, answered or not. That changed the population by 11%, and was the difference between a useful set and a flattering one.

Clustering, and why it is a modelling decision

Raw logs are dominated by repetition. Tathya's 7.9 crore quarterly sessions collapsed, under embedding clustering at cosine 0.86, into roughly 41,000 intents. The threshold is not hygiene; it defines the population. At 0.92, "when does the PM-Kisan instalment come" and "PM-Kisan instalment date for Bihar" are separate intents and the state-specific tail dominates the frame; at 0.78 they merge with "PM-Kisan status check" and the state dimension vanishes. Aparna's team ran both and reported the difference rather than choosing silently.

Allocating the sample

Proportional allocation mirrors traffic. Neyman allocation, from stratified survey sampling, minimises the variance of the overall estimate by giving stratum h a share proportional to NhSh — size times the outcome's standard deviation within it. For a pass/fail outcome Sh = √(ph(1−ph)), peaking at p = 0.5. Practically: strata where the model is reliably excellent or reliably terrible are cheap to estimate and deserve few items; erratic strata deserve more. Risk floors then override the arithmetic wherever a wrong answer is expensive.

Labels, agreement and the arithmetic of disagreement

Two labellers wrote an acceptability statement per item; a third adjudicated conflicts. On a 200-item overlap they agreed 86% of the time — but raw agreement flatters, since two labellers marking everything "acceptable" would agree 90% of the time by accident. Cohen's kappa corrects for chance: with observed agreement 0.86 and chance agreement 0.62, κ = (0.86 − 0.62) ⁄ (1 − 0.62) = 0.63, substantial but not excellent. Any stratum below κ = 0.60 went back for rubric revision before a single item entered the frozen set, because low kappa is almost never a rater problem and almost always a rubric problem.

Scoring a comparison properly

When Sanhita ran its old and new models over a 400-item set, the headline was 340 passes against 356 — 85.0% against 89.0%. Whether that gap is real turns not on the totals but on the items where the models differed; McNemar's test uses only those discordant cells.

With b = 18 and c = 34, the continuity-corrected statistic is (|18 − 34| − 1)² ⁄ (18 + 34) = 225 ⁄ 52 = 4.33, giving p ≈ 0.037: the improvement survives at the 5% level, just. Had the split been 22 and 30, the statistic would fall to 0.94 and p to 0.33, and the same four-point headline would be indistinguishable from noise. The second-order effect matters more than the test. Because only 52 items carried information, Sheth's 400-item set was effectively a 52-item experiment, and the 18 regressions were individually more informative than the 322 items the new model left alone. Experts read the discordant cells one by one; competent practitioners read the headline.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are worth stating as claims that can be checked rather than as advice.

Where the idea actively misleads matters more than where it merely fails. When the interface changes materially, the logs record what the old affordances permitted, and a set built on them certifies a redesign it cannot see. When the output is open-ended and quality is a matter of taste, pass/fail labelling forces a false binary and measures rubric compliance rather than usefulness. When the system is agentic, input–output pairs discard the trajectory: two runs can reach the same answer with one having called a write-enabled tool it should never have touched. And when a small cohort dominates volume, "representative of traffic" and "representative of users" diverge, and the set optimises for the loudest tenth of a percent.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product. When one model serves three surfaces, each product team wants its own set and the platform team wants one. Mature organisations do neither: per-surface representative sets owned by product PMs, plus a shared "platform floor" set — 150 to 400 items of safety, refusal and factuality behaviour — that every surface inherits and none may weaken. The honest version of the release gate names which set blocked a launch.

Two-sided. Mandvi Trade Networks, a marketplace for textile wholesalers, found correctness itself side-dependent: an answer to a buyer about typical price ranges is accurate and commercially damaging to sellers who never consented to that transparency. Mandvi ended with two sets, two rubrics, and — the part teams under-build — a third small set where the rubrics conflict, adjudicated by a policy owner rather than either side's PM.

Regulated. Sanhita could not export client borrower data for labelling. The workable pattern was federated: the labelling tool ran inside each client's virtual private cloud, only identifiers, labels and rubric references crossed the boundary, and the set Sanhita held was pointers and verdicts, not content. That costs central inspection, and so debugging speed. It also forces each label to cite the policy clause making it correct, so an RBI-facing audit traces a verdict to an authority rather than an annotator's opinion.

Hardware plus software. Chilika Instruments sells cold-chain monitors with a voice interface to dairy cooperatives. Inputs are audio from one microphone in one acoustic environment, and fleet firmware differs by up to fourteen months, so the set is stratified by device generation and noise band as well as intent, and items are audio files rather than transcripts — transcribing first hides exactly the failures the set exists to catch.

AI-native. Where the model is the product, the set stops being a test and becomes the roadmap: strata are capability bets. Aparna's Odia stratum was a language-support commitment made by the evaluation team six months before it reached any planning document.

6. Eight nuances that separate expert from competent

1. Freeze the rubric as hard as the items. Teams version the item list and edit grading guidance in place. The tell-tale is a score that moves several points with no model or item change; the expert reflex on hearing "we tightened the rubric a bit" is to treat every prior score as unusable for comparison. The obvious reading — a better rubric is simply better — is wrong, because rubric and items jointly define the instrument, and changing either resets the series.

2. A headline from a floored sample is not a quality estimate until re-weighted. The tell-tale is a headline that moves when someone changes a floor. Tathya's raw 640-item pass rate was 81.4%; re-weighted to production shares it was 84.9%, because over-sampled hard strata dragged the unweighted mean down. Both numbers are legitimate and answer different questions; the expert always says which one is on the slide.

3. The deduplication threshold is a policy, not a parameter. The tell-tale is a data scientist who cannot state it without checking. Collapsing near-duplicates decides whether the set measures intents or phrasings, and phrasing robustness is often precisely what a distilled model loses first. The obvious reading — dedupe harder to avoid redundancy — deletes the variation the evaluation existed to probe.

4. Labels are acceptance regions, not answer strings. The tell-tale is a rubric written as exact-match target text. For "my father is 61, can he get the widow pension for my mother," an acceptable answer must decline the premise, name the right scheme and assert no amount; many wordings satisfy that and none is the answer. Sets built on exact strings fail fluent correct answers and reward mimicry of the labeller.

5. Logs inherit the product's survivorship. The tell-tale is a set with no items in a category the product cannot currently serve. If Tathya has never offered an appeal-letter draft, no log contains a user asking for one twice: the first refusal taught them not to. Experts supplement the log-drawn core with a written frontier stratum, kept and scored separately, never averaged into the representative number.

6. Contamination arrives through retrieval, not only training. Everyone guards fine-tuning data. The subtler leak is a retrieval index or prompt-example library that has absorbed golden-set questions and their adjudicated answers, at which point the system looks up the answer key at inference time. The tell-tale is a pass rate that jumps on exactly the items the set contains while support volume is unchanged; the diagnostic is to hash golden inputs and scan the index before every release.

7. Saturation destroys information silently. The tell-tale is a stratum at 97% for three consecutive releases. Celebrating and deleting are both wrong: deleting removes the only guard against regression, celebrating hides that the stratum now costs money and yields nothing. Experts keep the items, drop them from the headline, move the budget to a new stratum, and record the decision so a later fall is still caught.

8. The golden set is a political object. Whoever chooses the strata chooses what the organisation optimises for two quarters, and that person is usually a mid-level PM making a sampling decision on a Tuesday. The tell-tale is a set whose strata map suspiciously well onto the current team structure. Experts treat stratum definition as a roadmap conversation with the people who approve features, and write down what was excluded — the exclusion list being the most informative and least written document in any evaluation programme.

7. What actually changes across product types and stages

Much less changes than practitioners expect. Framing, clustering, stratification, adjudication and re-weighting are identical whether the product is a consumer app or a factory sensor; anyone claiming enterprise evaluation is a different discipline is describing a budget constraint, not a method. Three things genuinely differ: the unit of analysis, the cost per label, and who may declare an answer correct.

Table 4 — where the differences are real.
ContextWhat genuinely changes
ConsumerLabels cheap, volume enormous; the constraint is finding rare scenarios. Stratify by segment and language, not only intent.
B2B / enterpriseCost per label rises tenfold. Stratify by account and contract term; one account's edge case outranks a hundred small-account repeats.
Platform / marketplaceCorrectness is side-dependent: two sets, two rubrics, a conflict set adjudicated above both PMs.
HardwareItems are raw signals; fleet heterogeneity becomes a stratum, and refresh tracks firmware, not quarters.
AI-nativeThe set doubles as the roadmap; adding a stratum is a capability commitment.
Seed stageNo usable logs. Seed from support and sales transcripts; replace within eight weeks of real traffic.
Scale-upLog volume exceeds what one person can read; sampling discipline starts paying for itself.
Large incumbentGovernance dominates; the failure mode is a set nobody owns because everybody uses it.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Tathya Labs: the average that hid the decision. Against golden-v1's 640 items, the frontier model scored 86.1% and the distilled model 84.4% — a gap Aparna's engineering lead called "within noise." Per language it was not: English fell from 91% to 90%, Hindi 88% to 87%, Marathi 85% to 79%, Odia 82% to 68%. Odia was 4% of traffic, so its collapse cost 0.6 points of headline. Aggregated, the models looked identical; disaggregated, the cheaper one was unusable for roughly 10 lakh queries a month, and those users were by Tathya's own segmentation the least able to verify an answer elsewhere.

Fig. 1 — Golden-v1 pass rates by language stratum. The aggregate gap is 1.7 points; the Odia gap is 14. A set stratified only by intent would have reported the aggregate and nothing else.

Sanhita Systems: buying the right 400 items. At ₹2,800 a label, Sheth could afford 400 items, not 4,000, and spent them where the regulator's attention was: 140 on clause citation, 120 on numerical consistency between note and financials, 80 on adverse-information disclosure, 60 on everything else — deliberately unrepresentative, and documented as such. Table 2 showed a real improvement overall, but the 18 discordant regressions clustered: eleven were adverse-information items where the newer model wrote smoother prose and dropped a qualifying sentence. Sheth shipped with a hard gate on that stratum alone. The risk officer accepted the artefact not because the score was high but because the exclusion list and adjudication trail existed.

Maanak Money: the set that certified a failure. Maanak, a Gurugram lender, built a 500-item set for its collections assistant from logs of completed conversations. It scored 94% on the first run and 95% on the third, while complaints to its grievance officer rose 38% over the same two quarters and one reached an ombudsman. The defect was the frame: "completed conversations" excluded the 23% of sessions the borrower abandoned mid-flow, and abandonment correlated almost perfectly with the assistant having said something confusing or intimidating. The set drew only from the population in which the product had already worked. Recovery took a quarter — frame re-drawn at session start, abandoned sessions labelled on whether the last assistant turn was a plausible cause — and the rebuilt set scored 67%. Maanak had spent roughly ₹18 lakh of engineering time optimising a number that could not fall; the real cost was two quarters in which a regression was invisible.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Table 5 — recurring failure modes, first symptom, catching question, and the cost of a late catch.
Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost if caught late
Frame conditioned on successScore stable while complaints riseWhat had to go right for a row to exist here?Quarters optimising an unfalsifiable number
Imagined items shown as realTopic mix unlike last month's logsShow me each item's session IDConfident release, incident within days
Unweighted headline, floored sampleHeadline moves when a floor changesThis is the pass rate of what?Wrong ship calls; trust in the number lost
Rubric driftScore moves with no model changeWhich rubric version produced last quarter's figure?The time series becomes uninterpretable
Contamination via prompt or indexGolden score climbs, live metrics flatHas anyone hashed these inputs against the index?A launch justified by a memorised exam
StalenessRefresh predates a policy changeWhat changed in the product since the freeze?Blind spot over the fastest-growing traffic
Over-reading small strataShip calls cited from 20-item groupsWhat is the interval on that stratum?Releases blocked or waved through on noise

Every one of these failures makes the number look better behaved, not worse. A wrong golden set is rarely erratic; it is smooth, flattering and stable, which is why it survives review. What catches all seven is a refusal to accept any score without its frame, weights and rubric version attached.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Representativeness versus difficulty. The measurement position: a set that does not mirror production cannot estimate production quality, and every departure from proportionality must later be undone by re-weighting. Its evidence is the record of survey sampling and of teams whose adversarial sets predicted nothing about live performance. The adversarial position: production is dominated by easy items, so a representative set spends most of its budget confirming what is known and has almost no power at the margin where releases are decided. Its evidence is benchmark saturation — sets that stopped discriminating between models years before the models stopped differing. The question would resolve if difficulty-weighted offline scores were shown to predict live incident rates as well as representative ones do. Nobody has shown it either way, and both camps cite anecdote.

Human labels versus model-generated labels. Past a few thousand items, adjudication dominates cost, and one camp argues that a strong model with a written rubric agrees with human adjudicators often enough — commonly reported at 80–90% on well-specified tasks — to justify labelling at fifty times the volume. The other answers that the errors are not random: judge models share failure modes with the systems they grade, so disagreements concentrate in exactly the hard cases the set exists to probe. The first position holds only if judge–human disagreement is uncorrelated with item difficulty. The measurements that exist suggest it is correlated — but not by how much, or how consistently across domains.

Offline gating versus online-only. The online school's strongest form is not that offline evaluation is useless but that it is unaccountable: a threshold gate creates an optimisation target with no feedback from the world, and teams reliably learn to move it. Its evidence is a literature showing weak correlation between offline proxies and live outcomes. The offline camp's strongest form is that experiments are available only to products with enough traffic and enough tolerance for harm — Sanhita cannot A/B test fabricated clauses on live credit decisions. In practice the camps converge on sequencing: offline sets as a floor against harm, online experiments as the arbiter of value. They still disagree about what to do when the two conflict, and that is settled inside companies by authority rather than evidence.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds a good set once. Someone who has internalised it differs in four visible ways. They ask about the frame before the size, knowing sample size is the cheapest thing to fix and frame bias the most expensive. They carry two numbers — the weighted production estimate and the per-stratum disaggregation — and notice that an executive asking for "the number" is asking a question with no single answer. They treat a stable, high score as a prompt to investigate, because every failure mode here manifests as reassurance. And they know the blind spots by name: what was excluded, when the frame was last re-drawn, which strata are saturated, where labels are weakest — said unprompted, before someone else finds out.

12. What Menon and Sheth decided

On 6 February, Aparna Menon declined the distilled model as a full replacement. She approved it for English and Hindi, where the set showed no meaningful regression, and kept the frontier model for Marathi and Odia — about 71% of the projected saving, roughly ₹81 lakh a quarter. She funded an Odia data effort and ruled that no aggregate quality number would reach the board without its language disaggregation on the same slide. Her reasoning: the saving was real and the regression was real, and nothing required her to accept both as a package.

On 19 February, Kabir Sheth shipped v4 with a stratum gate — any release below 92% on adverse-information disclosure is blocked regardless of aggregate score. He also published Sanhita's exclusion list to clients, naming the three categories the set does not cover; two asked for one to be added and funded the labelling. His reasoning: an evaluation artefact's credibility comes from what it admits it cannot see.

Discussion questions.

1. Menon's split preserves quality for 4% of traffic at a cost of roughly ₹33 lakh a quarter. When would a purely commercial reading of that trade-off be the defensible one, and what does your answer imply about who should own stratum floors?

2. Sheth's set is deliberately unrepresentative of Sanhita's traffic. Is it a golden set at all on the section 2 definition? If not, what is it, and what else would Sanhita need before claiming to know its overall quality?

3. Maanak's set was competent in every respect except its frame. Which of the seven failure modes in Table 5 would your own team's most-cited quality number survive, and how would you find out this week rather than next quarter?

13. Going deeper

Table 6 — adjacent topics, and what each unlocks next.
What evals are and why PMs own themThe container: a golden set is an eval's test data; owning one implies owning the other.
Instrumentation with product analytics toolsUpstream: frame defects are almost always instrumentation defects.
Grading rubrics and LLM-as-judgeThe scaling path once adjudication cost binds; the second disagreement in section 10.
Feedback loops and data flywheelsHow production failures route into the next version, so the set tracks the product rather than lagging it.
Problem–model fitWhether a fixed answer key can exist for this task at all.
The ML lifecycleWhere freeze, refresh and contamination checks belong in the release cycle.
Data strategy and data acquisitionWhat to do about the frontier stratum logs cannot contain.
Labelling and annotationThe craft behind kappa: rubric writing, adjudication, annotator economics.
Model metrics: precision, recall, AUCWhat to report when the outcome is not binary, and how thresholds change it.
What's different when the feature is a modelWhy deterministic regression tests do not transfer.

Pukaar Systems: What the Pack Does Not Hear

An ambiguous decision case in AI and ML product management · Indian context

1. Sunday night, 15 November 2026

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday night, 15 November 2026, Supriya Vaidya sat at her dining table in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with three documents open and a board call in twenty hours. The first was her own slide, shown twice since September, reporting that Pukaar Sahaayak answered customers correctly 92.1 per cent of the time. The second was a memo from the largest client's chief operating officer putting the figure at 63.2 per cent. The third was a service-credit clause she had to initial by Friday.

Supriya had built the measurement programme behind the first number: twelve hundred real customer calls from the company's own logs, each read by two annotators and paired with a written statement of what a correct answer had to contain. Everyone called it the Pack, and it had ended the arguing about model releases from intuition. It had also, she suspected, been measuring the wrong thing since January, and the evidence that would settle how wrong was deleted every thirty days under a clause she helped negotiate.

On Monday she had to tell the board what Pukaar's accuracy actually was, what it would cost to know, and whether to sign the clause. She had no answer to any of the three she would defend under questioning.

2. Pukaar Systems, 2019 to 2026

Pukaar Systems was founded in Hyderabad in 2019 by Pranav Khasnis and two colleagues from a Chennai telephony firm. Its first product was dull and profitable: speech analytics on recorded calls for lenders who had to show the Reserve Bank of India that their collection agents followed the fair-practice code. By 2022 it had forty people in Madhapur and a reputation for being good at Indian telephone audio.

Pukaar Sahaayak launched in August 2023: a voice agent that answers inbound calls in seven Indian languages, checks a loan or payment against the client's core system, and either resolves the request or hands it to a human. By October 2026 Pukaar had 196 employees, fourteen clients and annual recurring revenue of ₹38.4 crore.

One decision from February 2024 shapes everything that follows. To win Rajgiri Gold Exchange, a Thrissur gold-loan non-banking financial company with 1,100 branches, Pukaar agreed to a data clause its competitors would not match: all call audio deleted within thirty days, audio never used to train or test any model, only redacted transcripts kept. The clause won the account, worth ₹5.76 crore a year by 2026, or ₹48 lakh a month against 8,00,000 connected calls, exactly ₹6.00 a call. Eleven of the fourteen clients later asked for the same clause and got it. The Pack, built in January 2026, was therefore built out of text, because text was all that survived thirty days.

3. The industry

India's conversational-AI market is not short of capable sellers: Jio Haptik, Yellow.ai, Gupshup, Ozonetel and Exotel all sell automated voice support, and Freshworks and Zoho bundle it into broader suites. Sarvam AI and the AI4Bharat group at IIT Madras have made Indian-language speech recognition far cheaper than in 2023 — good for Pukaar's margin, terrible for its differentiation.

Pukaar's buyers are regulated. Gold-loan and small-finance lenders answer to the RBI on fair practice, grievance redress and the integrity of what they tell a borrower about dues. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, every client must state a purpose for personal data and keep to it, and recordings of borrowers discussing arrears are about as sensitive as Indian retail finance gets. The sharper pressure is commercial: a transferred call costs a client roughly ₹18, so containment is what procurement watches.

Pukaar is exposed outside India too. Riverina Payments Exchange, a Melbourne remittance business serving the Australian Indian diaspora, signed in April 2026 for ₹4.32 crore a year, English and Hindi only, and its compliance function wants the methodology, not the headline. Rajgiri and Riverina together are ₹10.08 crore of the ₹38.4 crore book, 26.3 per cent.

Figure A. How the commitments fall across the calendar

Figure A. Pukaar Systems, February 2024 to December 2026.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In September 2026 Pukaar Sahaayak was offered 24,00,000 inbound calls across fourteen clients and connected 20,40,000, or 85.0 per cent; the rest were abandoned in the client's own menu first. Exhibit 1 shows what became of the connected calls: the agent closed 10,71,612 without a human, a containment rate of 52.5 per cent, and handed over or lost the other 9,68,388.

Direct cost was ₹3.10 a connected call, so September's variable cost was ₹63.24 lakh against revenue of ₹320 lakh, 19.8 per cent.

The Pack was assembled in January 2026 from Rajgiri transcripts because Rajgiri was 8,00,000 of the 20,40,000 connected calls, 39.2 per cent of traffic, and its logs were cleanest. It began with 1,264 items; in June, after engineers protested that a cluster was unanswerable — a mumbled account number, two questions at once — 64 were removed as ambiguous and the Pack became 1,200. Exhibit 3 reports the pass rate by release. The April-to-June jump is the one Supriya can no longer defend: April was scored on 1,264 items and June on 1,200, and 61 of the 64 removed items had been failures.

Between June and September the Pack rose from 89.6 to 92.1 per cent, and the number went into a board pack, a sales deck and, on 3 September, a proposal to Riverina claiming "91 per cent accuracy on a benchmark of real customer calls". Nobody lied; the sentence was true of the Pack.

Rajgiri's quality team audited 500 of September's recordings between 6 and 10 October and sent the memo on 22 October, twelve days after the audit closed. Exhibit 4 reports it: on Rajgiri's definition, 316 of 500 calls, 63.2 per cent, resolved without human help. Exhibit 5, Rajgiri's post-call SMS survey, says something different again: 4.07 out of 5 from 46,800 responses, 76.0 per cent of them four or five stars. On 3 November, twelve days before this Sunday, Rajgiri's chief operating officer, Sudheendra Marath, put the December renewal "on review" and proposed a service credit of 5 per cent of monthly fees, ₹2.40 lakh a month or ₹28.8 lakh a year, in any month where an agreed audit put first-contact resolution below 70 per cent.

The deeper discovery is in the failure breakdown. Of the 184 calls that did not resolve unaided, 71 failed because the agent misheard: a Kannada speaker's seven became a one, a Hinglish caller's "pending dikha raha hai" became a different complaint. Pack v3 cannot detect one of those failures. It is a set of transcripts, and it assumes the transcript is right. The February 2024 clause means the audio is gone.

5. The people

Supriya Vaidya, vice-president of product, Hyderabad, owns the Pack and the slide that quoted it, and holds that measurement must be rebuilt before further model work. Her bonus turns on net revenue retention, which Rajgiri dominates. She has told nobody that she argued for the audio-deletion clause in 2024 because it closed the deal.

Ranjan Barua, head of machine learning, Bengaluru, wants to ship the fine-tuned Indic model ready since October, which he believes lifts containment four points. He calls the Rajgiri audit "an audit of their core banking system, not of our model", and is partly right: 44 of the 184 failures were correct understanding against stale data. He is not saying that his team has selected checkpoints on the Pack since June, which makes it no longer an independent measure.

Prithvi Vakharia, speech lead, Pune, has argued since 2024 that word error rate on code-mixed speech is the binding constraint, and Exhibit 1 supports him: the 2,38,680 Hindi calls flagged code-mixed contained at 40.0 per cent against 57.1 per cent for the rest. He wants audio retained, and would gain most from an audio programme. He does not mention that his flag is a heuristic of unmeasured precision.

Saumya Jhaveri, annotation lead, Jaipur, runs the thirty-person team at the vendor Prastaav Data Exchange and labelled the Pack. Agreement between her two annotators was 82 per cent on payment-status items and 61 per cent on complaints; she adjudicated the rest herself. She is not saying that for eleven weeks mid-year her trained team was swapped for four new joiners.

Parag Mirchandani, chief financial officer, Mumbai, wants model cost down: moving 60 per cent of calls to a smaller in-house model saves ₹0.70 a call on 12,24,000 calls, ₹8.57 lakh a month and ₹1.03 crore a year. He backs evaluation in principle and asks why it cannot be done for under ₹2 lakh. He has not told the board that two March-quarter renewals carry similar audit language.

Sreelakshmi Panicker, customer-success lead, Kochi, speaks to Rajgiri weekly. The client will accept nothing but real calls labelled by people it can meet, she says, and she has quietly promised Marath a "joint evaluation" before December. She is not saying that she showed Rajgiri the 92.1 per cent in August as reassurance, which is part of why the memo reads as it does.

Rameez Daruwala, sales head, Melbourne. Riverina is his account and his quota. He wants a documented evaluation set by 20 November, which he thinks wins a ₹22 lakh expansion, and the 91 per cent left in the proposal. He has not said that Riverina's procurement team has already asked whether the benchmark included Australian English.

Priyamvada Seshadri, general counsel and data-protection officer, Chennai. Audio cannot be kept for evaluation, she holds, without fresh consent and a contract amendment per client, and re-consent across fourteen clients is a nine-week exercise with no guaranteed outcome: the DPDP Act permits processing for a stated purpose, and "evaluation of our automated system" was never stated. She has not said that one client's counsel has already refused informally.

Roksana Zielinska, senior data scientist, Warsaw, hired in 2025 for Riverina, proposes synthesising 6,000 calls with text-to-speech in the seven languages and grading them with a stronger model as judge, the only route she sees that covers rare cases. She has not said that her previous employer abandoned the approach after the judge agreed with human reviewers only two-thirds of the time on Indian-language audio.

7. Voices

"Sudheendra asked me a question on Friday I could not answer. He said: your Pack has twelve hundred calls, and none of them is a call where your machine could not hear the customer. Why would I pay for a test that cannot fail?"

Sreelakshmi Panicker, chat message to Supriya, 7 November

"I understand the audio problem. I am asking a narrower question. We are at 19.8 per cent of revenue in variable cost and I have a ₹1.03 crore saving sitting in a branch nobody will merge. What is the cheapest measurement that lets me merge it?"

Parag Mirchandani, email, 9 November

"Riverina will not accept 'we are rebuilding our benchmark'. They will accept a documented set with a known composition, even a small one. Give me something by the 20th."

Rameez Daruwala, Melbourne, call at 6.30 am IST, 11 November

8. The options as Supriya sees them

Option P: an audio-first Pack across consenting clients. Obtain fresh consent and contract amendments, keep audio for evaluation only, and build 2,400 items sampled to the live language and intent mix from nine clients, each labelled by two annotators with an adjudicator on disagreements. Exhibit 6 puts it at ₹11.10 lakh and nine weeks, which lands in the third week of January. It is the only route that can see the 38.6 per cent of failures that are mishearing. It rests on Priyamvada's fourteen conversations, and it arrives after the renewal.

Option R: rebalance the Pack she has. Reweight Pack v3 to the September mix, add 400 transcript-only items from Sampige Credit Exchange and one other client to cover Telugu and Marathi, and republish with the composition disclosed. ₹2.22 lakh, three weeks, ready by 7 December — affordable, defensible about text understanding, and structurally blind to the largest failure class.

Option S: synthesise and let a model judge. Roksana's 6,000 generated calls, spoken by text-to-speech in seven languages and graded by a stronger model, with a 300-item human spot check. ₹5.99 lakh, four weeks. It covers rare cases and Australian English, needs no consent, and nobody at Rajgiri will believe it.

The three options on one page are themselves a problem she has not named. All three keep the unit of measurement at the call turn, while Rajgiri measures the episode: the 62 callers who rang again in 48 hours are invisible to each. All three assume one set can serve a Thrissur lender and a Melbourne remittance firm at once, and that labels are the easy part — which Exhibit 4's single-reviewer footnote and Saumya's 61 per cent should unsettle.
