9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Rajgiri decides on 1 December. Signing the credit clause at the current measured level puts ₹28.8 lakh a year at risk against an account worth ₹5.76 crore; refusing it, Sreelakshmi believes, risks the renewal. Riverina wants the methodology in writing by 20 November, five days away, with Rameez's ₹22 lakh expansion attached. Parag has approved ₹2 lakh of evaluation budget this quarter and will go to ₹6 lakh with a board resolution. Priyamvada's amendments cannot be compressed, Saumya's trained annotators are committed elsewhere until 5 January, and Ranjan's model is ready: every week it waits costs containment he can quantify and quality nobody can.

Supriya closed her laptop at ten past one on Monday morning: four slides, three routes, two numbers for the same month, and one question unresolved — whether what she needed to build was a better test set, or a different definition of what counted as a correct call in the first place. The board call was in eighteen hours.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1, 4 and 5, reconcile 92.1, 76.0, 63.2 and 52.5 per cent. What population and definition of success sits behind each, and which belongs in the board pack?
  2. From Exhibit 2, list every way the Pack's sampling could bias the pass rate, and say whether reweighting the existing items fixes each.
  3. Exhibit 3 looks like steady progress. What did removing 64 items do to the series, and what rule should govern dropping an item from a test set?
  4. Ranjan has chosen checkpoints on the Pack since June. What does that do to the 92.1 per cent, and what would you change about how the set is held and used?
  5. Saumya reports 61 per cent agreement on complaints, and Rajgiri assigned cause with one reviewer. How much of the disagreement here is a modelling problem and how much a labelling problem, and how would you tell them apart?
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November. What does Supriya do this week, what does she tell the board about the 91 per cent already in Riverina's proposal, and what one sentence should replace the credit clause in the Rajgiri contract?

Building a Golden Set from Real Usage

On the second Monday of March 2026, Ananya Rao, senior product manager for AI quality at Vivechan Systems, a Bengaluru-based SaaS company that sells an AI support copilot to mid-market Indian D2C retailers, opened a spreadsheet with fifteen rows in it. The fifteen rows were her company's entire test suite for the copilot's new model version — fifteen questions someone on her team had typed from memory eighteen months earlier, things like "What is the return policy?" and "Can I cancel after dispatch?". The copilot answered all fifteen correctly. It had also, the week before, told a customer of one of Vivechan's retail clients that a defective blender could be returned for a full refund after ninety days, when the client's actual policy allowed seven. The retailer absorbed the refund and escalated to Vivechan's account team. The fix cost nothing in engineering time and everything in trust: the retailer's ops head asked, reasonably, how Vivechan tests the copilot before a release. Ananya did not have a good answer.

What was on Ananya's desk, 9 March 2026
SignalValue
Copilot conversations logged, Feb 202640,000
Conversations escalated to a human agent3.1%
Refund paid on the mis-stated policy incident₹4.1 lakh
Questions in the existing manual test set15

Vivechan's engineering team wanted to ship a new base model within three weeks — it was cheaper to run and, on their internal hunches, "felt smarter." Ananya's job was to say whether it was actually better, worse, or merely different, and to do it with evidence a retailer's ops head would accept, not with fifteen remembered questions. What she needed, and did not yet have, was a golden set: a fixed, representative sample of real questions the copilot had actually been asked, each one paired with a correct answer someone had signed off on.

1. The idea

A golden set is a fixed, versioned collection of real inputs to a system, each paired with a labelled expected outcome, used repeatedly to check whether the system's outputs are acceptable. "Fixed" matters: unlike a live dashboard, a golden set does not change between one evaluation run and the next, so a score of 86% today and 91% next month is a real comparison, not noise from a shifting yardstick. "Labelled" matters too: each item carries not just a question but a verdict — the right answer, or the boundaries of an acceptable one — decided in advance by a human, not inferred after the fact from whichever answer the model happens to give.

The term has two lineages. Information-retrieval researchers built "gold standard" relevance judgments for search benchmarks such as TREC in the early 1990s, so that different search algorithms could be compared against the same fixed set of queries and known-correct results. Machine-learning practitioners borrowed the phrase for labelled test data more broadly through the 2000s and 2010s. Product teams adopted "golden set" specifically as large language models entered production software after 2022 and PMs needed a repeatable way to answer "is this release better?" without re-litigating the question from scratch every time. The single sentence Ananya could say in a meeting without sounding glib: the golden set is the fixed, labelled question paper the model has to pass before we ship it, built from what our users actually asked — not what we imagine they would ask.

2. How it actually works

Building a golden set from real usage is a sampling problem wearing a labelling problem's clothes, and the steps practitioners tend to skip are the ones between "pull the logs" and "write the answers." Ananya's team worked through six steps.

Define the sampling frame. She fixed a window — February 2026's 40,000 conversations — rather than "all conversations ever," because usage from a year earlier, before Vivechan added three new retail clients, no longer represented what the copilot would face next quarter. Cluster and deduplicate. Raw logs are full of near-identical repeats — "where is my order," "wheres my order," "order not arrived yet" — so her team used embedding similarity to group the 40,000 conversations into roughly 1,150 distinct question clusters before sampling, otherwise a stratified sample would just be a popularity contest for the most common phrasing. Stratify, don't randomly sample. A pure random sample of clusters would mirror the raw frequency of topics, which means it would almost never include the rare, high-stakes categories — product-safety complaints, policy exceptions — that matter most when they go wrong. She defined five strata by topic and set a minimum floor for risk-bearing categories regardless of how rare they were in the logs. Redact. Every sampled conversation was scrubbed of customer names, phone numbers and order IDs before anyone labelled it, both for privacy and so labellers judged the answer, not the person. Label with adjudication. Two reviewers independently wrote the expected outcome for each item; disagreements went to a third, senior reviewer, because for a meaningful share of real questions there is no single obviously correct answer, only a defensible range. Version and freeze. The finished set was saved under an immutable identifier, golden-v1, so that six months later, when usage had shifted again, the team could build golden-v2 without silently overwriting the record of what v1 had contained.

Fig. 1 — the pipeline from raw logs to a frozen, labelled golden set, including the adjudication loop back into freezing.

3. A worked example

Ananya's data lead ran the numbers on the February log. After deduplication, the 1,150 clusters fell into five strata by topic. A purely proportional sample of 200 items, drawn in proportion to each stratum's share of traffic, would have included only 8 product-defect questions — because defect complaints were rare, at 4% of volume, even though a wrong answer there was the costliest kind of mistake. Her team instead set a floor of 20 items for any stratum touching safety or money, and let the remaining budget fill proportionally. The arithmetic, shown rather than asserted:

Golden-v1 sampling plan, 240 items, ₹300 per item to label (two reviewers + adjudication share)
StratumShare of Feb trafficProportional countFloor appliedFinal sample
Refund policy31%74—74
Exchange window24%58—58
Delivery delay28%67—67
Order cancellation13%31—31
Product defect4%102020
Total100%240250

Raising product-defect from its proportional 10 to a floor of 20 added 10 items, taking the set from 240 to 250 and the labelling bill from ₹72,000 to ₹75,000 — a 4% cost increase to fix the stratum most likely to trigger a five-figure refund or a regulatory complaint. Three weeks later, after a second defect-related incident involving a mislabelled electrical appliance, Ananya's team ran the second pass: they doubled the product-defect floor to 40. Total sample size rose to 270, labelling cost to ₹81,000 — a further 8% increase — in exchange for a stratum with roughly four times its original statistical power to detect a regression. The lesson she took from watching the number move: the floor is not a nicety, it is where most of the marginal risk reduction per rupee actually lives, because rare-but-severe categories are exactly where a small sample is too noisy to trust.

4. The nuances a learner must become aware of

A golden set is not a regression test set, and neither is live monitoring. A golden set is a broad, representative snapshot used to score overall quality before a release; a regression test set is a narrow, growing list of specific past failures the team never wants to see again; live monitoring watches production traffic after release for problems neither set anticipated. Vivechan needed all three, and conflating them — as the fifteen-question spreadsheet effectively did, functioning as a weak version of all three at once — is how teams end up under-tested in every direction simultaneously.

Representativeness and coverage pull against each other. Logs show what users actually asked, which is exactly the golden set's strength, but logs cannot show what users would ask an adversarial user, a first-time visitor, or a user in a scenario the product has never yet encountered, such as a new client's return policy going live for the first time. A log-only golden set systematically under-samples the edge cases a team most needs to catch before they happen for real.

Labels are judgment calls, not data entry. For "what is your return policy," the correct answer is fixed and checkable. For "the product arrived late, what should I do," a defensible answer might validate the complaint, apologise, and offer one of two remedies — reasonable reviewers can disagree on which remedy, or on tone. Ananya's team tracked inter-rater agreement, the rate at which two independent labellers reached the same verdict, and treated any stratum below 80% agreement as needing a clearer rubric before it could be trusted, not as ready to grade.

Golden sets go stale. A set frozen in March reflects March's product catalog, March's policies and March's client roster. When Vivechan onboarded a new retail client in May with a different exchange window, golden-v1 quietly stopped covering a real and growing slice of traffic — not because anything in it was wrong, but because the world it described had moved.

It must never leak into training. If golden-set questions, or close paraphrases of them, end up in the model's fine-tuning data or in the few-shot examples baked into its prompt, the model is being tested on material it has effectively seen the answers to. The resulting score is contaminated and will not predict real-world performance; the set must be held out with the same discipline a university applies to an exam bank.

Sample size limits what a score can tell you. A 20-item stratum can distinguish a wild swing from a stable result, but it cannot reliably detect the difference between 82% and 87% pass rates — the noise band is wider than that gap. Ananya's team treated small strata as good for catching gross regressions, not for fine-tuning marginal decisions between two close model versions.

It cannot explain why a model failed, and it cannot see what users never got to ask. A golden set tells you that an item failed, not the mechanism behind the failure, and it inherits survivorship bias from the product itself: if the copilot has never once offered a store-credit option, no log will contain a customer accepting one, so the golden set will never surface that the option should exist at all.

Before relying on a golden set, a newcomer should ask: who adjudicates disagreement and on what authority; how often is it refreshed and what triggers a refresh outside the calendar; which categories were deliberately excluded, and why; and whether anyone has checked that the labels are not quietly present in the model's own training data.

5. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and scale

How the same discipline changes shape by product type and company stage
ContextWhat changes
ConsumerEnormous log volume; the hard problem is diversity of scenario, not sample size — most effort goes into finding the rare cases, not counting the common ones.
B2BFew conversations per account; stratify by client and contract terms, not just topic, because one enterprise account's edge case can matter more than a hundred small-account repeats.
MarketplaceTwo audiences, two golden sets — buyer-side and seller-side questions need separate sampling and separate labels, since a correct seller answer can be an incorrect buyer answer.
Early-stageNo logs yet, or too few; the set must be seeded from support-ticket transcripts, sales-call notes, or deliberately written scenarios, and revisited within weeks once real logs exist.
Large companyLog volume and labelling budget both scale up; governance gets heavier — legal and trust teams review sensitive strata before anything is frozen for company-wide use.

6. Common mistakes

Cherry-picked questions dressed up as a golden set. Symptom: the model looks excellent in every demo and then fails within days of a real release, as it did for Vivechan's original fifteen. Underlying misunderstanding: treating the set as a checklist of what the product should do, written from imagination, rather than a sample of what customers actually do. Cheapest diagnostic: compare the topic distribution of the "golden set" against the topic distribution of last month's real logs; a wide gap is the tell.

Never refreshing it. Symptom: the golden-set score keeps climbing release after release while support escalations quietly rise in parallel. Underlying misunderstanding: treating the set as a permanent monument rather than a living instrument that must track a moving product. Cheapest diagnostic: check the set's last-updated date against the date of the last catalog or policy change.

Loose or inconsistent labels. Symptom: the same model, scored twice by different graders, produces noticeably different pass rates. Underlying misunderstanding: treating labelling as clerical data entry rather than judgment work that needs a written rubric and adjudication. Cheapest diagnostic: measure inter-rater agreement on a small overlapping sample before trusting the full set.

Train-test contamination. Symptom: the model scores suspiciously well on the golden set while genuine user complaints do not fall to match. Underlying misunderstanding: reusing golden-set examples as few-shot prompt examples or fine-tuning data, so the model has effectively memorised the exam. Cheapest diagnostic: audit the training and prompt-example data for overlap with golden-set item IDs before every release.

7. What good looks like

Six weeks after freezing golden-v1, Ananya's team ran both the old and new model against it. The old model passed 71% of the 270 items; the new one passed 84% overall — but on the product-defect stratum specifically, the new model's pass rate fell from 90% to 68%, because the newer, cheaper model was more willing to promise refunds outside policy in exactly the way that had triggered the March incident. Because the stratum had been deliberately oversampled to 40 items, the drop was a real signal, not noise. Ananya held the release, asked engineering to add a policy-lookup step for defect questions specifically, and re-ran only that stratum three days later: 91%. The full model shipped the following week. Escalation rate for defect-related conversations stayed flat rather than rising, and no further five-figure refund incidents followed that quarter.

Closing

Ananya froze golden-v1 at 270 items, versioned and stored with its labels and its adjudication notes, and set two standing rules: no release ships without a golden-set run, and any release that drops below 90% on the safety-and-money strata specifically is blocked regardless of its overall score. She put a refresh on the calendar for every client onboarding and every policy change, not just once a quarter. What she flagged to learn next, and why: grading rubrics and LLM-as-judge methods, because manually adjudicating every item does not scale once the set reaches into the thousands; and feedback loops and data flywheels, because the real prize is routing production failures automatically back into the next version of the golden set, so the test keeps pace with the product instead of the other way around.

Two questions worth sitting with:

If your product's golden set were audited tomorrow, could anyone tell you which real-world scenario each item came from, and who decided the correct answer was correct?

What is the most severe question your users are not yet asking — and how would you know, if the only evidence you trust is what already happened in the logs?
case20v1-aipm.golden.set:
Ibaarat Labs: Building a Golden Set from Real Usage

A decision case in AI and ML product management

1. Opening

On the morning of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Ishaan Joglekar stood at the whiteboard in Ibaarat Labs' Baner office in Pune, looking at two numbers he had written side by side: ₹12.0 lakh and ₹7.2 lakh. The first was what the company's current language model cost to answer customer queries in September. The second was what a cheaper model would have cost for the same traffic. As head of product, Ishaan had to tell his team by the end of the day how they would test the cheaper model, because the largest client's renewal review was fixed for Monday, 2 November, and that client would want to know whether the saving came at the price of worse answers.

The company had no trustworthy test set, and only two weeks in which to build one.

2. Company background

Ibaarat Labs was founded in 2021 by two engineers who had left a Pune software services firm. Its product, Ibaarat Reply, drafts and sends answers to customers of lenders and insurers over WhatsApp and in-app chat, in Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, English and the code-mixed Hinglish that most customers actually type. Its sixty-two staff served eleven clients: lenders, two insurers and a two-wheeler financier. Billings were about ₹75 lakh a month, roughly ₹9 crore a year. The largest client, a Chennai lender, contributed 28 per cent of that, or ₹21 lakh a month.

The market was crowded. Haptik, Yellow.ai, Freshworks and Zoho all sold conversational support. Clients bought accuracy on routine queries and comfort that answers would stay inside the Reserve Bank of India's fair-practice expectations and IRDAI's grievance timelines. Ibaarat's pitch was vertical competence, not the cheapest bot.

3. The situation

In September, Ibaarat Reply handled 4,80,000 conversations, an average of 16,000 a day. Each cost the company ₹2.50 in model fees, so the month's bill was ₹12,00,000. A newer model quoted at ₹1.50 per conversation would have cut the bill to ₹7,20,000, saving ₹4.8 lakh a month, or ₹57.6 lakh a year. With festive volumes arriving before Diwali on 8 November, when EMI reminders and payment queries climb, the saving was tempting.

The trouble was evidence. Earlier in the year the team had tested changes against a set of 200 prompts that a data scientist had generated with a large model. Almost everything passed. Yet when Gitanjali Rao in Chennai had a reviewer read 300 randomly chosen live conversations in August, the picture differed. Exhibit 2 sets the two results side by side. The synthetic set passed 192 of 200, or 96.0 per cent. The live sample passed 252 of 300, or 84.0 per cent, a 12-point gap. Within the live sample, the 90 code-mixed Hinglish conversations passed only 63 times, or 70.0 per cent, against 189 of the other 210, or 90.0 per cent. The invented prompts were too tidy. Real customers wrote "emi kat gaya but status pending dikha raha" and asked two things at once.

Ishaan's problem was what to test against. A golden set, a fixed collection of real inputs each paired with a human-labelled correct outcome, would let the team score any change the same way every time. The raw material already existed in September's logs. Exhibit 1 shows how they divided by intent.

4. The people

Hemant Deshpande, the machine-learning lead in Bengaluru, wanted to switch models at once. He argued that each week of delay cost about ₹1.1 lakh in avoidable fees (₹4.8 lakh a month over roughly four and a third weeks) and that a quick synthetic set was good enough for a first comparison.

Ines Carvalho, a data scientist working from Lisbon favoured the same route for a different reason: synthetic prompts could cover rare cases, such as bereavement or fraud complaints, that might never appear in a random sample.

Gitanjali Rao, customer-success lead in Chennai, spoke to the largest client every week. She wanted real Tamil and Hinglish conversations in the set, since her client's customers wrote that way, and warned that the client's quality team would trust only real transcripts.

Hiral Shah, handling privacy from Ahmedabad, accepted logs but insisted that names, phone numbers and loan numbers be removed before any reviewer saw them, in line with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and with each client's contract on data use.

5. The options

Ishaan sketched three courses of action. Exhibit 3 sets out their costs and Exhibit 4 the calendar.

Option A: a stratified golden set from real logs. Draw 600 conversations from September's logs in the proportions of the recommended column of Exhibit 1, redact personal data automatically, and have two reviewers independently label each one with the expected outcome, the facts a good answer must contain and anything it must never say. A senior reviewer would settle the roughly 15 per cent of items where the two disagreed. The upside is fidelity to what customers actually send. The cost is ₹1.50 lakh and two working weeks, finishing on Thursday, 29 October, four days before the renewal review.

Option B: a synthetic set. Have a stronger model write 600 realistic prompts from the intent list and have one reviewer label them. It would be ready in a week and cost ₹0.47 lakh. The risk is the one Exhibit 2 has already shown: tidy prompts flatter every model, so a pass would prove little.

Option C: borrow the client's quality scores. The Chennai lender's quality team scores tickets for its human agents, and had offered about 3,100 scored conversations. Ibaarat would map those scores to its own rubric. The labels would carry the client's authority at a direct cost of ₹0.76 lakh. But the data covered only payment status and documents, and contractual data-sharing steps would take about six weeks, so the review would arrive first.

Workings. A: 600 items × 2 reviewers × 6 minutes = 120 hours at ₹800 = ₹96,000; 15% of 600 = 90 disputed items × 10 minutes = 15 hours at ₹2,000 = ₹30,000. B: 600 × 4 minutes = 40 hours at ₹800 = ₹32,000. C: 20 hours at ₹800 = ₹16,000; 40 engineering hours at ₹1,500 = ₹60,000. Each row's total equals its three cost columns.

Exhibit 4. Calendar for the decision, 14 October to 8 November 2026.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, why did the synthetic set and the live sample disagree, and what does the gap between Hinglish and other conversations imply about what a golden set must contain?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, what is the case for and against over-sampling complaints? How would you report a single headline score from an unevenly sampled set?
  3. Using Exhibit 3 and the calendar, which option fits the deadline, and what is the monthly saving worth compared with the cost of a wrong decision at the renewal?
  4. What would Hiral Shah need to see before approving the use of logs, and how might you modify Option A to answer Hemant's concern about speed and Ines's concern about rare cases?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. A golden set is the test data of an evaluation: it is only as good as its resemblance to real use. The question is not which route is cheapest, but which route produces a set the team and the client will both believe, in time to use it. Exhibit 2 shows that an unrepresentative set can overstate quality by double digits.

One defensible path. Choose Option A, with two refinements. First, keep 100 of the 600 items sealed, so that tuning on the other 500 cannot inflate the final score. Second, ask Ines to write a small supplement of rare-case prompts, marked synthetic and scored separately. Report results by intent and weight them by the share-of-volume column of Exhibit 1, so that over-sampling complaints does not distort the headline.

Why. Option B is cheap but has already misled the team once. Option C misses the deadline and covers two of six intents. Option A costs ₹1.50 lakh, finishes before the renewal review, and its price is small against ₹57.6 lakh a year of potential saving and ₹21 lakh a month of renewal exposure. It also becomes an asset against which every later change can be scored. Hiral's redaction requirement is a design constraint, not an obstacle, and Hemant's switch should wait for the score.
exp20v2-aipm.model.metrics:
Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC

AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management

1. A dashboard that looked finished

On Monday 7 September 2026, Sunanda Pathak, product lead for risk at Prahari Payments Network, a Pune-based acquirer that processes card and UPI payments for about 60,000 small merchants, opened a validation report from Pranav Shekhawat, the data scientist in Bengaluru who had built the company's new fraud model. The report covered one month of held-out transactions: 10,00,000 payments, scored by the model after the fact and compared with what chargebacks and merchant disputes later revealed. Its headline read “accuracy 99.15%, AUC above 0.9.” Pranav's note said the model was ready, pending one decision: what score should trigger a block-and-review.

Sunanda had two constraints. Prakash Sundaram, the head of finance, had told her that every fraudulent payment that got through cost Prahari about ₹4,000 in net loss after recoveries. And the operations team in Pune could manually review no more than 1,000 flagged payments a day. The decision looked technical but was a question about money and people: how many genuine customers would Prahari inconvenience to stop how much fraud? She suspected that “99.15% accurate” answered neither half.

2. The idea

A classifier is a model that sorts cases into two groups, here “fraud” and “genuine.” It can be wrong in two different ways. A false positive is a genuine payment wrongly flagged; a false negative is a fraud that slips through. Correct calls are true positives (fraud caught) and true negatives (genuine payment left alone). Counting the four outcomes gives a confusion matrix; every metric here is arithmetic on its four cells.

Precision asks: of everything the model flagged, what share was truly fraud? It is true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. Recall asks: of all the real fraud, what share did the model catch? It is true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. The terms come from information retrieval in the 1950s and 1960s, where researchers asked how many retrieved documents were relevant. AUC, the area under the ROC curve, descends from signal-detection theory developed for radar operators in the 1940s, and entered machine learning in the 1990s. ROC stands for receiver operating characteristic.

A single error rate hides which mistakes are being made. The sentence Sunanda could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: “Precision tells us what our reviewers will waste, recall tells us what our customers will lose, and AUC tells us whether the model can separate the two at all.”

3. How it actually works

The model does not output “fraud” or “genuine.” It outputs a score between 0 and 1 for every payment, and a human chooses a threshold: payments scoring at or above it are flagged. Practitioners leave this step implicit, yet precision and recall belong to a model plus a threshold, not to the model alone.

Pranav's validation month contained 5,000 frauds and 9,95,000 genuine payments, a fraud rate of 0.5 per cent. At a threshold of 0.50 the four cells were as follows.

Threshold 0.50Actually fraudActually genuineRow total
Flagged3,500 (TP)7,000 (FP)10,500
Not flagged1,500 (FN)9,88,000 (TN)9,89,500
Column total5,0009,95,00010,00,000

Exhibit 1. Confusion matrix for the validation month at threshold 0.50. TP = true positive, FP = false positive, FN = false negative, TN = true negative.

The arithmetic follows. Precision is 3,500 divided by 10,500, or 33.3 per cent: one flag in three is real. Recall is 3,500 divided by 5,000, or 70 per cent. Accuracy, the share of all calls that were correct, is (3,500 + 9,88,000) divided by 10,00,000, or 99.15 per cent, which is where the dashboard headline came from. Now consider a lazy system that never flags anything. It would be right on every genuine payment and wrong on every fraud, for an accuracy of 9,95,000 divided by 10,00,000, or 99.5 per cent. The lazy system beats the model on accuracy while catching nothing, which is why Sunanda set accuracy aside.

AUC handles the threshold problem by refusing to pick one. Sweep the threshold from strict to lenient and record, at each setting, the true positive rate (which is simply recall) and the false positive rate (false positives divided by all genuine payments). Plot one against the other and you have the ROC curve. AUC is the area beneath it, between 0.5 (a coin flip) and 1.0 (perfect separation). Its most useful reading: pick one random fraud and one random genuine payment, and AUC is the chance the model scored the fraud higher.

A miniature version makes this concrete. Take four frauds scoring 0.90, 0.80, 0.60 and 0.35, and five genuine payments scoring 0.70, 0.40, 0.30, 0.20 and 0.10. There are 4 × 5 = 20 fraud-genuine pairs.

The model ranks a fraud above a genuine payment in 17 of 20 pairs, so AUC is 0.85. No threshold was used: AUC judges only the ordering of scores.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Exhibit 6. The same data as Exhibit 5. The cheapest threshold is the interior one, 0.30.

The cheapest setting is 0.30 at ₹58.8 lakh, which is ₹9.6 lakh a month less than 0.50 (68.4 minus 58.8). It needs about 770 flags a day, inside the review team’s 1,000.

Second pass. Suppose Prakash revises the cost of a missed fraud from ₹4,000 to ₹8,000, because chargeback penalties from the card networks had been left out. The model is unchanged. Missed-fraud costs double to ₹200, ₹120, ₹72 and ₹40 lakh, and totals become 201.8, 128.4, 94.8 and 94.0 lakh. The optimum slides to 0.20, but only by ₹0.8 lakh over 0.30, and 0.20 would need 1,650 reviews a day against a capacity of 1,000. The best threshold moves with costs and capacity; AUC did not move at all.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Accuracy is not neutral; the base rate decides it

A model that catches nothing scores 99.5 per cent accuracy here. Before trusting any accuracy figure, ask what the always-predict-the-majority baseline would score.

Precision depends on how common the event is

Recall and false positive rate describe the model’s behaviour on each class separately and hold steady when the mix changes; precision does not. Take a hypothetical model with recall of 80 per cent and a false positive rate of 2 per cent.

Fraud rateFraudsGenuineTPFPPrecision
0.5%5,0009,95,0004,00019,90016.7%
5%50,0009,50,00040,00019,00067.8%

Exhibit 7. Same model, 10,00,000 payments, two fraud rates. Precision = TP / (TP + FP): 4,000 / 23,900 and 40,000 / 59,000.

A model tested on a fraud-enriched sample looks far more precise than it will be live.

AUC measures ranking, not decisions

Two models with equal AUC can behave very differently at the one threshold you will use. A product manager needs the operating point, not only the area.

ROC can flatter rare-event problems

The false positive rate divides by the huge genuine class, so 19,000 false alarms register as only 1.91 per cent. A precision-recall curve, plotting precision against recall, makes the pain visible.

Scores are not probabilities

A score of 0.30 does not mean a 30 per cent chance of fraud unless the model is calibrated, meaning its scores match observed frequencies. AUC is blind to calibration, so a badly calibrated model can have a superb AUC.

Metrics are only as good as the labels

“Fraud” here means a payment later charged back. Disputes arrive over 60 to 90 days, so recent transactions look cleaner than they are, and undisputed frauds count as genuine.

6. How it looks in different products

In consumer products, a false alarm is a person at a checkout with a declined card; recall is usually traded down until friction is tolerable. In B2B products such as Prahari’s, a false flag that holds a settlement can threaten a merchant’s cash flow, so its cost varies enormously by merchant size. One blended ₹120 hides that; mature teams set thresholds by segment. In marketplaces, there are two sets of victims: a fraudulent seller harms buyers, while a wrongly suspended honest seller withdraws supply.

Scale changes the discipline as well. An early-stage company has few labelled frauds, so recall estimates carry wide error bars and the threshold should be reviewed weekly. A large company has abundant labels but layered rules, models and human review, so the question shifts to the whole pipeline. Regulators such as the Reserve Bank of India and NPCI expect documented fraud monitoring, making the threshold a governance decision too.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data. Symptom: a triumphant dashboard beside a rising loss line. Diagnostic: compute the accuracy of the never-flag baseline; if it is close, the metric is uninformative.

Treating 0.5 as the threshold. Symptom: reviewers are idle or drowning. Misunderstanding: the software default is taken as a recommendation. Diagnostic: tabulate cost and review load at four thresholds, as Exhibits 3 and 5 do.

Quoting AUC as if it were business value. Symptom: a stakeholder hears “0.94” and assumes 94 per cent of fraud is caught. Misunderstanding: AUC is a ranking probability. Diagnostic: ask “at what threshold, and what are the counts?”

Evaluating on a rebalanced sample. Symptom: precision in production is a fraction of what the test promised. Misunderstanding: precision is treated as a model property. Diagnostic: recompute precision from recall and false positive rate at the live base rate, as in Exhibit 7.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Sunanda’s decision has the metric chosen before the model is judged, from costs written down by finance and operations. The confusion matrix is on the page, several thresholds are tabulated with cost and workload side by side, and the base rate matches production. Someone has also stated what would change the answer: the cost of a missed fraud and the size of the review team.

9. What Sunanda decided

She set the threshold at 0.30 and told Prakash and Pranav why in three sentences: it minimised monthly error cost at ₹58.8 lakh on the agreed inputs, it fit within review capacity at about 770 flags a day, and it would be revisited when finance finished its chargeback-penalty study, since at ₹8,000 per miss the ranking of thresholds nearly tied. She also asked for a weekly report of precision, recall and flag volume, because a threshold is a hypothesis about costs that production must keep confirming. Pooja Srinivasan, the analytics lead in Singapore, would build the precision-recall view by merchant segment.

What to learn next: offline versus online evaluation, because every number above came from a past month and says nothing about how fraudsters respond once the model is live; ranking metrics, for products where the order of a list matters more than a yes-or-no call; and fraud and risk models, where these ideas meet adversaries who adapt.

Two questions to sit with. First, name a decision in your own product where a false positive and a false negative have very different costs: who has actually written those costs down, and would they agree on the figures? Second, if your model’s AUC improved from 0.94 to 0.96 next quarter, what would you check before telling anyone that customers were better off?

Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC

AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management · near-expert depth

1. Two rooms, one arithmetic

On Friday 12 June 2026, in a converted godown on Wardha Road in Nagpur, Ila Ingale opened a printout she had asked for three times. Ingale runs the public-screening line at Indriya Diagnostics Network, 34 imaging centres and radiography vans across Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh. Since March, Indriya has pre-read chest X-rays from district camps under India's National TB Elimination Programme, using Ikshana 3, licensed from Ikshana Vision Labs in Bengaluru. Anyone it flags is tested; anyone it does not goes home. The vendor datasheet reported an AUC of 0.94. It did not tell Ingale whom to send home.

Ishan Idnani, Indriya's lead data scientist in Bengaluru, had scored 1,20,000 films taken between 1 March and 31 May 2026 — 92 days — each followed by a molecular test, so the reference standard was complete. Of those films, 1,200 came from people with pulmonary tuberculosis: a prevalence of exactly 1.0 per cent. The tender imposed a sensitivity floor of 90 per cent; district laboratories could run about 320 confirmatory tests a day. Indumathi Iyer, chief radiologist in Chennai, wanted to know who owned whatever number was chosen.

Six days later in Jaipur, Zeenat Zariwala faced the mirror image. Zariwala directs trust and safety at Zardozi Style Bazaar, a fashion marketplace that did ₹740 crore of gross merchandise value in FY26 across 41,000 sellers and some 6,00,000 live listings a quarter. Zubeda Zargar's team in Hyderabad had built Zarrin Signal, which scores each listing for counterfeit risk. Zoravar Zutshi, who owns seller growth from Gurugram, brought his own number: takedowns and complaints both up 40 per cent quarter on quarter. A missed counterfeit meant a refund and a brand's lawyer; a wrong takedown meant an honest karigar in Bagru dark for nine days. Neither woman had a metric that could choose her threshold for her.

2. The idea, and the four camps

A binary classifier emits a score, not a verdict. A human converts score into verdict by fixing a threshold, and only then does the model make countable errors, in four cells: true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN), true negatives (TN). Precision, or positive predictive value, is TP/(TP+FP): of what we flagged, how much was real. Recall, or sensitivity, is TP/(TP+FN): of what was real, how much we flagged. The false positive rate is FP/(FP+TN). The ROC curve plots recall against it as the threshold sweeps from strict to lenient; AUC is the area beneath, and equals the probability that a random positive outscores a random negative.

The lineage explains the disagreements. Precision and recall come from Cyril Cleverdon's Cranfield retrieval experiments of the late 1950s, where the negatives were uncountable. ROC analysis comes from wartime signal detection, formalised by Tanner and Swets in 1954; Hanley and McNeil tied it to the Mann–Whitney U statistic in 1982. Neyman and Pearson supplied the spine in 1933: fix the tolerable rate of one error, minimise the other.

Four camps are live. The decision-theoretic camp holds that a metric is a loss function in disguise, so the only honest report is expected cost at the operating point you will ship; it signs “every threshold implies a cost ratio, so state it,” and not “model A beats model B” with no decision attached. The discrimination-first camp separates model quality from policy and treats AUC as the threshold-free leaderboard; it signs “higher AUC gives the team more options,” and not “optimise F1,” an arbitrary operating point dressed as a score. The calibration camp, descending from proper scoring rules, wants a probability judged by Brier score or log loss, because downstream systems multiply the score by money; it will not sign “AUC 0.94, therefore ship.” The online-only camp holds that every offline number is a hypothesis about a world that no longer exists; it signs “ship behind a holdback and measure,” and not a launch decided on a retrospective sample.

Take 10,000 cases containing 500 positives.

Model I wins on precision and F1, Model Z on recall. At a false-negative cost ten times a false positive, Model I is cheaper by 1,200 units; at forty times, Model Z is cheaper by 300. The metric does not reveal the better model; it encodes a price.

The interior minimum is not luck. If the score were a calibrated probability, the optimal rule would test whenever the posterior probability exceeded cFP/(cFP+cFN) = 450/75,450 = 0.60 per cent. The move that separates practitioners: the quantity to compare against that break-even is not average precision but marginal precision at the boundary. Loosening from 0.45 to 0.30 adds 10,782 flags, of which 90 are true — 0.83 per cent, above break-even, so take the step, and the total duly falls by ₹18.98 lakh. Loosening from 0.30 to 0.20 adds 11,922 flags of which 42 are true — 0.35 per cent, below break-even, so refuse, and the total rises by ₹22.15 lakh. Average precision at 0.30, 4.46 per cent, is more than seven times break-even and would have argued for loosening much further: the wrong statistic for the marginal question.

Capacity then intervenes. At 0.30 the pathway needs about 270 tests a day against a ceiling of 320; at 0.20 it needs 400, and a queue that grows without bound makes recall on paper stop corresponding to cases found. The 90 per cent floor separately eliminates 0.60 and 0.45. Cost, capacity and contract agreed on 0.30 — the only reason the meeting stayed civil — and Iyer's demand stands, because a threshold is a price, not a configuration value.

4. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Five conditions, each testable. One: the two errors cost differently and someone with authority will state the ratio. Indriya passes, because a government annexure did the pricing; Zardozi passes only after Zariwala forces it, since her false-positive cost includes churn that Zutshi's team, not hers, would feel. Two: the label means what the metric assumes. Indriya's is a molecular test; Zardozi's “counterfeit” is a panel adjudication that disagrees with itself on one listing in twelve, so recall against it has a ceiling no model can breach. Three: evaluation prevalence matches deployment. Four: the decision really is a threshold on a score — not a ranked feed, not a fixed review budget. Five: the population is stable.

The frame actively misleads in three situations. Where a fixed human capacity sets the cut, the operating point is a top-k rule and precision at a fixed score is unactionable. Where the output changes the outcome it predicts — a warning that deters abandonment — the quantity of interest is a treatment effect, and observed labels credit the intervention to prediction. And where the product is a ranking, a threshold discards what matters, the order.

5. Hard edges: two sides, two devices, two organisations

A cost ratio crossing three cost centres is a negotiation, which is why mature firms keep a signed threshold memo.

The regulated and hardware edges bite at Indriya. Software that triages patients is a medical device, so the CDSCO file, the tender's floor and the cost annexure are three objective functions written by three bodies. And the older computed-radiography plates in the vans produce a different score distribution from the city's direct detectors, so one threshold is a different clinical rule on different hardware; mature teams recalibrate per device class.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

Precision is not a property of a model

Recall and the false positive rate live inside a class and survive a change in prevalence; precision mixes the classes. Indriya's 72,000 urban films sit at 0.50 per cent prevalence, its 48,000 van films at 1.75 per cent, so at recall 92.5 per cent and a 20 per cent false positive rate urban precision is 333 of 14,661, or 2.27 per cent, and rural 777 of 10,209, or 7.61 per cent. The tell: an expert never takes a precision figure without its base rate.

Marginal, not average, precision answers the loosening question

The average summarises a decision already made; the margin is the one in front of you. The tell: 4.46 per cent is quoted and 0.35 per cent has never been computed.

AUC is a weighted average of within-group and between-group concordance

Pool two populations whose scores and prevalences differ in the same direction and AUC rises without the model improving any decision, because between-group pairs can outnumber within-group ones. The tell: pooled AUC above every stratum's, and features that proxy for site or device.

Discrimination and calibration are independent

A strictly increasing transformation of the scores leaves AUC untouched and changes every expected-cost calculation, because costs multiply probabilities, not ranks. The tell: AUC to three decimals, with observed frequency never plotted against predicted score by decile.

F1 is a cost ratio somebody chose by accident

The harmonic mean implies an exchange rate between the errors that depends on the base rate and has nothing to do with the business: in Exhibit 7 it prefers the policy costing ₹78.13 lakh more, in Exhibit 1 it bets the ratio is below 34. The tell: F1 in a quarterly objective.

Labels are produced by the process being evaluated

Indriya tested every validation film, which is expensive; in steady state only flagged patients are tested, so the unflagged group's positives turn invisible and recall drifts upward for free. The tell: recall improving quarter after quarter with no model change. The remedy is a budgeted random audit stream the model cannot see.

Rare-event metrics carry wide intervals

Recall of 92.5 per cent on 1,200 positives carries a standard error of 0.76 percentage points, about ±1.5 points; on the 360 urban positives it widens to ±2.7, so a 1.1-point subgroup gain is noise. The tell: recall to one decimal with no denominator in sight.

The human in the loop is part of the metric

Zardozi's reviewers restore 92 per cent of false positives and confirm 95 per cent of true ones, turning a precision of 33.8 per cent into 376 effective wrong takedowns and 120 added misses. The tell: model precision on the dashboard with no overturn rate beside it.

7. What changes across product types and stages

In consumer products the false positive is friction spread across millions, rarely priced; recall is traded down until complaints subside. In enterprise and B2B, errors are concentrated and named — one blocked settlement belongs to one customer with a contract — so thresholds are set per account tier. In platforms and marketplaces the two errors fall on different sides in different currencies: buyer harm is refunds and reputation, seller harm is withdrawn supply, and no scalar reconciles them. Hardware-plus-software adds a per-device distribution and a calibration drift no model work fixes. In AI-native products the classifier often has no usable score, only a self-reported confidence that is not a probability, so the substitute is a graded rubric and sampled review: measurement design, not a formula.

Stage changes what is measurable, not what is true. Early, positives are scarce and intervals wide, so fix a tolerable false positive rate and watch recall drift. At scale, labels are abundant but contaminated by feedback and layered rules sit above the model, so the honest question is end-to-end yield. What does not change: somebody writes down the cost ratio.

8. Three worked examples

Indriya splits the threshold by site

Idnani proposed 0.45 in the urban centres, where prevalence is low and false alarms plentiful, and 0.30 in the vans. The class-conditional rates give 306 urban true positives and 7,880 urban false positives, plus 777 and 9,432 rural: 1,083 of 1,200 cases found, recall 90.25 per cent, on 18,395 tests. That is 18,395 × 450 = ₹82.78 lakh of testing and 117 × 75,000 = ₹87.75 lakh of misses, ₹170.53 lakh in all — ₹8.89 lakh cheaper than 0.30 everywhere at ₹179.42 lakh, on 200 tests a day instead of 270. The catch is distributional, which is why Iyer objected: urban misses rise to 54 of 360, or 15 per cent, against 63 of 840, or 7.5 per cent, and recall lands 0.25 points above the floor — three films.

Zardozi tiers instead of choosing

The second example's lesson is structural: Zariwala used both points, auto-actioning the head where precision is 88.9 per cent and routing the middle to review. That turned a threshold question into a budget question.

Where it failed: Zanjeer Freight Exchange

Zanjeer Freight Exchange, a Surat load-matching platform, shipped Zimmedari Score in 2025 to predict whether a booked load would be abandoned by the carrier, requiring a deposit above 0.55. Validation on 40,000 loads showed AUC 0.787, and the rule went live. Abandonment did not fall, and short-haul carriers began to leave. 9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Accuracy on an imbalanced problem. Sign: rising accuracy beside a flat count of caught cases. Diagnostic: what would an always-negative model score? At Indriya, 99.0 per cent. Caught late, a quarter of engineering chases a metric that cannot move.

Threshold left at the library default. Sign: reviewers idle or drowning within a week. Diagnostic: name its owner and show its change log. Caught late, the cost is overtime and trust that does not return.

Evaluating on an enriched sample. Sign: production precision a fraction of validation while recall holds. Diagnostic: recompute precision from recall and the false positive rate at the live base rate. Caught late, the launch rolls back.

Pooling heterogeneous populations. Sign: pooled AUC above every subgroup's. Diagnostic: Exhibit 8's decomposition. Caught late, as at Zanjeer, a live policy taxes the wrong cohort and its supply walks away.

Selective labelling. Sign: recall improving with no model change. Diagnostic: is there a random audit stream the model cannot see? Caught late, every historical metric becomes unusable at once.

Adversarial response. Sign: precision decaying monotonically after launch with no data change. Diagnostic: cohort the score distribution by seller tenure. Caught late, the threshold chases a distribution it created.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

ROC versus precision–recall under imbalance. The PR camp argues that at 1 per cent prevalence the false positive rate divides by so large a denominator that real pain vanishes, as Exhibit 3 shows. The ROC camp answers that prevalence-invariance is the feature: recall and the false positive rate transfer across districts, whereas PR curves must be recomputed for each deployment. The first is wrong if deployment prevalence tracks evaluation prevalence; the second if decisions come from the curve rather than the operating point.

Calibration versus discrimination. The calibration camp rests on the fact that costs multiply probabilities: without calibration, Indriya's 0.60 per cent break-even cannot be applied to a raw score. The discrimination camp answers that calibration is a cheap post-hoc fix, isotonic regression on a holdout, whereas ranking power is irreducible. The first is wrong if recalibration is reliable across the subpopulations that matter; the second if miscalibrated scores feed automated pricing, as increasingly they do.

One composite metric versus a dashboard. The composite camp argues from organisational reality: a team without one number to move optimises nothing, and Fβ with a chosen β is defensible. The dashboard camp replies that any composite hides the cost ratio it encodes. The first is wrong if teams can hold four numbers at once; the second if such teams demonstrably drift.

Are offline metrics decision-grade? The online-only camp points at Zanjeer: 0.787 approved a policy that made things worse, and only live measurement caught it. The offline camp answers that Zanjeer suffered a bad offline analysis, not an indictment of offline analysis, and that experiments are slow and sometimes impossible: Indriya cannot randomise who gets screened.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the cost ratio before the model, and treats the threshold as a priced decision with an owner, a memo and a review date. They read a confusion matrix before a headline, ask for the base rate whenever precision is quoted, and compute at the margin. They report subgroup tables unprompted, and are made uneasy rather than pleased by a pooled number exceeding every part.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Ingale set a single threshold of 0.30: it minimised total cost at ₹179.42 lakh, met the floor with 92.5 per cent recall, and fitted the 320-test ceiling at about 270 a day. She rejected the per-site split despite its ₹8.89 lakh saving, on the ground that a 15 per cent urban miss rate against 7.5 per cent rural is a choice for the state mission, and sent it to them as a written option. Zariwala adopted the tiered policy, at ₹63.09 lakh on the audit and about ₹7.57 crore a quarter at scale, and replaced her team's F1 objective with three numbers: effective wrong takedowns, effective misses, reviewer reversal rate.

For discussion. First, the per-site split is cheaper, meets the floor and misses twice the share of urban cases: who may make that trade, and what would you need to see before signing it? Second, Zardozi's ₹1,987 false-positive cost rests on a 14 per cent churn estimate owned by another executive; if it were 7 per cent, which policy wins, and who should own the metric? Third, Zanjeer's 0.787 was arithmetically correct and practically worthless — what standing report, costing under a week a quarter, would have caught it before launch?

13. Going deeper

Problem–model fit comes first in logic: the metric follows from the problem type, and a ranking problem mis-framed as classification cannot be rescued by a better threshold. Descriptive statistics for PMs supplies the intervals that stop a 1.1-point subgroup move becoming a roadmap. Offline versus online evaluation is the sequel; section 10's fourth disagreement needs it. Ranking and relevance metrics take over where the order of a list is the product, and fraud and risk models add the adversary who reoptimises against your threshold. The ML lifecycle places the threshold among retraining and rollback; data strategy and data acquisition and labelling and annotation govern the denominators; what's different when the feature is a model explains why a threshold needs a change log. Quality as a distribution generalises from point metric to spread, and what evals are and why PMs own them carries the argument into generative systems, where measurement design is the work.

A case for discussion. Pune, October 2026.

1. Sunday night, 4 October 2026

The Title Clear war room on the fourth floor of Zameen Exchange's office off Baner Road in Pune was empty except for Harini Barve, a cold filter coffee, and three sheets of paper she had spent two hours moving around the table as though they were a puzzle that would resolve if arranged right. The first was the release note for Sanad v3, the company's title-risk model, which led with an area under the curve of 0.908 and the sentence catches 85 per cent of material title defects. The second was an audit memo from Jaipur which, taken at face value, implied the model caught rather less than a third of them. The third was a cost model from the chief financial officer recommending that the threshold be left where it was.

On Monday morning, 5 October, Harini had to sign one page: the score above which a resale file would leave the automated pipeline for full advocate review. Engineering freeze was Friday 9 October. Below it, a file was stamped Title Clear and sent to the buyer, the seller's broker and, in roughly one case in three, a housing-finance company that would lend against it on the strength of that stamp.

What made the page hard to sign was not an absence of numbers. There were a great many. The difficulty was that they disagreed, and the people who produced them each had a reason to prefer their own.

2. The company, and a signature from 2022

Zameen Exchange was founded in Pune in 2017 by Hitesh Vaze and two classmates from Nashik, on the observation that India's resale housing market was enormous, almost entirely offline, and distrusted by everybody in it. Primary sales had builders, brochures and RERA registrations. Resale had a broker, a photocopied sale deed and a buyer's uncle who knew someone at the sub-registrar's office.

The exchange began as a listings platform in Pune and Bengaluru in March 2019 and grew by doing the unglamorous work of collecting the paper. In November 2021 it packaged that paper into a product: for ₹4,500, Title Clear assembled the chain of sale deeds, the encumbrance certificate, the 7/12 extract, the society no-objection certificate and the sanctioned plan, checked them against the state registration record, and issued a report.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken on 14 February 2022, when Hitesh signed a master agreement with Sthir Housing Finance. Sthir agreed to accept a Title Clear report in place of its own panel advocate's opinion, cutting eleven days from its sanction cycle. In exchange, Zameen indemnified Sthir up to ₹50 lakh per transaction for any material defect in a file Zameen had marked clear. The agreement runs to 13 February 2027; amendment requires ninety days' notice, that is, by 15 November 2026.

That clause turned a missed defect from an embarrassment into a liability with a number attached, and made clear a contractual representation rather than an opinion. Harini had inherited it; she had not written it.

3. The market

By 2026 the resale segment was contested from several directions. Housing.com, 99acres and Magicbricks competed for the listing; NoBroker and Square Yards for the transaction; PropTiger and a dozen regional brokerages for the buyer's trust. SBI, HDFC Bank and LIC Housing Finance ran their own panel-advocate processes, thorough and slow. No platform had made title verification a product with a price and a promise attached — Zameen's advantage and its exposure.

State digitisation made the model possible and, perversely, fragile. Maharashtra's registration record was searchable and Telangana's Dharani portal machine-readable, but Rajasthan's Apna Khata and the Uttar Pradesh Bhulekh records were inconsistent, conversion orders often held only as scans at the tehsil. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 obliged Zameen to justify every seller document it retained, limiting how long it could keep the raw scans the model trained on. One order in six came from non-resident Indians buying from the Gulf, Britain and Australia, for whom the report was the whole basis of a purchase they would not see for a year.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Sanad v1, shipped in August 2023, was a rule set written by Lohit Barnwal's advocates: unregistered chain links, recent encumbrance entries, mismatched measurements, missing conversion orders. In June 2024 Hemal Chitale replaced it with a gradient-boosted model trained on four years of reviewed files; it reached an AUC of 0.871, and review volume fell a third.

In January 2026 the exchange opened Jaipur, Nagpur and Lucknow, where prices were rising and acquisition cost per listing was under half of Pune's. The documentary logic was worse than anybody modelled: the three contributed 13,200 of the 48,000 Title Clear files in the trailing year and a disproportionate share of the trouble. On 12 March 2026 a Sthir audit found two files marked clear in which a prior agreement to sell had not been discharged; Zameen settled both, and the agreement was amended to add a quarterly audit of 400 cleared files.

Through July and August Hemal rebuilt the model. Sanad v3 was evaluated on the completed files of the twelve months to 31 August 2026 — 48,000 files, of which 1,440 carried a recorded material defect, a base rate of 3.00 per cent. Pooled AUC rose from 0.871 to 0.908. Exhibit 2 sets out four candidate thresholds; Exhibit 3 breaks it down by city.

Two things have since turned out to be wrong, and a third is contested.

The first is the release note. Its headline recall of 85 per cent is measured at a threshold of 0.25, which flags 18,000 files a year, or 1,500 a month, against panel capacity of 1,100 a month. The operations plan attached to the same note assumes the production threshold of 0.60, at which recall is 50 per cent. Nobody noticed that the two halves describe different products.

The second is the ground truth. A defect enters the holdout as a positive only if somebody found it, and the people who find defects are overwhelmingly the advocates who review flagged files. Between 1 and 20 August 2026, three Jaipur advocates re-reviewed 600 files Sanad had scored below 0.40 and the pipeline had auto-cleared. They found 39 material defects, a rate of 6.50 per cent; Exhibit 6 sets that beside the holdout's figures.

The third is the cost of a missed defect, contested because the honest answer depends on a claim rate nobody has measured for more than a year (Exhibits 5 and 4).

5. Figure A — the sequence

6. The people

Harini Barve, vice-president, product — Title Clear (Pune). She owns the threshold, the report and the apology when it fails. Her position: the company cannot ship a number it cannot explain to a buyer in Pimpri or an NRI seller in Abu Dhabi. Her bonus tracks attach rate and lender acceptance, both of which fall if the report slows. Unsaid: she pulled the Tier-2 launch forward a quarter in late 2025 to make a target, so the model's weakness there is partly her own calendar.

Hitesh Vaze, co-founder and chief executive (Pune). He wants Tier-2 to keep scaling; the next funding round rests on it. His position: trust is binary, so the model should err towards flagging. Unsaid: he has told two prospective lenders Title Clear runs at "over 90 per cent accuracy", a figure off an early slide, never interrogated.

Hemal Chitale, principal data scientist (Bengaluru). She built v2 and v3. Her position: AUC is the only honest summary of a model whose threshold is unchosen; precision and recall describe an operating point, not a model. Unsaid: she had the city AUCs a fortnight before circulating the pooled figure, and led with the pooled one.

Lohit Barnwal, head of legal operations and the advocate panel (Jaipur). Forty-four empanelled advocates in six cities, each reviewing about 25 files a month. His position: no threshold is defensible while the labels are wrong, and Jaipur proves they are. His incentive is a larger panel, his budget. Unsaid: the audit's three advocates were paid per defect identified.

Hiten Marathe, chief financial officer (Pune). Fourteen months of runway, EBITDA loss ₹28.40 crore. His position: the threshold should minimise expected cost, and Exhibit 4 answers it. Unsaid: his ₹3.00 lakh per missed defect comes from one year in which only 96 claims were filed, and the ₹50 lakh cap has never been tested in litigation.

Lavanya Erukulla, vice-president, engineering (Hyderabad). Her team owns the pipeline and the freeze calendar. A per-city threshold is feasible, she says, but not by 9 October — the scoring service holds one global constant. Unsaid: a contractor in Amsterdam, Lieke Vermeer, built it and left in July, and nobody has read the retraining job end to end.

Latika Dhond, head of NRI customer success (Abu Dhabi). Her position: a false flag costs far more than the finance model allows, because an NRI seller whose file is held loses a buyer and does not return. Unsaid: two large broker partners have begun quoting Zameen's review delay as a reason to list elsewhere.

Harleen Grewal, head of lender partnerships (Gurugram). She negotiated the March amendment. Her position: the only metric that matters is the defect rate in Sthir's own audit sample, because the renewal turns on it. Unsaid: Sthir's credit team has asked privately whether Zameen would accept a lower cap for a longer term.

7. Exhibits

Figure B makes visible what Exhibit 2 hides in a column. The panel's 1,100 reviews a month sit between the 0.40 point, needing 800, and the 0.25 point, needing 1,500. No confusion matrix exists inside that band, so the recall achievable at today's capacity is unknown to fifteen percentage points.

8. Voices

"The 0.908 is correct and I will defend it. What I will not defend is anyone reading it as a promise about Jaipur. AUC says the ranking is good. It says nothing about where you cut."

Hemal Chitale, product–engineering review, 11 September 2026

"We argue about the third decimal of a model scored against labels my own advocates generated. Of course it looks accurate. I asked the question in Jaipur and got 39 defects in 600 files we had told buyers were clean. Whose signature is on those reports?"

Lohit Barnwal, email to Harini Barve, 24 August 2026

"Lohit's advocates were on a per-defect fee. I am not saying the finding is wrong. I want the same 600 files read by somebody paid by the hour before we rebuild the product around it."

Hiten Marathe, finance review, 29 September 2026

"A held file is not a delay for my sellers, it is a lost sale. The buyer in the Gulf has a sanction with a validity date and a wife who has seen three other flats. Your ₹9,200 is a spreadsheet."

Latika Dhond, chat thread, 1 October 2026

"Trust is binary. A buyer does not care that we catch seventy per cent. Flag more. We will hire advocates."

Hitesh Vaze, board sub-committee, 26 September 2026

"Sthir reads its own audit, and that says 2.75 per cent. Go to them in November saying the model is weaker than we thought, and we negotiate the renewal from the floor."

Harleen Grewal, call with Harini Barve, 2 October 2026

9. The options, as Harini currently frames them

Hold at 0.60. Ship v3 at the production threshold, bank the AUC gain as better ranking within the same review volume, and spend a quarter fixing the labels. It costs nothing in capacity and ₹2,513.28 lakh a year on Hiten's model — second-worst of the four, ₹334.08 lakh above the 0.40 minimum. It also means stamping clear at a recall of 50 per cent under a ₹50 lakh indemnity, with 42 claims open.

Move to 0.40. The minimum of Exhibit 4 at ₹2,179.20 lakh, and 800 reviews a month fits inside 1,100. Recall rises to 70 per cent. The objection: that minimum rests on the labels Jaipur disputes, and if the audit is right, true recall at 0.40 is nearer 28.77 per cent.

Move to 0.25 and grow the panel. Recall of 85 per cent, the number already in the release note. It needs 1,500 reviews a month: sixteen more advocates at ₹1.80 lakh of panel overhead each, ₹28.80 lakh, and eleven weeks of training. Annual error cost rises to ₹2,304.00 lakh and 16,776 clean files are pulled into review — 1,398 a month of Latika's held sales.

Split the product. Keep Title Clear in the three metros, where AUC exceeds 0.91, and sell the Tier-2 cities a cheaper "Title Report" with no verdict and no indemnity. It protects the lender relationship and abandons the growth story Hitesh has sold.

Harini had written all four on the whiteboard and then, at about eleven, a fifth line underneath: all four assume one number is the decision. The pipeline has one threshold because Lieke built one constant. The report has one verdict because the 2022 agreement needs a representation to indemnify. The cost model has one price per error because the register holds one year. None of those is a fact about title risk.

10. Deadline and hard constraints

The threshold must be in the release branch by Friday 9 October; the next freeze is 13 November. Notice to amend the Sthir agreement must be served by 15 November 2026, and Harleen will not serve it without a defensible number. Fourteen months of runway and an EBITDA loss of ₹28.40 crore cap panel growth at twenty advocates this year, each needing eleven weeks on state records. Under the DPDP Act, Zameen cannot retain the raw scans behind auto-cleared files beyond a stated purpose, which puts a clock on relabelling history. The next Sthir audit falls due in December; Diwali is on 8 November, after which resale volumes rise about a third for six weeks.

11. Questions for discussion

  1. From the counts in Exhibit 2, verify precision, recall and accuracy at 0.40. Why does accuracy fall as the model catches more defects, and what would a model that flagged nothing score?
  2. Hemal says 0.908 is the honest summary; no Tier-2 city in Exhibit 3 exceeds 0.761. Are both true? What is the pooled figure measuring that the review queue does not care about?
  3. F1 ranks 0.60 highest; Exhibit 4 ranks 0.40 highest. Both are arithmetically correct. What assumption does each embed, and which does the 2022 indemnity clause impose?
  4. Exhibit 6 offers three defect rates: 3.00, 2.75 and 6.50 per cent. What must you believe for each to be the right basis for a threshold? What one measurement would you commission before 9 October?
  5. If Jaipur is directionally right, every figure in Exhibit 4 is wrong in the same direction. Does that change which option you prefer, or only your confidence in it? Rework the 0.40 column at a 7.30 per cent base rate.
  6. What should Harini put on the page on Monday morning, and what should she tell the board on 26 October — about the number, about the release note already sent, and about what she still does not know?

At half past midnight she turned the sheets face down and wrote one more line on the whiteboard, a question rather than an answer: if the labels are wrong, which of these numbers is worth arguing about? The brokers would start calling at nine. Lohit's advocates were already awake in Jaipur. The release note had sat in lenders' inboxes for thirty-one days.

Bharosa Labs: Where to Set the Fraud Threshold

A decision case on precision, recall and AUC

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday, 1 October 2026, Mitali Sengupta stood at the whiteboard in Bharosa Labs' Bengaluru office with a marker in one hand and a printout of a single number in the other. The number was 99.88 per cent. It was the accuracy of the company's new fraud-scoring model, and the data science team had put it, in bold, at the top of their release note.

Mitali, head of product for the company's payments-risk product, did not trust it. The model would go live for all merchants on Friday, 16 October 2026, so that it would be settled in before Dussehra on 20 October and the festive weeks that lead to Diwali on 8 November. Before then she had to choose one number: the score above which a transaction is flagged as likely fraud. The release note could not tell her where to put it.

2. Company background

Bharosa Labs, founded in 2018 and headquartered in Bengaluru, sells payment collection and fraud screening to small and mid-sized online merchants: D2C brands, tutoring platforms, regional travel sellers. It sits on top of UPI rails run by NPCI and on card networks, and it competes for the same merchants as Razorpay and Cashfree, while merchants' own customers also pay through PhonePe, Paytm and bank apps. Bharosa serves about 4,200 merchants and processes roughly 10,00,000 transactions a month, worth about ₹300 crore at an average ticket of ₹3,000.

Its differentiator is a guarantee. For merchants on its premium plan, Bharosa absorbs the loss on any fraudulent transaction its screening failed to flag. That makes every missed fraud a direct cost to Bharosa, and makes the risk model the core of the product.

3. The situation

Through the summer the data science team rebuilt the fraud model. Version 2 was tested against the same replay of September 2026 traffic as the production version 1: 10,00,000 transactions, of which 2,000 (0.2 per cent) were later confirmed as fraud through chargebacks and customer complaints. On this holdout, the area under the ROC curve, or AUC, rose from 0.934 for version 1 to 0.962 for version 2. AUC measures how well a model ranks fraudulent transactions above genuine ones across all possible thresholds; 0.5 is a coin toss; 1.0 is perfect.

That is where the release note went wrong. Version 2 outputs a score between 0 and 1, and the default threshold of 0.5 produced the 99.88 per cent accuracy. Tarini Bhalla, the data scientist in Hyderabad who built the model, was candid when Mitali called her: a model that flagged nothing at all would score 99.80 per cent accuracy on this data, because 9,98,000 of the 10,00,000 transactions are genuine.

The team ran version 2 at three thresholds. Exhibit 1 shows the confusion matrix counts at each, and the metrics that follow from them. Precision is the share of flagged transactions that are truly fraud, true positives divided by true positives plus false positives. Recall is the share of all fraud that was caught, true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives. F1 is the harmonic mean of the two, and accuracy is the share of all transactions classified correctly.

Read across Exhibit 1 and the trade is plain. Lowering the threshold catches more fraud, with recall rising from 55 per cent to 89 per cent, but it flags far more genuine customers, and precision falls from about 79 per cent to 13 per cent. At 0.2, 11,800 of 13,580 flags (86.9 per cent), roughly 7 in every 8, are wrong.

The team's views were not uniform. From Hyderabad, Tarini argued for reporting precision and recall together and never accuracy. From Mumbai, Mukund Rastogi wanted every possible fraud stopped. In Kochi, Tushar Naik, who runs support, warned that every false flag becomes a phone call.

4. The people

Mitali Sengupta, head of product, Bengaluru. She owns the decision and the merchant relationship. She wants a threshold she can explain to a merchant.

Mukund Rastogi, head of risk, Mumbai. He carries the fraud loss budget and the guarantee. He wants recall as high as possible and argues that a missed fraud, at ₹6,500 on average, costs about sixteen times what an annoyed customer does.

Tarini Bhalla, senior data scientist, Hyderabad. She wants the team to stop quoting accuracy and to choose the threshold from costs rather than from habit,.

Tushar Naik, head of customer support, Kochi. His team handles calls from customers whose payments were blocked or sent for extra verification. He wants false flags held down before the festive volume arrives.

5. Exhibits: what each error costs

Mukund and Tushar supplied the two cost figures. A missed fraud costs Bharosa an average of ₹6,500 in refunded value and handling. A false flag, whether the payment is blocked or sent for an extra OTP step, costs an estimated ₹400 once support time, abandoned baskets and a little churn are counted. Exhibit 2 applies these to one month of traffic like the holdout. All figures are in ₹ lakh; 1 lakh is 1,00,000.

Exhibit 3 plots the same three operating points, with recall on the horizontal axis and precision on the vertical. Moving right buys fraud caught at the price of moving down. AUC summarises a related curve over every threshold, but the business lives at one point on it.

6. The options

Option 1: ship at the default threshold of 0.5. It is what the release note assumed. Precision is 78.57 per cent, so Tushar's team sees only 300 false flags a month,. But it misses 900 of 2,000 frauds, and Exhibit 2 puts the monthly cost at ₹59.70 lakh, almost all of it fraud the guarantee must absorb.

Option 2: push recall to the limit at 0.2. This is Mukund's instinct. It catches 1,780 of 2,000 frauds and leaves only 220 uncaught. But it flags 13,580 transactions, 11,800 of them genuine, and the total monthly cost rises to ₹61.50 lakh, above Option 1. Around Diwali, Tushar's team would be flooded.

Option 3: choose 0.3, and route flagged transactions to step-up verification rather than a hard block. Recall is 78 per cent and precision 28.57 per cent. Monthly cost is ₹44.20 lakh, the lowest of the three. The price is 5,460 flagged transactions a month, of which 3,900 are genuine customers asked for an extra OTP or a UPI PIN re-entry.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Why does accuracy of 99.88 per cent say so little about this model? What would a model that flags nothing score, and what does that reveal about class imbalance?
  2. What does the AUC improvement from 0.934 to 0.962 tell Mitali, and what does it leave unanswered?
  3. Using the definitions in Section 3, verify precision and recall at 0.3 from the counts in Exhibit 1. Why does F1 rank the thresholds differently from the cost in Exhibit 2?
  4. If the ₹400 cost of a false flag were wrong, how far could it move before the best option changed?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Model metrics are not trophies; each answers a different question. Accuracy asks how often the model is right overall, and is dominated by the majority class. Precision asks, of what was flagged, how much was truly fraud. Recall asks, of all the fraud, how much was caught. AUC asks how well the model ranks fraud above genuine across all thresholds. The right metric follows the cost of each error, and the threshold is a product decision, not a modelling one.

One defensible path: Option 3. Set the threshold at 0.3 and use step-up verification for flagged transactions. At 0.3 the monthly error cost of ₹44.20 lakh is ₹15.50 lakh lower than Option 1 (59.70 minus 44.20) and ₹17.30 lakh lower than Option 2 (61.50 minus 44.20). Over twelve months the saving against Option 1 is ₹186 lakh, or ₹1.86 crore.

Why it holds up. Moving from 0.5 to 0.3 saves 460 missed frauds, worth 460 × 6,500 = ₹29.90 lakh, at the price of 3,600 extra false flags. That is worthwhile as long as a false flag costs less than ₹29,90,000 / 3,600, about ₹831. Moving from 0.3 to 0.2 saves 220 missed frauds, worth ₹14.30 lakh, at 7,900 extra false flags, and is worthwhile only if a false flag costs under ₹14,30,000 / 7,900, about ₹181. Option 3 therefore wins for any false-flag cost between roughly ₹181 and ₹831, a wide band around the ₹400 estimate. F1 prefers 0.5 because it weights both errors equally, which they are not.

Conditions. Report precision, recall and cost, never accuracy alone. Track the actual false-flag cost in the first fortnight after launch, and keep the threshold adjustable per merchant.
