AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management

Feedback Loops and Data Flywheels

How usage becomes the data that makes the product better — and why capturing it is a design decision, not an accident.

A number that would not move

On the second Tuesday of March 2026, Kabir Anand pulled up the same chart he had been staring at since December. Kabir was Head of Product at Rasid Systems, a Gurugram-based company that sold an AI invoice-processing layer to mid-market manufacturers: point a vendor invoice at Rasid, and its model read the PDF, extracted invoice number, GST details, line items and amounts, and posted them straight into the client's ERP. The chart tracked Rasid's straight-through processing rate, or STP — the share of the roughly 40,000 invoices Rasid handled each day across sixty-one client accounts that required zero human touch. For two straight quarters, STP had sat at 71 percent.

The remaining 29 percent — about 11,600 invoices a day — fell into a review queue, where a team of accounts-payable clerks fixed whatever the model had gotten wrong before the invoice could post. Finance had priced that clerk time at roughly ₹18 per reviewed invoice. It was not, on its own, a crisis; it was a cost Rasid's clients had budgeted for. What made the chart matter that Tuesday was a prospective account, a large auto-components manufacturer, whose procurement team had made a 90 percent STP guarantee within two quarters of go-live a condition of signing a contract worth roughly ₹4 crore in incremental annual revenue. Kabir had one quarter of his four ML engineers' time to spend before the proposal was due. He could spend it extending Rasid's library of vendor-specific templates, a method the team understood cold and that reliably added a point or two of STP per quarter. Or he could spend it building something Rasid had never properly built: a pipeline that captured every clerk's correction as structured, reusable training data and fed it back into the model on a weekly cycle. One was a known, linear bet. The other was a bet on compounding — and Kabir was not yet sure Rasid's usage was large enough, or its corrections clean enough, for compounding to actually happen.

The idea

A feedback loop, in this context, is the mechanism by which the corrections, choices and outcomes generated by real usage of a system are captured, structured and routed back into the process that produced the original output, so that each cycle of the system uses the previous cycle's mistakes as raw material. It is a mechanism, not an outcome. A data flywheel is what happens when that mechanism runs fast enough and cleanly enough, over enough cycles, that the resulting improvement compounds: more usage generates more corrected data, which produces a better model, which attracts or retains more usage, which generates more data still. The flywheel is the compounding; the loop is the machinery that makes compounding possible. Not every working loop becomes a flywheel — that distinction matters enough to earn its own nuance below.

The idea did not arrive with a single inventor or a single date. Statistical process control gave manufacturing the discipline of feeding measured defects back into the process decades before machine learning existed. Search engines were closing the loop between clicks and ranking by the late 1990s. What changed around 2021 was the vocabulary: practitioners like Andrew Ng began arguing publicly for "data-centric AI" — the claim that, past a point, improving a model's data pipeline beats tinkering further with its architecture — and the flywheel metaphor, borrowed from Jeff Bezos's description of Amazon's business model, got attached to it as shorthand. The problem the whole idea solves is a specific and unglamorous one: a model trained once, on a fixed snapshot of data, starts decaying the moment the world it operates in drifts away from that snapshot, and the cheapest possible source of fresh, relevant labels is the very users who are already using the product and, whether they know it or not, correcting it. The sentence Kabir could say in a meeting without sounding glib: every correction a user makes is free labelled data, if you bother to capture and route it.

How it actually works

Walking the mechanism through Rasid's own pipeline makes the abstract version concrete. First, inference: the model reads an incoming invoice and predicts a value for every field — vendor name, GST number, line-item amounts, purchase-order reference — each with its own confidence score. Second, confidence routing: if every field clears a threshold (Rasid used 92 percent), the invoice posts automatically; that is the STP case. If any field falls short, the whole invoice routes to a clerk's review queue. Third, and this is where most teams' loops quietly break, correction capture: the clerk does not merely approve or reject the invoice; she edits the wrong fields to their true values. The loop only works if that edit is captured as a structured diff — field name, predicted value, corrected value, the exact model version that made the prediction, the vendor's template identifier, a timestamp — rather than collapsed into a single thumbs-up or thumbs-down. Fourth, those diffs accumulate in a label store, deduplicated so that one clerk fixing the same recurring vendor quirk forty times in a day does not get weighted as forty independent lessons. Fifth, before any retraining run, an active-learning batch selection step chooses which corrections are actually worth training on — prioritising rare fields, unfamiliar vendor formats and genuinely hard cases over a random or merely recent sample. Sixth, the retrained model is checked against a golden set: a small, independently curated, deliberately stable sample of invoices whose true values are already certain, used specifically to catch regressions that the flywheel's own recent data might otherwise mask. Seventh, a model that clears the golden-set bar is redeployed, often with its confidence thresholds retuned, since a genuinely better model can afford to auto-post more aggressively. The loop then closes: that redeployed model's own predictions generate the next round of corrections.

Fig. 1 — Rasid's feedback loop. The clerk's edit at stage 3 is the whole loop's raw material; if it is captured as a diff rather than a yes/no, stages 4–8 have something to work with.

Two steps in that walk are the ones practitioners most often skip, and both are invisible until they cause damage. One is versioning every correction to the exact model that produced the original prediction, not just the date it was made — without it, a bug fixed three model versions ago can keep showing up in the training data as though it were still live, teaching the new model to fix a problem that no longer exists while ignoring the ones that do. The other is keeping the golden set genuinely separate from the flywheel's own data, sampled and refreshed by a process the retraining pipeline never touches — without that separation, a model can look like it is improving every week and be quietly memorising the review queue's own quirks instead.

The arithmetic Kabir actually ran

Kabir's team modelled two scenarios before the quarter began. Both start from the same baseline: STP at 71 percent, a review queue of 11,600 invoices a day, and a review cost of ₹18 per invoice, for a daily cost of ₹208,800 and an annualised cost, over roughly 300 working days, of about ₹6.3 crore.

In the clean-correction scenario, the team assumed each week of properly captured, field-level corrections used in retraining would lift STP by about 1.6 percentage points for the first six weeks, while the richest, previously uncaptured signal was still being mined, decelerating to about 0.7 points a week for weeks seven through twelve as the easier gains were exhausted. That path reaches 80.6 percent by week six and 84.8 percent by week twelve — short of the client's 90 percent target within one quarter, but on a trend that would plausibly cross 90 percent early in the second quarter after go-live, which is a very different negotiating position than a flat 71 percent. At week twelve, the review queue shrinks to 6,080 invoices a day and the daily review cost falls to about ₹109,440, saving roughly ₹99,360 a day — close to ₹3 crore a year at Rasid's current volume, before counting the ₹4 crore ARR the trend line might help win.

Table 1 — Two scenarios for the same twelve-week loop, clean versus noisy corrections
WeekSTP, clean correctionsSTP, noisy correctionsReview queue/day (clean)Daily review cost (clean)
071.0%71.0%11,600₹2,08,800
680.6%74.8%7,760₹1,39,680
1284.8%76.5%6,080₹1,09,440

The second pass changes one input: label quality. Suppose, under end-of-shift pressure, clerks genuinely correct only about 40 percent of flagged invoices — the rest get approved with the wrong value still in place, or "corrected" carelessly back to something equally wrong. The useful label volume falls roughly in proportion, so the realised weekly lift is close to 40 percent of the modelled figure: about 0.64 points a week early on, decelerating to about 0.28 points a week later. That path reaches only 76.5 percent by week twelve, a full 8.3 points short of the clean-correction case, and the review queue barely moves — saving under ₹5 lakh a year instead of ₹3 crore. Capturing corrections was never the hard part; capturing corrections a rushed human actually got right was.

Fig. 2 — Same loop, same twelve weeks; the only input that changed is whether clerks' corrections were actually right.

Eight things worth being precise about

A loop is not automatically a flywheel

The loop is the mechanism; the flywheel is what happens only if that mechanism compounds faster than a rival's. Rasid can have a perfectly functioning correction-capture pipeline and still have no flywheel, if a well-funded competitor with the same client volume can stand up an equivalent loop in two quarters. A flywheel is a claim about relative speed of compounding, not about whether a loop exists.

More data is not the same claim as better data

Usage patterns generate biased samples of corrections: clerks tend to fix what is already close to right, because it is quick, and leave genuinely strange outliers half-corrected or skipped under deadline pressure. A loop fed only by the easy cases gets very good at the easy cases and stays blind to exactly the hard ones it most needs to learn.

Acceptance is not consent to correctness

When review is treated as a chore, users rubber-stamp outputs to move faster rather than genuinely checking them. An "accepted" prediction in the log can mean either "verified correct" or "not actually reviewed," and a loop that cannot tell the two apart will quietly teach itself to repeat its own mistakes with growing confidence.

There is a cold-start question about when to even build this

Structured capture, versioning, a retraining pipeline and an independent golden set are fixed engineering costs. Below some volume of usage, that infrastructure is not yet worth its own weight; a team that builds it too early spends a quarter on plumbing for a trickle of data that a spreadsheet would have handled just as well.

The flywheel cannot prove it caused the improvement

STP rising in the same weeks a retraining pipeline went live is suggestive, not conclusive. Vendor mix shifts, seasonal invoice volume, or a template fix shipped the same month can each move the number on their own. Without a held-back comparison group, the loop's advocates and the loop's actual contribution can quietly drift apart.

It is easily confused with a network effect, and is not one

A network effect makes the product better for other users as more people join. A data flywheel, left unexamined, may only be a private efficiency gain — it makes Rasid's own model better for Rasid, but tells a prospective client nothing about switching cost unless the improvement is large enough, and durable enough, to be visible from outside.

The people generating the labels have a stake in the outcome

Every correction in Rasid's label store came from a clerk whose working hours, and eventually whose job description, are bound up with how well the resulting model performs. A loop that is honest about what it is collecting and why tends to earn careful corrections; one that extracts labels as a byproduct nobody explained tends to earn quiet, hard-to-detect carelessness.

The right first questions are simple ones

Before trusting any feedback loop, a newcomer should ask: what exactly counts as a label here, and who decides it is correct? How much time passes between an action and the model update it feeds? And could this loop be quietly learning to serve today's best-served users even better, while never noticing the users it already serves badly?

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and small versus large

Consumer products typically run on implicit, passive signals collected at enormous scale — clicks, dwell time, scroll depth, what a user watched next. Any single signal is noisy and nearly free to collect, so consumer flywheels tend to win by volume, tolerating a great deal of noise because there is so much of it to average over. B2B products like Rasid instead collect explicit, professional corrections from a comparatively small number of trained users; each label is expensive to earn, in clerk time and attention, but far richer per unit, which is exactly why Rasid's loop design has to emphasise careful, versioned capture over raw scale. Marketplace products carry a two-sided version of the same problem: a lending marketplace's underwriting model can learn from both a borrower's repayment behaviour and a lender's manual risk override, and when the two disagree the platform has to decide, explicitly, which side's correction is the more trustworthy signal, while staying alert to either side trying to bend the model in its own favour.

Table 2 — How the same mechanism differs by product type
DimensionConsumerB2BMarketplace
Signal typeimplicit, passiveexplicit, professionaltwo-sided, sometimes conflicting
Volume per labelvery cheapexpensivemoderate, split across sides
Main risknoise averaged outsparse but biased sampleone side gaming the signal

Stage matters at least as much as product type. An early-stage team's loop is often a founder reading a sample of failed cases by hand and adjusting a rule set the same afternoon — slow to scale but fast to notice something genuinely new. A large company's loop is instrumented software: a purpose-built labelling interface, a scheduled retraining pipeline, an evaluation harness. That scale is what makes compounding possible at all, but it also makes the loop slower to redirect, and prone to getting very good at whatever it already sees often, while a golden set that is never deliberately refreshed with unfamiliar cases lets it stay quietly blind to the next new class of problem.

Where the same mistake keeps appearing

Four patterns recur across teams that build these loops for the first time, and each is cheap to diagnose once named.

Table 3 — Four recurring mistakes, what gives them away, and how to check
MistakeSymptomCheapest diagnostic
Capturing accept/reject only, not the diffRetraining runs, but field-level accuracy does not moveCheck whether the label schema stores the corrected value, or just a checkbox
Golden set drawn from the same pool as training dataOffline accuracy climbs every cycle; production stallsCompare vendor/template IDs in the training batch against the golden set
Assuming the loop runs itself once instrumentedAn early jump in STP, then a plateau or a reversalWeekly, have a second reviewer independently re-check a 50-correction sample
Calling the loop a "moat" before volume justifies itA strong investor slide; a rival matches it in two quartersCompute the accuracy gain per additional 1,000 labels — if flat, there is no flywheel yet

The first mistake destroys the loop's raw material before it is ever stored; the second lets a team congratulate itself on an exam it wrote using the answer key; the third assumes quality is free once capture exists, when in fact someone has to own it, continuously; and the fourth confuses having a mechanism with having an advantage, which is precisely the distinction the first nuance above exists to prevent.

What good looked like, twelve weeks later

Rasid's team spent the quarter building field-level correction capture wired directly into the review interface, versioned to both model and vendor template, and gave one experienced clerk formal ownership of a weekly quality sample — fifty corrections, independently re-checked, with disagreement rates tracked over time. The golden set was refreshed monthly from a pool of newly onboarded vendor formats deliberately withheld from training. STP reached about 87 percent by week fourteen: slower than the optimistic model, far ahead of the noisy-correction case, and visibly still climbing. Rasid took that trend line, not a single promised number, into the renewal conversation, and the client's operations team accepted a two-quarter ramp to 90 percent rather than a day-one guarantee. The loop did not stop when the quarter ended; it was folded into the ordinary weekly release cadence, owned by name, not remembered by accident.

What Kabir decided

Kabir gave the quarter's ML capacity to the feedback loop, not the template backlog, on the reasoning that a linear method always trails whatever unfamiliar invoice format appears next, while a genuinely compounding loop gets steadily better at the one problem that matters most: the format it has not seen before. He took the honest arithmetic — a twelve-week path to 84.8 percent, not 90 — into the sales conversation and turned it into a ramp clause instead of a broken promise. The natural next things to learn are how a golden set is built and kept honest as the flywheel around it changes, since that is what protects this loop from grading its own homework, and how data flywheels function as a genuine competitive moat in AI products, since not every working loop earns one. Two questions worth sitting with afterward: if your product stopped receiving corrected usage tomorrow, how long before its accuracy noticeably decayed, and does anyone actually know the answer today? And whose incentives are you quietly relying on when you assume this week's corrections are honest signal about next month's model?

Feedback Loops and Data Flywheels

A loop is a rate. A flywheel is a gain. Most of what gets sold as the second is the first — and is often still worth building, for entirely different reasons.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 2 September 2026, Nandita Kurup sat in a room off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru with three printed charts and a proposal she did not want to sign. Peepal Scan sold a chest-radiograph triage model to diagnostic chains: it read each film as it came off the plate, scored it for suspected abnormality, and pushed the high scorers to the front of a teleradiology worklist. Across 340 centres it saw 9,400 studies a day, at a sensitivity of 0.91 against a specificity of 0.88 — numbers that had not moved in eleven months.

The reason sat in the second chart. Every study was eventually read by a radiologist, so in principle Peepal Scan swam in ground truth; in practice the radiologist produced free text, and the extractor that turned reports into labels agreed with a careful manual re-read only 79 percent of the time. Her engineering lead, Rohan Pillai, had costed a structured-confirmation widget — two clicks forcing the radiologist to confirm or deny each model finding — at ₹3.1 crore and two quarters. The alternative was buying 40,000 externally annotated studies at ₹310 each: ₹1.24 crore, ten weeks, no workflow negotiation and no radiologist goodwill spent.

Two days later and 980 kilometres away, Vikram Sahni faced the mirror image. Vikram was VP Product at Ghungroo, whose vernacular audio-storytelling app had 18 million monthly listeners and logged 340 million play events a week. Ghungroo had no shortage of data. It had a recommendation model whose quality had improved 1.4 percent over four quarters despite a fourfold rise in logged events, and a catalogue team complaining that shows from unknown creators never escaped the lower slots. Deepa Iyer, his data scientist in Singapore, wanted 4 percent of impressions spent on randomised exploration — serving items the model did not rank first and logging the probability with which each was shown, at a cost of 246,000 listening minutes a day. The CFO asked the obvious question: why would a company collecting 340 million signals a week pay to collect worse ones?

Both are one question asked from opposite ends of a single mechanism, and neither is answered by the sentence in both companies’ decks — that usage creates data which creates a better product which creates more usage.

2. The idea, and the camps that disagree about it

Define terms precisely, because the looseness is where the money leaks. A feedback loop is a mechanism: outputs of a deployed system generate observations — corrections, choices, outcomes — which are captured, attributed to the version that produced them, and routed into the process producing the next outputs. A loop has a period (time from an action to the deployed model that learnt from it) and a yield (error removed per turn). A data flywheel is an economic claim layered on top: that quality improvement produces usage growth, which produces more observations and further improvement, at a rate a rival starting today cannot match. The flywheel is a gain term; the loop is a rate. A product can have an excellent loop and no flywheel whatever, and that is the normal case.

The history has three tributaries. Control theory came first — Shewhart in the 1920s, Wiener’s cybernetics in 1948 — establishing that you measure output, compare to target and feed back the difference, and that a loop’s stability depends on its delay. Sequential experimentation came second: Thompson’s 1933 sampling rule and the bandit literature, which established that a system choosing what to show also chooses what it will learn, so deliberate randomness is the price of unbiased knowledge. Applied machine learning came third: click models on search logs in the early 2000s, showing logged behaviour is confounded by the interface producing it, and the 2015 hidden-technical-debt paper, which named feedback loops a class of defect rather than a feature. The phrase most PMs use arrived last, around 2021, when the Bezos flywheel was welded onto the data-centric AI argument.

Three schools now disagree substantively. The accumulation school holds that in any long-tailed domain, proprietary observations compound into an advantage capital cannot buy, because the tail is visible only from inside production traffic. It signs: a rival with equal engineering and no traffic cannot match our tail error rate. It does not sign that volume alone improves a model.

The quality school — the data-centric position — holds the binding constraint is rarely how many observations you have but how well-defined the label is and whether the sample covers the hard regions. It signs: a thousand adjudicated labels on disputed cases beat a million passive ones. It does not sign that the loop is therefore a moat; it is silent on competitive dynamics.

The economist school, put most sharply by Hagiu and Wright and by the sceptics who wrote about the empty promise of data moats around 2019, holds that learning curves flatten and that most apparent data moats are switching-cost or distribution moats in borrowed clothes. It signs: show me the accuracy-versus-log-data curve before you say moat. It concedes the narrow tail and asks for evidence you are in it. Since 2023 a fourth position has hardened around foundation models: the scarce asset is no longer training labels but a small, adversarially chosen evaluation set and a few thousand preference comparisons, so the loop’s product is the eval, not the weights.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic experts actually run

The first quantity a practised operator asks for is not the size of the label store but the learning curve. Across a wide range of supervised tasks, error above an irreducible floor falls as a power law in training examples, roughly a · n−β, with β typically between 0.07 and 0.35. That exponent is the asset: it decides what a doubling buys. To halve excess error you must multiply the data by 21/β — about 10× at β = 0.30, and roughly 545× at β = 0.11, Ghungroo’s measured value.

Fig. 1 — The same sixteenfold increase in labels removes 39 percent of Peepal Scan's excess error and 18 percent of Ghungroo's. The exponent, not the volume, decides whether collecting more is a strategy.

Run Nandita’s options through it. Peepal Scan’s excess error over an estimated floor of 4.5 percent is 6.7 points, on 96,000 clean labelled studies, at a measured β of 0.28. Buying 40,000 studies raises n by 42 percent; excess error falls by 1.42−0.28 = 0.906, to 6.07 points — total error 11.2 to 10.6 percent, once, then stops. The widget yields 1,300 clean confirmations a day, taking n to 571,000 within a year: excess error 6.7 × 5.95−0.28 = 4.07 points, an error of 8.6 percent, still falling. The purchased data is a step; the widget is a slope.

The second quantity is the loop period: the maximum of three delays teams routinely confuse — when the label becomes knowable, how often you retrain, how often you can deploy. Confirmed truth for an indeterminate nodule at Peepal Scan waits on a follow-up CT, median 31 days, and as regulated clinical decision support its retraining and release run quarterly under a change-control protocol: four turns a year. Ghungroo knows in ninety seconds whether a listener stayed, retrains nightly and deploys continuously: about 300 turns. Ghungroo turns 75 times faster and learns almost nothing per turn; Peepal Scan turns four times and learns a great deal. What must be managed is the product of rate and yield, and teams optimise whichever is easier to measure.

The third quantity is the one almost nobody computes: the gain, the product of three sensitivities — observations per unit of usage, quality per observation, usage per unit of quality. Teams instrument the first two. The third makes it a flywheel, and is frequently zero. Peepal Scan’s volume is set by referring physicians who never see model sensitivity; however good it becomes, no additional radiograph is taken. Its loop, however steep, is a margin story, not a moat. Ghungroo’s third term is positive but its second is near zero at that scale, so the product is negligible. Both have loops worth funding and flywheels they do not have.

The fourth mechanic is what Deepa was arguing for. Logged feedback is produced by a policy — the ranker, the threshold, the interface — and measures that policy as much as the world. Ghungroo’s numbers make it vivid. Slot one is seen with probability near 1.0, slot five with 0.34. Item A in slot one plays 11.0 percent of the time; item B in slot five plays 5.1 percent, so A naively looks 2.2× better. Divide each by its exposure probability — the inverse-propensity estimate — and A scores 11.0 against B’s 15.0. B is better, has been demoted, will now be shown less and will supply less evidence next cycle. That is a degenerate loop: popularity mistaken for quality, and the catalogue team’s complaint revealed as a statistical artefact rather than a taste dispute.

The same structure appears wherever a threshold decides who gets reviewed. A confidence cut-off means the only labelled cases are ones the model already found hard; above the threshold nothing is observed, so confident errors are invisible by construction. The remedy is an audit slice — a random sample of auto-approved cases sent to review regardless of score. At Peepal Scan, 3 percent of normal-scored studies is 282 a day, about one radiologist-hour: the cheapest insurance in the system, and the line most often cut when budgets tighten.

4. When it applies, stated as claims you can test

The conditions below are testable, and each has a defensible answer for both protagonists. The usual failure is not disagreement about them but never asking.

Table 2 — Six conditions applied. A “no” is not a veto; it changes what the loop is for.
ClaimPeepal ScanGhungroo
C1. Truth arrives faster than the world driftsYes: 31-day truth, multi-year hardware driftYes, but trends turn over weekly
C2. Labels are not a selected slice of the inputsNo: needs a 3% audit of normalsNo: needs propensities and exploration
C3. Marginal accuracy per label is still materialYes, β = 0.28No, β = 0.11 at current n
C4. Quality gain is perceptible where behaviour changesPartly: radiologists notice, referrers do notYes, within a session
C5. A rival cannot rent equivalent labelsYes on Indian TB-prevalence tails onlyNo: play logs are commodity
C6. The loop's own output does not determine its labelsRisk: score visible before the readRisk: rank drives exposure, drives label

C6 deserves emphasis: if the interface shows the model’s answer to the person supplying the label, the label is contaminated. Peepal Scan’s own widget is exposed, since a radiologist who sees a confidence score before reading is measurably likelier to agree with it. The fix — capture the reading first, reveal the score after — costs nothing if decided early and is politically impossible to retrofit once radiologists like the convenience.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When irreducible error is high — expert disagreement is the practical floor — more data buys noise-fitting and a slow accumulation of confident wrongness. When a general model reaches close to your accuracy by prompting, your labels are worth only what they add above that baseline, for many text tasks after 2024, approximately nothing. And when regulation forecloses it: under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, data collected to deliver a service cannot be repurposed as training material without a lawful basis, making a health-data loop built on that assumption an expensive discovery at the first audit.

5. Hard edges: seams, regulators and things with wheels

Multi-product companies hit the shared-label-store problem. One store looks like an economy until one product’s distribution poisons another’s: a document model trained on pooled corrections from invoicing and contracts is best at neither, and the team contributing 80 percent of labels quietly sets the roadmap for the model the other team ships. Mature organisations version the store by product and accept duplication that looks wasteful on an architecture diagram and is not.

Two-sided products face conflicting labels. A freight marketplace learns from a shipper’s rating and a carrier’s acceptance, and when they disagree it must decide whose signal is truth — a product decision dressed as a data-engineering one, worsened because either side can learn to send the signal that suits them. The tell that such a loop is gamed is a signal distribution sharpening around a threshold the platform publicised.

Regulated products face the change-control seam: a model that improves weekly is, clinically or in lending, a system that changes weekly, and retraining cadence and release cadence are different clocks. The mature practice is a pre-declared change protocol — the boundaries within which retraining needs no fresh review — with the loop running continuously in shadow and promotion on the regulator’s clock. Teams that skip this cannot ship the improvement they have already paid for.

Hardware-plus-software bakes the sampling policy into silicon. Machaan Agritech ran 6,100 solar-powered cameras in cotton plots across Vidarbha and Telangana on 40 MB per device per day, so the edge model uploaded only frames it scored as uncertain. That upload rule is the propensity function, chosen by a firmware engineer on cost grounds, and for eighteen months it made confident errors structurally invisible. A one-in-500 unconditional upload surfaced a pink bollworm presentation under leaf shade that the model had been confidently missing. No volume of additional uncertain frames would have found it.

AI-native products invert the picture. Often there is no retraining at all: the loop’s output is an evaluation suite, preference pairs, a retrieval corpus and a library of failures that become few-shot examples or guardrails. The period collapses to hours and the asset is curatorial. The seam is organisational — those who see failures work in support, those who could fix them work in engineering, and the ticket taxonomy between them was designed for refunds.

What mature companies do, as distinct from what they say, is worth stating plainly. They book annotation as cost of goods, not research; they keep a vendor annotation team long after the public story says the flywheel is self-sustaining; they run a quarterly loop-health review reporting period, yield, label agreement and audit coverage rather than accuracy; and they give one named person the label store, because loops without an owner degrade silently and no dashboard alerts on an absence.

6. Nine things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The rate limit is almost never data volume. The tell is a label store growing by millions of rows against a model-version count that moved twice in a year. The obvious reading — that the team needs more data engineering — is wrong; the constraint is the release path, and adding data to a loop that cannot deploy is fuelling an engine with no gearbox.

Logged feedback measures your policy, not the world. The tell is offline replay beating production by a suspiciously stable margin. The naive conclusion is an online bug; usually the offline evaluation scores the model on data its own predecessor selected, which flatters any successor behaving similarly. Propensity logging must be designed in before the data exists; it cannot be reconstructed after.

Thresholding manufactures a blind region. The tell is accuracy inside the review queue improving steadily while customer complaints do not fall. The obvious reading is that customers are complaining about something else; more often the errors that now matter live above the threshold, where nothing is ever checked.

The learning-curve exponent is the asset. The tell is a team that quotes its dataset size to three significant figures and has never plotted accuracy against the logarithm of that size. Without the exponent every acquisition proposal is a guess, and the arithmetic of 21/β routinely turns a confident roadmap item into an obviously bad trade.

Compounding requires a usage response. The tell is a strategy document with quality charts and no retention or volume chart beside them. The obvious reading is that quality is self-evidently valuable; it may be, as margin, but a loop whose third term is zero never accelerates, and calling it a flywheel sets up a promise the team will be measured against for years.

Cadence should be set by drift, not taste. The tell is nightly retraining against a golden set last refreshed fourteen months ago. Faster is not better: each retrain carries regression risk, and a loop turning much faster than the world changes mostly re-learns the same thing while its measuring stick rots.

The model curates its own future data. The tell is rising accuracy alongside falling diversity in the incoming corpus — fewer distinct vendors, languages or presentations month over month. The comfortable reading is that the product is finding its market; sometimes the system has instead narrowed the world it can see, detectable only if diversity is instrumented deliberately.

Users adapt faster than models do. The tell is a widening gap between first-week and tenured-user accuracy. The comfortable reading is that experienced users get more value; the uncomfortable one is that they have learnt to route around the weaknesses, so measured accuracy improves while capability is flat and every new cohort meets the original product.

A label is an organisational artefact, not a fact. The tell is a model plateauing within a point or two of the inter-annotator agreement rate. If two qualified radiologists agree at κ = 0.72, a model trained on single-reader labels has a practical ceiling near 86 percent, and the quarter spent chasing 90 is spent fitting one reader’s idiosyncrasies. Experts adjudicate disputed cases rather than collect more, raising the ceiling instead of approaching it faster.

7. Product type and stage — and where the difference is imaginary

The genuine differences are in the price and the bias of a label, not the mechanics. Consumer products collect implicit signals that are nearly free, abundant and heavily confounded by the interface; their whole practical difficulty is de-biasing, which is why exploration budgets and propensity logging are consumer-scale disciplines that rarely appear in B2B stacks. B2B products collect explicit corrections from trained professionals: expensive, sparse, richer per unit, and biased by workload rather than layout — the queue gets honest attention in the morning and rubber stamps at six, a pattern visible in correction timestamps. Enterprise adds a decisive obstacle: the customer owns the data and the contract may forbid cross-tenant training, capping the loop at the largest single client. Platforms and marketplaces differ because both sides’ signals are strategic; hardware because the sampling policy lives in firmware and ground truth arrives with a field visit; AI-native products because the artefact improved is a prompt, a corpus and an eval suite rather than a weight matrix.

Where difference is asserted and is not real: the independently curated golden set, versioning every observation against the model and interface that produced it, a named owner, and the arithmetic of the learning curve. These are identical everywhere, and a team claiming their situation is too special for them is usually describing a loop that has not been built. By stage, early loops are humans reading failures on a Friday — unscalable, unusually good at spotting genuinely new problems; growth-stage loops are the first real instrumentation, where the classic error is building capture before deciding what a label means; mature loops are excellent at the frequent and blind to the rare, so the discipline shifts from collection to deliberate sampling of the tail.

8. Three loops with numbers, one of them broken

Pankhudi Beauty, a Jaipur beauty-commerce app, ran a small explicit loop against its own large implicit one. Its search ranker had 2.1 million weekly sessions of click data and a stubborn NDCG@10 of 0.61. Rather than mine more clicks, the team hired six judges producing 1,800 graded query-result pairs a week at ₹64 lakh a year, and gave 4 percent of impressions to exploration. Over nine months NDCG@10 rose to 0.68 and search-attributed conversion by 2.1 percent, worth ₹3.4 crore annualised. The ratio is the point: 70,000 human judgments moved a metric 80 million clicks had not, because the clicks were confounded by the ranking and the judgments were not.

Machaan Agritech’s unconditional-upload fix cost ₹41 lakh a year in bandwidth and one engineering month, and found a failure class representing 9 percent of true pest incidence in shaded canopy — in a product whose entire commercial claim was early detection. The team wrote one question into its design-review checklist: what does our sampling rule make impossible to see?

Baadban Freight Systems of Chennai is the failure, and the most instructive. Baadban predicted arrival times for full-truckload shipments and showed the prediction in the driver’s app, where the driver confirmed it with one tap; that confirmed value was written back as the label. Over five months, offline mean absolute percentage error fell from 21.4 percent to 8.9 percent, a chart shown at three consecutive board meetings, while consignee complaints about missed dock windows rose 38 percent. The model was being graded on its own output: drivers tapped to dismiss, the label became the prediction, and the loop converged on self-agreement while accuracy against reality decayed. It surfaced only when a cement client’s gate-in timestamps were reconciled against Baadban’s logs in a contract dispute.

Fig. 2 — Baadban's two error curves. The one management saw was computed against labels the model itself had written. The gap was 17 percentage points before anyone reconciled them.

Recovery took seven months and ₹2.4 crore. Baadban discarded eleven million confirmed-ETA rows, rebuilt labels from GPS geofence gate-in events available for 61 percent of shipments, and retrained to a genuine MAPE of 26.8 percent falling to 15.2 — worse than the fiction, better than the truth had been. The durable change was a rule in the data-contract review: no label may be derived from a field the model pre-populated. The cost of catching it late was not the ₹2.4 crore but the two commercial commitments made on a number that was never real.

The pattern across all six is that the loop's own instrumentation reports health while the mechanism degrades, because each is a failure of the measurement rather than the model. That is why loop-health review belongs in a separate meeting, with different numbers and, ideally, a different person presenting.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is data ever a moat? The accumulation position rests on real evidence: in narrow long-tailed domains — Indic-language speech, Indian GST invoice layouts, chest radiographs in a high-TB-prevalence population — no public corpus contains the tail, and the only route to it is production traffic. The economist position rests on evidence just as real: measured curves flatten, most incumbent advantage turns out on examination to be distribution or switching cost, and firms with far less data have repeatedly matched leaders. This resolves empirically and only per domain. Accumulation is wrong if a rival with a tenth of the data matches tail error; the economists are wrong if the exponent stays steep at ten times the current corpus. Both tests are cheap; both are rarely run.

Should production systems randomise? The counterfactual-learning camp holds that without logged propensities and some exploration every offline estimate is biased by an unknown amount, so exploration is not a cost but the price of knowing anything. Product leaders push back seriously: deliberately serving a worse result harms a real user, negligibly in an audio feed and not negligibly in clinical triage or a credit decision, and the ethics there are unresolved rather than merely inconvenient. The compromise most large firms reach — exploration on low-stakes surfaces, observational methods on high-stakes ones — is a truce, not a theory, and leaves the high-stakes estimates biased in ways nobody has solved.

What are proprietary labels worth after foundation models? One camp argues their marginal value collapsed after 2023, that a general model plus a few hundred well-chosen examples reaches the plateau, and that loops should be redirected into evals and retrieval corpora. The other argues this holds only where the task resembles the pretraining distribution, and that the tails these products live in — regional dialects, local document formats, under-represented populations — are exactly where general models are weakest and proprietary labels still pay. What would settle it is the exponent measured above the zero-shot baseline, which most teams never measure. The same split runs through synthetic data, demonstrably good at fixing an imbalance you have noticed and bad at finding the failure you have not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the loop period and the exponent before the dataset size, and treats a proposal without both as unfinished rather than optimistic. They budget the audit slice and the exploration slice as permanent line items and defend them in the quarter the budget is cut, knowing those are precisely the quarters a loop goes blind. They insist no label be derived from anything the model pre-populated, and check interface mockups for it rather than trusting the schema. They call an efficiency loop an efficiency loop in front of a board, reserving the word flywheel for cases where they can name the usage-response term and show its magnitude. They raise the ceiling by adjudicating disputed labels rather than reaching for it faster with more of them. And they give the label store a named owner with time on their calendar, having learnt that the characteristic failure of feedback loops is not error but silence.

12. What Nandita and Vikram decided

Nandita rejected the purchased studies and funded the widget, changing its design twice before approving it: the radiologist’s reading is captured before the model’s score is revealed, and 3 percent of normal-scored studies go for a second read. She also stopped calling the loop a flywheel in commercial material. Her reasoning: at β = 0.28 the slope is worth far more than the step, anchoring was the only irreversible decision in the proposal, and a quarterly cadence gave her four turns a year, none of which she could spend on contaminated labels.

Vikram approved exploration at 3 percent rather than 4, with the propensity logging that was its actual purpose, and a concession to the CFO: a six-month deadline and a required lift in successful plays for catalogue items outside the top decile, or it stops. He also killed a data-moat slide, on the grounds that at β = 0.11 Ghungroo’s advantage is its catalogue rights and creator relationships, and pretending otherwise had cost the team roadmap arguments it deserved to lose.

Three questions for discussion. First: Peepal Scan’s loop has a steep yield and no usage response, Ghungroo’s the reverse — if you could fund only one, which creates more enterprise value, and what would change your answer? Second: Baadban’s reported and true error diverged for five months under a board reviewing the number monthly; what artefact in that meeting would have caught it, and why do so few companies present it? Third: if exploration is the price of unbiased knowledge, what is a defensible exploration budget for a clinical triage product, and who should set it?

13. Going deeper

Building a golden set from real usage comes next, because every claim here about improvement is only as good as the independent set verifying it; it unlocks the ability to tell a loop that is learning from one memorising its own queue. Moats in the AI era supplies the discipline for the gain term, separating margin from defensibility. Problem–model fit matters because no loop rescues a task whose irreducible error sits above the threshold of usefulness. The ML lifecycle gives the release machinery — shadow deployment, canaries, change control — that sets your loop period. Data strategy and data acquisition generalises the buy-versus-build arithmetic Nandita ran. Labelling and annotation is where the ceiling is set. Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC lets you say which error the loop is actually reducing, rarely the one on the dashboard. And what’s different when the feature is a model covers the interface craft — confidence display, correction affordances, anchoring — that decides whether your product produces labels worth having.

exp20v2-aipm.working.with.ml:
AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management

Working with Data Scientists and ML Engineers

Bengaluru, 11 March 2025. Meher Vasal, head of product for underwriting at Ankahi Credit, an NBFC that disburses unsecured personal loans of up to ₹2 lakh through a mobile app, is looking at two numbers on her screen that do not agree with each other. The data science team, led by Devika Raman, has finished retraining the credit-scoring model and wants to raise the approval cut-off from a score of 640 to 660 on Ankahi's 300–900 scale. Devika's slide says the change will cut the 90-day default rate from 4.2% to 3.1%. Meher's own dashboard says the same change will shrink monthly approvals by roughly 1,600 loans, which is revenue the growth team has already promised investors ahead of Ankahi's next funding round in June. Both numbers are correct. Neither team disagrees with the other's arithmetic. What they disagree about is who gets to decide, and on what basis, because nobody at Ankahi has ever written down what "good enough" means for this model, who signs off on a change to it, or what evidence a proposal needs before it goes live. Meher has three days before the model ships to either build that shared basis for judgment or let the decision get made by whoever pushes hardest in Friday's leadership call. If she gets it wrong, Ankahi either bakes in more bad debt than its board tolerates or turns away thousands of creditworthy borrowers who will take a competitor's loan instead — and either mistake will resurface in a regulator's audit of the Reserve Bank of India's fair-lending guidelines long after this week is forgotten.

The idea

Working with data scientists and ML engineers, in the sense this topic addresses, means building a durable structure through which a product manager and the people who build and tune a machine-learning model share ownership of what "quality" means for that model, rather than the PM setting targets from outside and the ML team meeting them however they see fit, or the ML team setting targets from inside and the PM discovering the trade-offs after the fact. The problem this solves is specific: a data scientist and an ML engineer are unusual stakeholders in a product organisation because they hold technical authority a PM typically cannot independently verify — a PM can read a churn dashboard or a sales pipeline and form her own view, but she usually cannot re-derive a model's precision-recall curve or judge whether a training set is biased. That asymmetry, if left alone, produces exactly the standoff Meher is in: two competent people, each fluent in a different vocabulary, each holding a number they trust, with no agreed instrument for reconciling them.

The practice traces to the discipline that grew up inside large-scale machine-learning teams at companies such as Google and Netflix through the mid-2010s, later documented and popularised under the banner of MLOps by practitioners including Chip Huyen and Eugene Yan, and it has since been absorbed into how serious AI product teams at Indian companies such as Flipkart, Razorpay and CRED run their model lifecycles. Its core move is to replace opinion with a jointly authored evaluation — a concrete, agreed test that any candidate model version must pass before it ships, built jointly by the PM (who supplies the business consequences and the thresholds that matter) and the ML team (who supplies the technical means to measure them). The sentence Meher could say in Friday's meeting without sounding glib is this: "We don't ship a model change until product and data science have agreed, in writing, what we're measuring, what number is good enough, and who owns the call when the numbers trade off against each other."

How it actually works

The mechanics run in a loop, not a single meeting, and the steps practitioners most often skip are the second and the fourth. First, the PM and the ML lead jointly define the eval: the metrics that matter (here, default rate, approval rate, and a fairness check across income bands), the minimum bar for each, and which trade-offs are acceptable versus which require escalation. Second — the step teams skip — they agree on an error budget: an explicit, pre-negotiated amount of degradation on one metric that is acceptable in exchange for improvement on another, so that when a real trade-off appears (as it did for Meher and Devika), the rule for resolving it was set before either side had a stake in a particular outcome. Third, the ML team runs the candidate model against a held-out test set and a live shadow test, and reports results against the agreed metrics, not a metric they chose afterward. Fourth — also usually skipped — both sides review the specific loans or cases where the new model disagrees with the old one, not just the aggregate numbers, because aggregates can hide a change that is fine on average but catastrophic for one customer segment. Fifth, they make the ship decision against the pre-agreed budget, and log the reasoning so the next disagreement doesn't relitigate the same ground. Sixth, they set a monitoring cadence — typically weekly for a model this consequential — so that drift after launch is caught by the same shared dashboard, not by a customer complaint or a regulator's letter.

A worked example

Ankahi processes about 18,000 loan applications a month. At the current 640 cut-off, 61% are approved — 10,980 loans — and 4.2% of those default within 90 days, which is 461 defaulted loans. Ankahi's recovery rate on a defaulted loan is roughly 40%, so the average loss on a default, at a typical ticket of ₹85,000, is ₹51,000 (60% of ₹85,000). Monthly credit losses at the current threshold: 461 × ₹51,000 ≈ ₹2.35 crore. Devika's proposed cut-off of 660 drops approvals to 52% (9,360 loans) and defaults to 3.1% (290 loans), so credit losses fall to 290 × ₹51,000 ≈ ₹1.48 crore — a saving of ₹87 lakh a month. But the 1,620 fewer approvals also cost revenue: at an average interest-and-fee contribution of ₹3,000 per loan over its life, that is 1,620 × ₹3,000 ≈ ₹48.6 lakh a month in foregone income. Table 1 lays the comparison out.

Table 1. Threshold change: aggregate effect
MetricCut-off 640 (current)Cut-off 660 (proposed)
Approval rate61%52%
Approved loans / month10,9809,360
90-day default rate4.2%3.1%
Defaults / month461290
Credit losses / month₹2.35 cr₹1.48 cr
Foregone fee income / month—₹48.6 lakh
Net monthly effect—+₹38.6 lakh

On pure arithmetic, raising the cut-off wins by ₹38.6 lakh a month. But this is exactly the number that hides the disagreement, because it treats every declined applicant as identical. When Meher and Devika instead pull the 1,620 newly declined applications and review a sample of 200 by hand — the step teams skip — they find that a large share sit just below 660 with strong repayment history on other apps (visible via account-aggregator data under India's Account Aggregator framework) but thin formal credit bureau files, a pattern common among salaried borrowers new to formal credit. A second pass, where the ML engineers add three alternate-data features (utility payment regularity, UPI transaction consistency, employer verification) rather than simply raising the cut-off, recovers the default rate to 3.4% at the original 61% approval rate, because the model now separates genuinely risky applicants from thin-file-but-reliable ones instead of declining both. That version saves roughly ₹68 lakh a month in credit losses with no lost approvals at all — a better answer than either side's original proposal, and one that only surfaces because the eval forced a joint review of individual cases rather than a negotiation over one aggregate trade-off.

The nuances

An eval is not a KPI

A business KPI (approval rate, revenue) tells you whether the company is healthy. An eval tells you whether this specific model version is fit to ship. Conflating them leads teams to approve a model because company numbers looked fine that quarter, when the model itself degraded and something else compensated.

Shared ownership is not equal expertise

Meher does not need to know backpropagation, and Devika does not need to own the collections-cost model. Shared ownership means each contributes the piece the other cannot supply — consequences from the PM, mechanism from the ML team — not that both become generalists.

Aggregates can lie by omission

A model can hit its aggregate target while failing badly on a subgroup, as Ankahi's case shows. Any eval for a decision that affects real people needs a slice-level check, not just a headline number.

Error budgets must be set before the data arrives

An error budget agreed after seeing which side "wins" is not a budget; it is a post-hoc rationalisation. The discipline only works if the trade-off rule predates the specific trade-off.

Confidence intervals are not optional detail

A 4.2%-to-3.1% default improvement measured on a few hundred loans can be noise. A thoughtful PM asks the sample size and the confidence interval before treating a metric change as real, a question data scientists expect and welcome.

The model is not the only lever

Teams often assume the only choice is where to set a threshold, when a feature-engineering change, a policy overlay, or a manual review queue for borderline cases can dissolve the trade-off entirely, as it did here.

This does not tell you what the business should value

No eval framework decides whether Ankahi should prioritise growth or credit quality this quarter; that is a leadership call the eval merely makes legible, not a call the process makes for you.

Fairness metrics need a named owner

Checking for disparate impact across income or geography is easy to add to a slide and easy to skip in practice unless one named person is accountable for running it every release, since it rarely improves the headline metric that gets applause.

Consumer, B2B, marketplaces — and company stage

In a consumer product like Ankahi's, the eval usually centres on a single, high-stakes score per user (approve/decline, default risk) with fairness and regulatory checks as hard gates, because one wrong decision affects one person concretely and RBI's fair-lending expectations make disparate impact a compliance question, not just an ethics one. In B2B products — a demand-forecasting model sold to a retailer, say — the eval more often centres on the cost of forecast error to the customer's operations, and the customer's own ops team becomes a third party to the eval alongside the PM and the ML team. In a marketplace product, such as a lending-adjacent platform matching borrowers to multiple NBFC partners, the eval must hold for both sides of the match simultaneously, since a model that improves outcomes for lenders by tightening approvals can starve the borrower side of the marketplace of supply. Company stage changes the machinery more than the principle: an early-stage team of six can run this loop as a fifteen-minute weekly conversation with a shared spreadsheet, while a company at Ankahi's scale, with a model risk committee and RBI's model-governance expectations for NBFCs, needs the same loop formalised into a written policy, an audit trail, and a named accountable executive, because the informal version does not survive an external audit.

Common mistakes

The PM sets a target with no technical basis. Symptom: a target like "99% accuracy" appears in a roadmap doc with no reference to the model's actual error distribution. Underlying error: treating a model like a feature toggle rather than a probabilistic system. Cheapest diagnostic: ask the data scientist what accuracy the best possible model on this data could achieve; if nobody knows, the target is fiction.

The ML team optimises a proxy metric nobody asked for. Symptom: model AUC improves release after release while business complaints rise. Underlying error: the eval was written once and never re-validated against real outcomes. Cheapest diagnostic: pull ten recent complaints and check whether the model's proxy metric would have flagged any of them.

Aggregate-only sign-off. Symptom: a launch decision made from one slide with one topline number. Underlying error: skipping the case-level review. Cheapest diagnostic: request the ten most different decisions between old and new model before approving.

No monitoring after launch. Symptom: a model that was fine at launch quietly drifts as the applicant population shifts. Underlying error: treating the eval as a one-time gate rather than a standing dashboard. Cheapest diagnostic: check whether anyone can produce this week's default rate by model version without a special request.

What good looks like

Three months after the March standoff, Ankahi's credit model changes ship through a one-page eval document that Meher and Devika co-sign: three metrics, a pre-agreed error budget, a fairness check by income band, and a required case-level review of the twenty most divergent decisions. Devika's team proposes changes; Meher's team supplies the business consequences and signs off within the budget or escalates with a named reason when a proposal falls outside it. A shared dashboard, checked weekly by both of them for five minutes, catches a data-drift issue in July before it becomes a quarter of bad loans, because the eval never stopped running after launch. Neither of them remembers the last time a model change caused a Friday-afternoon fire drill.

Closing

Meher does not choose either the 660 cut-off or the original 640. She asks Devika's team for one more week to test the alternate-data feature set, and together they ship the version that keeps approvals at 61% while cutting defaults to 3.4%, with the individual-case review built into the release checklist going forward. The reasoning she carries out of that week is not "the ML team was right" or "the business team was right," but that the disagreement existed only because nobody had built the shared instrument earlier — and that instrument, once built, turned a threshold fight into a better model. What Meher should learn next is how to read a confusion matrix and a precision-recall trade-off well enough to ask her own sharp questions of a proposal, not to second-guess the modelling, because a PM who cannot follow the mechanics of her own eval cannot own it.

Two questions to sit with:

1. On a model you rely on today, could you and its builders both write down, independently, what "good enough" means for it — and would the two answers match?

2. If your team's next model change trades one metric against another, has anyone agreed in advance how much of one you'll give up for the other, or will that get decided in the room, by whoever argues harder?
