AI & Data Products · AI & ML Product Management · Near-expert reading

Working with Data Scientists and ML Engineers

How product managers and modellers come to share ownership of quality — the mechanics, the disagreements the field has not settled, and the seams where the arrangement usually breaks.

1. Two rooms, two weeks apart

Hyderabad, 4 February 2026. Shalini Bhandarkar, vice-president of product at Jaanch Diagnostics, is sitting with a printout she has read four times. Jaanch sells an AI triage service that reads chest X-rays at intake and marks the ones a radiologist should see first; its largest customer, a twenty-two-hospital chain across Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, puts roughly 100,000 films a quarter through it and is up for renewal on 18 February. Dr Anirban Basu, who leads Jaanch's ML group, wants to ship a model that raises sensitivity from 0.92 to 0.96. The chain's chief radiologist has separately written to Shalini to say that her registrars are already drowning in flagged films and that if the flag volume rises again she will recommend the contract be allowed to lapse. Both statements are true. Nobody at Jaanch has written down what the service is allowed to cost the customer in radiologist minutes, so the argument has nowhere to go except seniority.

Gurugram, 9 February 2026. Kabir Ranganathan, product manager for marketplace experience at Ladaan Logistics, has the inverse problem. Ladaan matches shippers to about 14,000 truck operators and quotes an arrival time at booking; its ETA model is the most-read number on the platform. Sneha Kulkarni's team has a candidate that cuts mean absolute error from 34 minutes to 31 across a 90-day backtest. In the two-week pilot on the Nashik–Hyderabad corridor, Kabir's operations lead counted a 19 per cent rise in "where is my truck" calls. Sneha's reading is that operations is looking at eleven days of noisy data. Kabir's is that a model can improve on average and still be worse at the only thing the number is used for: telling a shipper whether to keep a dock crew waiting. Peak season starts 1 March; whatever ships now runs until May.

Both cases look like disputes about a model. They are disputes about who owns the definition of quality, and in both companies that question has an answer only in retrospect, decided by whoever holds the room. This page is about the alternative: the machinery by which a product manager and the people who train and tune models come to hold one definition of quality between them — what it is, who disputes it, how it is actually operated, and where it reliably fails.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

Shared ownership of quality means that the product manager and the modelling team jointly author, and are jointly accountable for, the artefact that decides whether a model version is fit to ship — the evaluation: a fixed set of examples, measurements on them, a stated bar for each, and a pre-agreed rule for what to do when the measurements trade off. The claim is not that the PM should have opinions about models. It is that "good enough" is neither a business input handed down nor a technical output handed up, but a single object neither party can write alone, because it requires consequences the PM knows and mechanisms the ML team knows.

The problem it was invented to solve is an asymmetry. In most product work a PM can independently audit the evidence: she can read the funnel, talk to the customer, form a view. With a model she typically cannot re-derive the precision–recall curve or judge whether a training sample is representative, and the modeller typically cannot price a false negative. Leo Breiman's 2001 essay on the two cultures of statistical modelling set the culture that asks whether a model describes the data-generating process against the culture that asks only whether it predicts; the PM sits at a third vertex, asking whether it predicts well enough for a decision someone will regret. The practical vocabulary arrived later: the Netflix Prize in 2009, whose winning ensemble was never deployed because its engineering cost exceeded the value of its accuracy; Sculley and colleagues' 2015 paper on hidden technical debt in ML systems, which named the CACE principle — changing anything changes everything — and thereby killed the idea of a model as a component with a stable contract; Andrew Ng's data-centric turn around 2021; and the eval-driven discipline that spread through LLM product teams from 2023 onward.

Four schools now disagree, and the disagreement is real rather than terminological.

The specification school holds that the relationship should be a clean interface: the PM specifies the operating requirement — "no more than 28,000 flags per quarter, sensitivity at least 0.90" — and the ML team meets it however it likes. It would sign: the operating point is a business decision and must be expressible as a constraint the modellers can optimise against. It would not sign: the PM should be present when features are chosen or labels adjudicated.

The co-production school, the mainstream of applied practice today, holds that the eval set is the real product specification, must be built from examples the PM has personally inspected, and that error analysis is a joint activity. It would sign: a PM who has not hand-read two hundred model errors does not know what her product does. It would not sign: a numeric target in a PRD is a sufficient statement of quality.

The research-autonomy school, strongest in labs and frontier-model teams, holds that premature productisation of metrics locks a system into a local optimum and that modelling leadership should own quality until a capability threshold is crossed. It would sign: most PM-authored evals measure a proxy that will look embarrassing in eighteen months. It would not sign: shipping should wait on a co-signed document.

The assurance school, native to regulated finance and medicine, holds that neither builder nor PM should sign off, because both are invested; an independent validation function must. It would sign: the person who trains the model must not be the person who approves it. It would not sign: speed of iteration is a legitimate reason to compress review.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice is less a meeting than a division of authority along the model lifecycle, and the division is not where most organisations draw it. Figure 1 shows the stages and the two overlapping bands of authority.

The formal treatment is expected cost per decision. Write p for prevalence, s for sensitivity, t for specificity, N for volume, and cFN, cFP for the cost of each error type: expected cost is N·[ p(1−s)cFN + (1−p)(1−t)cFP ]. The modeller supplies the achievable (s, t) pairs — the curve. The PM supplies the ratio cFN/cFP. Neither alone can pick a point. Jaanch's numbers: 100,000 films a quarter at 8 per cent prevalence, so 8,000 true positives and 92,000 true negatives available.

Table 1. Jaanch Diagnostics: two operating points on the same model curve, one quarter, 100,000 films.
QuantityPoint A (current)Point B (proposed)
Sensitivity0.920.96
Specificity0.780.62
Net effect on the review queue, both operating points
Findings caught7,3607,680
Of which missed, not flagged (excluded from the review total below)640320
False flags20,24034,960
Total flags to review27,60042,640
Precision of a flag26.7%18.0%
Extra registrar hours (4 min/flag)—981
Extra review cost at ₹2,400/hr—₹23.5 lakh

The arithmetic converts an argument about model quality into a single price: Point B buys 320 additional catches for ₹23.5 lakh of radiologist time, roughly ₹7,360 per additional finding. That number is the whole negotiation. Anirban cannot say whether ₹7,360 per early catch is worth paying; Shalini cannot produce the curve. Written that way, the disagreement becomes a question the customer's clinical director can answer in one meeting — which is exactly what shared ownership buys.

Three steps are routinely left implicit, and they separate working practice from ritual. The first is the error budget agreed before the data arrives: a written statement of how much of one metric may be traded for how much of another, fixed before anyone knows which side benefits. Once a candidate model is on the table, every budget negotiation is a rationalisation. The second is the divergence review: pulling the cases where old and new model disagree and reading them individually, together. Aggregates are compatible with almost any distribution of harm; at Jaanch the 14,720 additional false flags clustered in portable-machine films from two district hospitals with older detectors, so the choice was never A versus B but "fix the domain shift or accept a cost concentrated on two sites". The third is eval-set design as a statistical exercise rather than a sampling convenience.

That third step decided Ladaan's case. Per-trip absolute error at Ladaan has a standard deviation of about 26 minutes. For an unpaired comparison — one set of trips scored by the old model, another by the new — detecting a three-minute difference at 80 per cent power needs roughly 2σ²(1.96+0.84)²/δ² ≈ 1,177 trips per arm. But ETAs can be scored in parallel: both models quote on the same trip, and the standard deviation of the difference is about 9 minutes because route, season and operator cancel. The paired requirement is 81×7.84/9 ≈ 71 trips — seventeen times less evidence for the same question. A PM who does not know this asks for an experiment the team cannot afford and then settles for an anecdote.

4. When the arrangement applies, and when it misleads

The case for joint ownership rests on four conditions, each testable.

Claim one: the errors have asymmetric, nameable consequences. True at Jaanch, where a missed finding and a wasted registrar hour are incommensurable; true at Ladaan, where a truck twenty minutes early costs nothing and one an hour late strands a dock crew. Where both error types cost the same, the modeller can optimise accuracy alone and the PM adds only delay.

Claim two: the ground truth is contestable. At Jaanch "actionable finding" is a judgement three radiologists render differently, so label definition is a product decision. Where truth is mechanical — did the payment settle, did the user click — joint authorship collapses to joint authorship of the thresholds.

Claim three: deployment differs from the training distribution in ways only the product side can see. Ladaan's backtest excluded the monsoon corridor closures Kabir's team handles weekly; Jaanch's test set under-represented portable films. Neither omission is visible from a notebook.

Claim four: the decision recurs. The machinery is worth building when model changes ship monthly for years; for a model that a vendor API will replace wholesale in two quarters, the honest answer is to skip it.

The idea becomes actively misleading in three situations. When the model is a pure capability play — a research team pushing a frontier where nobody yet knows what the product is — a PM-authored eval encodes today's use case and suppresses discovery of a better one. When offline metrics correlate poorly with the online outcome, as in most ranking work, a co-signed offline eval creates false comfort and ownership must move to experiment design. And when "shared ownership" gives a PM a veto over technical choices she cannot evaluate, it produces slower iteration with no better judgement.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

The arrangement assumes one model, one product, one PM. Most consequential models do not live there.

Multi-product platform models. Jaanch's detection backbone also feeds a tuberculosis screening product sold to state health missions. One curve; three operating points; three PMs with different cFN/cFP ratios, one of them set by policy rather than economics. Mature companies separate the model from the policy layer: the ML team owns and evaluates the scoring model against product-neutral metrics, and each product owns a thin, versioned threshold-and-routing policy with its own eval. What they claim in architecture reviews is that each product has its own model. What is usually true is that one team quietly retunes a shared backbone and the second-order effects land on whoever notices last.

Two-sided markets. Ladaan's ETA affects shippers and operators in opposite directions: a conservative ETA protects the shipper's planning and makes the operator look slow in the rankings that drive his load allocation, so an eval measuring only shipper-facing accuracy will systematically ship models that degrade supply. Two-sided products need at least one metric per side, with the error budget expressed as a constraint on the weaker side rather than a weighted average — averages let one side subsidise the other invisibly.

Regulated products. Jaanch's software is a medical device under India's CDSCO regime and its hospital customers answer to NABH accreditation; a competitor selling into Europe faces the EU AI Act's high-risk classification. Here the assurance school wins the narrow question of sign-off: a validation function independent of both PM and modeller signs the release. The seam is that independent validation evaluates the model against the documented intended use while the PM and ML team have quietly evolved the actual use. The gap is invisible until an audit, and then it is the only thing anyone talks about.

Hardware and software together. The portable-detector problem is the general case: the model's input distribution is set by a fleet of devices with independent refresh cycles, so an eval fixed in software drifts because hardware in the field drifts. Teams that handle this well stratify every eval by device generation and treat a device rollout as a model release.

AI-native products. Where the model is the product rather than a feature inside it — a generative assistant, an agentic workflow — there is no stable behaviour to hold fixed, offline metrics are weak, and graders are themselves models. The emerging practice is that the PM owns a small, hand-curated set of cases encoding product intent and reviews grader–human agreement, while the ML team owns everything upstream. This is markedly less settled than the binary-classifier case, and anyone who says otherwise is selling a platform.

6. Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A metric improvement and a product improvement are different events. The tell: a team reporting "AUC up 0.02" without saying what changed at the operating point actually in production. AUC integrates over thresholds nobody uses; a model can gain area and lose ground precisely where the business runs. The obvious reading — better ranking is better — is wrong because the product consumes one point on the curve, not the curve.

Labelling instructions are the specification. The tell: two annotators disagreeing and the dispute settled by a third annotator rather than by amending the guideline. Every ambiguity resolved in a chat thread is a product decision made by a contractor. The obvious reading is that labelling is data-collection overhead; it is where the product's definition is written.

Confidence intervals are a PM's tool, not a statistician's courtesy. The tell: a decimal reported with no interval and no sample size. A 3.1 versus 4.2 per cent movement on 300 cases is compatible with no movement at all. The expert asks for the interval first, because it says whether there is a decision to make.

Aggregate parity conceals concentrated harm. The tell: no slice in the eval report smaller than a quarter of the data. Models fail on structured minorities — one device generation, one language, one corridor — and those slices are where churn and regulatory exposure originate. The obvious reading is that overall accuracy is what customers experience; customers experience their own slice.

Changing anything changes everything. The tell: a proposal described as "just a feature addition" or "just a data refresh". Model outputs feed downstream thresholds, caches, human workflows and other models, so no change is local. Experts ask what consumes this output before asking how the model improved.

The threshold is rarely the only lever. The tell: a debate framed entirely as a number on a slider. Abstention — routing uncertain cases to a human — a policy overlay, a better fallback or three new features can dissolve a trade-off that looks binary. Framing the decision as A versus B is itself the error.

Shadow deployment beats opinion and costs less than an A/B test. The tell: a team choosing between "argue in the meeting" and "run a two-week experiment" with nothing in between. Scoring both models on live traffic without acting on the new one gives paired data at full volume with zero customer risk — the cheapest evidence available, and the most consistently forgotten.

Trust is built by conceding technical points, not winning them. The tell: a PM who has never said "your metric is right and my request was wrong" in front of the team. Modellers extend decision rights to PMs who follow evidence against their own preference; the converse is the fastest way to be routed around.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products ground truth arrives late and biased — you observe what happened to the recommendations you made, not the ones you did not — so ownership shifts from offline evals toward experiment design and guardrail metrics, and the PM's distinctive contribution is choosing what not to optimise. In B2B and enterprise the customer becomes a third author: Jaanch's eval means nothing unless the chain's clinical lead agrees with the label definition, which is why enterprise AI contracts increasingly specify metrics and thresholds in the master services agreement, and why a metric change is a commercial renegotiation. In platforms and marketplaces the eval must be multi-objective because the model's output is an allocation, and allocations have losers who do not file tickets. In hardware-plus-software the input distribution is owned by an organisation that does not read model release notes; stratification by device is the only defence. In AI-native products the model's behaviour is the brand, and owning a golden set of intent-encoding cases is closer to editorial direction than to measurement.

Stage changes the machinery more than the principle. At six people the loop is a shared spreadsheet and a Friday conversation, and formalising it is waste. At Jaanch's size — 140 people, a regulated device, one customer worth a quarter of revenue — the same loop must become a signed release record, because an informal agreement survives neither an audit nor the departure of the two people holding it in their heads. At the largest scale a central team owns evaluation infrastructure while PMs own eval content; the failure mode is that infrastructure ownership drifts into content ownership and evals become uniform, comparable and irrelevant to any specific product. What does not change with stage: someone must price the errors, and that someone is never the model.

8. Three worked cases

Jaanch, and the third option. Once the divergence review localised the additional false flags to portable films, Anirban's team stratified the eval by detector generation. On fixed-detector films, Point B cost 4,100 additional flags a quarter for 210 additional catches — ₹1,850 per catch, comfortably worth paying. On portable films it cost 10,600 flags for 110 catches, or ₹11,600 each. Jaanch shipped B for fixed detectors and held A for portables while retraining on 9,000 newly collected portable films. Aggregate sensitivity landed at 0.95 and review volume at 31,700 flags — worse than Point A on burden, better than either single-threshold option on cost per catch, and unreachable by any global threshold.

Ladaan, and the metric that measured the wrong thing. Sneha's shadow harness, run on 4,200 paired trips over nine days, confirmed the three-minute MAE gain at a 95 per cent interval of ±0.7 minutes: real. It also showed the improvement came almost entirely from trips under six hours, while on long-haul trips the model shifted from over-predicting arrival time to under-predicting it — and under-prediction is what generates a "where is my truck" call. Kabir and Sneha added an asymmetric loss — lateness penalised 2.4 times earliness, a ratio derived from Ladaan's own dock-detention charges of ₹450 per hour — retrained, and accepted an MAE of 32.1 minutes in exchange for a 41 per cent drop in under-predictions beyond twenty minutes. The aggregate metric got worse. The product got better.

Zimmedari Insure, and what failure looks like. A Pune health insurer built a model to auto-approve low-risk cashless claims, targeting 60 per cent auto-approval at 2 per cent leakage. The eval was authored entirely by the data science team and signed by a product manager who never inspected it. It was built on eighteen months of historical claims labelled "approved" or "rejected" by the manual process — so the model learned to imitate adjusters, including their habit of waving through claims from three hospital networks with which the insurer had rate agreements.

The offline eval was not wrong; it measured agreement with historical adjuster decisions, which is what it had been asked to measure and which was never the same thing as correctness. Nobody had written down that "correct" meant "the claim was genuinely payable", because the two definitions coincided in the training data and diverged in production once providers learned which claims sailed through. The recovery took seven months: a 3,000-claim re-adjudication by a senior panel that produced an independent gold set at a cost of about ₹38 lakh, a rebuilt eval stratified by provider network, reversion to manual review for network claims during the rebuild, and a standing rule that no eval label may be produced by the process the model replaces. Leakage returned to 2.4 per cent by month sixteen. The cost of one unasked question about what the labels meant was roughly ₹9 crore.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Labels inherited from the process being automated.
Early sign: the eval's ground truth is the legacy system's output. Diagnostic: "if the old process was wrong here, would our label be wrong too?" Cost late: a model that industrialises an existing bias, found only when the loss reaches the P&L, as at Zimmedari.
Metric drift by substitution.
Early sign: the metric quoted in this month's review is not the one in the eval document. Diagnostic: "which of these numbers is in the signed eval?" Cost late: a year of gains on a proxy, and no record of what was promised.
Aggregate-only sign-off.
Early sign: one slide, one number, no slices. Diagnostic: "show me the twenty cases where old and new disagree most." Cost late: concentrated harm on a segment that churns or complains to a regulator.
Eval-set overfitting by human search.
Early sign: steady small gains on the eval with flat live metrics. Diagnostic: "how many candidate models has this set scored?" Cost late: an evaluation that has silently become a training set.
Silent dependency breakage.
Early sign: a downstream team learns of a model change from its own alerting. Diagnostic: "who consumes this output, and were they told?" Cost late: incidents attributed to the wrong system for weeks on end.
Monitoring that watches only the model.
Early sign: dashboards show model metrics but not input distributions. Diagnostic: "what would a new detector fleet look like on this chart?" Cost late: months of degradation before anyone sees a cause.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should the PM do hand-labelling? The co-production position is that a PM who has personally adjudicated two hundred errors develops calibrated intuition no summary provides, and that the cost — three days — is trivial against the decisions it informs; the evidence is the consistent finding that error analysis relocates teams' attention from architecture to data. The opposing position holds that a PM's sample is small, unrepresentative, and prone to producing overconfident anecdote-driven priorities, and that the same three days spent on customer interviews would be worth more. For the first to be wrong, hand-inspection would have to systematically mislead rather than merely under-sample; for the second, error analysis would have to produce no insight beyond what aggregate slicing already shows.

Does independent validation improve quality or only assurance? The assurance school points to two decades of model-risk practice in banking and the fact that self-certifying teams under commercial pressure approve their own work; the opposing school points to organisations where validation became documentation that caught no real defect while adding six weeks to every release, and argues quality comes from those closest to the failure. Both describe real institutions. The disagreement would resolve if anyone had good data on defects caught per week of delay, and nobody does.

Are offline evals the right locus of ownership at all? One camp argues that the only honest measurement is online, that offline evals mainly measure resemblance to a curated past, and that ownership belongs in experiment design and guardrails. The other argues that online-only testing makes every learning cycle a customer-affecting risk, is unavailable in regulated or low-traffic settings, and produces organisations that cannot say what they believe before they ship. The positions are partly domain-specific — ranking versus diagnosis — but participants do not treat them that way, which is why the argument recurs.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the interval before the estimate and the slice before the average. She treats a label definition as a specification she is accountable for, and can state without notes what her product's two error types cost. She reaches for shadow deployment when a disagreement turns on evidence, and knows roughly how much evidence her question needs before she asks for it. She concedes technical points publicly and quickly, and reads the divergences rather than the summary. She can tell when the machinery does not apply — a research phase, a disposable model, a domain where offline and online diverge — and says so rather than imposing process as identity. Most tellingly, she is comfortable with a model shipping on a decision she did not make, because the rule for that decision was written before anyone knew who it favoured. Someone who has merely studied the topic can name evals, precision and recall, and drift, and still walks into Friday's meeting with one number and an opinion.

12. What each of them decided

Shalini did not choose between Anirban's model and the radiologist's complaint. She asked for the divergence review, took the device-stratified answer into the 18 February renewal as a two-threshold proposal with the cost-per-catch table above, and let the chain's clinical director set the portable-film threshold herself. The contract was renewed with a written flag-volume ceiling of 33,000 per quarter — a constraint Anirban now optimises against deliberately rather than discovering after the fact.

Kabir shipped the asymmetric-loss model on 27 February with a worse headline metric than Sneha had originally proposed, having first written down with her that lateness beyond twenty minutes was what the marketplace was actually managing and that up to two minutes of MAE could be spent to reduce it. The document took ninety minutes to write, and is why the next four releases needed no meeting at all.

  1. Jaanch's stratified solution produced a worse aggregate number and a better business outcome. What would have to be true of an organisation for that trade to be impossible to approve?
  2. Zimmedari's eval was internally valid and catastrophically wrong. Which question, asked by whom, would have caught it in week one — and why is that question so rarely asked?
  3. If independent validation caught no defect in Jaanch's last six releases, is that evidence the validation function is working or that it is theatre? What additional evidence would separate the two?

13. Going deeper

Stakeholder mapping and management — the general theory of which this is a hard special case; the technical-authority asymmetry recurs with security, legal and clinical stakeholders, and the same instrument works. What evals are and why PMs own them — the artefact the relationship is built on; without fluency in eval construction, joint ownership is a slogan. Problem–model fit — the prior question of whether a model should exist at all. The ML lifecycle — the stage map underlying Figure 1, and the vocabulary for locating at which stage a disagreement actually sits. Data strategy and data acquisition — the lever that dissolved Jaanch's trade-off, and the one PMs most underestimate. Labelling and annotation — where the specification is really written, as Zimmedari discovered. Model metrics: precision, recall, AUC — the minimum literacy for refereeing the disagreements above rather than deferring on them. What's different when the feature is a model — the design consequences of probabilistic behaviour, where the quality definition you co-authored meets the user.
